fixtures.answer:
## Question 1

         Many, but not all, procedural safeguards contemplated in the Sniadach line of

cases and in Vitek make the system less accessible to litigants. While providing a lawyer

to all civil litigants may improve access to justice, there are less expensive solutions.

Perhaps the Eldridge test could be altered to include the effect new safeguards have on

accessibility. Alternatively, agencies could be designed to improve access for pro se

litigants, perhaps by eliminating or modifying the adversarial system.

         Some Vitek/Restatement procedural safeguards do not inherently complicate the

system. For example, notice often does so only because the language used is needlessly

abstruse. Similarly, a notice of rights can clarify the system if written clearly and simply.

Having independent decisionmakers instead of clerks might cost more, but it also need

not complicate the system; the adjudicator has familiarity with the law and, if trained

properly, can make it more accessible.

         But for many procedural safeguards, there is an inherent conflict between

protecting litigants and making litigation less accessible. In-person hearings like the one

guaranteed in Sniadach create procedure, from paperwork to obscure rules. They are

inaccessible to indigent litigants, especially those who can't take paid leave from work.

Vitek notes that the hearing should be "sufficiently after the notice to permit the prisoner

to prepare," but a litigant cannot become familiar with obscure legal rules in a few weeks.

Similarly, many pro se litigants, like the mother in Lassiter, are ill-equipped to call

witnesses and conduct direct and cross-examination. Even a statement of fact from the

adjudicator complicates the proceedings for those without literacy in legal English.

         Unfortunately, many of these safeguards are often necessary, especially when

liberty interests are at stake. A hearing was necessary in Goldberg to protect welfare

recipients. Similarly, witnesses are necessary in cases with many factual questions, like

Doehr.

         One possible solution that the commentator suggests and that the civil-Gideon

movement advocates is to provide lawyers to many civil litigants. Using the Eldridge

test, the indigent party has a strong private interest in counsel, and a lawyer lowers the

risk of erroneous deprivation. But lawyers are expensive. And as Justice Powell notes in

Vitek, lawyers complicate proceedings just by being there. Proceedings for certain

liberties, like the parental rights in Lassiter, are so important that they benefit from such

complication. Perhaps with enough political will and money, such a system could be

implemented. Without it, mandating state-provided lawyers risks creating in civil courts a

situation like criminal justice in states where public defense is underfunded, defendants

meet their lawyers on the day of trial, and they have literally minutes in court.

         One solution to this conflict could be adding a fourth factor to the Eldridge test:

effect on accessibility. The current test purports to weigh private interests but fails to

consider this crucial factor. This test could make the system efficient by preventing

safeguards that complicate more than they help. The Turner court could have used this to

mandate the presence of a neutral social worker or a notice about "ability to pay", both of

which it briefly mentions. This test doesn't tell judges how to assess accessibility or low-

income people's needs, something they are ill-equipped to do.

         Another solution could be to design agency adjudications to better meet the needs

of their communities. While such a system might disrupt the balance between the

executive and judiciary, Congress controls federal courts through the N&PC and can

restrict their jurisdiction. Each type of case, from Social Security benefits to prisoner's

liberty interests, would go through a separate adjudication system. These would be

designed to meet each litigant's needs better; a welfare court could have social workers

and community members contribute. This allocates expertise efficiently but could create

a huge, inefficient bureaucracy. Too much division might itself create more complication;

one advantage of the court system is its ability to adjudicate diverse matters in a single

case. Furthermore, a patchwork of agency adjudication systems might require rural

litigants to travel to far-off agencies, not the local courthouse.

         A more radical way to design agency adjudications is to eliminate the adversarial

system and its impartial adjudicators altogether. Adjudicators and their clerks could go

out into their communities to conduct investigations. They would be more accessible to

the public. This eliminates many complex proceedings, lessens the need for lawyers, and

makes outcomes fairer. But it requires many more judges and many more facilities

scattered throughout jurisdictions. It would also require many new procedural safeguards.

Perhaps most difficult, this type of system requires a different conception of justice:

instead of a formidable justice in a marble courthouse that lowly supplicants approach,

justice would be on the street, among the people.

## Question 2

         The court must verify sua sponte that it has SMJ, IPJ, and Venue. DJ: Fillius is a

ME domiciliary (incorporation and PPoB), and defendants are NJ

domiciliaries(Strawbridge complete diversity). AIC is met ($3,300,000).

         AUJ: There's no federal cause of action, but there might be Smith-Grable AUJ

because the definition of mail-delivery in a federal statute is at issue. This is a mixed

question of law and fact. Taking it would flood the federal system with new cases, so

Smith-Grable is unlikely.

         IPJ: There's no general IPJ because the defendants are NJ

domiciliaries. NY has specific IPJ because the defendants purposely availed themselves

of the benefits of working in NY, where they made the corporate decisions in question

(International Shoe). This is fair and reasonable because they can be expected to be haled

into court in NY, and Newark is close to Manhattan. Long-arm and 42(k)(1)(A) give NY

IPJ. SDoNY has venue because the decisions were made in Manhattan (1391(b)(2)).

         AJ: JAMOL appeal doesn't fit under 1291 (no final judgment), Cohen (later

appeal possible), 54(b) (only one claim), 1292(a) (no injunction), or mandamus (no

immediate need/irreparable harm). 1292(b) DD may fit: Jorkin said it would be "good to

know" if she were wrong, but also that she "cannot imagine" she was. This statement

might be a sufficient signal to give the Second Circuit discretion to hear it.

         JAMOL: FRCP 50 requires that with all facts in the light most favorable to the

defense, a rational jury could have found the way this jury did. A rational jury could

believe the defendants' testimony, not believe their emails, and find they did not know of

the accident rate. Denying MJAMOL was proper.

         New Trial: FRCP 59 requires a judge to weigh law and justice on both sides. If

the emails weren't forged, the great weight of the evidence favors the plaintiff. The

defendants were likely lying. Jorkins properly granted a new trial.

-------------------------------------------

-------------------------------------------

## Question 3

         CP: Federal and NY CP law is the same, so there are no intersystem preclusion

issues. The SDoNY retrial (L1) had a final judgment, even if the 2d Circuit hadn't ruled

yet (it has). The facts, which concerned whether the defendants' decisions led to Fillius'

loss, are exactly the same, so it's the same claim (CNOF). The defendants are the same.

The plaintiffs are in privity: Slughorn is the sole owner of Fillius and she sued in that

capacity in L1. Slughorn is claim precluded.

         IP: Only Slughorn can raise IP because she won. If L1 was just a DJ case,

rendering-court-state (NY) preclusion law is used (Semtek), and no mutuality is required.

If L1 was both a DJ and a Smith-Grable AUJ case, the law is unclear: federal or NY

preclusion law may be used. If federal law is used, mutuality is probably met because

Slughorn and Fillius are in privity, making them effectively the same party (see privity

analysis above). If not, this is NMOCE, which is generally not permitted (Parklane). But

Slughorn couldn't intervene in L1 without violating diversity (NJ domicile). This case is

smaller, so the defendants have no new incentives. There is no evidence of new

procedural opportunities, so NMOCE is permitted here.

         There are three issues: Chudley needing a license, defendants acting outrageously,

and their actions causing a drop in stock price. Although there's no evidence of their

inclusion in the decision, all three must have been decided for L1 to come out as it did.

The first and third were necessary for L1 to award Fillius any damages and the second for

Fillius to get punitives. All were actually litigated and necessary to the decision, and the

same issues are in L2. Slughorn can issue preclude in L2, but she still needs to argue the

issue of damages, especially punitive damages (for which it would be difficult to

determine the "true amounts").

-------------------------------------------

-------------------------------------------

## Question 4

Directors and Officers Count

         No CP (not same parties); no IP (we lost).

         SMJ: Complete diversity: Tonks is a VA domiciliary and the defendants NJ

domiciliaries. AIC-deficient ($9,900). Maybe AUJ under Smith-Grable (Question 2), but

this is unlikely. If not, the count should be dismissed for lacking SMJ.

         SJ: Plaintiffs might try to use Count II as an anchoring claim. Even though the

decline in stock value and the crash both happened because Chudley flew drones, the

accident could have happened if Chudley had a license. There are two separate CNOFs,

so EDoVA can't exercise SJ.

         IPJ: The defendants are NJ domiciliaries, so no general IPJ. Nothing suggests they
sought the benefits of VA law by having Chudley have stockholders in VA; they didn't

control Tonks (International Shoe). It's not fair and reasonable for them to be sued in VA.

They weren't on notice, and it'd be inconvenient to VA courts to hear suits about NY

corporations. The count should be dismissed.

         Venue: Improper (absent special shareholder-derivative-suit venue law) because

all defendants live in NJ (1391(b)(1)) and the corporate decision not to get a license

happened in SDoNY (1391(b)(2)).               Failure to State a Claim: The complaint meets

notice pleading; the incident it refers to is clear (Conley no-set-of-facts). Using

plausibility, the latter half of ¶8 ("Their decision...") is conclusory. When omitted, the

remaining allegations are insufficient to bump from possibility into plausbility the

allegations that defendants acted outrageously and that they caused Tonks a $900 loss.

The complaint doesn't meet plausibility.

         Pleading standards (like FRCP 12(b)(6)) are likely procedural for HCOL

purposes, so VCOL between VA notice pleading and federal plausibility pleading.

York: If a complaint meets the notice standard but not the plausibility standard, the

standard determines the outcome of the case. State law; don't dismiss.

Hanna majority/Scalia: FRCPs are valid because Congress passed the REA. Scalia might

argue that being heard in court after meeting notice but not plausibility is not a

substantive state right and that the different pleading standards clearly conflict. Federal

law; dismiss. That's begging the question. Following Walker, narrowly construe 12(b)(6):

"The pleading does not state facts sufficient to constitute a cause of action." The

plausibility standard is federal judge-made law (Twiqbal), so go to twin aims of Erie.

Different pleading standards in the same state might encourage forum-shopping and lead

to inequitable administration of laws, e.g. when plaintiffs don't have enough information

to meet the plausibility standard (e.g. Twiqbal). State law applies; don't dismiss.

Harlan: Pleading standards don't generally affect primary conduct, except when

companies violate antitrust laws or discriminate because plaintiffs don't have enough

information to meet a higher pleading standard. This probably isn't enough to make it

substantive. Federal law; dismiss.

Ginsberg: When setting pleading standards, states control the amount of litigation

(policy). Consistent with Walker, 12(b)(6) only requires that there be a standard for

stating a claim, while VA law creates one. VA law; don't dismiss.

Stevens: Same test as Ginsberg, but plausibility and notice pleading clearly conflict, so

federal law; dismiss.

Chudley Count

         SMJ: DJ because Chudley incorporated in Delaware, PPoB in NY. Tonks is a VA
domiciliary. Complete diversity, and AIC met ($2,200,000). No AUJ; state claim.

         IPJ: VA doesn't have general IPJ over Chudley (only DE, NY do). Chudley was

sending the drone to a VA store, purposely availing itself of the benefits of doing

business in VA. Minimal contacts are met. It's fair and reasonable to be haled into court

in connection with supply delivery in VA (15 stores and $1,000,000,000 in VA

revenues). VA's long-arm and 42(k)(1)(A) give VA specific IPJ.

         Venue: Although the crash was in WV (1391(b)(2)), venue is proper in EDoVA if

Chudley had sufficient contacts EDoVA to have IPJ if it were a separate state (1391(d)).

Chudley likely has stores in EDoVA, but the more relevant contacts are the store the

drone was being sent to. If it was on its way to EDoVA, venue is likely proper; if it was
on its way to WDoVA, it should be transferred there.

         Failure to State a Claim: See VCOL above. The complaint meets the notice

standard (similar to Form 11); it specifies the drone number and puts Chudley on notice

about the event. It also meets plausibility; Chudley admits it likely wouldn't have flown

there if they'd investigated, making it plausibly negligent.

$2,000,000,000 Punitives

         For HCOL, damages are substantive and VA (Second Restatement) would apply

law of the state relevant to the issue of negligence. Longbottom works in WV (even

though his division covers VA and WV) and the crash happened there because Chudley

didn't investigate its flight paths in WV. WV law probably applies.

         If so and notice pleading applies (see above), the court won't dismiss (¶15 says

"reckless"), but Tonks will have difficulty proving recklessness. If plausibility applies,

nothing in the claim makes recklessness plausible (failure to investigate insufficient), so

the $2,000,000,000 punitives should be dismissed.

Separation

         SJ is improper because of different CNOFs (see above). Count II has SMJ, but

Count I doesn't (unless Smith/Grable). Count I should be dismissed.

         The directors were improperly joined. T/O is not the same (20(a)(2)(A)) and there

is no commmon question of law or fact (accident/failure to investigate is separate from

not getting license) (20(a)(2)(B)).
         The court can also separate under Rule 42.

feedback.headline: Complete coverage across all four questions; the losses sit in a handful of specific steps
feedback.overview: Question 4 is your best work. You caught the $9,900 amount-in-controversy deficiency, refused supplemental jurisdiction on a reasoned common-nucleus analysis, ran plausibility pleading at the paragraph level, and combined the Erie and horizontal choice-of-law layers into the conditional conclusion the punitive damages demand required. That combination is the hardest thing this exam asked for. What costs you is narrower: the Rules Enabling Act step is stated backwards, Klaxon never appears, personal jurisdiction over Chudley is resolved for the plaintiff without confronting the facts cutting the other way, and Question 2 canvasses the appellate bases without ever resolving the appeals or stating the recommendation the judge asked for.

strengths.label: Sorting safeguards by whether they inherently complicate
strengths.detail: Separating notice and an independent decisionmaker from hearings, cross-examination, and written findings let you show why added process defeats itself for an unrepresented litigant rather than merely that it costs money. That internal framing is the core of the question and most answers never reach it.
strengths.answerExcerpt: But for many procedural safeguards, there is an inherent conflict between protecting litigants and making litigation less accessible.

strengths.label: Three alternatives, each tested against its own drawback
strengths.detail: Adding an accessibility factor to the Mathews balance, redesigning agency adjudication by case type, and an investigatory model each came with the objection to it. That answers the second prompt instead of gesturing at it.
strengths.answerExcerpt: a patchwork of agency adjudication systems might require rural litigants to travel to far-off agencies

strengths.label: Each appellate basis rejected on a named ground, and the two post-trial standards kept apart
strengths.detail: You did not assert non-finality and stop. Section 1291, Cohen, Rule 54(b), 1292(a), mandamus, and 1292(b) each got a stated reason. Applying the reasonable-jury test to the JAMOL motion and the weight-of-the-evidence test to the new trial then let you explain the judge's split ruling rather than treat it as a contradiction.
strengths.answerExcerpt: Cohen (later appeal possible), 54(b) (only one claim), 1292(a) (no injunction)

strengths.label: Privity worked by hand, and the intervention bar caught
strengths.detail: You built privity from sole ownership and control instead of assuming it. You then spotted that Slughorn could not have intervened in the first action without destroying diversity, which is the fact that turns the Parklane could-have-joined factor in her favor.
strengths.answerExcerpt: But Slughorn couldn't intervene in L1 without violating diversity (NJ domicile).

strengths.label: Plausibility run at the paragraph level
strengths.detail: Naming the second half of paragraph 8 as conclusory, setting it aside, and then asking what the remaining allegations do for outrageousness and causation is the taught sequence performed rather than summarized.
strengths.answerExcerpt: the latter half of ¶8 ("Their decision...") is conclusory

strengths.label: Erie and horizontal choice of law layered, then combined
strengths.detail: You resolved choice of law to West Virginia on the record facts and joined it to the pleading standard to reach a conditional answer on the punitive damages demand. Either layer alone would have left the demand unresolved.
strengths.answerExcerpt: If plausibility applies, nothing in the claim makes recklessness plausible (failure to investigate insufficient)

improvements.label: Question 1 — the case against broad state-paid counsel is doctrinal, not political
improvements.whatHappened: Lassiter appears only for the weight of the parental interest. The claim that state-paid counsel will not arrive rests on "political will and money."
improvements.whyItMatters: Lassiter supplies a presumption against state-funded counsel in civil cases, and that presumption holds even where incarceration is at stake. Paired with Turner's choice between providing counsel and simplifying procedures, it is what makes your alternatives necessary rather than merely preferable.
improvements.howToImprove: Add one sentence stating the Lassiter presumption and pairing it with Turner's either-or. Pay for it by cutting the closing image about justice in a marble courthouse, which costs several lines and carries no analysis.

improvements.label: Question 2 — only one of the two appeals was analyzed, and no recommendation was given
improvements.whatHappened: The canvass runs against the JAMOL appeal alone. The defendants' appeal from the new-trial grant never gets its own appealability analysis. The memo never states the bottom line the judge asked for.
improvements.whyItMatters: Two orders were appealed and the clerk was asked what to do about the appeals. An unstated recommendation cannot earn the points reserved for it. The new-trial grant is non-final for the same reason the JAMOL denial is: merits litigation continues after both.
improvements.howToImprove: Open with the recommendation to dismiss both appeals, run the bases once, and say expressly that the same analysis disposes of the new-trial appeal. Pay for it with the opening paragraph verifying diversity, arising-under, personal jurisdiction, and venue in the district court, which is at most bonus here and can shrink to a clause.

improvements.label: Question 2 — 1292(b) leans the wrong way and one requirement is never applied
improvements.whatHappened: You quoted the judge saying she "cannot imagine" she was wrong and still concluded the order "might be a sufficient signal" for a discretionary appeal.
improvements.whyItMatters: That remark is the element failing: there is no substantial ground for difference of opinion. Double discretion also went unapplied — section 1292(b) requires permission from both the district court and the court of appeals, and this judge certified nothing.
improvements.howToImprove: Name the three requirements — a controlling question of law, substantial ground for difference of opinion, and material advancement of the litigation — then say which one the judge's own words defeat, then add the double-permission point. Recover the words from the same district-court jurisdiction paragraph.

improvements.label: Question 3 — the opening line is broader than what follows
improvements.whatHappened: You opened by saying federal and New York preclusion law are the same, so there are no intersystem preclusion issues. Two paragraphs later you correctly treat which sovereign's preclusion law governs as the pivot for issue preclusion.
improvements.whyItMatters: The exam gives New York the federal claim preclusion rule, so the shortcut holds for that branch. It does not hold across the board: New York departs from federal law on mutuality, and that departure is exactly what your issue preclusion analysis runs on.
improvements.howToImprove: Limit the opening to claim preclusion and say the two bodies of law converge there. Pay for it by cutting the suggestion that under federal law "mutuality is probably met because Slughorn and Fillius are in privity," which sits against your own privity holding — if they are the same party, the nonmutual branch is unnecessary.

improvements.label: Question 4 — the Rules Enabling Act step is stated backwards
improvements.whatHappened: "FRCPs are valid because Congress passed the REA" inverts the inquiry, and Sibbach never appears.
improvements.whyItMatters: This step carries the Hanna majority track on the most heavily weighted analysis in the exam. Validity is the question the Act poses, not something the Act's existence answers.
improvements.howToImprove: Use the course's formulation: a FRCP is valid if it does not abridge, enlarge or modify a substantive right, and under Sibbach if it really regulates procedure. Then say whether Rule 8(a)(2) and Rule 12(b)(6) really regulate procedure here. The words come from that inverted sentence plus "That's begging the question," which does no work. Incidentally, the course calls the standard plausibility pleading rather than the portmanteau you used.

improvements.label: Question 4 — personal jurisdiction over Chudley is resolved without the facts cutting against it
improvements.whatHappened: You found specific jurisdiction in Virginia from the drone being sent to a Virginia store, and folded the 15 stores and $1 billion in revenue into the fairness discussion.
improvements.whyItMatters: The drone never arrived in Virginia, and Tonks operating his controller from Virginia is his own activity rather than the defendant's contact with the forum. The store count and revenue are contacts unrelated to this claim, so they belong to general jurisdiction, where the standard is whether Chudley is at home there.
improvements.howToImprove: Take the two bases in order. Say why the store count and revenue do not make Chudley at home in Virginia. Then argue both sides of specific jurisdiction: the drone was dispatched toward Virginia, but it never arrived, and the collision, the physical evidence, and the witnesses are all in West Virginia. Pay for it by cutting your speculation about whether the destination store lay in the Eastern or Western District down to one clause.

improvements.label: Question 4 — Klaxon is missing, so the move to Virginia's choice-of-law rules is unexplained
improvements.whatHappened: You asserted that Virginia's Second Restatement approach governs the punitive damages question without saying how a federal court gets there.
improvements.whyItMatters: This is the one gap a reader cannot fill from your surrounding reasoning. A federal court sitting in diversity uses the forum state's choice-of-law rules, and Klaxon is the authority for that step. Without it the West Virginia conclusion floats.
improvements.howToImprove: Add one sentence naming Klaxon and stating the forum-state rule, then keep your existing Second Restatement application. Pay for it by dropping the quoted text of Rule 12(b)(6) in your Walker line; the course prefers you not quote a source of law beyond a word or two.

revisionPlan: 1. Question 2: put the recommendation to dismiss both appeals in the first sentence, then run the bases once and apply the result to the new-trial appeal as well as the JAMOL denial.
2. Question 2: rework 1292(b) so the judge's "cannot imagine" remark defeats the substantial-ground element, and add the requirement of permission from both courts.
3. Question 3: confine the opening convergence point to claim preclusion, leaving the preclusion-law choice live for issue preclusion.
4. Question 4: replace the Rules Enabling Act sentence with the abridge-enlarge-modify formulation plus Sibbach's really-regulates-procedure test, applied to Rule 8(a)(2) and Rule 12(b)(6).
5. Question 4: split personal jurisdiction over Chudley into general and specific, and argue both sides of specific using the drone's failure to arrive and Tonks's own operation of the controller.
6. Question 4: name Klaxon before applying Virginia's choice-of-law approach.

7. Fund every addition from the passage named on its card: the marble-courthouse image, the district-court jurisdiction paragraph, the mutuality-by-privity sentence, the quoted rule text, and the Eastern-versus-Western District speculation.
feedback.exampleRevision:
Instead of: "Hanna majority/Scalia: FRCPs are valid because Congress passed the REA... That's begging the question."

Try: "Hanna majority: Rules 8(a)(2) and 12(b)(6) are directly on point, so they apply if valid. A FRCP is valid under the Rules Enabling Act if it does not abridge, enlarge or modify a substantive right; under Sibbach, if it really regulates procedure. These Rules set what a filing must contain and when it may be tested, which really regulates procedure. That a stricter standard kills the punitive damages demand does not change the character of the Rule. Federal law; dismiss. The counter is Walker: read 12(b)(6) narrowly to require only facts sufficient to state a claim, leaving sufficiency to state law. That reading separates the Rule from the Supreme Court's own interpretation of it, and is hard to sustain."

What changed: validity is now a question you answer rather than an assumption, the course's formulation and Sibbach carry it, and the narrow-construction counterargument is stated and answered.
feedback.closing: Fix the Rules Enabling Act step and the general-versus-specific split on Chudley first; both sit on the 23-point question. Question 2's missing recommendation is the cheapest point on this exam to recover.

fixtures.bandRationale: Reference defect lists first, so both sides carry one. Same-exam H reference: Q2 misstates Rule 50 practice (asserts there was 'no delayed JAMOL to be renewed' and uses the superseded JNOV label), leans toward 1292(b) on a misreading of the order, and buries appellate jurisdiction behind an SMJ/IPJ/venue paragraph; Q4 collapses the pleading question with 'Virginia, as the forum state, will follow notice pleading since it's purely procedural, so there's no HCOL analysis' and so never runs the vertical choice-of-law analysis at all; its IPJ and venue treatments are one-clause each; and it repeatedly hedges over who the plaintiff is. Same-exam P reference: SMJ announced as a bare conclusion, finality inverted (treats the Rule 59 order as final), general jurisdiction over Chudley asserted from store presence, and the pleading/Erie question compressed to a sentence about whether pleading is procedural. Same-exam LP reference: gets appellate jurisdiction backwards (JAMOL denial called a final order), asserts arising-under jurisdiction without analysis, concludes Virginia law applies to the tort by mislocating the collision, and treats the complaint as satisfying both pleading standards so the Erie tracks resolve nothing. DS reference (different year, sole DS comparator, weighted as a full comparator): one-sentence answer to 1c, effects-test reliance, and some conclusory turns — but sustained argued canvassing on the policy question and complete multi-track Erie runs on two separate issues with alternatives preserved throughout. Pairwise verdicts. Versus LP: stronger, not close — every weighted core here is resolved with reasoning attached. Versus P: stronger — no bare-conclusion jurisdictional disposals, and the punitive-damages question is actually resolved through both required layers. Versus H: stronger on the 23-point question (full Erie run the H reference omits entirely, paragraph-level 12(b)(6), AIC deficiency and CNOF-based refusal of supplemental jurisdiction, Rule 20(a)(2)(A)-(B) plus Rule 42) and comparable-to-stronger on Q3; roughly comparable on Q1 and Q2, where the H reference cites more of the assigned readings and this answer canvasses the appellate bases more cleanly but leaves the recommendation unstated. Versus DS: weaker as a total performance. Q2 is the gap — the canvass is there but the new-trial appeal's appealability is never analyzed, no recommendation is given, the 1292(b) lean is off, and the JAMOL merits rest on thin reasoning that conflicts with the answer's own credibility assessment two paragraphs later; and the Hanna-majority track fails on the REA formulation the course expects by name. That is not the sustained resolution across every weighted question that the DS reference maintains. Comparable-to-stronger than the H reference, short of DS: high H.
fixtures.whyNotHigher: Not DS because Q2 (10 pts) canvasses without resolving — the defendants' new-trial appeal never gets its own appealability analysis, the memo states no recommendation on the appeals, and the 1292(b) lean misreads the order's 'seems really straightforward' language — and because the Hanna-majority track on the most heavily weighted question inverts the REA inquiry and never reaches Sibbach's 'really regulates procedure.' Boundary evidence for the 'high' lean sits on Q4 (23 pts), where this answer does what the H reference does not: a complete multi-track Erie run, paragraph-level plausibility analysis on both counts, a reasoned CNOF refusal of supplemental jurisdiction after identifying the AIC deficiency, and the combined Erie-plus-HCOL conclusion on the punitive-damages demand.
fixtures.whyNotLower: Not P because no heavily weighted core is left as a bare conclusion: SMJ is run through citizenship, AIC and an arising-under alternative; the appellate bases are each rejected on named grounds; preclusion is worked through privity, Semtek and Parklane with the intervention bar caught; and the punitive-damages demand is resolved through both the Erie and horizontal choice-of-law layers rather than one. The P reference, by contrast, announces SMJ in a clause, inverts finality, and asserts general jurisdiction from store presence.

judgeFindings.problem: Mutuality is an issue preclusion concept, not a claim preclusion one, so the stated reason the choice matters is wrong. The card also treats the student's opening line as a straightforward error when the exam expressly gives New York the federal claim preclusion rule, which makes the shortcut correct for that branch.
judgeFindings.correction: Rewrote the card as a narrower point: the opening sentence is broader than what follows, because New York departs from federal law on mutuality and that departure is what the student's own issue preclusion analysis runs on.

judgeFindings.problem: The Stevens entry is one of the vertical choice-of-law tracks on the most heavily weighted analysis in the exam, and it reaches a different disposition from the Ginsburg entry. Funding a one-sentence addition by cutting a track tells the student to thin the framework the question was built around.
judgeFindings.correction: Replaced the payer with the quoted text of Rule 12(b)(6) in the Walker line, which the course's own guidance against quoting sources of law beyond a word or two makes expendable.

judgeFindings.problem: The sentence would read the same on any competent answer and adds nothing the surrounding sentences do not already say.
judgeFindings.correction: Deleted; the overview now moves from what the Question 4 work accomplished directly to the specific steps that failed.

judgeFindings.problem: As phrased this reads as a complaint about the student's shorthand, which costs no credit, rather than about the missing analysis.
judgeFindings.correction: Rewrote so the point is the unapplied requirement: section 1292(b) needs permission from both the district court and the court of appeals, and no certification was made here.

fixtures.label: 2015 answer — H
fixtures.answer:
## Question 1

       There may be an inherent conflict between simplified procedures and greater

protections. State agencies, such as the offices that award drivers’ licenses, often play an

adjudicatory role; they use simplified procedures to make decisions which may have

radically negative impacts on citizens. Often, there’s no opportunity to contest such

decisions, or opaque bureaucratic systems obscure the opportunities for pro se litigants to

protect their rights. When an adjudicatory system is challenged on procedural due process

grounds and additional protection is proposed, the courts often employ Matthew/Eldridge

balancing to determine whether to add the procedure. This balancing test always

measures the government’s interests in reducing costs against the interests of the party

concerned and the risk of erroneously depriving that party of liberty or property. Such a

test demonstrates that the government’s interest in efficiency often conflicts with private

party’s interests in increased due process. However, the governmental interest in cheaper

adjudicatory processes is in some cases aligned with the interest of indigent plaintiffs. In

child custody suits as in Turner, the simplified process may have served the interests of

the mother trying to recover child support payments - she may not have been able to

navigate a more complex process. If one proposes lawyers as the solution, then lawyers

must be provided both for defendants and for plaintiffs.

       But should lawyers be guaranteed; must there be a Gideon for civil actions - was

SCOTUS wrong in rejecting the right to counsel in Turner? If legal representation is

required for all adjudications, then the systems of justice would be swamped; imagine the

DMV offices standing still. The justice system would probably respond by simplifying

methods of ending cases early, which would result in an increase in the mistaken

dismissal of meritorious claims (much like what happened as a result of the heightened,

plausibility pleading standard). However, perhaps efficiency and judicial economy would

readjust naturally, as the agency systems would be forced to reform their adjudication

methods in response to the overwhelming flood. Regarding fairness, more lawyers would

provide greater protection for defendants - the mother in Lassiter certainly would have

benefited from the assistance of a lawyer. However, as previously mentioned, in cases

like child custody claims, lawyers would need to be provided to both sides. SCOTUS in

Turner indicated that doing so would create more complications, leading to more

complex processes, thus counteracting the potential for lawyers to simplify procedures

and running counter to the commentator’s dichotomous representation of protection

versus simplification. Additionally, some argue lawyers don’t lead to fairer outcomes for

the parties involved; in their article, Barton & Bibas claim there’s no difference in

outcomes when lawyers are provided. They point to Gideon’s legacy: overworked public

defenders, unable to adequately represent clients, and a criminal system that’s adjusted to

the pressure by becoming wholly dependent on plea bargaining. A similar, detrimental

outcome might occur on the civil side. Then again, more lawyers may lead to a move

away from agencies that employ simplified processes and towards the formalized court

system that generally provides more protection than agencies. Originalists may be

proponents of such a shift, but the competitive advantage of agencies and their ability to

quickly and competently deal with matters would disappear.

       While I would argue that requiring lawyers would flood the civil system and thus

force radical change and a recognition of the unconscionable and possibly

unconstitutional lack of due process in agency decisions that deny liberty and new

property interests, I’m forced to admit that lawyers do not necessarily simplify processes

and arguably do not provide more protection and just outcomes. As Pollock & Greco

argue, counsel should be provided when “basic human needs” or physical liberty are at

stake, but in other cases, certain protections may not require more complex systems and

greater state expenditures. Vitek recommends written notice. Currently, many defendants

don’t actually receive notice. Email and text message notification may be cheaper and

more effective. The Restatement of Judgments (2nd) recommends that issues be

formulated in reference to specific rules. Creating basic forms and tools for litigants

would systematically make adjudications simpler, clearer, and more consistent (while

forms are provided, they aren’t necessarily aligned with common law requirements - see

plausibility pleading). Other protections may require initial investments but could be

drawn out of a rotating fund; in order to protect against erroneous deprivation, the

government could post bonds on behalf of plaintiffs. Plaintiffs would then have an

opportunity to contest before the property is actually seized, and the government would

be protected by its own bond system. Lastly, lawyers could relinquish their monopoly on

the justice system; specialized counsel may be more efficient and effective in providing

greater civil protections in certain cases.

-------------------------------------------

-------------------------------------------

## Question 2_

       The appellate court has DJ but probably not SMJ through FQJ Smith/Grable

exception; the federal government has an interest in uniform interpretations of the Mail-

Only Act (MOA), but exercising FQJ would sweep many drone cases into the federal

courts and defining “mail” is a fact-bound issue. The court has DJ because Fillius is suing

on behalf of CC against SFU. There is complete diversity between CC (nerve center in

NY and incorporated in DE) and SFU (domiciled in NJ), and the AIC is 300K or $3.3

million. If CC is considered the defendant, there is diversity: Fillius is incorporated and

PPoB in Maine. There is general IPJ over SFU through Daimler (may as well be at home

in NY) with the long-arm statute or specific IPJ (R4k1(a) piggybacks on NJ long-arm

statute), as SFU have minimal contacts and it would be fair and reasonable to try the case

in NY. Venue properly laid: 1391(B)(2).

       There is no appellate jurisdiction under 1291 because there was no final order, and

no jurisdiction under rule 54(b), as there’s no final judgment for any individual claim. No

final order with respect to the issue, so no interlocutory appeal under Cohen. Possible

jurisdiction under 1292(b) as the trial court wrote there’s an issue for which there could

be substantial difference of opinion and a district court decision could materially advance

the ultimate termination of the litigation. However, the issue may be too fact-bound for

an appellate court and so the appellate court should not exercise jurisdiction under

1291(b) - the trial court’s familiar with all information from discovery regarding the

failure to seek a permit. No 1292(a)(1) jurisdiction because there’s no injunction and no

writ of mandamus because the plaintiff won’t suffer any irreparable harm and no need

for a supervisory writ.

       JJ was technically correct in denying the JAMOL motion. Although SFU had a full

opportunity to be heard, because the initial JAMOL (before the jury verdict) was denied,

there’s no delayed JAMOL to be renewed for a JNOV. If the appellate court reviews the

motion for JAMOL, it will be de novo, and the court could find that the first JAMOL

motion should have been granted, as the evidence clearly appeared to show SFU knew of

the drone collisions. JJ was right to grant a new trial motion, as Fillius convinced JJ he

made a mistake, and the summary judgment ruling in favor of CC was not harmless error.

The granting of the new trial motion is not reviewable on appeal without exceptional

circumstances.

-------------------------------------------

-------------------------------------------

Answer-to-Question-__3_

       NY state court has venue because 1391(B)(2). SFU should file for dismissal on the

theory of claim preclusion. SS is suing SFU over the same issue that Fillius (or CC, if

they were the plaintiff) did: outrageous conduct regarding knowledge of the accident rate.

It’s the same transaction or occurrence and would use the same evidence as the

stockholder’s derivative suit. There’s privity, as SS had a significant degree of effective

control of the first lawsuit; she made all decisions on behalf of Fillius. If CC were the

plaintiff in the first case, then there’s strictly no privity here, but SS’s control of the first

lawsuit probably trumps the legal fiction of corporation as plaintiff in stockholder

derivative suits. There was final judgment on the merits in the federal court; the lawsuit is

over and wasn’t dismissed for procedural reasons but was decided by a jury and affirmed

on appeal.

       SS will try to issue preclude (NMOCE or OCE) my client on a factual matter. The

issue is the same as before; whether SFU knew of the accidents and acted outrageously in

ignoring it. In NY state court, mutuality is not required for issue preclusion, so questions

of who was the first plaintiff are irrelevant; federal preclusion law would forbid NMOCE

(Erie issue?). This issue was actually litigated, given that the precise question was raised

and the jury determined an award (SFU had every reason to defend themselves

vigorously in suit 1). Given that punitive damages were awarded in the first lawsuit by

the jury, after they determined that SFU knew of the accident rate, the finding regarding

the outrageousness of SFU’s failure to obtain a license was necessary to the final decision

(so no Rios/ gratuitous to decision). However, a court may decide that collateral estoppel

should not be permitted here because SS had full opportunity to have her interests heard

in court during lawsuit 1.

       Semtek: since the first court was a federal court with DJ, the subsequent, NY state

court is to use the law of the state in which the first court sat, and give as much preclusive

effect as that state would to the judgment. Since the first court was in NY, the state court

will follow issue preclusion rules of New York, which do not require mutuality (Hart). If,

however, the first federal court had FQJ under Smith/Grable exception, and the state

court finds the parties in lawsuit 2 are not in privity, then the state may follow federal

common law and forbid NMCE because of 1738 and the rendering court would have

precluded the case.

-------------------------------------------

-------------------------------------------

Answer-to-Question-__4_

       If TT is the plaintiff for both claims, then SFU could move to dismiss count 1

against them for lack of independent SMJ and no supplemental jurisdiction (following

Exxon). SFU can argue venue wasn’t properly laid in the Eastern District of Virginia, as

defendants don’t reside there, the events or omissions that gave rise to the claim didn’t

occur there, and there are other districts in which the case could’ve been brought. There

was no general nor specific IPJ because SFU don’t live in Virginia nor significantly

benefit from VA; so SFU can contest IPJ through special appearance.

       If CC is the plaintiff for claim 1, then SFU could move to claim preclude the suit.

There’s the same claim regarding liability for decreased stock prices. CC and SFU are the

same parties, and there was final judgment on the merits in the NY case already. Virginia

requires more stringent preclusion standards than NY, and require full mutuality, but

these requirements are met.

       Count II against CC could be dismissed for lack of IPJ or failure to properly lay

venue. There’s DJ because the AIC is at least 200K, CC is in NY & DE, and TT lives in

Virginia. Specific jurisdiction requires minimal contacts between the defendant, forum

and subject matter (although McGee suggests plaintiff’s interests are relevant too). The

federal long arm statute piggybacks on Virginia’s long arm statute. CC purposefully

availed itself of the benefits of Virginia, but it still may not be fair and reasonable to try

the case there - it’d be much better to try the case in West Virginia, where the brunt of the

harm was felt. Venue was improper as well because CC isn’t in Virginia, the

events/omissions occurred in West Virginia, and the case could have been brought

somewhere else.

       CC can move to dismiss the punitive damage claim (FRCP 12). Virginia, as the

forum state, will follow notice pleading since it’s purely procedural, so there’s no HCOL

analysis and the complaint sufficiently notified CC of the transaction/occurrence giving

rise to the claim. Virginia is a 2nd restatement state, so the court will conduct HCOL

analysis for the issue of whether recklessness is necessary for awarding punitive damages

(Klaxon: federal court in diversity uses rules of state in which its sitting). If it’s

procedural, then punitive damages will be rewarded, but if it’s substantive, then look to

the center of gravity. The collision occurred in WV, Longbottom’s office and alleged

negligence occurred in WV, and so the court will use WV law and forbid punitive

damages for negligence. TT cannot use NMOCE for the negligence issue in Virginia

because Virginia requires full mutuality.

       CC could alternatively move to transfer the case to WV. Since the first court was

not a happy court (either for lack of PJ or improperly laid venue), the transferee court will

use its own COL rules. WV is a first restatement state and the crash occurred in WV, so

TT won’t be able to get punitive damages from CC. WV follows the plausibility pleading

standard, so all conclusory statements in the complaint regarding CC’s negligence are

ignored. TT will not be able to use NMOCE on the negligence issue in his case because

the issue being decided is not the same as the issue in NY court - in NY it was over the

failure to get a license and here it’s vicarious liability for Longbottom’s negligence.

       FRCP 42 allows for the court to separate the trials for efficiency reasons. Since the

alleged misfeasance is different for each claim, the court will probably separate. If TT is

the plaintiff for both claims, there’s no permissive joinder for CC as the defendant in

claim 2 because there are different transaction or occurrences at issue. However, if SFU

are considered 3rd party defendants in claim 2 because liability shifts to them, then T/O is

not required to join them; under rule 18(a), TT can join even if CC was the plaintiff in

claim 1.

feedback.headline: Strong on preclusion and appellate jurisdiction; the 23-point question is missing its two biggest analytical blocks
feedback.overview: Two pieces of real analysis held up. Question 2's appealability canvass names and rejects each route in turn — no final order under 1291, no Rule 54(b) certification, no collateral order under Cohen, no injunction under 1292(a)(1), no mandamus — and lands on the right recommendation. Question 3 leads with claim preclusion, grounds privity in Slughorn's own allegation that she made every litigation decision, then runs issue preclusion in the alternative and applies Semtek and Hart rather than just naming them. The problem is Question 4. It carries 23 points, and two of its heaviest blocks never happen: the vertical choice-of-law analysis of notice versus plausibility pleading, and the paragraph-by-paragraph pleading run against a complaint the exam reproduced in full. Both personal-jurisdiction holdings are disposed of in a clause each. On Question 2 the merits reasoning rests on a preservation rule stated backwards.

strengths.label: Named readings and concrete reform proposals
strengths.detail: The alternatives section does what a policy answer has to do: it proposes specific measures — electronic notice, forms tied to actual legal requirements, a government-funded rotating bond fund with a chance to contest before seizure, loosening the bar's monopoly — and ties them to Vitek and the Restatement. Setting Barton & Bibas against Pollock & Greco produces an argument rather than a gesture at access to justice.
strengths.answerExcerpt: the government could post bonds on behalf of plaintiffs

strengths.label: Complete run through the appealability checklist
strengths.detail: Each route is named and rejected with a stated reason rather than abandoned once one answer appeared. That sequencing is what earns the points on a jurisdiction question. One of the reasons misreads the order; see the 1292(b) note below.
strengths.answerExcerpt: no jurisdiction under rule 54(b), as there's no final judgment for any individual claim

strengths.label: Claim preclusion first, issue preclusion in the alternative
strengths.detail: Leading with claim preclusion is the right order, and control-based privity is applied to the facts rather than asserted. Running issue preclusion anyway answers the prompt's demand for all possible uses. Semtek picks the governing preclusion law, and the Smith/Grable wrinkle is flagged as the thing that would change the answer.
strengths.answerExcerpt: SS had a significant degree of effective control of the first lawsuit

strengths.label: Horizontal choice of law and the Happy Court Rule
strengths.detail: Klaxon routes to Virginia's Second Restatement approach, and the center of gravity is located with facts — the collision, Longbottom's office, the alleged failure to investigate — producing the correct West Virginia result on punitive damages. The Happy Court Rule is then used accurately on transfer: the transferor was not a happy court, so the transferee's choice-of-law rules travel.

strengths.label: Venue applied prong by prong

improvements.label: Question 1 — the conflict is about complexity, not only cost
improvements.whatHappened: The essay locates the conflict in money and system capacity: lawyers for everyone would swamp the courts and stall the DMV. The other dimension, which the quotation is actually about, never appears.
improvements.whyItMatters: Added protections can defeat an unrepresented litigant on difficulty alone, even with unlimited funding. Presenting evidence requires knowing the rules of evidence. A written statement of findings is hard to read unaided. A bond requirement assumes you know what a bond is and how to get one.
improvements.howToImprove: Name two or three protections from the due process cases and say how each raises the difficulty of using the system — Doehr's bond, Vitek's written statement of findings and hearing, Goldberg's pre-termination hearing. Then say plainly that this problem does not depend on cost. Pay for it by cutting the paragraph imagining the justice system flooded and readjusting naturally.

improvements.label: Question 1 — state Turner's holding as a holding
improvements.whatHappened: Turner is used for the asymmetry point and for the observation that counsel adds formality, but its rule is never stated.
improvements.whyItMatters: That rule is the pivot for the second half of the question. It is what lets you reject state-paid counsel as the necessary resolution without abandoning the litigant.
improvements.howToImprove: Write the either/or: when very serious interests are at stake, the state must either provide counsel at its expense or simplify and rationalize its procedures so they are usable. Your reform proposals then become the second branch of a constitutional command rather than free-floating suggestions. One sentence, paid for by trimming the originalists aside.

improvements.label: Question 2 — the preservation rule runs the other way
improvements.whatHappened: The answer treats the denial of the pre-verdict Rule 50 motion as removing any renewed motion to decide. A denied pre-verdict motion is what preserves the renewed post-verdict motion; it does not foreclose it.
improvements.whyItMatters: This is the merits half of a 10-point question, and the invented bar is doing the work the standard should be doing. The answer then hedges toward roughly the right result without ever saying what test applies.
improvements.howToImprove: State the standard: view the evidence favorably to the non-movant and ask whether a reasonable jury could find for that party. Apply it to these facts — three unrebutted emails against the defendants' own testimony — and conclude that a reasonable jury could not have found late knowledge. Recover the words from the opening paragraph on the trial court's diversity jurisdiction, personal jurisdiction, and venue, which the memo was not asked for; cut it to a clause. The course uses JAMOL, not JNOV.

improvements.label: Question 2 — the new trial grant needs its own standard
improvements.whatHappened: The grant is defended on the ground that the judge was convinced she had erred and that the summary judgment ruling in favor of Chudley was not harmless. That misidentifies who won summary judgment and is not the basis for a new trial here.
improvements.whyItMatters: The reason the two rulings can coexist is that the new-trial standard is more permissive than the JAMOL standard and is reviewed far more deferentially. Without naming it, you cannot explain why granting one and denying the other is not a contradiction.
improvements.howToImprove: Say the verdict was against the great weight of the evidence, which suffices for a new trial, and that the grant is reviewed for abuse of discretion. Add a clause on why that is a lower bar than JAMOL. Pay for it by deleting the sentence about exceptional circumstances for reviewability, which repeats the jurisdiction analysis you already did.

improvements.label: Question 2 — the 1292(b) analysis misreads the order
improvements.whatHappened: The answer says the trial court wrote that there could be substantial difference of opinion on the issue. The order says the opposite — that the judge cannot imagine being wrong and the issue seems straightforward.
improvements.whyItMatters: That statement negates the substantial-ground element directly. Reaching the right recommendation by a different route leaves the strongest available reason on the table.
improvements.howToImprove: Swap the inaccurate characterization for the accurate one, which costs no words: the judge's own description of the issue as easy defeats that element. Add that certification requires both the district court and the court of appeals to agree.

improvements.label: Question 3 — the federal branch needs Parklane and Slughorn's domicile
improvements.whatHappened: The answer says federal preclusion law "would forbid" non-mutual offensive preclusion. Federal law makes it discretionary, not prohibited, and Parklane — the source of that discretion — is never named even though the alternative branch depends on it.
improvements.whyItMatters: The decisive factor is whether Slughorn could easily have joined the SDNY action. She could not: she and the defendants are all New Jersey domiciliaries, so joining her would have destroyed complete diversity. That fact converts a rule recitation into an applied answer.
improvements.howToImprove: Replace "federal preclusion law would forbid NMOCE" with the discretionary standard, name Parklane, and run the could-have-joined factor against the New Jersey domicile. The words come from the opening sentence laying venue in New York state court under 1391(b)(2); the federal venue statute does not govern a state court, and that line can go entirely.

improvements.label: Question 4 — the vertical choice-of-law question on pleading is never reached
improvements.whatHappened: The answer says Virginia will follow notice pleading because pleading is purely procedural, so no choice-of-law analysis is needed. That treats a federal district court as bound by state pleading practice and collapses the vertical question into the horizontal one.
improvements.whyItMatters: This is one of the two conditions that decide the punitive damages demand: it survives only if pleading is lenient and Virginia punitive damages law applies. Skipping it removes the largest analytical block in the heaviest question.
improvements.howToImprove:
Walk the taught sequence.
1. State the two conditions separately: which pleading standard governs, and which state's punitive damages law governs.
2. Run York outcome-determinativeness and say it is inconclusive, because the standard determines the punitive demand but not the case.
3. Take the Hanna majority route: Rule 8(a)(2) and Rule 12(b)(6) are on point, and a FRCP is valid under the Rules Enabling Act if it does not abridge, enlarge, or modify a substantive right; under Sibbach it is valid if it really regulates procedure. Say whether these rules do.
4. Argue Harlan's primary-conduct question both ways.
5. Try the Walker narrow-construction move and say why it is hard here — you cannot sever Rule 8 from the Supreme Court's reading of it.
Pay for this by cutting the closing Rule 18(a) and third-party-defendant speculation, and by keeping only one of the two sentences about whether Tonks can use non-mutual offensive issue preclusion.

improvements.label: Question 4 — the complaint was reproduced and never worked paragraph by paragraph
improvements.whatHappened: The answer says all conclusory statements about Chudley's negligence are ignored. No paragraph is named, no element is matched to a paragraph, and the punitive damages demand is never cut separately from the claim.
improvements.whyItMatters: A complaint printed in full signals that a complete run is wanted. The decisive point is available and missed: the pleaded facts about the failure to investigate flight routes support negligence, but negligence is not the recklessness West Virginia requires for punitive damages. That is how the demand falls while the claim survives.
improvements.howToImprove:
Take the steps in order.
1. Name paragraph 8's bare causation assertion and set it aside as conclusory.
2. Take the four negligence elements the exam gives — duty, breach, causation, damage — and name the paragraphs (9 through 12) pleading facts as to each.
3. Say whether what survives makes each element plausible.
4. Run the cut again, separately, for the $2 million punitive damages demand, and identify which element of recklessness has no facts behind it.
The words come from the "if CC is the plaintiff for claim 1" aside, which is worth a clause rather than a paragraph.

improvements.label: Question 4 — both personal-jurisdiction holdings are asserted, not analyzed
improvements.whatHappened: The individuals are dismissed in one clause because they do not live in Virginia and do not significantly benefit from it. Chudley's general jurisdiction is never tested against the 15 stores and $1 billion in Virginia sales.
improvements.whyItMatters: These are separate holdings the memo was asked for, and each has a fact the other side will press. For the individuals, the deciding point is that a corporation's contacts are not attributed to its officers and directors personally — otherwise a decision made in New York would make them suable wherever a shareholder lives. For Chudley, substantial in-state sales do not make a Delaware and New York corporation at home in Virginia.
improvements.howToImprove:
Take the bases in order.
For the individuals: Rule 4(k)(1)(A) routes to Virginia's long-arm, which reaches the constitutional limit, so run minimum contacts under International Shoe and say no alleged contact is theirs rather than the corporation's, citing Shaffer for non-attribution.
For Chudley: test general jurisdiction against Daimler's at-home standard and reject it on the numbers, then take specific jurisdiction and treat the plaintiff's operating the controller from Virginia as the plaintiff's own activity, not Chudley's.
Recover the words by cutting the McGee aside about the plaintiff's interests, which decides nothing here.

revisionPlan: Rewrite the Question 4 pleading passage at paragraph and element level, and cut the punitive damages demand separately from the negligence claim.

Add the vertical choice-of-law run on notice versus plausibility pleading to Question 4, funded by deleting the Rule 18(a) speculation and one of the two duplicative non-mutual offensive preclusion sentences.
Give each Question 4 personal-jurisdiction holding a minimum-contacts run: non-attribution of corporate contacts for the individuals, the at-home standard for Chudley.
Replace the Question 2 preservation sentence with the JAMOL standard applied to the unrebutted emails, and defend the new trial on the great weight of the evidence.
In Question 3, state the federal standard for non-mutual offensive preclusion as discretionary, name Parklane, and run the could-have-joined factor against Slughorn's New Jersey domicile.
In Question 1, add the complexity dimension of the conflict and state Turner's either/or holding, paid for by cutting the flooded-courts speculation.
feedback.exampleRevision:
Instead of: "WV follows the plausibility pleading standard, so all conclusory statements in the complaint regarding CC's negligence are ignored."

Try: "Paragraph 8 asserts that Chudley's decision caused the collision. That is bare causation with no supporting facts, so set it aside. What remains is paragraphs 9 through 12: Chudley never investigated whether its flight routes were crowded, and the collision rate was known internally. Duty and breach are plausible on those facts, and paragraph 13 supplies damage, so Count II survives. The $2 million punitive demand is a separate cut. West Virginia law governs punitive damages here and requires recklessness. Nothing in paragraphs 9 through 12 alleges that Chudley knew the route was crowded and flew it anyway; failing ever to look is carelessness, not conscious disregard. The demand should be dismissed even though the claim stands."
feedback.closing: The preclusion and appealability work shows you can run a checklist to the end. Do that on Question 4's pleading and Erie blocks, where the points are.

fixtures.bandRationale: Reference defect lists, run at equal scrutiny. DS (same exam): reaches several contestable bottom lines (finds the derivative count fails plausibility, treats Chudley's Virginia contacts as supporting specific jurisdiction, uses 1391(d) in a strained way, misstates the punitive figure) — but canvasses six Erie approaches, runs paragraph-level plausibility, tests the common-nucleus question, and resolves every sub-question. P (same exam): inverts appellate jurisdiction ('The R59 motion finished the trial so appellate jurisdiction is valid'), relies on a case no longer part of the course for the Rule 50 record limit, invents a ten-day waiver on 1292(b), asserts general jurisdiction over Chudley in Virginia, and disposes of the pleading vertical-choice question in two sentences — but covers Smith/Grable, the Exxon limit, Rios/Russell, Gonzalez/Migra, a full horizontal choice-of-law run, and a plausibility cut on each count. LP (same exam): holds the JAMOL denial appealable as a final order and partly grounds appellate jurisdiction in the trial court's subject-matter jurisdiction, applies Virginia law to the drone tort, finds general jurisdiction over Chudley and proper venue under 1391(b)(1), and never addresses the punitive damages demand separately or supplemental jurisdiction at all — though it does run the Erie tracks and cites Turner's substitute safeguards well. H (2009, sole H comparator, full weight): dense sustained canvassing with preserved alternatives throughout — Erie tracks including Walker/Gasperini narrowing and Harlan, transfer and its choice-of-law consequence, Russell/Kelley/Cromwell nuance on actually-litigated, Smith exception, Parklane factors — its defects are localized (some hedging on numerosity, a shaky waiver-of-remand point). Pairwise verdicts. Versus LP: stronger. The student gets finality right where LP inverts it, canvasses the full set of interlocutory escape hatches, applies Semtek and Hart cleanly, and reaches the correct West Virginia punitive damages result and the correct Rule 20/42 conclusion that LP largely skips. Versus P: comparable. The student is better on appellate jurisdiction and on venue application; P is better on the Question 2 merits, on running plausibility against the complaint, and on breadth of authority. Both leave the Erie/vertical-choice core essentially undone, and both dispose of at least one jurisdictional holding by assertion. Versus H: weaker. The student has no sustained alternative-canvassing anywhere; the 23-point question omits the Erie structure and the pleading run entirely and disposes of two personal-jurisdiction questions in single clauses. Versus DS: clearly weaker on every heavily weighted question. That places the answer at P — above the LP reference, level with the P reference, below H.
fixtures.whyNotHigher: H requires mostly sound resolutions and rich analysis with real errors confined to some cores. Here the 23-point question loses two of its largest analytical blocks — the vertical choice-of-law run on notice versus plausibility pleading, and the paragraph-and-element pleading analysis of a complaint the exam reproduced in full — and disposes of both personal-jurisdiction questions and the subject-matter jurisdiction of the derivative count by assertion rather than analysis. The Question 2 merits rest on an inverted preservation rule and a misread of the summary judgment ruling. That is core analysis underdeveloped or unresolved, not localized error, and it falls well short of the H comparator's sustained canvassing of alternatives.
fixtures.whyNotLower: LP is reserved for answers whose heavily weighted cores combine wrong results with conclusory, inverted, or skipped analysis. This answer resolves the 10-point appellate-jurisdiction question correctly and with the full set of escape hatches tested, runs claim and issue preclusion with Semtek and Hart applied rather than named, applies 1391 prong by prong twice, reaches the correct horizontal choice-of-law result on punitive damages with Klaxon and the Second Restatement, deploys the Happy Court Rule accurately, and identifies both the Rule 20 misjoinder ground and Rule 42 severance. The LP comparator, by contrast, inverts finality and gets general jurisdiction, venue, and the governing tort law wrong on the same exam.

fixtures.label: 2015 answer — LP
fixtures.answer:
## Question 1

       The writer is correct to conclude that there is a real conflict between the principles

of procedural due process and simplicity in the American legal system. She could just as

easily have used the terms we used most often this semester to describe these principles:

fairness and efficiency. Examples of this conflict include measures like preclusion that
increase efficiency but potentially reduce litigants’ ability to defend themselves, or

doctrines like Erie that go to extreme lengths to ensure that litigants are safe from “home

cooking” prejudice at the price of relatively inefficient and complicated litigation.

       But the evolution the writer traces isn’t quite the black-and-white duality she

implies. Justice Breyer’s opinion in Turner isn’t so much a 180-degree departure from the

court’s previous jurisprudence that attempted to expand procedural due process

safeguards as it is a left turn--a recognition that it’s time to try something new, and in so

doing, strike a balance between these two principles that have been at war since the birth

of American jurisprudence.

       The U.S. Supreme Court (SCOTUS) has long recognized this conflict, and their

solutions have indeed complicated legal processes. In Sniadach, among the first of the

Court’s focus on PDP that began in the late-60s and early-70s, the Court required that

Wisconsin provide sufficient notice and opportunity to be heard to a debtor whose wages

were garnished. One year later, in Goldberg the Court required that New York City and

State provide a hearing before depriving a beneficiary of government assistance of her

benefits. In Vitek v. Jones in 1980 the court outlined a host of irreducible minimums of

PDP including adequate notice, an in-person hearing, an opportunity to present and

confront witnesses, and even a legal counselor (who may or may not be a lawyer).

       Not long after, SCOTUS reached the verge the verge of mandating civil counsel in

Lassiter, but refrained, and has since moderated--2011’s Turner v. Rogers was unable to

garner a single vote for civil counsel. They’ve probably come to the conclusion that the
writer has yet to: while lawyers at state expense could very well be necessary (though

probably not sufficient, as the writer claims), it would be shortsighted to mandate that

states incur this expense and the inevitable inefficient slowdown of the legal system that

such a measure would entail without attempting alternate reforms first.

       Justice Breyer outlined some of these reforms in his Turner opinion, noting that

“they lack the drawbacks inherent in recognizing an automatic right to counsel.” These

include enhanced notice, use of simple forms, a simplified hearing process, and making

express findings about D’s ability to pay. These suggestions echo calls for reform from

legal commentators like Bibas and Barton who argue that “the task now...is to make civil

lawsuits simpler and more accessible to nonlawyers.” In other words, pro se reform.

       Organizations like the AJS, the NCCS, and other academics are seeking to take

Breyer’s suggestions even further. While these developments may frustrate advocates of

a right to civil counsel like Pollock and Greco, even Breyer appears to agree with one of

Bibas/Barton’s major conclusions: “It is far more important to fund appointed lawyers in

serious felony cases than it is to provide them in, say, housing court.” Until now, the

Court has focused on adequate PDP for those from whom property or liberty would be

taken by the government. The writer’s proposal optimistically and ambitiously exceeds

these measures, but unfortunately fails to meet the most important standard in a

complicated, ossified, difficult-to-navigate legal system: practicability.
