## Question 2_

       (a) The 2nd Circuit (2COA) should hear Fillius, Inc.’s (FI) FRCP 50 JAMOL
appeal, but should not hear the director and officers’ (D&Os) appeal regarding Judge

Jorkins’ (JJ) granting of a new trial. The 2nd Circuit has appellate jurisdiction over the

JAMOL appeal because SDNY had FQJ (embedded question of federal law re: “mail

delivery”) & DJ (complete diversity, Strawbridge + AIC > 75k) and the JAMOL appeal

is a final order. It will review JJ’s decision de novo. 2COA should not review JJ’s grant

of a FRCP59 motion for new trial, because the grant or refusal of a new trial is a matter

within the discretion of the trial judge and is not reviewable on appeal except in

exceptional circumstances, such as a clear abuse of discretion. (Yeatts). No such abuse of

discretion is present here. While 2COA could not have review the MSJ order regarding

the definition of “mail delivery” at the time of the order, it could now, and D&Os should

have appealed on this basis as well. Now they’re precluded.

       (b) While there is some doubt regarding JJ’s finding on the definition of “mail

delivery,” her post-trial rulings appears to be correct.

       JAMOL: The evidence does appear to suggest that the D&Os knew about the high

collision rate and were therefore reckless in not seeking an FAA license. That said, it’s

not impossible that a rational jury could decide the way they did. Perhaps the emails

appeared forged. Thus, a rational jury could have decided the way they did, and JJ’s

ruling is appropriate.

       New Trial: However, even if a rational jury could have found as this jury did, a

judge may give a new trial on the grounds that the verdict is “against the clear weight of

the evidence.” (Yeatts). The problem here is that JJ appears to suggest that her MSJ re:

“mail delivery” definition will be reviewed in the new trial. It won’t, because she just

granted FI’s motion for a new trial on the issue of D&Os’ knowledge of the high accident
rate, not the MSJ.

-------------------------------------------

-------------------------------------------

## Question 3_

       D&Os can use claim preclusion to defend against SS’s suit. NY state court will
give at least as much preclusive effect, maybe even more, than the subsequent federal

court. (Hart).

       Claim Preclusion:

       Same claim: While SS brings here a tort claim rather than the shareholder’s

derivative claim she brought in the last suit, the claim is based in the same T/O. Same

evidence, same facts, etc.

       Same parties: Gonzales and our in-class “Joey Rich/JR, Inc.” hypothetical suggest

that SS is in privity with FI, and the parties are therefore the same.

       FJOM: The final judgment was on the merits (SS won).

       Claim preclusion is probably dispositive, but if SS can prove somehow that she is

not in privity, SS could issue preclude the D&Os in NY state court on the issue of 1) their

knowledge of the high collision rate; and perhaps on 2) the definition of “mail delivery,”

which is crucial to the determination of negligence or recklessness.

       To get past claim preclusion, SS would have had to prove she was not in privity

with FI. This lack of privity would hurt her in many courts, which require strict mutuality

for issue preclusion/collateral estoppel (CE). NY state courts, however, have no mutuality

requirement for CE.

       Knowledge:

       Same Issue: Yes. The fact of knowledge.

       Same Parties: Not necessary in NY, see above (mutuality).
       Actually litigated: Yes, evidence was raised by FI (emails), denied by D&Os

(testimony). This was a crucial question in the previous case, and both parties were

highly motivated to litigate it.

       Necessary to the decision: Yes. This finding made the difference between

negligence and recklessness, the key issue in the second trial.

       “Mail Delivery” Definition: While JJ believed this to be a matter of fact, the NY

state court may not see it that way, and it may be necessary to SS to argue this “issue” as

a matter of fact.

       Same issue: Yes. The definition of the term, which at least one commentator

believes is a mixed question of law and fact.
       Same parties: As above, not necessary in NY.

       Actually litigated: Yes, the issued was raised (both parties filed cross motions on

the matter) and determined (JJ granted MSJ).

       Necessary to the decision: Yes. It was appealable, and the jury could not have

reached a determination on negligence or recklessness without it.

-------------------------------------------

-------------------------------------------

## Question 4_

       First, HCOL:
       EDVA will probably apply VA procedural law (Klaxon). What substantive law

will EDVA DCt apply? VA is a 2nd restatement state, so EDVA will weigh the relevant

states’ interests and the transaction’s “center of gravity,” or where most of the facts are.

Because the facts regarding the collision with TT’s drone are mostly in VA (some in

WV) and VA has an interest in governing conduct that occurs in its territory, EDVA will

probably apply VA law to the tort claim. It could have applied WV law (and perhaps seen

a significantly different outcome on the tort claim), but the fact that collision occurred

just over the border is insufficient to negate VA’s interests in governing conduct that

occurs in its territory (drone flights by its citizens and companies that do business within

its borders). EDVA will probably apply NY law to the shareholder’s derivative claim

because the company is publicly traded in New York, and NY has a similar interest in
governing the conduct of the companies that trade therein, particularly when that conduct

has a significant effect on their stock price. This is not the ideal outcome for CC, as VA’s

standards for punitive damages are plaintiff-friendly.

       (a) There are several grounds upon which our clients can move to dismiss under

Rule 12(b).

       SMJ isn’t one of them. There appears to be FQL because there in an embedded

question of federal law (definition of “mail delivery”). (Smith-Grable exception). If there

weren’t FQJ, there would still be DJ because complete diversity (VA v. NJ) and AIC >

75k.

       Personal jurisdiction is a grounds for dismissal as per Rule 12(b)(2). EDVA
piggybacks off CA’s long-arm statute via FRCP 4(k)(1)(a). It’s improbable that VA has

personal jurisdiction over the defendants. First, there’s a question as to whether the

concept of privity extends to personal jurisdiction. D&Os are in charge of the company,

but the company is publicly traded. I’ll proceed as though privity has no bearing on IPJ

questions regarding a company’s D&Os. D&Os here have insufficient minimal contacts

with the D, the forum (VA) and the subject matter (Intl. Shoe). The D&Os haven’t

personally purposefully availed themselves of VA law, they didn’t personally direct the

harm into the forum, and they couldn’t have expected to be haled into VA for the actions

of a company of which they are simply D&Os. That said, VA’s interest in providing

effective means of redress for its citizens is strong here, and the ease of getting

information and witnesses may be easier in VA than in NY.

       Venue is another ground for dismissal under §1391(b), as per Rule 12(b)(2),

because (1) defendants don’t reside in EDVA; (2) the events occurred in WDVA and

WV; (3) the action may be brought properly in other districts (WDVA, DNJ).

       Finally, while we could argue that TT has failed to state a claim, it’s likely that this

argument will be unsuccessful. TT must meet the pleading standard, but there’s a conflict

here: SCOVA says pleading standard is notice, SCOTUS says standard is

Twombley/Iqbal. VCOL problem. While it appears that TT has pled sufficiently to meet

both standards (the complaint appears to have successfully crossed the line from possible

to plausible even after crossing out legal conclusions), I’ll perform VCOL analysis here:

       York: Not outcome determinative, so use federal rule: Twiqbal.

       Hanna Majority: The SCOTUS rule is applicable (on point) and appears to be valid.
SCOTUS is interpreting a FRCP 8(a), and in so doing is probably acting appropriately

under REA, though it could be argued that the standard “abridges” a VA citizen’s

substantive right in other cases. Scalia would say it’s an easy call: SCOTUS’

interpretation of FRCP 8(a) is on point, so there’s no need to look at state law. Use

Twiqbal.

       Harlan Concurrence: No problems here. While CC is a big company, it appears

unlikely to modify its primary conduct to take advantage of the state rule. May use

Twiqbal.

       Ginsburg (Shady Grove/Walker): VA’s state law here appears “powerful” in that

it’s a marked departure from FRCP with serious consequences for litigants, and Ginsburg

would try hard to construe the federal rule narrowly. She would probably struggle to do
so however, as the rules are in direct conflict. Perhaps she would construe the federal rule

narrowly in just this case, and in so doing revive the post-Twombley perception that

plausibility pleading only applies to certain types of cases.

       (b) This claim will be much tougher to dismiss.

       As above, FQJ is present under Smith-Grable because embedded federal question

of “mail delivery.” If no FQJ, TT cannot bring the claim against CC because it doesn’t

satisfy AIC requirement for DJ.

       General IPJ. CC is “essentially at home” in VA because its VA operations are

sufficiently continuous and systematic (like Wal-Mart).

       Venue, proper under §1391(b)(1).

       It’s unlikely that the claim will be dismissed for failure to state a claim (FRCP

12(b)(6)). Because TT has pled adequately under both standards, the VCOL analysis is

the same as above.

       (d) Because the tort claim against the D&Os will probably be dismissed, this won’t

be necessary. If, however, that claim is not dismissed, we’ll argue that the parties were

joined improperly under FRCP 20(a)(2). While there is a common issue of fact (drone

flights conducted negligently), we have a strong argument that the claims are based on

different T/Os, and should be tried separately.

       (addtl.) Issue preclusion (on the same issues as in SS’s preclusion argument) may

play a role here. Though the parties are different and VA requires full mutuality,

interstate preclusion rules require that a subsequent state court give as much preclusive

effect to a rendering federal court’s judgment as a state court in the state in which the

rendering federal court sat would. The rendering court is in NY, and NY has no mutuality

requirement. EDVA DCt should apply NY state preclusion law and require no mutuality.

feedback.headline: Three heavily weighted questions stop at the conclusion where the course teaches a checklist
feedback.overview: Question 1 and the vertical choice-of-law run in Question 4 are your best work. The essay argues from named authority — Sniadach, Goldberg, Vitek's minimum list, Lassiter, Turner's substitute safeguards — and takes a position on both halves of the prompt. The Erie run works York, the Hanna majority track, Harlan's primary-conduct test, and Ginsburg/Walker, and concedes honestly that the conflict cannot be construed away. But the primary allocations elsewhere are conclusions. Question 2 asserts finality in one clause and never canvasses the routes off the final order rule. Question 3 never asks which body of preclusion law a New York court applies to a federal judgment, so the no-mutuality conclusion is unsupported. Question 4 inverts the amount in controversy on both counts, which erases supplemental jurisdiction, and the $2 million punitive damages demand is answered by cross-reference.

strengths.label: Position taken and defended with course authority
strengths.detail: You argue the conflict is real but not a reversal, and you use Turner's substitute safeguards to show what the Court preferred over counsel. Reading Turner as offering a choice rather than a refusal is what lets you answer the second half of the prompt.
strengths.answerExcerpt: they lack the drawbacks inherent in recognizing an automatic right to counsel

strengths.label: Two post-trial standards kept apart
strengths.detail: You explain why the same judge on the same record can deny judgment as a matter of law and still grant a new trial, and attach a review standard to each ruling. Catching that the judge appears to expect her summary judgment ruling to be revisited at the retrial is a sharp read of her order.
strengths.answerExcerpt: even if a rational jury could have found as this jury did, a judge may give a new trial on the grounds that the verdict is "against the clear weight of the evidence."

strengths.label: Issue preclusion elements tied to record facts
strengths.detail: You run the elements twice, on knowledge and on the "mail delivery" definition, and each element rests on something that happened — the emails against the testimony, the cross-motions, the two trials. That is application, not recitation, and you correctly identify mutuality as the live obstacle.
strengths.answerExcerpt: Actually litigated: Yes, evidence was raised by FI (emails), denied by D&Os (testimony).

strengths.label: Personal jurisdiction over the individual defendants
strengths.detail: You test each contact against these three people rather than the company: no purposeful availment of their own, no harm they personally directed, no expectation of suit in Virginia for corporate acts. Arguing Virginia's interest and witness convenience the other way is the both-sides treatment a close issue merits.
strengths.answerExcerpt: they couldn't have expected to be haled into VA for the actions of a company of which they are simply D&Os

strengths.label: Erie argued in multiple voices
strengths.detail: You apply York to this conflict, take the Hanna majority track through Rule 8(a) and the Rules Enabling Act, ask whether this defendant would change its primary conduct, and then admit Ginsburg would struggle to construe the conflict away. Conceding the weak point of your own path is worth more than a clean assertion.
strengths.answerExcerpt: She would probably struggle to do so however, as the rules are in direct conflict.

improvements.label: Question 1 — the complication mechanism is asserted, never worked
improvements.whatHappened: You recast the conflict as fairness against efficiency. That captures cost. It misses the other half of what the quotation claims: the protections are themselves complicated, so an unrepresented litigant cannot use them. You write that the Court's solutions "have indeed complicated legal processes" and then move on.
improvements.whyItMatters: The essay's central claim is that added process can defeat itself even when the state pays for nothing extra. Without that step, the answer reads as a budget argument, and the practicability conclusion at the end rests on cost alone.
improvements.howToImprove: Take two or three protections and say what a person without a lawyer must do to use them. Presenting evidence at a Goldberg-style hearing requires knowing the rules of proof. A written statement of findings under the Vitek list may require proposed findings and is hard to read unaided. The Doehr bond requires understanding and reaching a bond market. Pay for this by cutting the preclusion and Erie illustrations in your opening paragraph; both sit outside the procedural due process line. Mathews v. Eldridge is the course's balancing test and belongs in an essay about how much process is due.

improvements.label: Question 1 — "pro se reform" is a label, not a proposal
improvements.whatHappened: Your alternatives to counsel stop at Breyer's list and the phrase "pro se reform." The organizations are named but nothing they do is described.
improvements.whyItMatters: The prompt asks what should be done short of state-paid counsel. A concrete recommendation earns credit here; a category name does not.
improvements.howToImprove: Name two measures and say what each fixes: standardized forms that elicit the financial information the court needs, and non-lawyer assistance of the kind Justice Powell contemplated in Vitek and the Court gestured at in Turner. Add the institutional obstacle — courts that do not treat access to justice as their job, and a bar that treats non-lawyer help as competition. Pay for it by trimming the narration of Sniadach and Goldberg to a clause each; you have already established the line.

improvements.label: Question 2 — the appealability checklist is not here
improvements.whatHappened: Appellate jurisdiction is the primary allocation of this question, and you dispose of it in one clause: the appeal "is a final order." None of the routes off the final order rule appears — no 1292(a)(1), no 1292(b), no Rule 54(b), no Cohen, no mandamus.
improvements.whyItMatters: This is a checklist the course teaches you to walk in order, and the facts were built to be run against it. The judge's own written order is where the 1292(b) work happens: she called the issue important, which touches the controlling-question element, but she also said she cannot imagine being wrong, which defeats substantial ground for difference of opinion.
improvements.howToImprove:
Brain off here and walk the taught steps.
1. 1291 finality — say which posture you have, and say what the grant of a new trial does to the finality of the case as a whole.
2. 1292(a)(1) — no injunction.
3. 1292(b) — controlling question of law, substantial ground for difference of opinion, material advancement, plus double discretion and the ten-day window.
4. Rule 54(b) — express determination and no just reason for delay, and say how many claims there are.
5. Cohen — final as to the issue, collateral to the merits, effectively unreviewable later.
6. Mandamus — clear and indisputable right, exigency, sound judicial administration.
Cut the sentence grounding appellate jurisdiction in the district court's jurisdiction, and the closing "now they're precluded" sentence; those words pay for steps 2 through 6.

improvements.label: Question 2 — two conclusions that do not follow
improvements.whatHappened: You ground the Second Circuit's appellate jurisdiction in the fact that SDNY had subject matter jurisdiction. Those are different questions. You then say the defendants "should have appealed" the summary judgment ruling and are "now precluded."
improvements.whyItMatters: The second point inverts the rule. An interlocutory ruling generally cannot be appealed when made and is reviewed after final judgment, so not appealing it earlier forfeits nothing. Preclusion is a different doctrine and does not operate within a single case.
improvements.howToImprove: Delete the subject matter jurisdiction sentence. Replace the forfeiture claim with the accurate point: the summary judgment ruling merges into the eventual final judgment and can be challenged on appeal from it.

improvements.label: Question 3 — which body of preclusion law governs is never asked
improvements.whatHappened: You move from a federal SDNY judgment straight to New York's no-mutuality rule. The step licensing that move is missing. Your opening sentence gestures at it but is garbled, and Semtek is never named.
improvements.whyItMatters: This is intersystem preclusion, and it is the pivot the question turns on. Without it the no-mutuality conclusion is an assertion, and the reader cannot tell whether you knew federal law might supply a different answer.
improvements.howToImprove:
Walk it in order.
1. Name the rendering court and the jurisdiction it exercised.
2. If it sat in diversity, Semtek directs the later court to New York preclusion law, which has no mutuality requirement under Hart.
3. You asserted in Question 2 that SDNY also had arising-under jurisdiction over the embedded Mail-Only Act issue. Say what that does — which law governs when the rendering court had both is unsettled, so state the options and argue rather than pick silently.
Pay for this by cutting the two repeated "not necessary in NY" lines under your issue-preclusion headings to one. Also fix the slip that Slughorn won the prior suit; the corporation did.

improvements.label: Question 3 — the could-have-joined inquiry is missing
improvements.whatHappened: You reach nonmutual offensive issue preclusion without asking whether Slughorn could easily have joined the SDNY action, which is the Parklane factor weighed before allowing it.
improvements.whyItMatters: The facts answer the question in her favor and you leave the point on the table. She and the SDNY defendants are all New Jersey domiciliaries, so joining would have destroyed complete diversity. She could not have joined, which removes the main objection to offensive use.
improvements.howToImprove: After you establish no mutuality, state the could-have-joined factor and apply the domicile fact to show joinder was jurisdictionally impossible. Take the words from the claim-preclusion section, where "Same evidence, same facts, etc." and the second privity paragraph repeat what you have already established.

improvements.label: Question 4 — the amount in controversy is inverted on both counts, and supplemental jurisdiction disappears
improvements.whatHappened: You find diversity on the derivative count against the individual defendants, where the amounts are $900 and $9,000, and deny it on the Chudley count, where they are $200,000 and $2,000,000. Both are backwards. Because of that inversion the derivative count never looks jurisdictionally deficient, so supplemental jurisdiction is never analyzed and 1367 is never named.
improvements.whyItMatters: The exam built the two counts with those numbers to force the supplemental jurisdiction chain. Missing it costs the whole subject matter jurisdiction analysis, not one sentence.
improvements.howToImprove:
Run it as steps.
1. Identify the anchoring claim — the Chudley negligence count, diversity, amount plainly satisfied.
2. Note the derivative count fails the amount in controversy, then consider arising-under jurisdiction over it through the embedded federal issue.
3. 1367(a): is there a common nucleus of operative facts? Be honest that it is doubtful — different defendants, little shared evidence, only a loose drone connection.
4. 1367(b): the individual defendants were joined under Rule 20, so supplemental jurisdiction over the plaintiff's claim against them is carved out. Exxon offers no reading that saves a single plaintiff aggregating against multiple defendants outside the class-action-fairness setting.
Cut the digression about whether privity extends to personal jurisdiction, which you raise and then set aside; those words pay for this. The course says arising under jurisdiction, not federal question.

improvements.label: Question 4 — general jurisdiction over Chudley on the wrong standard, and no specific jurisdiction at all
improvements.whatHappened: You find Chudley "essentially at home" in Virginia because its Virginia operations are continuous and systematic. Those are two different standards. On a $280 billion business, Virginia is a fraction of a percent. You then never analyze specific jurisdiction over Chudley.
improvements.whyItMatters: Under Daimler's at-home standard Chudley is at home in Delaware and New York, so the general jurisdiction conclusion fails. Specific jurisdiction is the only route left, and it is the closer question.
improvements.howToImprove: Test the suit-related contacts one at a time — the plaintiff's Virginia domicile, a drone bound for a Virginia store that never arrived, and the plaintiff operating the controller from Virginia. That last one is contact the plaintiff created, which World-Wide Volkswagen says does not count against the defendant. Then run the fairness factors, which point toward West Virginia where the collision and the evidence are. Pay for this by cutting your general jurisdiction paragraph to a single sentence stating the at-home conclusion.

improvements.label: Question 4 — the punitive damages demand is answered by cross-reference
improvements.whatHappened: The partner asked about the $2 million punitive damages demand directly. Your whole treatment is that the pleading analysis "is the same as above." You also never name a paragraph of the complaint as conclusory, though the complaint was reproduced in full.
improvements.whyItMatters: A complaint can plead the claim adequately and the demand inadequately, and this one does. The demand needs recklessness, and West Virginia law says failure to investigate does not ordinarily show it.
improvements.howToImprove:
Work the sequence against the text.
1. Name the conclusory paragraphs and set them aside — paragraph 8's assertion that the joint decision caused the drop states an element without facts.
2. Take the negligence elements in turn — duty, breach, causation, damage — and name which paragraphs plead facts going to each.
3. Say whether what survives makes each element plausible rather than merely possible.
4. Run the cut again, separately, for the punitive damages demand: the pleaded facts support negligence but do not push recklessness across the line.
Pay for this with the words spent in part (b) restating that the pleading and vertical choice-of-law analysis is the same as in part (a).

improvements.label: Question 4 — horizontal choice of law rests on an inverted fact and misuses Klaxon
improvements.whatHappened: You write that the facts about the collision are "mostly in VA (some in WV)." The crash was ten miles inside West Virginia. You also say the federal court will apply Virginia procedural law under Klaxon, and you run choice of law on the claims generally rather than on punitive damages.
improvements.whyItMatters: Punitive damages are the only issue on which the two states differ, so that is the only issue choice of law needs to resolve, and the last event was the West Virginia collision. Klaxon sends a diversity court to the forum state's choice-of-law rules; it does not import state procedural law, and in the horizontal analysis procedural questions take forum law anyway.
improvements.howToImprove: Say the sequence out loud: the demand falls only if plausibility pleading applies and West Virginia substantive law applies, so resolve Erie first and choice of law second. Then run the Second Restatement on punitive damages specifically, noting that punishment and deterrence are interests West Virginia has in conduct over its own land, and that this is not a case with a preexisting relationship between the parties. Do not take the shortcut of calling punitive damages procedural. In the Erie run, add Sibbach and ask whether Rule 8(a)(2) and Rule 12(b)(6) really regulate procedure. Pay for this with the generic center-of-gravity recitation opening Question 4. The course's term is plausibility pleading.

revisionPlan: Question 1: add the usability mechanism and two concrete alternatives, paid for by cutting the preclusion and Erie illustrations.
Question 2: replace the finality clause with the six-step appealability checklist, using the judge's own order to work the 1292(b) elements.
Question 3: insert the intersystem preclusion step before you reach mutuality, and say what the possible arising-under basis does to it.
Question 4: recheck the dollar figures against each count, then run supplemental jurisdiction as anchor claim, 1367(a), 1367(b).
Question 4: analyze specific jurisdiction over Chudley contact by contact, and state general jurisdiction with the at-home standard.
Question 4: run the plausibility cut against numbered paragraphs and named elements, then run it again separately for the punitive damages demand.
feedback.exampleRevision: Appellate jurisdiction first. Under 1291 the circuit hears final decisions. JJ granted a new trial on the knowledge issue, so merits litigation in SDNY continues and no judgment has been entered; the denial of the renewed Rule 50 motion in this posture does not end the case. No injunction, so no 1292(a)(1). 1292(b) is the closest route: JJ's order calls the "mail delivery" question important, which supports a controlling question of law, but she also writes that she cannot imagine being wrong, which is the substantial-ground element failing on her own words; and 1292(b) is double discretion in any event. Rule 54(b) needs multiple claims and an express finding of no just reason for delay; there is one claim and no such finding. Under Cohen the ruling is not collateral — the meaning of "mail delivery" is the merits. Nothing extraordinary supports mandamus. 2COA should dismiss both appeals.
feedback.closing: The habit to break is stopping at the conclusion where the course has given you a checklist. When you write "there is appellate jurisdiction" or "New York has no mutuality requirement," treat that sentence as the last line of an analysis you still owe.

fixtures.bandRationale: Equal-scrutiny defect lists for the same-exam references. DS reference: reaches a defensible-but-contrary bottom line on the Rule 50 denial, treats 1292(b) as possibly satisfied on a strained reading of the judge's order, asserts general jurisdiction analysis compactly, and mislabels Rule 4(k)(1)(A) as '42(k)(1)(A)' throughout — yet it canvasses every escape hatch, separates the two counts on SMJ with the amount in controversy correctly identified, runs supplemental jurisdiction, does plausibility at the paragraph level (¶8), runs five Erie voices, and resolves the punitive damages demand through both the choice-of-law and pleading steps. H reference: says Virginia notice pleading is 'purely procedural, so there's no HCOL analysis' and skips the Erie chain almost entirely, garbles who the plaintiff is in the derivative posture, uses JNOV, and misstates Rule 50 preservation — but canvasses all appellate-jurisdiction routes and runs Semtek plus the arising-under branch on preclusion law. P reference: opens with 'The trial court had SMJ (diversity, non-AIC deficient)' as a bare conclusion, finds general jurisdiction over Chudley on a continuous-and-systematic rationale, relies on authority no longer part of this course for the Rule 50 record limit, and reduces the whole vertical choice-of-law question to one sentence — but it canvasses 1291, Rule 54(b), Cohen, mandamus, and 1292(b) including the ten-day point; names intersystem preclusion authority; identifies the derivative count as amount-in-controversy deficient and discusses 1367; and reaches West Virginia law and the failure of punitives. Pairwise verdicts. Versus DS: clearly weaker — the student skips the appealability canvass, the preclusion-law pivot, supplemental jurisdiction, and the punitive damages demand, all of which the DS reference works. Versus H: weaker overall. The student's Erie run is better than the H reference's, but the H reference does the two things the student does not do at all — the full appellate-jurisdiction canvass (10 pts) and Semtek plus the mixed-jurisdiction preclusion-law branch (12 pts). Versus P: comparable overall. The student is stronger on Question 1 (more case-specific, quotes Turner's safeguards, engages both readings) and clearly stronger on the Erie voices; the student is weaker on Question 2 (no escape-hatch canvass at all where P runs them), weaker on Question 3 (no preclusion-law authority where P names intersystem authority), and weaker on Question 4's core chain (inverted amount in controversy both ways, no supplemental jurisdiction, punitive damages demand skipped, choice of law resting on an inverted fact, where P gets to West Virginia law and dismissal of punitives). Versus LP reference: clearly stronger — the student's essay is a real argument on the assigned question with course authority rather than an off-topic excursion, and its element-by-element preclusion work and personal jurisdiction analysis are genuinely applied rather than conclusory. That places the answer at P: issue recognition is broad and some analysis is rich, but several heavily weighted cores are underdeveloped, inverted, or unresolved.
fixtures.whyNotHigher: Not H because the two questions whose primary allocations turn on a single canvass — appellate jurisdiction in Question 2 and the choice of preclusion law in Question 3 — are asserted rather than analyzed, and both same-exam references at H and above run them. Question 4 compounds this with two inverted amount-in-controversy conclusions, no supplemental jurisdiction or 1367(b) analysis, a general-jurisdiction rule error on Chudley with no specific-jurisdiction alternative, and the $2 million punitive damages demand disposed of by cross-reference. The strong Erie run and the essay are not enough to offset core analysis that is missing rather than merely wrong.

Question 1 is a genuine argument on the assigned prompt built from named cases and readings with a stated position on both halves; Question 3 applies the preclusion elements to specific record facts on two separate issues; and Question 4 contains real fact-attached analysis on personal jurisdiction over the individual defendants, venue, joinder, and a four-voice Erie chain. The LP reference, by contrast, is fragmentary and conclusory on its weighted cores and takes its policy essay outside the course frame.

fixtures.label: 2015 answer — P
fixtures.answer:
There is no inherent conflict with PDP’s focus on protecting the defendant and the idea that at some point proceedings get so complex or important that a lawyer is needed to achieve this. They are both factors to the same balancing test: how can the courts make sure to obtain the correct outcome with minimal harm to all parties involved. The introduction of appointed council is expensive –harm to the government – and complicates matters, thus decreasing the efficiency of the court system. However the introduction of a lawyer into proceedings is one, but not the only way, to balance the need for finding the correct outcome with the expense in doing so.

Having full jury trials could obtain the correct outcome for every matter in dispute. This is expensive so courts cut down on the PDP afforded in the name of efficiency.  Having a judge, not a clerk, make decisions (Sniadach) is more expensive but a judge will take more care in issuing decisions so have a lower error rate, justifying the cost. If the base error rate is thought to be very low, there is less PDP required. This also occurs when the pleading standards are high for the plaintiff and the proof needed can be evaluated objectively – medical testimony or documents instead of the credibility of live testimony.

When harm is minimal, such as with disability benefits (Eldrige), PDP requirements are relaxed but when irreparable harm will occur such as with need-based disability benefits (Goldberg) PDP must provide more protections because of the harm that would result in an incorrect decision. This is tempered against the harm to the plaintiff. In the interests of finding the correct outcome the defendant must have some sort of opportunity to rebut the accusations when there would be no harm to the plaintiff by slight delay (Fuentes). In contrast, when there would be harm by delay the plaintiff can proceed ex parte if a hearing is available soon afterward (Mitchell). The goal is to find a middle ground where the harm to the plaintiff is balanced against the harm that seizure would cause the defendant. If there is some way to mitigate the harm to one of the parties, such as posting a bond or posting a counter-bond, then the PDP will be adjusted to minimize the amount of work that party must do.

With all risks balanced how do you achieve the best outcome with the required level of PDP? Gideon remedy was providing council for criminal defendants, but overworked public defenders don’t substantially decrease risk of error; they simply triage and plea. Civil cases, which can be just as damaging as incarceration, should not follow Gideon in finding a feel-good but do-little solution of lawyers for all. They should give the litigant the chance to proceed with their case.

There are other ways to have mostly correct outcomes without expending resources on state-appointed council for all litigants, fitting into the balancing approach as a modified Eldrige test. Eldrige said the PDP, and thus the right to appointed council depends on the private interest, the risk of erroneous judgment, and the governments interest in preserving scarce legal resources. Courts usually find that the government interest outweighs the other factors when deciding categorically to not provide council in civil cases.

I argue that in addition to toning back the devotion to the government interest prong – litigants should have the genuine opportunity to petition the court or a civil legal aid bureau for appointed council for high impact but low monetary civil cases related to basic needs (Pollock) – a fourth branch of Eldrige is needed: the availability and satisfactory nature of waiving PDP to proceed with the case. If the litigant can waive some PDP to provide for a simplified procedure in exchange for a heightened risk of erroneous decisions the litigant should be allowed that choice. This would allow, for example, a pro se litigant to forgo motions for SJ in exchange for there being a speedy hearing on the merits of the case by a judge or administrator. There would be a higher risk of erroneous judgment, but this would be offset by ease of access.

This process must incentivize the government as a cost saving measure to set up a court system with PDP tradeoffs that is navigable by pro se litigants. The more pro se litigants view the process as fair, the more they would utilize it. The more the judiciary views the tradeoffs as unfair, the more they should appoint council for pro se litigants when they assert their rights to full PDP to increase incentives on the government for reform.

There will always be a bias towards litigants with lawyers. The goal of reform should not be fewer cases; the goal should be giving aggrieved parties the access the court system no matter their resources. Access to justice for all is key in providing trust in the judiciary: if a litigant thinks the deck is too stacked against them they will seek alternative redress.

The trial court had SMJ (diversity, non-AIC deficient). Under 28USC1291 the appeal must be after a final order. The R59 motion finished the trial so appellate jurisdiction is valid. There were two claims under R54(b) (Liberty Mutual), the negligence claim and the recklessness claim. There was no express determination that the negligence claim was appealable, even though it was separable from the recklessness claim. There is no Cohen exception under 28USC1291 on the issue of “mail delivery” because the issue was not collateral to the merits and it was reviewable later. Mandamus is not appropriate here because there is no flagrant abuse of discretion.

The directors should’ve appealed the “mail delivery” determination under 28USC1292(b) because Judge Jorkin’s writing stated that the controlling question of law of if Chudley had to have a permit was special, it is likely to reoccur with other drone operators, and the proceedings are very high-cost. There are substantial grounds for difference of opinion, and Judge Jorkin indicated this in the writing. Finding on the issue would materially advance resolution. However, the defendants didn’t file a motion within ten days so this approach is waived.

The appeals court shouldn’t allow appeal on the R59 motion for a new trial. The decision to grant a new trial is not reviewable except for the most exceptional circumstances, and the standard of review is a clear abuse of discretion (Yeatts). Judge Jorkin does not meet this high bar. The judge can make credibility determinations, unlike R50 motions, and this serves as a judicial brake to runaway juries. Judge Jorkin may have felt that like in Yeatts the clear weight of the evidence favored Fillius but not enough to succeed in JNOV, therefore R59 was the only way to proceed.

The JAMOL was properly renewed as a JNOV under R50 (Unitherm), but Judge Jorkin improperly rejected it. Under a R50 motion like a R56 motion all inferences are made in favor of the non-movant (Reeves). Unlike a R56 where the record is the evidence produced in discovery, R50 only looks at the evidence presented at trial. The appeals court would review this de novo. Doing so, all reasonable inferences are made in favor of the defendants. Thus, the emails directly contradicting the defendants are controlling. Therefore there is no rational way a jury could find that the defendants didn’t know about the accident rate of the drones prior to the FAA announcement and thus the R50 should’ve been granted.

The defendants could use claim preclusion against Slughorn’s offensive posture. She asserts exactly the same claims. This does not fall under the bond exception because there is no liquid market in judgment recovery. Slughorn is in privity with Filius; she substantially controlled Filius’s activities as the executive officer and sole shareholder (Gonzalez). The second trial produced a final judgment on the merits – Filius won and collected judgment. The state court must give as much preclusive effect as the federal court would have (Migra); the federal court had SMJ over the claims so there’s no Marrese problem. The policy behind claim preclusion is that judicial efficiency favors not letting parties have multiple tries at the same judgment; Slughorn can’t just keep filing suits until she gets all that she thinks she’s owed, spending judicial resources and the defendants’ time in the process. The interest in finality precludes this. Yes, the initial court may have been wrong, but it could also have also been wrong in Slughorn’s favor, but would she want to re-litigate then?

The defendant’s cannot use issue preclusion against Slughorn because she won, but if she is not barred by claim preclusion she can use it against them. The issue of timing of knowledge of Chudley’s accident rate was actually litigated and determined in the suit by Filius. It was necessary to the decision (Rios); it was the linchpin required to find recklessness and there were no rulings in the alternative (Russell). The issue was even between the same parties, see above, but mutuality is not required in NY.

Both claims are sufficient to put their respective defendants on notice (Dioguardi), but unlike the complaint against the directors the complaint against Chudley fails the plausibility pleading standard (Twombly, Iqbal). Absent the conclusion that Chudley was negligent in flying its drone through the forest all that is left is the allegation that there was a crash, Chudley was responsible. This is not enough to say that Tonks plausibly wins in court.

The court has SMJ over count I. The count is AIC deficient but there is a Smith-Grable exception. The question of whether Chudley needed an FAA permit is a contested federal issue embedded in the state cause of action that won’t open the floodgates into federal court. The answer to this question is a substantial federal interest due to the abundance of drone users and it is a clear issue of law, not fact. If this is held to be insufficient, claim I may be joined under R20(a)(1) because it’s the same T/O, even though it’s AIC deficient. Exxon green-lit this for two plaintiffs, one defendant, but not one plaintiff, two defendants. The policy for it would be that since it is the same T/O and one part meets AIC the case is obviously substantial enough to warrant a federal forum. The policy against it would be that it allows pulling minor matters into one omnibus case where different defendant’s interests could conflict to the advantage of the plaintiff who forced them all into one case together.

The court has SMJ over count II independent of count I. The parties are diverse – Tonks is a domiciliary of VA, Chudley is of DE (incorporation) and NY (nerve center). Both the compensatory and punitive damages put it over the AIC requirement. Adding the directors, NJ domiciliaries does not destroy this.

There is no problem with abstention because there are no concurrent state proceedings (Colorado River) or other issues (Pullman/Burford/Younger).

VA does not have IPJ over the directors. They are not domiciliaries of VA, so specific IPJ is needed. They didn’t purposefully avail themselves of the protections of VA law even though their company did. There were no minimum contacts with VA (International Shoe). This may not save them though since being hauled into court for your actions in a state where your business is ubiquitous may not offend the traditional notions of fair play and substantial justice (Volkswagen); their actions hurt all stockholders. VA though is not the best forum for litigating count I because all of the documents and witnesses are in NY (McGee), so count I will likely be dismissed unless the directors consent.

Count I also lacks venue: the directors don’t reside in VA (28USC1391(b)(1)), the substantial parts of the events didn’t occur in VA (28USC1391(b)(2)), and there is another district where action may be brought: NY (28USC1391(b)(3)).

VA has general IPJ over Chudley. Chudley’s presence in the state is so continuous and systematic that it is essentially at home in VA (Perkins).

Count II has venue under 28USC1391(b)(2) because a substantial part of the events occurred in VA.

Since the suit is filed in VA, HCOL uses the second restatement. Thus all procedural rules will be VA law but all substantive laws will be where the center of gravity of each issue is. The center of gravity of this case could be in VA (Babcock) since Tonks was flying the drone from VA. There is likely a better argument though that WV law should apply because the drone was part of the WV fleet, Tonks’s drone was flying in WV, and the crash and all evidence is in WV. Unlike Neumeyer, VA law doesn’t give Tonks more protections than WV law, but the idea that lex loci delictus should apply absent a good reason is compelling to prevent forum shopping. Therefore, the court will use WV substantive law.

Pleading and mutuality are likely procedural since they would not influence pre-litigation behavior. Pleading though may be ruled substantive; it is an important consideration as to how much knowledge you need when deciding to file a lawsuit. If it is, count II will also be dismissed for failing to meet WV code-pleading standards using R12(b).

The punitive damages will not be awarded under WV substantive law. Per Longbottom, there was no knowledge of the risk, and so no conscious decision to disregard it as required to award punitive damages. Chudley could thus file a R56 motion for summary judgment on that claim.

Count I will be dismissed for IPJ and venue, and also may be severable from count II. Count II, using WV substantive law, may be dismissed for failure to plead. If it is not, the punitive damages will be thrown out under WV recklessness law.

feedback.headline: Real strengths in jurisdiction and post-trial analysis; the two heaviest questions each lose a required structure
feedback.overview: Your best work is specific and fact-applied. On Question 2 you keep the Rule 59 and Rule 50 standards apart and reach the JAMOL result by weighing the three contemporaneous emails against the defendants' testimony. On Question 4 you run Count II's diversity fully, catch the amount-in-controversy problem on Count I, and land on the controlling reading that Exxon does not license one plaintiff suing two defendants. But the two most heavily weighted questions each lose a required structure. Question 4 (23 pts) never runs Erie on the notice-pleading-versus-plausibility conflict, decides general jurisdiction over Chudley in two sentences and gets it wrong, and answers the separation question in three words. Question 1 (25 pts) never names Turner, the case the prompt is built on.

strengths.label: Cases used against their facts
strengths.detail: Sniadach's judge-versus-clerk decisionmaker, Goldberg's means-based benefits against Mathews' documentable disability determination, Fuentes against Mitchell on pre- versus post-seizure hearings. That comparative work is what makes the balancing claim persuasive rather than asserted.
strengths.answerExcerpt: when irreparable harm will occur such as with need-based disability benefits (Goldberg) PDP must provide more protections

strengths.label: A concrete reform proposal, not a funding wish
strengths.detail: A fourth Mathews factor for waiving process in exchange for a simplified route, with a worked pro se example, answers the prompt's second bullet with something a court could actually adopt.
strengths.answerExcerpt: a fourth branch of Eldrige is needed: the availability and satisfactory nature of waiving PDP

strengths.label: Two post-trial standards kept distinct and applied to the record
strengths.detail: Abuse-of-discretion review and the judge's credibility power uphold the new trial; the different Rule 50 standard then yields error on the denial. Reaching that through the specific emails rather than a general sufficiency statement is what earns the points.
strengths.answerExcerpt: the emails directly contradicting the defendants are controlling

strengths.label: Privity established on facts
strengths.detail: Naming Slughorn's control of the corporation's litigation as sole shareholder and officer is what makes the claim preclusion bar work, and you checked that the rendering court had jurisdiction before relying on the judgment.
strengths.answerExcerpt: she substantially controlled Filius's activities as the executive officer and sole shareholder (Gonzalez)

strengths.label: Subject matter jurisdiction run completely
strengths.detail: Citizenship, nerve center, amount in controversy, and the point that adding the New Jersey directors does not destroy diversity. You then saw Count I as deficient on amount in controversy and moved to Smith-Grable with the floodgates factor applied to drone operators rather than recited.
strengths.answerExcerpt: The count is AIC deficient but there is a Smith-Grable exception.

strengths.label: Horizontal choice of law argued both ways to a conclusion
strengths.detail: You identify the Second Restatement, argue Virginia's center of gravity against West Virginia's on named facts, and then choose. Carrying West Virginia law through to the recklessness standard and the punitive damages result is the payoff.
strengths.answerExcerpt: the drone was part of the WV fleet, Tonks's drone was flying in WV, and the crash and all evidence is in WV

improvements.label: Turner is missing from the question built on it
improvements.whatHappened: The prompt quotes and turns on Turner, and the essay never names it. The holding that matters therefore never appears: when very serious interests are at stake, the state must either provide counsel or simplify and rationalize its procedures.
improvements.whyItMatters: Your own recommendation — simplified procedures a pro se litigant can navigate — is Turner's second branch. Without the case you present as your invention a route the Court already opened.
improvements.howToImprove: Name Turner and use its substitute safeguards as your model: notice that ability to pay is the critical issue, a form to elicit financial information, an opportunity to respond about financial status, and an express finding on ability to pay. Add Lassiter for the presumption against state-paid counsel in civil cases, and Vitek's minimum-factors list when you say what a simplified scheme must still contain. Pay for this by cutting the second paragraph on jury trials and error rates, which repeats a balancing point you have already made.

improvements.label: The conflict is framed as cost, not as complexity
improvements.whatHappened: The essay treats added process as expensive and inefficient. The course's point is different: each added protection is itself a barrier, because an unrepresented litigant must handle evidentiary rules, bonds, and written decisions.
improvements.whyItMatters: That barrier exists even with unlimited money, so a cost-only frame cannot explain why more process can make outcomes worse for the people it protects. Your pro se navigability paragraph is one sentence away from this and never develops it.
improvements.howToImprove: State the mechanism early: the Sniadach line and Goldberg produced real protections and simultaneously made proceedings harder to use without a lawyer. Then let the fourth-factor proposal answer that specific problem. The words come from the Gideon paragraph, which can lose two sentences without losing its point.

improvements.label: The finality rule is stated backwards
improvements.whatHappened: You write that the Rule 59 motion "finished the trial so appellate jurisdiction is valid." A grant of a new trial is not a final decision under 1291, precisely because merits litigation continues.
improvements.whyItMatters: Two different rulings are before the court. Grounding both on one inverted proposition means your bottom lines, even where tolerable, rest on nothing a court could use.
improvements.howToImprove:
In place of that sentence, say what each order does to the case.
1. The new-trial grant sends the case back for a second trial, so nothing is final.
2. Because that second trial is still to come, the denial of the post-verdict Rule 50 motion does not end the litigation either.
Your existing treatment of Rule 54(b), the collateral order doctrine, and mandamus is sound and can stand as written. The course uses JAMOL rather than JNOV.

improvements.label: 1292(b) read against the judge's own words
improvements.whatHappened: You treat the order as indicating substantial ground for difference of opinion. Her statement that the issue seems really straightforward is what defeats that element. You also treat a ten-day filing point as the obstacle rather than the certification requirement.
improvements.whyItMatters: 1292(b) requires both the district court's certification and the court of appeals' acceptance. Neither happened, and no amount of party diligence supplies them.
improvements.howToImprove: Walk the three elements in order: a controlling question of law, substantial ground for difference of opinion, and materially advancing the ultimate termination of the litigation. Say that her characterization of the issue as straightforward kills the second. Add the certification-and-acceptance point in a clause. The words come from the mandamus sentence, which can be one clause.

improvements.label: The branch where federal preclusion law might govern is never opened
improvements.whatHappened: You assume throughout that New York preclusion law supplies the answer, and never ask whether the SDNY was also exercising arising-under jurisdiction on the embedded mail-delivery question.
improvements.whyItMatters: That branch is the harder half of the memo. If federal law governs, New York's abandonment of mutuality does not settle things, and the offensive nonmutual analysis under Parklane becomes necessary — including whether Slughorn could easily have joined the SDNY action. She could not: she and all three defendants are New Jersey domiciliaries, so her joinder would have destroyed diversity. You ran Smith-Grable a page later, so you had the tools.
improvements.howToImprove: Flag the jurisdictional basis of the SDNY judgment as unsettled, say which way you would guess, and run Parklane's could-have-joined inquiry on the New Jersey domicile facts. Pay for it by deleting the bond-exception aside about a liquid market in judgment recovery.

improvements.label: No vertical choice-of-law run on the pleading conflict
improvements.whatHappened: The Virginia notice-pleading versus federal plausibility-pleading clash is handled as a substantive-versus-procedural characterization inside the horizontal analysis. A federal court choosing between a state and a federal pleading standard is a vertical question.
improvements.whyItMatters: This is the structure the course tests most often, and on your own reasoning it decides the fate of Count II. Omitting it costs more than any other single gap in the paper.
improvements.howToImprove:
Run the sequence separately and before the horizontal analysis.
1. Identify the conflict and ask whether a Federal Rule is directly on point — Rules 8(a)(2) and 12(b)(6) are.
2. Try the narrow construction move under Walker and say why the conflict cannot be avoided here.
3. Test the Rule under the Rules Enabling Act, which bars a rule that abridges, enlarges or modifies a substantive right, and under Sibbach, which asks whether it really regulates procedure.
4. Give the alternative track for a reader who finds no Rule on point: outcome determination under York, and the twin aims, argued both ways on whether a pleading standard influences primary conduct.
The words come from the abstention paragraph, which these facts do not raise, and from trimming the plausibility discussion of the directors' complaint, which plainly passes and needs one sentence.

improvements.label: General jurisdiction over Chudley is wrong and specific jurisdiction is never attempted
improvements.whatHappened: Two sentences assert that Chudley is essentially at home in Virginia. Fifteen stores and a billion dollars in sales do not make a national retailer at home there under Daimler.
improvements.whyItMatters: That shortcut lets you skip the specific jurisdiction analysis the facts were built for, which is where the points are.
improvements.howToImprove: Reject general jurisdiction under Daimler in a clause, then run specific jurisdiction on the suit-related contacts: a delivery bound for but never reaching Virginia, and Tonks's own choice to operate his controller from Virginia, which is his conduct rather than Chudley's (World-Wide Volkswagen). Close on reasonableness, where the crash site, physical evidence, and witnesses all sit in West Virginia. Delete the two at-home sentences, and move the forum-convenience reasoning you wrote under Count I here, where it belongs.

improvements.label: Venue for Count II decided in one clause on the wrong facts
improvements.whatHappened: You conclude a substantial part of the events occurred in Virginia. The hotel is in the Western District and the crash was in West Virginia, so the Eastern District's only connection is that the plaintiff lives there.
improvements.whyItMatters: 1391 operates at the district level, and plaintiff residence is not a basis. You ran the subsections properly for Count I; doing the same here would have flipped the result.
improvements.howToImprove: Take 1391(b) in order for Count II as you did for Count I — residence of defendants, then substantial part of the events or property, then the fallback — and name the districts. Two sentences, paid for by shortening the Count I venue paragraph, whose result you can state once.

improvements.label: The partner's separation question is not answered
improvements.whatHappened: "may be severable from count II" is the whole answer, and it sits against your earlier statement that Count I is the same transaction or occurrence.
improvements.whyItMatters: The partner asked whether the cases must be separated, which is a Rule 20 question first: same transaction or occurrence, and a common question of law or fact. Only then does the remedy follow.
improvements.howToImprove: Do the joinder work once, in the sentence in your supplemental jurisdiction paragraph that already asserts the same transaction or occurrence: the FAA license decision and the drone collision overlap thinly, though the collision rate arguably put Chudley on notice as to both. Reuse that answer here and name the remedy — dismissal for misjoinder, or severance under Rule 42. The words come from the closing paragraph, which restates conclusions you have already given.

revisionPlan: Question 1: name Turner and its four substitute safeguards, add Lassiter, and state the complexity-as-barrier mechanism before your reform proposal; cut the jury-trial and error-rate paragraph to pay for it.
Question 2: give the new-trial grant and the Rule 50 denial each its own finality answer under 1291, and fix the 1292(b) element the judge's own language defeats.
Question 3: flag the arising-under basis of the SDNY judgment as unsettled and run Parklane's could-have-joined point on the New Jersey domiciles; delete the bond-exception aside.
Question 4: insert the vertical choice-of-law run on the pleading conflict before the horizontal analysis, using the words from the abstention paragraph and the trimmed plausibility discussion.

Question 4: reject general jurisdiction under Daimler and run specific jurisdiction and reasonableness; run 1391(b) subsection by subsection for Count II; answer the separation question under Rule 20 with severance as the remedy.
feedback.exampleRevision:
Instead of: "Pleading and mutuality are likely procedural since they would not influence pre-litigation behavior."

Try, opening a separate vertical choice-of-law passage: "The federal court must decide whether VA notice pleading or federal plausibility pleading governs. Rules 8(a)(2) and 12(b)(6) are directly on point, and a Walker-style narrow reading cannot avoid the conflict — the two standards demand different factual detail for the same complaint. The REA bars a rule that abridges, enlarges or modifies a substantive right, and Sibbach asks whether the rule really regulates procedure. Rules 8(a)(2) and 12(b)(6) set what a filed paper must contain, so the federal standard governs. If no Rule were on point, York cuts toward VA law because the standard disposes of the punitive damages demand but not the case. On the twin aims, Chudley says no drone operator picks flight routes with a pleading rule in mind; Tonks answers that pleading rules decide whether claims are filed at all, and so what conduct gets deterred."

What changed: the conflict is named, the Rule-on-point question is decided first, the REA and Sibbach tests appear, and the primary-conduct point is argued from both sides instead of asserted in a clause.
feedback.closing: The habit that produced your Question 2 merits analysis and your horizontal choice-of-law passage — pick the standard, apply it to named facts, decide — is what the Erie run and the specific jurisdiction analysis were waiting for.

fixtures.bandRationale: Reference defect lists first, so both sides carry one. DS reference: reaches a wrong bottom line on the JAMOL denial (calls the denial proper), finds specific jurisdiction over Chudley in Virginia on contacts the model treats as too thin, treats 1292(b) as possibly satisfied without confronting the judge's "cannot imagine" language, and miswrites the punitive figure — yet every weighted question is canvassed with alternatives preserved (a full multi-justice Erie run, Rule 20 elements, supplemental jurisdiction with a two-CNOF analysis, Semtek plus the arising-under branch plus NMOCE fairness factors, and two developed institutional-reform proposals in Q1). H reference: Q4 skips the vertical choice-of-law run entirely by declaring pleading "purely procedural" for the forum, garbles who the plaintiff is across Q3 and Q4, offers an incorrect Rule 50 renewal theory in Q2, and floats a Rule 18 joinder move that does not fit — but its Q1 engages Turner, Lassiter, Vitek and the assigned commentators, and its Q3 runs Semtek, Hart and the arising-under wrinkle. P reference (sole P comparator, weighted as a full comparator): shallow and mechanical throughout, inverts the Rule 23 numerosity reasoning, disposes of appealability in a bare list, and leaves several conclusions conclusory — but it runs the full Erie sequence and reaches every question. LP reference: grounds appellate jurisdiction partly in the trial court's subject matter jurisdiction and calls the JAMOL denial final, reaches the wrong JAMOL merits result, states diversity is satisfied on a $9,900 claim and never discusses supplemental jurisdiction at all, and finds Chudley at home in Virginia and venue proper under 1391(b)(1) — though it does run the full VCOL sequence and engages Turner. Pairwise verdicts. Versus DS: clearly weaker — Erie absent where DS runs it across both counts, Rule 20 unanswered where DS runs the elements, two threshold rulings (general jurisdiction, Count II venue) disposed of in a clause and wrong, and Turner unmentioned. Versus H: weaker overall. The two answers share the Q4 Erie hole, but H covers Q1 and Q3 more fully (Turner, Lassiter, Vitek; Semtek, Hart, the arising-under branch) while this answer's Q1 never reaches Turner and its Q3 stops before the arising-under branch it had already built elsewhere. This answer does beat H on Q2's merits and on Q4's supplemental-jurisdiction/Exxon analysis, but not enough to close the Q1 and Q3 gaps. Versus P: comparable. This answer is better on Question 2's merits and on Smith/Grable plus the Exxon reading, and its HCOL passage is fact-applied rather than recited; the P reference is better on the Erie sequence, which is exactly this answer's largest hole. Breadth, the proportion of sound resolutions, and the pattern of underdeveloped weighted cores match. Versus LP: stronger. This answer resolves Q4's subject matter jurisdiction correctly including the amount-in-controversy deficiency and supplemental jurisdiction, gets the JAMOL merits right on the actual evidentiary record, and runs venue subsection by subsection for Count I, where LP's corresponding cores are inverted or skipped. Verdicts place it between LP and H and comparable to the P comparator, so P.
fixtures.whyNotHigher: Not H because the two heaviest questions each lose a weighted core. On Question 4 (23 pts) the Erie/vertical choice-of-law analysis is essentially absent — the pleading conflict is folded into the horizontal analysis, so York, the Hanna majority's treatment of Rules 8(a)(2) and 12(b)(6), the Rules Enabling Act/Sibbach formulation and the Walker/Ginsburg construction attempt never appear — and the separation question is answered in three words with no Rule 20 predicate, while general jurisdiction over Chudley and Count II venue are each disposed of in a clause and come out wrong. On Question 1 (25 pts) the essay never names Turner, the case the quotation is built on, and frames the conflict predominantly in cost/efficiency terms without developing complexity-as-barrier. H requires mostly sound resolutions with rich analysis and real errors on some cores; here the errors sit on the cores themselves and one major structure is missing rather than mistaken.
fixtures.whyNotLower: Not LP because the heavily weighted cores are not a pattern of wrong results reached conclusorily. Question 4's subject matter jurisdiction is fully run and correct, including the amount-in-controversy deficiency on Count I, Smith/Grable applied to the embedded mail-delivery issue, and the controlling reading of Exxon foreclosing supplemental jurisdiction; the horizontal choice-of-law analysis states the operative rule and argues Virginia against West Virginia on named facts to a sound conclusion. Question 2's merits are resolved correctly on the actual evidentiary record with the Rule 50 and Rule 59 standards kept distinct, and Question 3's claim preclusion analysis establishes privity on the facts and reaches the right disposition. The LP reference, by contrast, inverts the diversity analysis on a $9,900 claim, never reaches supplemental jurisdiction, and gets the JAMOL merits wrong.
