fixtures.label: 2019 answer — DS
fixtures.answer:
## Question 1

SMJ
No SMJ through AUJ: no embedded federal question (Mottley) and no crucial embedded
federal issue (Smith-Grable).

Look to Diversity, with requirement for complete diversity. HGInc. domiciled by place of
incorporation (MA) and PPoB (MA). Droobles domiciled in NH. Issue is Riddle, who
may be domiciled in RI or MA. Riddle born in RI, maintains RI voter registration, and
spends every weekend in RI. But, has paid MA income taxes for 15 years and owns
apartment in MA where he sleeps on weeknights. Possible that court will see domicile in
RI since he still travels back and demonstrates no intent to change voter registration; also
possible court sees domicile as MA, where he spends most of his time, has his place of
business, and where he pays taxes. If latter, dismiss for lack of complete diversity.

If Riddle kicked out for lack of SMJ, no sufficient AIC for suit against Droobles

(50,000<75,000) and suit against Droobles must be dismissed. If Riddle not kicked out
for SMJ, look to whether Droobles can be joined through supplemental jurisdiction since
there is no independent jurisdiction for Droobles suit (insufficient AIC for DJ). Likely
that Droobles suit not permissible under §1367, since Droobles' suit was a claim by a
plaintiff against a party joined by Rule 20(a)(2).

PJ
No general IPJ over Droobles in MA or over Riddle if domiciled in RI: there is general

IPJ over Riddle if domiciled in MA, but then suit kicked out for SMJ.

Specific IPJ if long-arm to limits of Constitution and DP through minimum contacts and
traditional notions of fair play (International Shoe). 4(k)(1)(a) says FDC uses long-arm of
state in which it sits: MA has valid long-arm.

Probably fine for Riddle: offer for purchase received in MA, has MA office, and conducts
most business external to suit in MA (purposeful availment of state and could reasonably
foresee being haled into court; contra: J. McIntyre and Daimler).

Less sure for Droobles: no advertising in MA so unlikely he targeted sales in MA (J.
McIntyre). Goods regularly flow (25% of business), but no intentional availment or
solicitation. Suggests no IPJ over Droobles: can dismiss.

Venue
No venue under 1391(a): Droobles and Riddle not domiciled in same state. Look to

1391(b).

Substantial portion of events occurred in MA: gum taste test, receipt of emails, and
receipt of business valuations (last act for Tort purposes). Relies on court determining
that an email is where a person receives it: within realm of possibility. If website
constitutes property, could argue that website exists where content is created and
uploaded. Since HG creates all content, property impacted in suit could reasonably be in
MA. Likely cannot dismiss for lack of venue.

If MA not valid under 1391(b), couldn't use 1391(c) since venue also proper in NH.

Pleading

Likely cannot dismiss for failure to state a claim. Under Twiqbal, remove conclusory
statements and determine plausibility of remaining facts. Complaint alleges with
specificity via email that meeting at Droobles estate occurred, that HG received repeated
emails from Riddle including threat to reduce value of company, that HG has never been
to Droobles estate, and that value of HGInc. dropped. Court could argue that, since emails
were not provided, these are not adequate preliminary facts--this is unlikely.

No substantial policy reasons to dismiss case for failure to plead: unlikely to be a high-
cost discovery case since all companies are small and complaint deals with short time
period.

Notice and Service of Process
Service likely sufficient, since Droobles and attorneys received complaint.

Discrepancy between FRCP and MARCP. Erie analysis to determine whether motion to
dismiss for failure to provide separate document satisfying MARCP 4(a)(1)(h).

York outcome-determinative says MARCP results in dismissal while FRCP does not, so
use MARCP. Harlan says how lawyers file and notify unlikely to impact pre-litigation

conduct, so use FRCP. Under Scalia, FRCP valid since it doesn't "abridge, enlarge, or
modify" a state substantive right (permissible under REA) and applicable since it "really
regulates procedure" (Shady Grove): use FRCP. Under Ginsburg, FRCP valid under REA
but not applicable since no actual conflict: FRCP more permissive than MARCP and
doesn't bar additional requirements listed in MARCP 4(a)(1)(h), so use MARCP.

If following York or Ginsburg, dismiss. If following Harlan or Scalia, no dismissal for
failure to provide additional sheet unless other elements of FRCP 4(a)(1) not met.

-------------------------------------------

-------------------------------------------

Answer-to-Question-__2_

Summary judgment available if no genuine issue of material fact and movant entitled to
judgment as a matter of law (FRCP 56).

SJ for Public Access
Moving party bears burden of persuasion on affirmative defense. Must produce evidence
that, if unrebutted, would require a rational trier of fact to find in their favor (Celotex).

Defense a substantive question and only available in MA: do HCOL to determine
whether permissible. HCOL carries if transferor court had proper PJ and Venue. As stated
above, venue likely proper but unclear if MA District Court (MADC) had PJ over
Droobles. HCOL done by state choice-of-law rules.

If MADC had PJ, use HCOL analysis from transferor state (MA). MA is 2nd
Restatement: use Lex Loci Delicti (LLD) plus relevant state interest. Last event is loss of
value, which was likely in MA. HGInc. incorporated in MA, suggesting value is there.
Emails determining value also sent to HG in MA, so discovery of loss occurred in MA.
Could also have been where video filmed (NH) or edited (unknown), but likely to be
receipt of email (MA). Competing state interests: two parties voluntarily engaging in
business in MA but one party has nearly insignificant connections to MA and does all

business in NH. Center of gravity unclear, since most of this occurred online. Could
argue NH has greater access to witnesses but that MA has greater access to any paper
dealings of Riddle. Court likely to use LLD and use MA law with small possibility of NH
law.

If MADC did not have PJ, use HCOL analysis from transferee state (NH). NH is 1st
Restatement: use LLD. LLD likely in MA (see above). Use MA law.

If using NH law, cannot use this defense since only exists in MA. Motion will fail.

If using MA law, have access to affirmative defense and likely success. Law applies to
shareholders. HG is majority shareholder and has constant access to the public through
social media outlets: business model relies on website, Facebook, Instagram, Twitter, and
other accounts. Videos and posts involve HG's face and he bills himself as followers'
"independent voice." All revenue stems from posts, suggesting access is constant and
ready. Court may not consider social media a traditional media outlet under statute, but

seems unlikely.

Court likely to grant motion: nothing in record suggests HG doesn't have access to public.

SJ for Liability
No conflict in law; no HCOL analysis.

Moving party (HG) bears burden of persuasion. E1 met by testimony from Evans that

Droobles and Riddle participated in production of video, supported by fact that Droobles
shared tape in email and was present in video. E2 met as video had been edited: HG
testifies he wasn't there, Evans testifies HG wasn't there, and Droobles statement "I do not
accept that" became "I accept that." E3 met by diminished ad revenue (reduced standing).
E4 implied by devaluation of business (would want to know if offer for $5,000,000 was

anomalous and other offers closer to $3,900,000 or if other concurrent factors dropped
value).

Biggest challenge is lack of proven reputation damage (element three). While intuitive
that reputation based on independent evaluation would be tarnished by allegations of
purchased sponsorship, would want to prove that no other elements could have caused
drop in value. Still possible that judge would conclude no genuine issue of material fact
and grant judgment for HG as matter of law.

-------------------------------------------

-------------------------------------------

## Question 3_

No.

No final judgement: no §1291 appeal. No final judgement on one claim while other
claims still being adjudicated and can delay to appeal until after judgment entered: no
54(b) appeal. On the merits, no final order, and is reviewable later: no appeal under
Cohen Exception. No trial judge certification of important decision: no §1292(b) appeal.
No injunction: no §1292(a)(1) appeal. Not a class: no 23(f) appeal. Writ of Mandamus
possible to force decision to allow appeal (§1651), but unlikely that court of appeals will
find requirement for speed or high likelihood that petitioner is correct.

-------------------------------------------

-------------------------------------------

## Question 4_

Claim Preclusion
No HCOL: CP law the same. Same claim asserted: same T&O as L1. There's privity:
same defendant and plaintiffs had control over the litigation in L1. Dismissal with
prejudice final. Unclear if on-the-merits: if a federal court is sitting in diversity, borrow
the law of the state where the rendering court sits and give at least as much preclusion as
the rendering state (Semtek). L1 in Federal NH court using DJ, so give at least as much
preclusion as NH state. NH will probably see dismissal with prejudice as on-the-merits,
since it came after a SJ that decided Droobles participated in scheme.

If on merits, either party can preclude. If not, no preclusion.

Only preclusive if SMJ was valid in L1(Marrese).

Issue Preclusion

Droobles won no issues in L1: he cannot preclude.

HG and GW might be able to preclude. Ruling sufficiently final: settled with no appeal.
Same issues as in L1. Unsure if settlement means issue was actually litigated, but likely

that summary judgment in favor of HGInc. means issue of whether Riddle&Droobles
committed the tort was actually litigated. Determination of common scheme suggests
Droobles' liability is severable from Riddles' liability and would allow preclusion (contra:
Russell).

If all above factors were met, would do HCOL for mutuality using Semtek. Use NH law:
NH requires strict mutuality. Could argue that HGInc. not same party as HG (inc. v.
person) so issue preclusion would not run. Could argue that HGInc. is the same party as
HG since HG is majority stakeholder, CEO, and Chair of Board, so issue preclusion
would run.

-------------------------------------------

-------------------------------------------

## Question 5_

State court: AUJ or DJ under Ben-Hur/Exxon irrelevant.

No conflict between FRCP and NHRCP: no Erie.

Class Certification Requirements

Numerosity possible. 22 shareholders that are geographically dispersed: suggests joinder
too difficult. 20 potential suits only $15,000 (.015%x1,000,000): members unlikely to
litigate on their own (lawyers and filings too expensive). All cases arose in MA: IPJ
should be fine over all unnamed members, so numerosity preserved (Shutts).
Discretionary, but judge would probably grant.

Commonality likely. Common scheme involved in all suits (diminution of value) and
same/similar issues of law and fact, like whether the actions met standard of business
disparagement.

Typicality likely. Named plaintiff typical of class, since all seeking similar compensation
for same wrong (only difference is amount). HG has no conflicting incentive: arguably,
has bigger incentive to fight for class since he is majority stakeholder. Only potential

issue is refusal since he has more at stake (unlikely, since he settled L1).

Representativeness likely. Named plaintiff a member of the class and aggrieved in the
same way.

Requirements Specific to 23(b)(3)
Seeking damages; certify as 23(b)(3).

Predominance likely. Common issues predominate; discovery and testimony like the
same. This is essentially identical to commonality analysis (Wal-Mart).

Superiority likely. See numerosity argument. But, no experts involved--litigation could
be cheap so could do individual suits.

-------------------------------------------

-------------------------------------------

## Question 6_

Claim preclusion: add that all dismissals (including for FNC, SMJ, PJ, and venue) are
now on-the-merits. Expansion of preclusion will likely increase efficiency but decrease
fairness to those who lack sophisticated understanding of court system.

Such a policy would support judicial efficiency by reducing refilings and dismissing
current cases. Parties would be incentivized to bring all claims at once, preventing future
suits and expediting decision-making. There's social benefit in having cases consolidated:
expedites restitution and helps parties to move on. Parties would also be discouraged
from filing frivolous lawsuits designed to harass defendants and instead focus on the
merits of the case. Parties would be encouraged to abstain from forum shopping for fear
of dismissal. This would also push more cases into state court, as parties wouldn't want to

risk having improper SMJ. This would support federalism, state adjudication of state
issues, and equitable administration of laws within the same region. Making permissive
counterclaims compulsory would encourage plaintiffs to research prior to filing to gain a
complete picture. Keeping cases in state court could be beneficial to plaintiffs--
particularly middle and low-income individuals--since federal courts tend to be more
favorable to big corporations.

The scheme also meets Vitek factors since it leaves intact the right to the first trial and all

associated due process protections.

The policy could be seen as balancing power between plaintiff and defendant, since
plaintiff would be held to a higher standard of review and would be subject to
consequences for mistakes that arguably should be corrected prior to filing. Could also

incentivize corporations to choose FSCs that don't fight the public interest.

However, such a policy would be unfair--particularly for pro se clients without
knowledge of FRCP. Since the complexity of FRCP favors large corporations and those
who can afford expensive counsel, adding more procedural dismissals to the "on-the-
merits" category could incentivize crafty lawyering on behalf of defendants to get more
cases dismissed with prejudice through purely procedural means. A particular issue
would be with hidden FSCs: claims against corporations would be dismissed by the
handful because it's likely many plaintiffs are unaware they've even signed an FSC or that
the clause will not be challenged despite unconscionability or unfair bargaining practices.
Challenging to seriously argue that plaintiffs should have their suit claim-precluded

simply because they poorly interpreted FRCP or didn't know about a claim they could
have filed.

Requiring all permissive counterclaims could lead to issues under Twiqbal, where
plaintiffs are unable to plead with enough specificity prior to discovery to prevent these
cases from being dismissed.

Including FNC in this proposal would give judges even more discretionary power, since

they would have the ability to dismiss a case forever simply because they thought it could
be better adjudicated elsewhere.

These two desires would also likely clash: parties could be obligated to abandon
legitimate permissible claims for fear of disrupting SMJ, PJ, or venue.

When weighing these policies, Eldridge test tells us that private interest in having chance
to correct mistakes and reserve right to sue probably doesn't outweigh government
interest in efficiency. Unlikely to cause too much erroneous deprivation; scheme still
allows full case in front of a judge with opportunity to present evidence.

Could mitigate issues by simplifying FRCP for SMJ, PJ, and venue. Removal of AIC
requirements would allow more cases into federal court but make DJ easier to understand.
Removal of DJ entirely would simplify the boundary between state and federal court and
speed up growth of state law development. This is unlikely to prejudice out-of-state
defendants: frequent movement obviates distinction between in-state and out-of-state.

Could also mitigate issues by providing access to counsel (unlikely by Lassiter/Turner
precedent and fact that plaintiff would be receiving counsel) or providing non-counsel
safeguards like simple guides to FRCP, non-lawyer advocates to explain and guide
plaintiffs, or online filing that explains potential consequences prior to submitting file.

feedback.headline: Question 1's jurisdiction chain and Erie run are the strongest work here; Question 4 leaves both of its decisive questions unanswered
feedback.overview: The Question 1 subject matter jurisdiction chain and the Erie run are the best analysis on the exam. You joined Droobles under Rule 20, then applied the 1367(b) bar to a plaintiff's claim against a Rule 20 party, and you said why — that is the step most answers leave open. You then ran Erie as four competing approaches and stated the mixed result instead of forcing one. Question 2's choice-of-law gateway, worked through both the transferor and transferee branches before Rule 56, is the same quality of work. The problems sit in two places. Question 4, worth 8 points, never separates Harry from Ginny on privity, and it asserts New Hampshire preclusion law without asking whether Massachusetts law travels with the transferred judgment. In Question 1, the personal jurisdiction analysis over Droobles runs three sentences and stops before relatedness and before fairness and reasonableness.

strengths.label: Supplemental jurisdiction resolved rather than left open
strengths.detail: Reaching 1367(b) and naming why Count II is barred settles the point most answers abandon at 1367(a). You also stayed off the reading of 1367 the course no longer permits.
strengths.answerExcerpt: Droobles' suit was a claim by a plaintiff against a party joined by Rule 20(a)(2)

strengths.label: Erie run as four approaches with an honest mixed result
strengths.detail: York, Harlan on primary conduct, Scalia with the Rules Enabling Act and Sibbach, and Ginsburg on applicability each produce a different answer, and saying so is more useful than manufacturing one outcome. Reading FRCP 4 as a floor the state rule supplements is the crux of the Ginsburg branch, and you found it.
strengths.answerExcerpt: If following York or Ginsburg, dismiss. If following Harlan or Scalia, no dismissal

strengths.label: Domicile argued both ways with the consequence drawn
strengths.detail: Weighing the Rhode Island indicia against the Massachusetts ones is only half the work; drawing the payoff — that Massachusetts citizenship sinks the whole complaint, including the count against your own client — is what makes the analysis useful to the partner.
strengths.answerExcerpt: If latter, dismiss for lack of complete diversity.

strengths.label: Happy court rule stated, both branches run
strengths.detail: Putting horizontal choice of law ahead of Rule 56 is what part (a) requires. Running both branches to show they converge on Massachusetts law through the supplied last-event rule is what makes the conclusion usable no matter how the Question 1 jurisdiction call comes out.
strengths.answerExcerpt: HCOL carries if transferor court had proper PJ and Venue.

strengths.label: Record matched to the supplied elements
strengths.detail: Each of the four tort elements is tied to named discovery items rather than to a narrative of the evidence, and identifying causation as the weak link is the honest read of this record.
strengths.answerExcerpt: E2 met as video had been edited

strengths.label: Complete finality answer in one paragraph
strengths.detail: For 3 points you canvassed 1291, Rule 54(b), Cohen, 1292(b), 1292(a)(1), 23(f), and mandamus, and grounded the 1291 conclusion in the reserved-damages posture rather than merely announcing non-finality.
strengths.answerExcerpt: On the merits, no final order, and is reviewable later: no appeal under Cohen Exception.

strengths.label: Numerosity argued on the actual numbers
strengths.detail: You placed 22 members between the thresholds and argued dispersion and the roughly $15,000 stake rather than asserting a headcount rule, and you had the small per-member stake cutting in favor of certification, which is the right direction.
strengths.answerExcerpt: members unlikely to litigate on their own (lawyers and filings too expensive)

strengths.label: Access to justice integrated, with concrete mitigations
strengths.detail: The disadvantages are specific — unrepresented litigants, procedural dismissals as a target for aggressive lawyering, hidden forum selection clauses. Noticing that your two proposals pull against each other is analysis, not hedging, and the closing mitigations are concrete.
strengths.answerExcerpt: parties could be obligated to abandon legitimate permissible claims for fear of disrupting SMJ, PJ, or venue

improvements.label: Question 1: personal jurisdiction over Droobles stops halfway
improvements.whatHappened: The specific jurisdiction analysis is three sentences ending in "no intentional availment or solicitation." The fact that decides the contacts question goes unused: Droobles ships 25% of his gum directly to Massachusetts customers with no intermediary. You cite J. McIntyre for the absence of targeting, but the course uses that case as the contrast for direct sales with no middleman, which is Droobles's posture. Relatedness — gum sales versus a deepfake claim — is never named as the hard question. There is no fair and reasonable step, so International Shoe is recited but only half applied. The general jurisdiction denial is asserted without the Daimler reasoning about whether 25% makes Droobles essentially at home.
improvements.whyItMatters: This is a heavily weighted sub-issue on a 25-point question, and the credit is in the application rather than the recitation.
improvements.howToImprove:
Take the bases in the order the course lists them.
1. Really at home: New Hampshire only.
2. Daimler essentially at home: 25% of sales is not the substantial, continuous, systematic presence required.
3. Consent: none.
4. Specific: Massachusetts long-arm plus 4(k)(1)(A).
5. Minimum contacts linking Droobles, Massachusetts, and this claim: direct shipment with no intermediary, Massachusetts as his largest market, against no office, no advertising, no solicitation, a passive order-taking website.
6. Fair and reasonable: Massachusetts's interest in its businesses, location of the valuation evidence, Droobles's convenience.
Pay for this by cutting the "No substantial policy reasons to dismiss" paragraph in your pleading section.

improvements.label: Question 1: the pleading analysis never works paragraph by paragraph
improvements.whatHappened: You named plausibility pleading and the strike-then-assess sequence and pointed at several allegations. No paragraph is identified as conclusory, and the surviving allegations are never mapped onto the four supplied tort elements.
improvements.whyItMatters: The exam reproduced the complaint in full, which is the signal that a full 12(b)(6) run is wanted. Naming the conclusory material by paragraph is the first taught step, and without a paragraph number that step has not been performed.
improvements.howToImprove:
Run it in order.
1. Set aside paragraph 20's "on information and belief" scheme narrative as conclusory.
2. For each of the four elements, name the paragraphs pleading facts that go to it.
3. Say whether what survives moves each element from possible to plausible, and name the contested one — here, Droobles's own participation.
This is a rewrite of the allegation list you already have rather than an addition, so number the paragraphs instead of describing them. The course's term for the standard is plausibility pleading rather than the portmanteau.

improvements.label: Question 1: the state summons rule needs a characterization step before Erie
improvements.whatHappened: The answer jumps from "Discrepancy between FRCP and MARCP" straight to the Erie tests. The step in between is missing: characterize MARCP 4(a)(1)(H) for horizontal choice of law, which under Klaxon sends a Massachusetts federal court to Massachusetts's own rules.
improvements.whyItMatters: Without that step nothing explains why a Massachusetts rule is in the case at all, and the Erie analysis floats free of it.
improvements.howToImprove: Add one clause naming Klaxon and the operative point: anything arguably procedural is procedural, so the forum state's rule is the one in play. Cut "Service likely sufficient, since Droobles and attorneys received complaint" to pay for it. Separately, the defendant-residence provision is 1391(b)(1) and the fallback is 1391(b)(3); relabeling costs no words and your substance on all three was right.

improvements.label: Question 2: the defendants' claimed memory gaps are never assessed
improvements.whatHappened: Droobles and Riddle both say they cannot remember because of cold medicine and the flu. The answer never asks whether that testimony creates a genuine dispute of material fact.
improvements.whyItMatters: It is the only response the non-movant has on this record, and it is the point on which the two motions cut in opposite directions. Your conclusion on part (b) is also left unstated, which forfeits the payoff of the element-by-element work you did.
improvements.howToImprove: Say whether an absence of memory controverts affirmative documentary evidence — the better view is that it does not — and then state your conclusion on (b) outright. Pay for it by deleting the branch "If using NH law, cannot use this defense," which your own analysis had already ruled out. Use "Harry" rather than "HG" where you mean the person, since the defense's terms turn on the shareholder-versus-entity distinction.

improvements.label: Question 4: which state's preclusion law travels with the transferred judgment
improvements.whatHappened: The answer states "Use NH law: NH requires strict mutuality" and gives no reason for choosing New Hampshire. Judgment was entered in New Hampshire but the case was filed in Massachusetts, and the two states diverge on mutuality.
improvements.whyItMatters: That choice decides whether Ginny can use non-mutual offensive issue preclusion at all. Asserting it turns the analytic core of an 8-point question into a coin flip, and your own happy court reasoning from Question 2 was sitting right there: a proper transfer changes the courthouse, not the law, which points to Massachusetts and its abolition of mutuality.
improvements.howToImprove: Walk it: Semtek sends you to the preclusion law of the state where the rendering court sat; identify which state that is after a transfer; argue Massachusetts through the happy court rule while preserving the contrary reading that one looks to the face of the New Hampshire judgment; state the mutuality consequence each way. Pay for it by cutting the Marrese aside on subject matter jurisdiction and the line "If on merits, either party can preclude. If not, no preclusion." The course calls this intersystem preclusion, not a choice-of-law question.

improvements.label: Question 4: Harry and Ginny are treated as one party for privity
improvements.whatHappened: Privity is asserted collectively — "plaintiffs had control over the litigation in L1" — for both shareholders at once.
improvements.whyItMatters: The distinction is the claim-preclusion payoff. Harry's 65% stake plus his control of the first suit supports privity with the corporation; Ginny's 5% with no showing of control does not, which is why she escapes claim preclusion and is the one positioned to use issue preclusion offensively. Collapsing them loses both halves.
improvements.howToImprove: Split the claim-preclusion discussion into Harry and Ginny and give each the ownership and control reasoning. You already wrote the material: the observation that Harry is majority stakeholder, CEO, and Chair belongs in the privity analysis, not in the mutuality discussion. Move it rather than adding words, and keep claim preclusion and issue preclusion in separate blocks.

improvements.label: Question 5: trade the Shutts sentence for the choice-of-law point
improvements.whatHappened: You invoke Shutts to establish personal jurisdiction over absent members, a topic the question expressly took off the table. The course uses that case for whether a single state's law can be applied to all class members' claims.
improvements.whyItMatters: With members spread across California, Washington, and Oregon, differing state law is the one live threat to commonality and superiority here, and it goes unmentioned.
improvements.howToImprove: Delete the Shutts sentence and spend the words saying that each member's claim gets its own choice-of-law treatment, then explain why that does not defeat commonality on these facts — every member was injured by one scheme and the tort is the same in all fifty-one states.

improvements.label: Question 6: label the chosen proposal and tie both to the elements they displace
improvements.whatHappened: Your own proposal — treating procedural dismissals as on the merits — is clearly stated. The permissive-counterclaim option is discussed but never labeled as the listed one you adopted, and it is interleaved with your proposal so a reader must reconstruct which argument attaches to which idea.
improvements.whyItMatters: On a 15-point question with an explicit instruction to pick one, a reader who cannot tell which proposal you adopted cannot credit the argument. Neither proposal is tied to the doctrine it would change, so the analysis sits above the rules it displaces.
improvements.howToImprove: Open with one sentence naming the listed option you chose and one naming your own. For each, name what it displaces: the compulsory-versus-permissive line in Rules 13 and 20, the actually-litigated and necessary-to-the-judgment requirements, mutuality, and privity. Add the notice constraint on binding nonparties (Mullane). Pay for this by cutting the unsupported claim that federal courts favor large corporations and by tightening the Vitek and Eldridge passages, which currently announce conclusions rather than apply factors.

revisionPlan: Rewrite Question 1's personal jurisdiction section taking the bases in order, using the direct-shipment fact, naming relatedness as the hard question, and closing with fair and reasonable.
Renumber the Question 1 pleading discussion so it sets aside paragraph 20 first and then maps surviving paragraphs onto each of the four elements.
Add the Klaxon characterization step before the Erie run and correct the venue subsection labels.
In Question 2, decide whether the claimed memory gaps create a genuine dispute, and state a conclusion on the liability motion.
In Question 4, separate Harry from Ginny on privity, then argue whether Massachusetts or New Hampshire preclusion law travels with the judgment and give the mutuality consequence each way.
In Question 6, name the listed option you adopted in your first sentence and tie both proposals to the preclusion elements they would displace.
feedback.exampleRevision: Specific IPJ over Droobles: MA long-arm to constitutional limits, 4(k)(1)(A). Contacts: Droobles ships 25% of his gum straight to MA customers with no intermediary, unlike J. McIntyre, where the goods reached the forum through a distributor, and MA is his largest market — purposeful availment. Against: no office, no agent, no advertising, no solicitation, a passive order-taking website. Harder question is relatedness: the claim is about a deepfake, not gum. Droobles says the MA sales have nothing to do with the video. HG says the endorsement of that gum is why Droobles wanted HG discredited, so sales and tort share a subject matter, and Droobles knew the loss of value would land in MA. F&R: MA has an interest in protecting a MA business, the valuation evidence is in MA, and Droobles already transacts with MA customers, though the recording and the key witness are in NH. Closer than the contacts alone suggest; relatedness likely carries it for HG.
feedback.closing: Work Question 4 first: split Harry from Ginny on privity, then argue which state's preclusion law follows the judgment after the transfer. Then rebuild Question 1's personal jurisdiction section so it runs through relatedness and fair and reasonable.

fixtures.bandRationale: Reference defect lists first, so both sides of each comparison carry one. DS reference (different year, sole DS comparator, treated as a full comparator): relies on the effects test as an operative personal jurisdiction framework, disposes of one sub-question in two sentences, hedges the forum non conveniens vertical-choice question by assuming its way past the substantive/procedural characterization, and reaches a class-certification conclusion resting on facts it says it would need to go get. Its distinguishing quality is sustained canvassing — every branch is opened, both sides run, and alternatives preserved across all subparts. Same-exam H reference: leaves the 1367(b) question expressly unresolved ('Unclear after Exxon'), builds its specific-jurisdiction argument on an effects-test comparison, disposes of venue in a single sentence with no subsection analysis, and mis-states the Massachusetts sales percentage. Same-exam P reference: never resolves supplemental jurisdiction ('Maybe there's SJ'), uses Calder/Griffis as the operative jurisdictional test, skips the transfer step entirely in Question 2 and applies New Hampshire choice-of-law rules directly, and claim-precludes Ginny along with Harry. Same-exam LP reference: concludes there is no venue anywhere, garbles the Erie analysis into a second conflict it invented, answers Question 2 with a bare recitation of the Rule 56 standard and no application, and spends much of Question 6 on criminal-law consequences outside the course frame. Pairwise verdicts. Versus LP: stronger, decisively — every question here receives an applied analysis and a stated conclusion, and Question 2 in particular runs the record against the elements. Versus P: stronger. The student resolves 1367(b) correctly where P leaves it open; avoids the effects test where P makes it the operative framework; performs the transfer/happy-court step in Question 2 that P skips; is broader and better applied on Question 3; and is comparable on Question 5 and Question 6. P's advantage is confined to Question 4, where it engages the Massachusetts/New Hampshire transfer question the student misses, but P then botches Ginny's claim preclusion, so even there the exchange is close to even. Versus H: comparable overall. The student is better on the Question 1 SMJ chain (1367(b) resolved rather than left open), better on venue, better on Question 3, and equal or better on the Question 2 choice-of-law gateway; H is better on Question 4 (which distinguishes Harry from Ginny and squarely raises the Massachusetts-versus-New Hampshire preclusion question) and on the depth of its jurisdictional and Question 6 doctrinal tethering. Weighting by points, the two answers trade advantages on the 25- and 11-point questions and split the 8- and 3-pointers, which places the student at the H reference's level. Versus DS: weaker — the DS reference sustains open branches and preserved alternatives on every subpart, whereas this answer leaves Question 4's dispositive choice unmade and half-runs the International Shoe test.
fixtures.whyNotHigher: Not DS because two weighted questions lack the sustained canvassing the DS reference maintains throughout: Question 4's outcome-determinative choice between Massachusetts and New Hampshire preclusion law is asserted rather than argued, and the Question 1 personal jurisdiction analysis recites International Shoe without the relatedness or fairness-and-reasonableness steps and without the direct-shipment fact that carries the contacts question. Both are places where alternatives were available and not preserved.
fixtures.whyNotLower: Not P because the core analyses are, with one exception, resolved rather than left hanging: the supplemental jurisdiction chain reaches the 1367(b) bar and states why, the Erie problem is run as four distinct approaches with the mixed result stated, the Question 2 choice-of-law gateway is worked through both branches before Rule 56, and Questions 3 and 5 are complete and proportionate. The P reference by contrast leaves supplemental jurisdiction unresolved and skips the transfer step in Question 2 altogether.

fixtures.label: 2019 answer — H
fixtures.answer:
## Question 1

Claims are under state law, so no AU. No Smith-Grable. SMJ from diversity. Anchoring
claim is against Riddle, as he meets AIC and diversity if he is indeed a citizen of RI, as
the complaint alleges. But this is questionable, and we need to look at domicile: although
he was certainly a RI resident up through business school (Mas) and continues to vote in
RI and spends time there on weekends, he works in MA, spends most of his time there,
and owns an apartment there. If Riddle is MA domiciliary, complete diversity
(Strawbridge) broken and no SMJ. Supplemental jurisdiction over Droobles, who is
diverse but AIC deficient. Unclear after Exxon whether under 1367(b) AIC deficiency
defeats supplemental jurisdiction over joined defendant. If yes, the claim against
Droobles must be dismissed for SMJ lack.

4(k)(1)(a) MA federal court piggybacks off of MA state long arm. Hard to dismiss
anchoring claim against Riddle for IPJ. General IPJ over Riddle if domiciled in MA (but
then SMJ problem as above), or if essentially at home due to continuous and systematic
contacts with state. This is likely. Harder to establish general IPJ over Droobles, because
Daimler requires a large proportion of its business be done in forum state. Is 20%
enough? If no general IPJ, then argue against specific IPJ. International Shoe minimal
contacts questionable: didn't purposefully reach into MA or purposefully avail itself of
MA laws (no advertising). Maybe the volume of business in MA enough to indicate to
Droobles that MA was regular place of using the product, but merely placing product in
stream of commerce usually not enough (McIntyre, Volkswagen). Plus, not really
Droobles's product that is at issue. What about intentional tort? This is a bit like Griffis v.

Luban effects test: brunt of tort felt in forum, but probably not aimed specifically at MA
itself. Not enough to know that the plaintiff resided within the forum. so insufficient
contacts for specific IPJ.

Venue proper under 1391(b)(2) because the events leading to the action (loss of business
value) were in MA.

Dismiss for insufficient process if MA procedure rules apply, since HG didn't attach
required additional documents. HCOL MA will use this rule, because procedure defined
broadly. But FRCP don't require. So run Erie. York: the difference in rule is the
difference between dismissal and survival, outcome-determinative, so use state law
(really concerned with federalism and fed vs. state just being change in courthouse, not in
law). Harlan: Would just change attorney behavior in filing, no way to affect primary
conduct of parties (which is true domain of states), so use federal law. Scalia/Hanna:
REA is source of law, presumably valid (Sibbach: does it really regulate procedure?
certainly yes). Also, an FRCP has never been held invalid so that is an ever-so-slight
consideration. Applicable here because it covers exact same requirements and process as
MA rule. Use federal. Ginsburg/Hanna: Same validity analysis, but avoid conflict
through applicability prong. State interest here in making sure defendants know how to
access justice system and defend themselves, with a particular eye to poorer defendants.
Protect that interest by saying MA rule is merely a further requirement upon accepted
FRCP, and no clash. Use state law.

Possibly dismiss for failure to state claim under Twiqbal plausibility pleading standard.

Eliminate conclusory statements and then see if remaining factual allegations nudge
claim across line from possible to plausible. There's a good amount of facts alleged, but
do they make the claim plausible? HG is relying on a lot of assumptions based only off of
the one email. Major assumption that "I don't accept" line was edited. Central questions:
will court believe that the claim is so unlikely to succeed on the merits so as to not justify
judicial resources spent on proceedings? Also don't want to subject defendants to
harassment by frivolous lawsuits.

-------------------------------------------

-------------------------------------------

Answer-to-Question-__2_

A) We want MA law for the defense to apply in NH court so HG can't recover as matter
of law. It's hard to argue that the defense is procedural, so do an HCoL analysis. If MA
fed court not happy, then NH state HCoL applies (Klaxon). First restatement, so lex loci
delicti. The last element of the tort was the loss of value to HG, which occurred in MA.
So apply MA law.

If MA was a happy court: MA fed court uses MA state HCoL (Klaxon), so Second
Restatement. Look at individual issues, not whole case: so here look just at the public
access defense (not the tort claim). HG is domiciled in MA, and the media outlets HG
uses would be MA outlets or at least HG would broadcast from within MA. Relationship
between parties (HG's use of Droobles's product) in MA. For keeping laws uniform and
avoiding frankenlaw: questionable whether MA or NH tort law would apply (last act in
tort in MA, but substantial evidence in NH, and second restatement would account for
that) neutral factor here. However, Babcock/Neumeier indicates reduced willingness to
apply a state's law to protect foreign parties (Droobles is from NH). State interest in
protecting own citizens would actually cut against its applying its own law here. So tough
call.

If MA law permitting the defense applies, the crucial question of fact would then be
whether HG had constant and ready access to public or media outlets. Do Celotex
analysis. Burden of persuasion on Droobles here, probably met because of Harry's social
media presence. In its cross motion, HG would need to show that there is a genuine
dispute of fact in order to survive the motion.

B) Not clear that evidence in deposition record overwhelmingly favors movant as
happened in Scott v. Harris. So go through Celotex analysis. HG has burden of
persuasion at trial for Droobles's lability for the tort. Burden of production probably met:
if unrefuted, the emails from Droobles to Riddle and from Riddle to the anonymous
account, contextualized by Lily's testimony, may require rational trier of fact to find for
HG. But Droobles/Riddle probably also meet their resulting burden of production:
genuine issue of fact for trial in that no memory of the events. Court must read record in
best light for non movant, so probably won't grant summary judgment.

-------------------------------------------

-------------------------------------------

Answer-to-Question-__3_

Not immediately appealable because not a final judgment under 1291. Liberty Mutual.
No damages have been awarded yet. Can't use 1292(A) because not an injunction.
Probably can't use 1292(b) because, even though may argue that several of the
requirements for double discretion met, there's just not many special aspects of this case
that would convince a trial judge that an immediate appellate court decision is required on
an issue. Judge gave no indication that he was stumped by the case. Not 54(b) because
even though there are two claims (Droobles and Riddle), neither is final, and both are
extremely related. Definitely no Cohen exception. Can't get writ because no risk of
irreparable harm.

-------------------------------------------

-------------------------------------------

## Question 4_

All states here use same claim preclusion law, so an inter system analysis is not needed
for claim preclusion. Harry will probably be claim precluded. It's the exact same claim,
and probably a final judgment on the merits: even with the settlement, the court still
dismissed the case with prejudice. Harry is probably in privity with HG: even though he
is not the sole shareholder, he is the majority shareholder, CEO, and "runs the business."
This is likely enough to show that Harry sufficiently controlled HG during the previous
litigation. Ginny probably won't be claim precluded. She is probably not in privity with
HG, since she is merely the VP and owns only 5% of its shares.

Droobles may be issue precluded on his participation in the business disparagement
scheme:

For Mutuality: We are in NH state court now, with the rendering court being NH federal.
Sitting in diversity, so use federal common law to determine preclusion law: the law of
the state of the rendering court is applied (Semtek). But is this NH or MA law? If the NH
federal court applied NH law, this isn't an issue. NH preclusion law would apply. But if
the transfer from MA fed court carried MA law with it, this may mean that the relevant
state law for the NH fed court is MA law, in which case no mutuality is required. We
want a mutuality requirement, though, so argue that the rendering NH federal court's

power is what is important, not the law of the MA fed court that was transferred over, and
therefore use the law of the state in which the federal court literally sits. NH requires
strict mutuality. If strict mutuality, Ginny cannot issue preclude Droobles. But Harry may
still be able to, due to privity (see above). If no mutuality requirement, then Ginny would
be permitted to use ONMCE.

For Actually Litigated: could make the argument that the issue was dropped due to the
settlement, but this seems weak. Summary judgment on the issue was granted. For
Necessary to Decision: do summary judgments have enough finality to constitute a
decision? It's questionable here, as no final judgment was entered; the suit was dismissed.
We could also make an argument based on Rios that the issue decided was gratuitous, as
HG settled with Riddle and the suit was dismissed. Though the facts are pretty different
here from Rios, Droobles likewise had no chance to appeal the summary judgment ruling
on his participation, and so should not be precluded from contesting the issue here.

Under Hart, court may be able to grant more preclusive effect than rendering court, but
this is unclear. Hope that it doesn't for the issue preclusion question.

-------------------------------------------

-------------------------------------------

Answer-to-Question-__5_

First look at SMJ. Only care about named plaintiffs for diversity (Ben-Hur). Harry would
have the anchoring claim here: his AIC is $650k as the 65% shareholder. Does not matter
that Ginny as a named plaintiff doesn't meet AIC, just need one (Exxon). SMJ met.

Rule 23 may not be met if due to numerosity. There are over 20 but under 40 members,
so look at other factors. Smallest claim would be for $15k, which is not insubstantial. We
could argue that these claims aren't small enough to justify a class. However, the
geographic dispersion (shareholders on the west coast) cuts in favor of certifying.
Commonality easy to meet, even after Wal-Mart, because there is a single T/O for the
same loss of value for all claims being brought by the class. Though the value of Harry
and Ginny's claims substantially larger and maybe atypical of class, the crux is they legal
theory is still the same, and due to the structure of the proposed division of damages, their
incentives will be to maximize damages for everyone. This also accomplishes
representativeness. We could perhaps argue that Harry himself wasn't aggrieved in the
same way as the other class members, as he was personally attacked by the ad. This may
alter his incentives compared to the rest of the class.

This is a suit for damages, so 23(b)(3). Predominance very likely met due to commonality
analysis above. Schutts resulting in increased HCoL analyses unlikely to be a problem

because we can probably use one state's law for all claims (NH or MA) due to there being
a single T/O. For superiority of a class action to individual suits, we could make a related
argument to the numerosity concerns above: the claims aren't too small individually.

-------------------------------------------

-------------------------------------------

Answer-to-Question-__6_

Additional proposed rule: Remove the Parklane factor of plaintiff ease of joining L1 in
applying ONMCE. So now, the fact that P2 could have easily intervened in L1 is
irrelevant to determining whether they could exercise ONMCE in L2 against D1. The
policy interest here may be in not coercing additional potential plaintiffs into intervening
in litigation they may not want to, for fear of having to re litigate a contentious or
expensive issue should they choose to bring a subsequent suit.

The primary advantages of the first (the exam's) proposal would be judicial efficiency in
subsequent suits and greater finality. If more issues are disposed of in L1, fewer resources
need to be spent down the line in hearing these issues. There's even more resource-saving
if we can preclude issues upon which no time or effort was spent at all. All parties still
had their day in court, so the rule seems equitable. What's more, If rules around raising
particular issues and defenses during L1 were loosened (for example, loosening the
immutability of the pre-trial order), there would be an even stronger argument that the
parties had sufficient opportunities to have issues heard in the initial litigation.

However, there are many more downsides. There would ironically be a loss of efficiency
for the initial litigation, as the parties would now be incentivized to raise every possible
issue, as this will always be more strategically desirable than losing on every one by

default. One could also make a due process argument that an issue warrants its own day
in court, analogous to parties. Losses in court will become much more severe and far-
reaching to the losing party if they don't raise issues, perhaps functionally depriving them
of rights further down the road. This system will also advantage wealth and experience
with the legal system even more than at present, as good lawyering in recognizing every
potential issue becomes vital. Even if you may have easily won on the merits of an issue
in L2, you will lose if your attorney failed to raise it in L1. Indeed, corporations and other
repeat players in the legal system will easily pick up which issues they must routinely
raise, while everyone else will be disadvantaged. Preclusion doctrine is obscure enough to
where one would need an actual attorney, not just an expert of some type (see Powell in
Vitek) to navigate it. Litigation will also cost more if there are more issues to adjudicate.

The second proposed rule would make it easier to apply ONMCE, as a party could now
do so even if they could have joined the original litigation. Any expansion of ONMCE
has some clear general issues. It would encourage potential plaintiffs to sit on the
sidelines of litigation. Though we may be concerned about not forcing a party to join, we
are probably more concerned with efficiency in consolidating lawsuits when possible. On
top of this, the threat of ONMCE would make defendants much more likely to settle in
order to avoid any final judgment that subsequent plaintiffs could use against them.
Though we generally want parties to settle for the sake of judicial efficiency, there should
be some concern over the power imbalance that is created. Circumstances may arise
where the defendant is willing to pay exorbitantly more than P1 may individually be
justly owed, as P1 has outsized bargaining power when D1 is threatened by the specter of
many more subsequent plaintiffs using a ruling against it.

feedback.headline: Questions 2 through 4 carry frameworks to a resolution; Question 1, worth 25 points, leaves four of its five grounds open
feedback.overview: Your best passages are analysis, not coverage. The Erie run on the Massachusetts summons rule walks York, Harlan, Scalia, and Ginsburg each to a disposition, with the Rules Enabling Act and 'really regulates procedure' stated correctly. Question 2 runs both the happy-court and unhappy-court branches of horizontal choice of law. Question 4 finds the pivot — whether the transfer carried Massachusetts preclusion law to the New Hampshire federal court — and traces the mutuality consequence for Ginny. Question 3 is complete. Question 1 is the problem, and it is the biggest question on the exam. The supplemental jurisdiction bar is called 'unclear' when the course treats it as settled; specific personal jurisdiction is built on the effects test rather than purposeful availment and fair and reasonable; venue is one sentence; the plausibility discussion poses its own question and never answers it. Question 5 also runs a rule backwards: small per-member stakes support certification rather than cutting against it.

strengths.label: Domicile treated as the live question it is
strengths.detail: Making the client's jurisdictional argument turn on contested facts rather than on the complaint's label, then tracing the Strawbridge consequence for the whole case, is the move that pays.
strengths.answerExcerpt: If Riddle is MA domiciliary, complete diversity (Strawbridge) broken and no SMJ.

strengths.label: The Erie sequence run to a disposition on each test
strengths.detail: Each approach ends in 'use federal' or 'use state,' and the Ginsburg branch supplies an actual state interest instead of asserting no conflict. This is the strongest passage in the answer.
strengths.answerExcerpt: Ginsburg/Hanna: Same validity analysis, but avoid conflict through applicability prong.

strengths.label: Both choice-of-law branches run, conditioned on the happy court question
strengths.detail: Because you could not resolve whether Massachusetts was a happy court, you ran the analysis on both sides of that question instead of assuming one. The Babcock/Neumeier point — that a state's interest in protecting its own citizens argues against using its law to shield a foreign defendant — uses the factor rather than gesturing at it.
strengths.answerExcerpt: If MA fed court not happy, then NH state HCoL applies (Klaxon). First restatement, so lex loci delicti.

strengths.label: Every avenue closed with a reason, in proportionate space
strengths.detail: Reserved damages defeat finality under 1291, no injunction for 1292(a), no certification for 1292(b), no fully resolved claim for 54(b), plus Cohen and mandamus. This is what a three-point answer should look like.
strengths.answerExcerpt: Not 54(b) because even though there are two claims (Droobles and Riddle), neither is final, and both are extremely related.

strengths.label: Privity distinguished by control, not by status
strengths.detail: Separating Harry from Ginny on the 65% stake, the CEO role, and actually running the business gets privity right for the reason the doctrine cares about. The no-chance-to-appeal argument on 'necessary to the decision' is your own move.
strengths.answerExcerpt: This is likely enough to show that Harry sufficiently controlled HG during the previous litigation.

strengths.label: The contested requirement identified
strengths.detail: Recognizing that a class of this size requires argument from the facts rather than a threshold, then reaching for geographic dispersion, targets the one requirement here that is genuinely in doubt.
strengths.answerExcerpt: There are over 20 but under 40 members, so look at other factors.

strengths.label: Structure obeyed and access to justice made substantive
strengths.detail: One listed proposal, an original second one located inside course doctrine, and real distributional analysis. The repeat-player point and the settlement-pressure distortion are the two best paragraphs on the exam.
strengths.answerExcerpt: corporations and other repeat players in the legal system will easily pick up which issues they must routinely raise, while everyone else will be disadvantaged

improvements.label: Question 1 — resolve the 1367 question instead of leaving it open
improvements.whatHappened: The $50,000 claim against Droobles cannot be aggregated with the claim against Riddle, so it needs supplemental jurisdiction. You wrote that it is 'Unclear after Exxon whether under 1367(b) AIC deficiency defeats supplemental jurisdiction over joined defendant.'
improvements.whyItMatters: The course treats this as settled. Droobles was joined under Rule 20, and 1367(b) ousts supplemental jurisdiction over a plaintiff's claim against a person joined under Rule 20 when it would be inconsistent with 1332's amount requirement. Exxon tolerates amount-deficient claims where the added parties are plaintiffs, not additional defendants. This is the most concrete dismissal ground your client has.
improvements.howToImprove:
Brain off, and walk the taught steps.
1. Name the anchoring claim and its basis: the $950,000 claim against Riddle under 1332.
2. Name the joinder rule that brought Droobles in: Rule 20, same transaction or occurrence.
3. Apply 1367(a) and say what makes it one common nucleus here — the single deepfake scheme and the alleged Riddle–Droobles agreement.
4. Apply 1367(b) and dismiss Count II.
The hedge sentence itself pays for the steps.

improvements.label: Question 1 — specific personal jurisdiction needs the taught framework
improvements.whatHappened: The analysis runs through 'Griffis v. Luban effects test: brunt of tort felt in forum,' and the fair and reasonable prong is never reached.
improvements.whyItMatters: The effects test is not part of this course's personal jurisdiction toolkit, and skipping fairness stops the analysis halfway. The facts you want survive inside the correct framework: direct internet sales shipped to Massachusetts customers go to purposeful availment, and Droobles' knowledge that HG operates only in Massachusetts goes to relatedness.
improvements.howToImprove:
Run the enumerated bases in order.
1. General: Droobles is an individual not domiciled in Massachusetts, and 25% of sales volume is not substantial, continuous, and systematic under Daimler.
2. Specific, contact side: Rule 4(k)(1)(A) borrows the Massachusetts long-arm; direct shipments with no intermediary are purposeful availment; relatedness is the hard part, because the suit arises from the video rather than from gum sales.
3. Specific, fairness side: extent of contacts, defendant's convenience, plaintiff's interest, forum's interest, judicial system's interest including witnesses and evidence, and choice of law.
Deleting the effects-test discussion pays for the fairness step. The record says 25% of sales go to Massachusetts, not the 20% you use against Daimler.

improvements.label: Question 1 — venue needs the subsections walked in order
improvements.whatHappened: Venue is one sentence asserting 1391(b)(2) on the location of the loss of business value.
improvements.whyItMatters: Venue is brain off, and the whole payoff is mechanical completeness. A bare conclusion does not show that you know why the other subsections fail.
improvements.howToImprove:
Three clauses:
1. (b)(1) is unavailable because the two defendants reside in different states.
2. (b)(2) is satisfied, and give more than one fact — the Massachusetts endorsement video, the Riddle–Harry emails on Harry's end, HG's Massachusetts operations.
3. (b)(3) is foreclosed because a proper (b)(2) district exists.
Fund this by cutting the speculation about whether 20% is enough, which the Daimler threshold already answers.

improvements.label: Question 1 — the plausibility analysis is never worked against the complaint
improvements.whatHappened: You state the method, then ask 'There's a good amount of facts alleged, but do they make the claim plausible?' and shift into judicial resources and harassment policy without answering.
improvements.whyItMatters: The exam reproduced the entire complaint, which is the invitation to run the analysis against its text. A recited method earns little; the credit is in matching paragraphs to elements and reaching a conclusion on the element that is actually in doubt.
improvements.howToImprove: Set aside the conclusory portions of paragraph 20, the 'on information and belief' allegation of the scheme, because it asserts the element rather than pleading facts. Then match what remains to the four elements: participation in production, paragraphs 12–14 and 16; false video, paragraphs 12–14; harm to business reputation, paragraphs 6–8; resulting loss of value, paragraphs 18–19. Then answer your own question on the participation element, where the recording made on Droobles' phone, at his request, in his own conference room is your strongest inference. The two closing policy sentences and the 'major assumption' musing pay for it. One note: the course calls this plausibility pleading.

improvements.label: Question 1 — say that Droobles is an individual
improvements.whatHappened: The citizenship discussion never notes that the gum business was never incorporated.
improvements.whyItMatters: One clause forecloses any argument that the business carries its own citizenship.
improvements.howToImprove: Write that Droobles is a New Hampshire citizen by domicile and the unincorporated business generates no separate citizenship. Take the words from the repeated observation that Riddle's domicile is 'questionable.'

improvements.label: Question 2 — the Public Access motion needs the record
improvements.whatHappened: After the choice-of-law work, the merits of Droobles' motion are one clause: 'probably met because of Harry's social media presence.'
improvements.whyItMatters: Droobles bears the burden of persuasion on an affirmative defense, so his production burden is the heavy one, and the answer has to show it carried.
improvements.howToImprove: Name the testimony that establishes constant and ready access — Harry's own account of the website, the social media accounts, the dependence on internet traffic, and his posting of a denunciation video — then say that even reading inferences for HG no genuine dispute remains. Compressing the frankenlaw aside, which you already call neutral, pays for it.

improvements.label: Question 2 — say why memory gaps do or do not create a genuine dispute
improvements.whatHappened: You conclude that Droobles and Riddle 'probably also meet their resulting burden of production: genuine issue of fact for trial in that no memory of the events.'
improvements.whyItMatters: That is the crux of HG's motion, and it is asserted rather than argued. An absence of memory is not affirmative contrary evidence, so the question is whether a jury could rest a verdict on it. Your conclusion may be defensible, but only with that step shown.
improvements.howToImprove: Tie HG's record items to the elements they prove — the email from Droobles' account with the 'Keep this quiet!!!!!' subject line and an attached video matching the deepfake's five-minute-twenty-two-second length, forwarded hours later to an account since deleted, plus Lily Evans' uncontradicted account of being handed the phone. Then say whether professed illness-induced memory loss is enough against that, and why. Cutting the Scott v. Harris framing sentence to a clause pays for it.

improvements.label: Question 4 — weigh both readings of the transfer
improvements.whatHappened: You resolve the Massachusetts-versus-New Hampshire preclusion-law question by advocacy: 'we want a mutuality requirement, though, so argue that the rendering NH federal court's power is what is important.'
improvements.whyItMatters: The entire mutuality outcome turns on this pivot, so the competing reading deserves its merits. If Massachusetts was a happy court, the transfer is a change of courthouse rather than of law, and Massachusetts preclusion rules travel with the case.
improvements.howToImprove: Name the happy court rule and say in a clause what it does to a transfer out of a proper forum. Give the opposing reading a clause, then say which is stronger and why. Cutting the Hart sentence, which currently raises a point and abandons it with 'Hope that it doesn't,' pays for it.

improvements.label: Question 4 — keep the two doctrines separate at the end
improvements.whatHappened: You conclude Harry is claim precluded, then write that 'Harry may still be able to' issue-preclude Droobles.
improvements.whyItMatters: If Harry's personal claim is barred, he has no second suit in which to use issue preclusion, so the sentence reads as a conflation rather than an alternative holding. The labels slip too — it is Ginny, a non-party to the first suit, whose use would be nonmutual and offensive.
improvements.howToImprove: Rewrite that sentence rather than adding one: because Harry is barred, the issue preclusion question matters only for Ginny, whose posture is nonmutual and offensive, and the mutuality rule you selected decides it.

improvements.label: Question 5 — small individual stakes support certification
improvements.whatHappened: You treat the $15,000 per-member figure as an argument against a class: 'these claims aren't small enough to justify a class,' and repeat the inversion under superiority.
improvements.whyItMatters: This runs the rule backwards. Small individual stakes are what make separate suits impractical, so they support numerosity and superiority both. Repeating the inversion compounds it, and it lands on the one requirement genuinely in doubt here.
improvements.howToImprove: Flip it: with roughly $15,000 at stake, no member would rationally sue alone, which together with dispersion across California, Washington, and Oregon makes joinder impracticable. The question expressly excluded subject matter jurisdiction, so cut the Ben-Hur and Exxon opening and spend those words on numerosity and superiority.

improvements.label: Question 6 — take a position and offer a concrete fix
improvements.whatHappened: Both proposals get advantages and disadvantages, but the answer never recommends anything.
improvements.whyItMatters: On fifteen points, evaluating the considerations is the analysis. Concluding that the tension cannot be resolved is allowed, but it has to be stated as a position and defended.
improvements.howToImprove: Add a concrete mitigation for the proposal you would adopt — a case-management or notice mechanism that blunts the cost you identified — and a closing position saying which way you come out and why. Trimming the sideline-sitting paragraph, which repeats the Parklane rationale you already stated, pays for both.

feedback.exampleRevision:
Instead of "Supplemental jurisdiction over Droobles, who is diverse but AIC deficient. Unclear after Exxon whether under 1367(b) AIC deficiency defeats supplemental jurisdiction over joined defendant," work the steps:

Anchor is the $950K claim v. Riddle under 1332 (assuming RI domicile). Count II v. fixtures.bandRationale:
Reference defect lists first. The DS same-exam reference has real flaws: it concludes there is likely no specific PJ over Droobles, its venue discussion wanders into speculative property-location theorizing, its Q4 issue-preclusion section says 'Droobles won no issues in L1: he cannot preclude' without developing offensive/defensive posture, and its Q6 second proposal drifts into simplifying SMJ/PJ/venue rather than an expansion of preclusion. But every one of its six answers runs its analysis to a resolved conclusion with the elements against named facts (Q1 walks each Erie test to a disposition, Q2 marshals element-by-element record support E1–E4, Q4 names Semtek and Marrese and traces mutuality). The P same-exam reference resolves each question but its Q2(b) merits analysis is a paragraph, its Q4 concludes 'not actually litigated... the parties settled' without engaging the summary judgment grant, and its Q6 is competent but thinner on doctrinal mechanics. The LP reference misstates venue outright ('No venue'), leaves Q3 as a single fragment, and diverts Q6 into criminal-law policy. The H comparator (different year, sole H reference, full comparator) has substantial errors too — it hedges the Rule 23 numerosity thresholds oddly ('above the 25 party minimum'), its Erie discussion is diffuse, and parts of its class-action analysis are speculative — but it sustains rich two-sided reasoning across every question it reaches.

Pairwise verdicts. Versus LP: clearly stronger — every question here is resolved with reasoning, no doctrinal inversions of the LP kind, no off-topic policy. Versus P: stronger. This answer's Q3 is complete where P's is a checklist, its Q4 resolves the Semtek/transfer pivot with an advocated position and adds a Rios argument where P concludes 'not actually litigated' without engaging the SJ grant, its Q2 HCOL run is deeper (both branches plus Babcock/Neumeier), and its Q6 is substantially richer in doctrinal mechanics and access-to-justice analysis. P's Q1 is somewhat better on 12(b)(6) (element-by-element with paragraph cites) and on the 1367(b) conclusion, but the overall performance here is broader and deeper. Versus the H comparator: comparable. Both sustain two-sided analysis across the board with real errors on core questions; this answer's Q3 and Q6 are tighter, its Q4 pivot-handling is at least as good, and its Q2 HCOL work matches the comparator's transfer/Ferens analysis in quality. Versus DS: weaker. On the 25-point question the DS reference resolves the 1367(b) question, runs both general and specific PJ to conclusions, develops venue with reasons, and works 12(b)(6) against specific allegations; this answer leaves 1367(b) unresolved, frames PJ on the effects test the course has removed, disposes of venue in one sentence, and abandons its own 12(b)(6) question unanswered. That is a materially thinner performance on the most heavily weighted item. Interval is P-to-DS; the answer sits closer to the H comparator than to either endpoint, so H.
fixtures.whyNotHigher: Not DS because the 25-point question — the largest on the exam — leaves its most concrete dismissal ground ('unclear after Exxon whether under 1367(b) AIC deficiency defeats supplemental jurisdiction') unresolved, frames specific PJ on an effects test rather than purposeful availment plus fairness and never runs the fairness prong, disposes of venue in a single sentence, and poses but never answers the plausibility question. The DS reference, whatever its own outcome errors, carries each of those paths to a framed resolution.
fixtures.whyNotLower: Not P because the core analyses are resolved rather than underdeveloped: Q3 is complete, Q4 identifies and argues the MA/NH rendering-court pivot with a consequence traced through mutuality plus an original Rios argument, Q2 runs both HCOL branches with state-interest reasoning and correctly allocates the summary judgment burdens, and Q6 obeys the prompt structure with genuine doctrinal mechanics and integrated access-to-justice analysis. That is a better total performance than the P reference across four of six questions. Lean is low because the weighted Q1 defects (1367(b), effects test, one-sentence venue, unanswered 12(b)(6)) press toward the P boundary.
