fixtures.label: 2019 answer — LP
fixtures.answer:
1.

SMJ

AUJ: Probably no fed COA (Mottley/Holmes), but maybe Smith-Grable AUJ. Congress has substantial federal interest in passing Business Disparagement (BD). However, using fed jurisdiction for state-law COA might overwhelm federal court with cases. Also fact-bound, not just law. Likely no AUJ.

DJ: HG is citizen of MA with nerve center. Hertz. DD is citizen of NH. TR is RI citizen but might be citizen of MA for paying taxes, job, home there. If TR MA citizen, no DJ. If TR RI citizen, DJ exists. Claims alleging joint liability against multiple defendants valued on entire amount claimed so million$ meets AIC. Likely DJ.

Venue

No venue under §1391(b)(1): defendants domiciled in NH and RI, not MA. No venue under

§1392(b)(2): substantial events happened in DD estate in NH. Under §1391(b)

(3) no venue since action may be brought somewhere else. No venue.

PJ

No general IPJ, since DD domiciled in NH, TR domiciled RI and will likely object to PJ. Federal court "piggy-backs" on the long-arm statute of the state in which it sits. 4(k)(1)(a). MA, RI, NH all have long-arm going to lengths of constitution. BD is substantive not procedural and fed court in diversity uses COL in state sits in for substantive. Klaxon. RI/NH 1st restatement so blood in NH video filmed in DD house. MA 2nd restatement so has substantial interest because all businesses in MA and center of gravity there, with TR having home there.

Minimal contacts: TR works/has home in Boston and DD ships products to MA so availed themselves to MA. International Shoe, McGee. TR has home in Boston and HG in Boston so convenient there and fair. RI only 1-hour train ride from Boston so arguably fair too. However, NH is further by train to MA, 3 hours, so might not be fair. Shorter drive 1 hour so possibly fair. IPJ exists.

Due Process

Notice

Likely timely enough to respond (Roller), method appropriate (Flowers), but maybe not adequate information, but will detail why in Eerie.

Opportunity to be heard

Damages so no property at stake. Plaintiff has to show Clerk signed off so not wrongful. Little risk of erroneous deprivation.

Eerie

Conflict between FRCP4(a)(1) and MARCP4(a)(1), also requiring separate paper on summons form detailing courthouse address and nearest public transportation to courthouse. If using FRCP, don’t dismiss. If MARCP, dismiss. Issue seems procedural so substantive in VCOL, use Eerie analysis.

Also conflict with federal business disparagement (BD) law and MA BD law, with public access defense stating that plaintiff can’t recover if has access to public or media. Use Eerie.

York: Outcome determinative since outcome dependent on state vs. fed law so state rule in effect since using FRCP and MARCP differ in results and federal vs MA BD law differ in results.

Harlan: Is primary conduct affected?

For MACP4(a)(1) probably not since moved forward procedural purpose to increase access to adequate notice of due process. Could argue that hinders lawyering in making them do more work, but not the primary conduct. Probably use federal law.

For BD, could argue that HG legally savvy large entity, can affect pre-litigation conduct. However, in this case, pre-litigation conduct probably wouldn’t differ as HG denounced video and then sued. Probably use federal law.

Scalia SG: FRCP is source of law so use valid and applicable test. REA really regulates procedure so valid (Sibbach), not substantive right to  “abridge, enlarge, or modify” lawsuits. Applicable since both rules have to do with summons forms and Supremacy clause so use fed law.

Supremacy clause for federal BD law vs MA BD law so fed law overrules state law.

Ginsburg SG: Similar to Scalia test, but FRCP4(a)(1) applied narrowly (Walker) to preference state policy and elude conflict. MA implies interest in requiring lawyers write out separate paper on summons form detailing courthouse address and nearest public transportation to courthouse. Therefore, state’s interest overrules.  Don’t use FRCP and instead MARCP.

For BD, MA also has interest in judicial efficiency since savvy entities with access to public and media can probably counter falsehoods in media and not need to go to court for frivolous lawsuit. Probably use MA BD law.

Stevens SG: FOR CP4(a)(1) and BD, Stevens might side with Ginsburg since fed law can’t displace state law if intertwined with state-created right. However, might side with Scalia since in inquiry necessary to sort out whether a state procedural rule, would probably find doesn’t count as substantive right or remedy to overrule FRCP or fed BD law.

2.

To succeed summary judgment, HG has to show

1. That there is no disputed material of issue of fact and succeed in a motion for summary judgment, a movant must show

2. Movant entitled to judgment as matter of law

Yet evidence viewed more favorably to nonmoving party.

3. If couldn’t appeal, then likely not necessary to decision.

4.

Claim preclusion

CP doesn’t apply to DD because can only be offensive posture.

CP requires same claim, same parties, and final judgment on the merits. It is efficient to try these cases together and they are logically related with a central nucleus of fact. Harry and Ginny have the same claim of BD. For Harry or Ginny, they are part of HG as shareholders so claim preclusion in MA, NH, and RI might apply. Gonzalez. However, can be argued that since there are more stakeholders that they might not be same party. Settlements can count as on the merits in final judgment because the parties already decided appropriate money and for an efficient judicial economy we wouldn’t want renegotiations coming back to court or going to other courts.  Harry and Ginny can likely CP.

Issue Preclusion

For Harry and Ginny, if Smith-Grable AUJ, then probably no IP since federal judgments should be similar across the board. Parklane. Yet Harry and Ginny joining the lawsuit might have ruined diversity. This can promote a wait and see attitude which court wouldn’t want for inefficiency.  For DD, non-mutual defensive collateral estoppel is usually allowed. Blonder-Tongue. If same parties, we as D want to preclude P from relitigating an issue we lost on. Since TR gave money we say we lost. Plaintiff can say they didn’t have fair opportunity in court but have to prove it. For DD, likely IP.

5.

Commonality, Numerousity, Typicality, Representativeness needed in FRCP23a to be considered class action.

Commonality

Commonality of evidence can be the same since Harry, Ginny, and HG will use emails, video, and other forms of evidence discovered above. However, we could argue that Harry, Ginny, and HG did not suffer the same injury as Ginny suffered substantially less financially, Harry had his reputation hurt (non-financial), and HG also lost a lot of money, HCOL can also end commonality since different state laws applied. However, NH is 1st restatement so MA law will apply so there is likely commonality.

Numerousity

If below 20 plaintiffs, likely to lose. If above 40, likely to win. HG made up of Harry, Ginny, and 20 other stakeholders, so has numerousity. Since other stakeholders mostly in Western states, court also more likely to certify claims. Since amount in controversy is large amount, a million$, court likely to certify class.

Typicality

The named plaintiffs, Harry and Ginny, likely have similar incentives, to recoup losses they incurred from TR and DD.

Representativeness

We want to determine if class members were aggrieved in the same way as named plaintiffs. We could argue that since Harry and Ginny have more at stake, they were aggrieved in a different way from other plaintiffs and not representative. We could also say that differences in state law from other plaintiffs could create different incentives so Harry and Ginny not representative. Anchem. However, it is more likely that since Harry, Ginny, and other stakeholders of HG all lost money due to reputation loss, despite different stakes, Harry and Ginny are representative and aggrieved in the same way, with people not likely precluded.

23(b)

Not likely limited fund restriction since more for bankruptcy cases where only certain amount of money that D can pay so runs out. Not a structural 23(b)(2) case seeking injunctive relief. Likely falls under damages class actions.

Damages

Superiority

If million$ considered large individual claim, class action not needed. If considered small, likely needed and superior. Class member interests are similar so likely superior. However, HCOl differences in state law might make better for individual suits.

Predominance

If already proved commonality, probably proved predominance.

6.

Expanding claim preclusion to any claims that could have been brought in the first case would create many sweeping changes. In favor of expanding CP, judicial resources would be conserved even further. If you can’t try another case for similar reasons, then P is incentivized to bring in all evidence at once and finality will make it so the court will not waste money on cases with a similar result or using the same evidence. Lawyers will have fewer lawsuits so either get paid more per lawsuit or become less relevant in general. We can prevent the P from pestering the D with numerous, often frivolous lawsuits. If P will forum shop, we can ensure that they choose the forum of their liking.

However, expanding CP to any claims that could have been brought up in the first case also creates many issues. Those who cannot afford a lawyer or an adequate lawyer will face severe access to justice problems. In criminal cases, those who are falsely convicted will not be able to bring in new discovered evidence and will therefore remain wrongfully convicted. With public defenders being stacked against the D.A., police evidence, and public sentiment to crack down on crime, defendants are likely to lose. Since defendants will be more likely to rely on public defenders, and public defenders are overworked already, the issue of false convictions will severely worsen. One possible alternative is that cities will hire more public defenders to stop the increased urgency of false convictions, but this is unlikely.

In civil cases, those who cannot afford an adequate lawyer will probably be more likely to lose a case since those with money can hire expensive firm lawyers to gather all of this evidence through discovery and the lawyers that defendants have will not be able to compete and be more likely to lose the case. In our unequal capitalist society, those with less money will face further hardships, deepening inequality. However, one could argue that for civil cases, the urgency of finality in expanding CP would help non-lawyers become more active in representing people, civil right to counsel could become a possibility, or know your rights programs would become more common for pro se litigants to defend themselves more accurately, especially considering the high rate of pro se litigants in general in civil suits. Still, it isn’t likely that these positive outcomes would come from expanding CP. It is more likely that the negatives would expand. For example, cities might try and blanket target people for tickets or other simple quality of life offenses to continue making money off of them. Since many low-SES and POC will not be able to win their cases, the cities will reap huge financial profits with little incentive to do otherwise. Therefore, marginalized communities would likely become more over-policed and marginalized in general.

feedback.headline: Strong Erie work; Questions 2 and 3 and half of Question 6 are unanswered
feedback.overview: Your best analysis is the vertical choice-of-law run on the Massachusetts summons rule in Question 1: York, Harlan on primary conduct, Scalia and Ginsburg under Shady Grove with the narrow-construction move from Walker, Stevens, and the Rules Enabling Act point stated in the form the course expects. Question 5 is proportionate and mostly sound. The rest is a completeness problem. Question 2 carries eleven points and is effectively unanswered. Question 3 contains no appealability analysis. Question 1 loses two of its largest components, the section 1367 bar and the entire 12(b)(6) run. Question 4 never reaches the question of which state's preclusion law governs after the transfer, which is what the exam built the two mutuality regimes to generate. Question 6 answers half of what it asks and spends its longest stretch on criminal law.

improvements.label: The amount in controversy against Droobles, and then section 1367
improvements.whatHappened: You wrote that joint-liability claims against multiple defendants are valued at the entire amount claimed, so the million-dollar figure satisfies the amount in controversy. The request for relief seeks only $50,000 from Droobles, and a single plaintiff cannot aggregate across defendants to reach $75,000.
improvements.whyItMatters: This is the one subject-matter jurisdiction defect specific to your client, and it is the hinge of the question. The wrong aggregation rule closes off the whole supplemental jurisdiction analysis.
improvements.howToImprove:
Run it as steps.
1. Name the anchoring claim: the $950,000 claim against Riddle under 1332, complete diversity under Strawbridge, turning on the domicile conclusion you already reached.
2. Ask whether Rule 20 joinder is proper, both claims arising from the one deepfake scheme.
3. Ask whether the Droobles claim shares a common nucleus with the anchoring claim, and say what makes it one: same video, same recording session, same loss of value.
4. Apply the 1367(b) carve-out, which bars supplemental jurisdiction over a plaintiff's claim against a person joined under Rule 20 where it would be inconsistent with 1332's amount requirement.
The due process and "Opportunity to be heard" passage and the Supremacy Clause sentences pay for it.

improvements.label: The 12(b)(6) ground is missing entirely
improvements.whatHappened: The exam reproduces the complaint in full and you never test it under plausibility pleading. No paragraph is sorted and Iqbal appears nowhere.
improvements.whyItMatters: A complaint printed in full is the exam's clearest signal that a plausibility run is wanted, and this is one of the largest scoring blocks in a 25-point question.
improvements.howToImprove:
Work the sequence against the paragraphs.
1. Set aside paragraph 20's "on information and belief" allegations as conclusory.
2. Match what remains to the four elements the exam supplies: participation in the production; a false video; harm to the business's reputation or standing; that harm causing loss of value. Paragraphs 12-14 go to the fake video, paragraph 16 to the recording made on Droobles' own phone at his own request, paragraph 11 to Riddle's threat, paragraphs 6-8 and 18-19 to injury and loss of value.
3. Say whether what survives nudges Droobles' participation from possible to plausible, and name the element that fails if one does.
The "For BD" segments you added under York, Harlan, Scalia and Ginsburg pay for it. There is no federal business disparagement law in this problem; the exam says the tort exists in all fifty-one states.

improvements.label: Specific personal jurisdiction stops at one contact sentence
improvements.whatHappened: You have the long-arm and the 4(k)(1)(A) piggyback, and no general jurisdiction. Then minimum contacts is one sentence about shipping gum to Massachusetts. You never ask whether gum shipments relate to a deepfake claim, and none of the facts pointing the other way appear: no advertising, no salesforce, no solicitation, a website that only responds to visitors. Fairness is reduced to train travel times.
improvements.whyItMatters: Relatedness and the fairness factors are where the points sit on this ground, and relatedness here is genuinely contestable in both directions.
improvements.howToImprove: After the piggyback step, argue contacts on both sides: direct shipment to Massachusetts customers without an intermediary as purposeful availment, contrasted with Nicastro stream-of-commerce, then the exculpatory facts above. Add Daimler to the general jurisdiction line, since 25% of sales is not an at-home affiliation. Then run fairness and reasonableness on Massachusetts's interest in protecting a Massachusetts business, where the evidence of harm sits, and party convenience. The train-time and driving-distance sentences pay for it.

improvements.label: Venue decided on a single clause
improvements.whatHappened: You closed off 1391(b)(1) and 1391(b)(3) correctly, then rejected 1391(b)(2) on the sole ground that substantial events happened at the New Hampshire estate.
improvements.whyItMatters: 1391(b)(2) asks whether a substantial part of the events occurred in the district, not where the most events occurred, and your Question 4 answer depends on whether Massachusetts was a happy court.
improvements.howToImprove: Weigh the Massachusetts events: the endorsement video on the Boston Common, Harry's side of the email exchange, HG's Massachusetts operations, and the loss of business value felt there. Then state whether Massachusetts is a happy court. The Stevens paragraph, which adds little to your Scalia and Ginsburg discussions, pays for it.

improvements.label: Neither summary judgment motion is analyzed

improvements.whyItMatters: Eleven points sit here, and this question is a record-marshalling exercise. A standard stated without application earns almost nothing.

For Droobles: he carries the burden of persuasion on the Public Access defense, and Harry's own testimony about the website and social accounts establishes constant and ready public access. For HG: attach record items to each of the four elements (participation in production; false video; harm to reputation; loss of value) — the "Keep this quiet!!!!!" email with the .mp4, the identical five minute twenty-two second runtime, the forward to the anonymous account, and Evans's testimony that Droobles summoned her and had her record on his own phone. The wrongful-conviction and public-defender paragraph in Question 6 pays for it.

improvements.label: The choice-of-law chain that decides whether the defense exists
improvements.whatHappened: The Public Access defense exists only in Massachusetts, and the case sits in a New Hampshire federal court after transfer. You never ask whether Massachusetts law applies there. The sentences you wrote under the Question 1 personal jurisdiction heading also put the last event completing the tort in New Hampshire, at the filming.
improvements.whyItMatters: Without this chain Droobles' motion has no legal basis at all. The exam tells you the last event necessary to complete business disparagement is the loss of business value, and that landed in Massachusetts.
improvements.howToImprove: Run the chain: a federal diversity court uses the forum state's horizontal choice-of-law rules under Klaxon; on transfer from a happy court the transferee court keeps the transferor's choice-of-law analysis (Ferens), pointing to Massachusetts and its Second Restatement approach; New Hampshire's First Restatement gets you to Massachusetts too, because the loss of value occurred there. Then weigh the place-of-injury presumption against the New Hampshire meeting and recording, and conclude. Move the horizontal choice-of-law sentences from under the Question 1 personal jurisdiction heading down here rather than writing new ones.

improvements.label: No appealability analysis
improvements.whatHappened: The only sentence under this heading is about preclusion firmness, and it assumes the answer instead of giving it.
improvements.whyItMatters: Three points for a short checklist makes this the cheapest scoring on the exam.
improvements.howToImprove:
Walk the routes, one line each.
1. Section 1291: no final decision, damages reserved and no judgment entered.
2. Rule 54(b): no express determination and no partial final judgment directed.
3. Section 1292(a)(1): no injunction.
4. Section 1292(b): no certification by the district court.
5. Cohen collateral order: a liability ruling goes to the merits and is reviewable after final judgment, so nothing is effectively unreviewable later.
6. Mandamus: no irreparable harm or usurpation of power.
The repeated horizontal choice-of-law objections in Question 5 pay for these lines.

improvements.label: Which state's preclusion law governs after the transfer
improvements.whatHappened: Judgment was entered in New Hampshire in a case filed in Massachusetts. Massachusetts has abolished mutuality and New Hampshire keeps it, so the two produce opposite results for Ginny. The question is never raised.
improvements.whyItMatters: This is intersystem preclusion, and the exam supplies the two mutuality regimes precisely to generate the conflict. It decides the outcome for Ginny.
improvements.howToImprove: Name the issue as intersystem preclusion and run it with Semtek. Then resolve the transfer wrinkle out of your Question 1 conclusions: if Massachusetts was a happy court, the transfer is a change of courthouse and Massachusetts preclusion law follows, so Ginny can use NMOCE; if Massachusetts venue or personal jurisdiction was lacking, New Hampshire's strict mutuality defeats her because she was not a party in the same posture. Either resolution earns credit if you reason to it. The Smith-Grable and diversity-spoiling asides pay for it.

improvements.label: The preclusion postures are pointed the wrong way
improvements.whatHappened: You open with the statement that claim preclusion cannot apply to Droobles because it works only offensively. Droobles, as the defendant in the second suit, is exactly the party who raises it against Harry. You then conclude that Droobles can use nonmutual defensive collateral estoppel, but he lost the summary judgment ruling and holds no issue he could preclude on.

improvements.howToImprove: Keep the two doctrines separate and walk each. Claim preclusion against Harry: same claim arising from the deepfake, final judgment on the merits (your judicial-economy argument for the stipulated dismissal is good), and party identity through privity. Then run privity on the facts, which is what splits Harry from Ginny: his 65% stake and control of the HG litigation against her 5% and no showing of control. Issue preclusion: same issue, actually litigated, necessary to the judgment, plus both sides of whether a revisable summary judgment ruling is firm enough. Rewrite the Blonder-Tongue sentences in place rather than adding words.

improvements.label: The stakes argument runs backwards

improvements.whyItMatters: It is the small per-member stake, roughly $15,000 each, that makes individual suits impractical and supports both numerosity and superiority.
improvements.howToImprove: Say that each holder's share of the $1,000,000 is small, so joinder is impracticable and one adjudication beats twenty suits. Drop the horizontal choice-of-law objection, which your own Question 1 reasoning already answers.

improvements.label: The invented second proposal is missing

improvements.whyItMatters: Roughly half of a 15-point question is unattempted.

Expanding privity to bind persons whose interests were effectively represented is one workable option: on the claim preclusion side it makes intervention nearly compulsory, and it runs into the limits on binding absentees without notice under Mullane. The over-policing and municipal-ticketing passage pays for it.

Declaratory judgment practice combined with expansion lets a sophisticated party force all disputes into a forum it selects, and forum choice matters because of horizontal choice of law under Klaxon. Rule 42 gives the trial judge severance and ordering tools to contain the resulting complexity. Keep the access-to-justice argument. The civil-right-to-counsel and know-your-rights sentences, which you discount immediately afterward, pay for it.

fixtures.bandRationale: Reference defects first, so both sides of each comparison carry a real list. The DS reference concludes there is no specific PJ over Droobles and no venue problem it fully resolves, hedges the on-the-merits question in Q4, and its Q2 liability analysis leaves element three unresolved. The H reference invokes an effects-test framing that is outside the current course, is uncertain about 1367(b) after Exxon, and treats the defendants' memory gaps as enough to defeat summary judgment without much interrogation. The P reference asserts a $50,000 AIC defect but then hangs supplemental jurisdiction on it loosely, concludes Harry and Ginny are both claim precluded without splitting them, and treats $15,000 per member as defeating numerosity and superiority. Pairwise verdicts. Versus DS: far weaker — the DS answer resolves every weighted question, including a full 12(b)(6), both summary judgment motions with burden allocation, the complete appealability list, and Semtek-driven mutuality. Versus H: weaker — the H answer runs an Erie sequence comparable to this student's but also resolves 1367(b), both SJ motions with Celotex, the appeal routes, and the MA/NH preclusion choice, and completes both halves of Q6. Versus P: weaker — the P answer covers every question with real application, including a paragraph-and-element 12(b)(6), an HCOL-anchored Public Access analysis, both Celotex motions, the happy-court preclusion choice, and two developed Q6 proposals with course citations; this student leaves an 11-point question and a 3-point question effectively blank, omits 12(b)(6), and completes only half of a 15-point question. The LP reference covers everything it is asked but disposes of weighted cores conclusorily and with inversions; this answer has a better Erie run and a stronger Rule 23 discussion, but pays for it with two skipped questions, an inverted AIC rule that swallows the supplemental jurisdiction core, an inverted claim-preclusion posture rule, and a policy question that is half-done and largely off-topic. fixtures.answer:
## Question 1

SMJ:

       No AUJ: No Federal COA. No imbedded Federal issue, so no smith-grable

exception.

       No DJ: Insufficient AIC, so no DJ. Citizenship: HG=MA(PPoB & Place of
Incorporation). DD is a citizen of NH. However, AIC is only $50k.

       SJ: Maybe there's SJ because this claim ("Claim 2," against DD) is from the same
case/controversy as Claim 1 (against TMR). Since SJ has to be anchored by Claim 1, we
first analyze SMJ over the Claim 1.

SMJ over Claim 1:

       No AUJ: No Federal COA. No imbedded Federal issue, so no smith-grable
exception.

       DJ: Probably yes. $950k AIC is sufficient, and parties are probably diverse.
Citizenship: HG=MA(PPoB & Place of Incorporation). TMR is probably domiciled in
RI. Although TMR bought an apartment in MA and pays MA tax, he still returns to his
RI home every weekend (and he votes in RI). Buying an apartment and paying taxes in
MA is probably insufficient to change where he's domiciled since he returns to his RI

residence every weekend (Mas v. Perry).

IPJ: We should look at IPJ over TMR too because the Court might decline to exercise SJ
over Claim 2 if Claim 1 (the anchoring claim) got dismissed (1367(c)(4)).

General IPJ: No general IPJ over either TMR or DD. GenIPJ over TMR only if he's an
MA citizen (probably not, discussion in DJ). TMR has systemic and continuous presence
in MA (Shoe, Perkins), but General IPJ based on continuous presence probably does not
apply to individuals. No GenIPJ over DD. He's a NH citizen.

Specific IPJ: There might be specific IPJ over both TMR and DD(Calder v. Jones, but
see Griffis v. Luban). HG can argue that TMR and DD intentionally aimed their tortious
conduct to MA residents, so there should be specific IPJ (Calder). MA was the focal
point of HG's injury. HG's main audience is probably MA residence since all of the
photographs and videos Harry makes feature MA landmarks. However, TMR and DD
can argue that mere knowledge that HG and its audience resides in MA is not sufficient to

establish that the defamation was directed at MA residents (Griffis).

Venue: Probably proper under 1391(b)(2). Venue would be proper under b1 if TMR is an
MA residence (but probably not). Not proper under b3 (venue would be proper in RI/NH
court). The loss of value of HG occurs in MA, and this is "a substantial part of the events
giving rise to the claim" (last event necessary). So, proper under 1391(b)(2).

Failure to State a Claim: Under Twiqbal plausibility pleading, we must establish

plausibility with sufficient factual support, striking out conclusory statements. The
complaint states a claim with sufficient specificty. We ignore ¶14 and the last two
sentences of ¶20 for being conclusory. Analyze each element of Business Disparagement:
(i) Evidence of participation via anonymous email
(ii) Allegedly false video beacuse Harry never set foot at Drooble's estate (¶13)

(iii) Evidence of reputation harm via youtube video
(iv) Evidence of loss of value via drop in ads revenue
Complaint is nudged accross the line from possible to plausible.

4(a)(1): MARCP requires an additional paper with the address of the courthouse and a
description of the nearest public tranportation. FRCP does not require this. There's a
VCOL issue here. Hooray, Erie!

Under York, the difference would be outcome determinative for the whole suit. Apply
state law.

Under Harlan in Hanna, the difference probably will not affect anyone's pre-litigation
connduct. Apply FRCP.

Under Hanna majority/Scalia, Rule 4(a)(1) directly speaks to the question at issue
(applicable) and probably really regulate procedure (Sibbach). Therefore, it is valid under
the REA. Apply FRCP.

Under Walker/Ginsburg analysis, we can narrowly construe FRCP 4(1)(a) as merely

setting a minimum requirement, but open to any additional requirements. MARCP
4(a)(1)(H) merely sets additional requirements not inconsistent with the FRCP.
Therefore, state law controls.

The Erie tests give mixed results. Dismiss if MARCP applies, otherwise probably not.

HCOL issue? Probably not because MARCP rule is clearly procedural for HCOL
purpose, so no need to do HCOL analysis here. Apply procedural law of the forum state
(MA).

-------------------------------------------

-------------------------------------------

## Question 2

TMR and DD probably met at their office. The email and mp4 are strong evidence
establishing the meeting between TMR and DD. Neither TMR or DD affirmatively
denied that they had a meeting (but they said they have no memory of it). However, HG
has no evidence regarding the modification of video.

(a)

HCOL issue is important here. If MA Public Access Defense ("PAD")applies, then DD's
summary judgment may be granted. Otherwise, no. Whether PAD applies is a substantive
law issue (not procedural), so apply NH HCOL rule (1st restatement). We apply the law
of the state where the last act necessary to complete the tort occured (lex loci deliciti).

The loss of value of HG occurs in MA, and this is last event necessary to complete the
tort of "Business Dispagaragement." So, MA substantive law applies and PAD can be
asserted.

Apply Celotex (Brennnan), first, to DD's motion. DD has the burden of persuasion at
trial because PAD is an affirmative defense. DD has to show that HG has "constant and
ready access to the public or media outlets." Can DD produce evidence that, if
unrebutted, would compel any reasonable jury finding in his favor? Probably yes. ¶6, 7,

which Harry himself testified for, are probably strong evidence that DD can assert PAD.
It's clear that HG has access to various media outlets (¶6). In addition, the fact that HG
can generate revenues from Ads is a strong evidence that HG as a significant number of
audience (¶7).

Now, burden of production shifts to HG. HG would have a hard time trying to show they
do not have constant and ready access to the public. Therefore, Summary Judgement for
DD based on PAD will probably be granted.

(b)

Apply Celotex (Brennnan) to HG's motion. HG has the burden of persuasion at trial to
show that DD and TMR are liable for Business Disparagement. Can HG produce
evidence that, if unrebutted, would compel any reasonable jury finding in his favor?
Probably no. HG can probably establish that a meeting occured between DD and TMR. In
addition, they may claim the YouTube video and TMR's "your company will be worth

less" statement evince that DD and TMR modified and distributed the false video.
However, that's not a very strong argument. A jury may reasonably believe that another
person obtained the mp4 without DD's or TMR's knowledge, modified it, and distributed
it (DD and TMR might have nothing to do with this). Therefore, HG's motion for
summary juddment will not succeed.

-------------------------------------------

-------------------------------------------

## Question 3

Not appealable. Damage has not been awarded. Not a final judgment, so not appealable
(Liberty Mutual). No injunction. No issue collateral to the merits. No trial Judge
recitation for double discretion 1292(b). No certification for Rule 54(b). No special harm
for mandamus.

-------------------------------------------

-------------------------------------------

## Question 4

Claim Preclusion: Harry and Ginny are claim precluded.

         Same claim. The complaint by Harry and Ginny ("Ha&Gi") clearly assert the same
claim. That is, Business Disparagement based on Riddle/Harry deepfake video.

         Same party (in privity). Ha&Gi are in privity with HG (Gonzalez). Harry is the
CEO and the Chair of the Board. Ginny is the Vice President of the Board. They probably
exercised substantial control over the initial litigation ("L1") by HG. In addition, Ha&Gi
probably got some money from L1 settlement. So, their interest has been adequately
represented.

         Final Judgment on the Merit. L1 dismissal through settlement is probably
considered on the merit. First, as a policy matter, the interest of Ha&Gi was clearly
represented in L1. Second, the settlement with HG only makes sense if HG's shareholders
would be claim precluded. DD and TMR would be effectively paying double damage for
their tort if HG's shareholders are not claim precluded. Finally, the trial court issued a
judgment "with prejudice," indicating that the same claim should not be brought back to
court.

Issue Preclusion:

       Interstate Preclusion. The New Hampshire State Court should at least apply as
much preclusion as the court that renders the judgment in L1 (Semtek). However, which
one is the "rendering" court? MA or NH Fed Court? If the MA Fed Court was a Happy

Court, then a strong argument can be made that the transfer to NH Fed Court was merely
a change of courtroom. So, MA preclusion law should apply. However, a
counterargument can be made by applealing to simplicity. It'd be simpler if we can
determine the applicable preclusion law just by looking to the court that actually renders
the judgment. In this case, it's the NH Fed Court. So maybe NH preclusion law applies. If
MA Fed Court was the "rendering" court, then NH State Court need to apply no
mutuality for IP. Otherwise, apply NH strict mutuality requirement.

       Same issue. Clearly the same issue (Business Disparagement based on
Riddle/Harry deepfake video).

       Same parties. Not an issue if we're giving as much preclusive effect as MA IP law
(no mutuality). If NH law applies, then L2 does not have the same party as L1 (but can
we argue they're in privity, therefore the same "plaintiff"? maybe not), so no IP.

       Not actually litigated. The issue was not actually litigated in court. The parties
settled.

       May not be necessary to the decision. Unclear what motivates the settlement since

the discussion were not made public.

Therefore, no issue preclusion, but there's claim preclusion.

## Question 5

Under Rule 23, we need to consider four things:

- Commonality: Class members suffered the same injury (reduction in share value). The
claim depends on a common contention, that DD committed Business Disparagement,
capable of class wide resolution. Difference of damage awards to different members
should not be an issue here because it can be prorated. There might also be a different
HCOL issue here because plaintiffs are located in different states.

- Typicallity: Harry and Ginny have the same incentive as the other class members (to
get as much damage awards as they can).

- Representativeness: Harry and Ginny are probably representative. Although they own
more shares in the company compared to other members, this is probably insufficient to
cast doubt on their representativeness. Their interest is clearly alligned with other
shareholders here.

- Numerosity: Unclear because the number of class members is between 20 and 40. Is it
practicable for each member to bring their own lawsuit? probably. Each of the 1.5%
shareholders have $15k at stake here, so each of them can probably bring their own suit.

Plaintiffs are quite diverse (from four different states), so court are more likely to
consider the numerosity prong fulfilled.

Rule 23 requirements are probably met. This is a damages class action under 23(b)(3), so
there's two additional prong to fulfill.

- Superiorirty: All plaintiff have at least $15k of claim, so it's unclear whether a class
action is superior. Furthermore, there's might be a HCOL issue here because plaintiffs are
located in different states.

- Predominance: Common issue certainly predominate. See Commonality.

On balance, we can probably defeat class action by contesting
Commonality/Numerosity/Superiority.

## Question 6

       The first suggestion exapands issue preclusion by barring the losing party from
litigating an issue they could have raised in Litigation 1. This will surely promote
efficiency. By enforcing this rule, parties will not be able to "test out" their arguments in
multiple law suits. Rather, they will be incentivized to raise all issues and arguments to
win Litigation 1.

       However, the proposed rule face an issue more problematic than gratuitious
decision (Rios). Applying this new rule, it is entirely possible for a non-decision to have a
preclusive effect (even when the issue has never been litigated!). This is especially
problematic when combined with the lack of mutuality requirement (e.g. NY issue
preclusion law). If this new proposal were to be implemented, it has to be safe-guarded

by strict mutuality requirement. Non-mutual party should not be issue precluded just
because a different party in L1 did not raise the issue, especially if the non-mutual party
in L2 could not have joined L1. We need to make sure that a party had their full day in
court before precluding them (Marrese). Mutuality requirement will likely solve this
issue. As a policy matter, it's probably not unfair to issue preclude a party who chose not
to raise the relevant issue in the previous litigation.

       Furthermore, expanding preclusion rule can be burdensome for indigent litigant

since they might not understand complicated legal rules (Lassiter, Vitek). Applying this
rule, pro se litigants might be unjustly precluded in subsequent cases because they did not
bring up the relevant issue when they could have. One way to solve this problem is to
apply the new rule only to parties who are able to afford counsel.

         Another possible way to expand issue preclusion is to dispense with the "necessary
to the decision" requirement. This new rule would dispense with both the necessary and
finality element. For example, if an issue has been decided in Litigation #1, Court #2
adjudicating Litigation #2 need not wait until Litigation #1 goes to judgment to issue
preclude.

         Since litigation often takes a long time, dispensing with the "finality" requirement -
and by implication, the "necessary" requirement - can be beneficial, especially when an
important issue is decided relatively early. Under the current issue preclusion law,
subsequent courts are unable to use that decision to issue preclude because there's no
judgment yet. In contrast, under the new rule, subsequent courts do not have to wait for

L1 judgment to issue preclude. This will promote efficiency since litigation can take a
long time to reach judgment. In the meantime, other courts might be litigating the same
issue.

         However, there are significant drawbacks with this proposal. A decision on an issue
might be gratuitious (Rios), and we do not want gratuitious decision to preclude
subsequent litigants. In response to this criticism, it can be argued that if this proposed
rule is in place, courts - knowing that their decisions can be grounds for preclusion - will

no longer make "gratuitious" decision. Although, it is unclear if this response is
convincing. Furthermore, a decision regarding an issue might change during the course of
the litigation as new evidence comes to light. One possible way to mitigate this criticism
is by requiring that to have a preclusive effect, the decision has to be "reasonably certain"
and "unlikely to change."

       My proposed expansion of issue preclusion may be beneficial for pro se litigants.
Indigent litigants might not have the knowledge or resources to go to trial. By expanding
issue preclusion, pro se litigants can "piggy back" on others who have litigated the same
issue (even when there's no judgment yet). In addition, the proposal can be interpreted as
an attempt to simplify and "level down" our legal process (Turner). Removing the
"necessary to the decision" requirements for issue preclusion will make it easier for pro-
se litigants to use issue preclusion rules to their benefit.

feedback.headline: Complete coverage and a full Erie run; four decisive steps missing or inverted on the heaviest questions
feedback.overview: Your strongest work is the summons-rule problem in Question 1. You identify the vertical choice-of-law question, run York, Harlan, Hanna/Scalia with the Rules Enabling Act and Sibbach, and Ginsburg's narrow-construction route, then say what follows for the motion. The 12(b)(6) run is also real work: named paragraphs set aside, then each tort element matched to record paragraphs. Four steps that decide outcomes, however, are missing or inverted, and all sit on heavily weighted material. Question 1 raises supplemental jurisdiction and then abandons it, so Count II never gets a bottom line. Question 1's specific jurisdiction turns on where the harm was aimed, without the long-arm step, purposeful availment, or fairness weighing. Question 2 picks New Hampshire's choice-of-law rules without asking whether the Massachusetts court was a happy court. Question 4 declares the issue never actually litigated even though summary judgment had been granted on participation, which closes off the non-mutual estoppel question your own preclusion-law work was building toward.

strengths.label: Complete Erie sequence on the Massachusetts summons rule
strengths.detail: You treat a fictional state rule with no federal counterpart as a vertical choice-of-law problem and run all four tests, including the Rules Enabling Act plus Sibbach formulation and Ginsburg's floor-versus-additional-requirement reading of FRCP 4. Naming the mixed results and then stating what follows for the motion is what the question wanted.
strengths.answerExcerpt: The Erie tests give mixed results. Dismiss if MARCP applies, otherwise probably not.

strengths.label: Plausibility pleading worked at the paragraph and element level
strengths.detail: Cutting specific paragraphs before testing what remains, then tying each element of the tort to record paragraphs, is the taught sequence performed rather than recited.
strengths.answerExcerpt: We ignore ¶14 and the last two sentences of ¶20 for being conclusory.

strengths.label: All three venue subsections addressed, with facts
strengths.detail: You do not stop at the subsection that decides the question. You reach (b)(1), (b)(2) and (b)(3), and you ground the (b)(2) result in where HG's loss of value occurred rather than asserting it.
strengths.answerExcerpt: Probably proper under 1391(b)(2).

strengths.label: Rule 56 burden structure applied to an affirmative-defense movant
strengths.detail: You notice that Droobles carries the trial burden on the Public Access defense, which raises what he must produce, and you cite the deposition paragraphs that carry it. That is the difference between stating Celotex and using it.
strengths.answerExcerpt: DD has the burden of persuasion at trial because PAD is an affirmative defense.

strengths.label: Appealability closed route by route
strengths.detail: Three points, and you name the finality defect and then close 1292(a)(1), the collateral-order route, 1292(b), Rule 54(b) and mandamus in a few clauses. Nothing more was available here.
strengths.answerExcerpt: Not a final judgment, so not appealable (Liberty Mutual).

strengths.label: Which state's preclusion law follows the transfer, argued both ways
strengths.detail: You name Semtek, ask which court is the rendering court after the transfer, use the happy court rule for the change-of-courtroom argument, and then state the competing simplicity argument. The mutuality consequence of each branch is spelled out, which is what makes the argument usable.
strengths.answerExcerpt: If the MA Fed Court was a Happy Court, then a strong argument can be made that the transfer to NH Fed Court was merely a change of courtroom.

strengths.label: Numerosity handled with the soft middle
strengths.detail: You refuse to assert a threshold, treat the number as genuinely arguable, and use geographic dispersion as the tiebreaker.
strengths.answerExcerpt: Unclear because the number of class members is between 20 and 40.

strengths.label: An original second proposal with a concrete safeguard
strengths.detail: Dropping the necessary-to-the-decision and finality requirements is a genuine expansion distinct from the listed options. Pairing the listed proposal with a strict mutuality limit is your sharpest move, and the access-to-justice analysis runs through the argument instead of sitting at the end.
strengths.answerExcerpt: it is entirely possible for a non-decision to have a preclusive effect

improvements.label: Question 1 — supplemental jurisdiction raised and then dropped
improvements.whatHappened: You write that there may be supplemental jurisdiction over Count II, turn to the anchor claim, and never return. Rule 20 and 1367(b) are never named. Count II is left without a bottom line on the 25-point question.
improvements.whyItMatters: Count II seeks only $50,000, so supplemental jurisdiction is the only thing keeping it in federal court. The motion against your own client turns on that step.
improvements.howToImprove:
Finish the steps in order.
1. Name the anchoring claim and its jurisdictional basis: Count I against Riddle, diversity, $950,000.
2. Say how Droobles was joined — Rule 20, same T/O in the single deepfake scheme, with the common question whether a Riddle/Droobles scheme existed.
3. Run 1367(a): say what makes this a CNOF here.
4. Run 1367(b): this is a claim by a plaintiff against a person joined under Rule 20 in a diversity case, so the bar applies and Count II goes.
Pay for it by deleting the second appearance of the arising-under paragraph, which you state twice in identical words.

improvements.label: Question 1 — the personal jurisdiction analysis is missing its main steps
improvements.whatHappened: Specific jurisdiction over Droobles rests on Calder and Griffis and on where the harm was aimed. There is no long-arm step, no purposeful availment, no relatedness, and no fairness weighing. General jurisdiction over Droobles is disposed of in one clause with no comparison to Daimler's at-home standard. None of the record facts about the gum business appear, and this course does not run personal jurisdiction on an effects test.
improvements.whyItMatters: The facts you skipped are the ones that decide it: 25% of sales go to Massachusetts, the highest-volume state, and Droobles ships direct to customers with no intermediary, which is the contrast with stream of commerce in Nicastro.
improvements.howToImprove: Take the bases in order. Rule out general jurisdiction because 25% of sales is nowhere near at home under Daimler. Note the Massachusetts long-arm reaching constitutional limits and 4(k)(1)(A). Argue minimum contacts both ways under International Shoe: the 25% figure and direct shipment for jurisdiction, no office, no salesforce, no advertising and a passive website against it. Then weigh fairness and reasonableness — Massachusetts' interest in its own businesses, evidence and witnesses there, low burden on Droobles. Spend the Calder/Griffis exchange on that weighing.

improvements.label: Question 1 — the 1391(b)(1) aside states the subsection wrong
improvements.whatHappened: You write that venue would be proper under (b)(1) if Riddle is a Massachusetts resident. Droobles resides in New Hampshire, so no single state houses all defendants and (b)(1) is closed whatever Riddle's domicile.
improvements.whyItMatters: (b)(1) turns on all defendants residing in one state, and the slip costs you a subsection you had otherwise handled cleanly.
improvements.howToImprove: Replace the conditional clause with the reason (b)(1) is unavailable: the two defendants reside in different states. Note also that the course term for the standard you applied is plausibility pleading.

improvements.label: Question 2 — the transfer step is skipped before a choice-of-law rule is picked
improvements.whatHappened: You apply New Hampshire's First Restatement rule because the case now sits in New Hampshire. You never ask whether the Massachusetts federal court was a happy court so that its choice-of-law analysis travels with the transfer. Ferens and Klaxon go unnamed.
improvements.whyItMatters: This threshold decides whether the Public Access defense exists at all in an 11-point question. You use the happy court rule in Question 4, so the step was available to you at the point it mattered most. Both branches land on Massachusetts law here, but the path is what is graded.
improvements.howToImprove:
Run it in order.
1. Ask whether the Massachusetts federal court had personal jurisdiction and proper venue — a happy court.
2. If happy, its choice-of-law analysis follows the transfer under Ferens, and a diversity court uses the forum state's rules under Klaxon, so Massachusetts rules apply.
3. If unhappy, New Hampshire's rules apply, and lex loci delicti points to the last event completing the tort, the loss of value in Massachusetts.
4. Say both branches reach Massachusetts substantive law, while noting the New Hampshire contacts — the meeting and the recording — that cut the other way.
Pay for it by cutting your opening paragraph on the meeting evidence; that material belongs in part (b).

improvements.label: Question 2 — HG's motion decided without the strongest record items
improvements.whatHappened: Your conclusion rests on the YouTube video and Riddle's "worth less" statement. Evans' testimony that Droobles convened the meeting and handed her his phone is never used. Neither is the "Keep this quiet!!!!!" email, its forwarding to an anonymous account that was then deleted, or the matching 5:22 runtime and near-identical dialogue.
improvements.whyItMatters: Those items carry the inference of participation, and Rule 56 is decided on the record actually assembled. Either conclusion is defensible, but only against the evidence that pushes hardest the other way.
improvements.howToImprove: Name each item and say what inference it supports, then say why a jury could still find otherwise. Recover the words from the second recital of the Celotex standard in part (b), which you already stated in part (a).

improvements.label: Question 4 — the actually-litigated element decided on the wrong record
improvements.whatHappened: You write that the issue was never actually litigated because the parties settled. The court had already granted summary judgment finding that Riddle and Droobles participated in the scheme, and that ruling is the litigated determination.
improvements.whyItMatters: The error ends the analysis early. Because you find no issue preclusion, you never reach the plaintiffs' non-mutual offensive use against Droobles, which is where your Massachusetts-versus-New Hampshire mutuality work was headed. The best part of Question 4 goes unspent.
improvements.howToImprove: Walk same issue, actually litigated, necessary to the judgment, then mutuality. Treat the summary judgment ruling as the litigated determination and ask instead whether that ruling followed by a stipulated dismissal is sufficiently firm, since such orders are revisable but rarely revised. Then reach Ginny's non-mutual offensive use against Droobles, with Parklane as the limit. Cut the double-damages policy paragraph under "Final Judgment on the Merit"; the with-prejudice language carries that point alone. The course calls this intersystem preclusion rather than interstate.

improvements.label: Question 4 — Harry and Ginny treated as one for privity
improvements.whatHappened: Both are held claim precluded on the same reasoning. The record supplies a discriminator you never use: Harry holds 65% and effectively controlled the first suit, while Ginny holds 5% with no evidence of control.
improvements.whyItMatters: Privity turns on control and representation, so the two plaintiffs come out differently. Ginny is likely not bound, and that changes what the second suit looks like.
improvements.howToImprove: Split the discussion in two sentences: Harry's controlling stake and control of the first action bind him; Ginny's small stake and the absence of control evidence do not, subject to discovery. Take the words from the speculation that Harry and Ginny received settlement money, which the record does not support.

improvements.label: Question 5 — the small per-member stake is used backwards
improvements.whatHappened: You treat each member's roughly $15,000 as a reason to doubt superiority, on the ground that each member could sue alone.
improvements.whyItMatters: It runs the other way. Modest individual stakes are what make separate suits impractical, so they support certification.
improvements.howToImprove: Say that $15,000 spread across members in three distant states makes individual suits impractical, which is what superiority asks. One clause, no added length.

improvements.label: Question 5 — the closing sentence contradicts the analysis
improvements.whatHappened: After concluding that the Rule 23 requirements are probably met and that common issues certainly predominate, the last sentence says the class can probably be defeated on commonality, numerosity and superiority.
improvements.whyItMatters: The question asks for a prediction, and the reader is left without one.
improvements.howToImprove: State the prediction — certification is likely — then name in one clause the ground you would press as Droobles' counsel anyway.

improvements.label: Question 6 — the fairness limit needs its authority, and the due process objection needs developing
improvements.whatHappened: Your mutuality safeguard is the best idea in the answer, but the fairness limit on non-mutual offensive use is argued without Parklane. The objection that a party would be bound through someone else's litigation without notice is gestured at rather than worked.
improvements.whyItMatters: This is the second-heaviest question. Naming the governing authority shortens the argument and strengthens it at once, which is exactly what a word cap rewards.
improvements.howToImprove: Cite Parklane where you argue that a party should not be bound by an issue another party failed to raise, and add the notice constraint on binding non-parties in one or two sentences. Pay for it by cutting the duplicated efficiency point — you make the litigation-takes-a-long-time argument twice.

improvements.label: Both sides argued unevenly across Questions 1, 4 and 5
improvements.whatHappened: You argue both ways on Riddle's domicile, on the Erie tests, and on which court is the rendering court. General jurisdiction over Droobles, the contacts case against him, the actually-litigated element, and the Rule 23 bottom line are each disposed of in a single clause.
improvements.whyItMatters: Every one of those single-clause disposals is on a contestable point, which is where the argument is expected. The habit shows up in three questions, so it is worth fixing once.
improvements.howToImprove: When you write a one-clause conclusion, ask whether a competent opponent would contest it. If so, add the opposing sentence and answer it. Fund that from passages restating a standard you already gave — the second Celotex recital in Question 2 and the duplicated efficiency point in Question 6.

feedback.exampleRevision:
Instead of: "SJ: Maybe there's SJ because this claim ('Claim 2,' against DD) is from the same case/controversy as Claim 1 (against TMR)."

Try a run that finishes: Count II seeks $50k, below §1332's threshold, and no aggregation across defendants saves it, so it needs SuppJ. Anchor: Count I v. fixtures.bandRationale: Reference defect lists first. DS reference: never addresses the MA-versus-NH transfer ambiguity in its Q4 preclusion law (it simply says the rendering court is the NH federal court), asserts Droobles' minimum-contacts case away fairly quickly, and its Q2(b) element run guesses at causation evidence; still DS because every path is canvassed and framed. H reference: leaves 1367(b) unresolved and hedges it on an Exxon reading the course no longer permits, runs PJ partly on an effects test, gives venue one conclusory sentence, and discusses SMJ in Q5 after being told not to. P reference (sole P comparator, different year): disposes of SMJ in one clause ('The trial court had SMJ (diversity, non-AIC deficient)'), asserts an Exxon single-plaintiff-multiple-defendant route, muddles IPJ over the directors into a self-contradicting paragraph, and its policy essay is generic. LP reference: concludes 'No venue' on a clearly available 1391(b)(2) record, gives a three-line Q2, and diverts its policy answer into criminal-law consequences. Pairwise verdicts. Versus DS: WEAKER — DS resolves 1367(b) via Rule 20, runs the happy-court branching in Q2 both ways, and marshals the elements against the discovery record; the student leaves 1367 hanging and never reaches Ferens. Versus H: WEAKER overall, though not uniformly — the student is stronger on venue (all three subsections, fact-based) and on the paragraph-and-element 12(b)(6) run, and its Q4 transfer/rendering-court discussion is as good as H's, but H clearly outperforms on Q2's choice-of-law threshold (11 pts), on Q4's privity split and actually-litigated element (8 pts), and on the Q1 IPJ and 1367 analysis. Versus P: STRONGER — the student's core analyses are framed and applied to named facts rather than announced, no threshold is disposed of by bare conclusion except general IPJ over Droobles, and the Erie, Celotex, Semtek and Rule 23 runs are all resolved; the P comparator repeatedly states conclusions without the path. Versus LP: clearly STRONGER. That leaves the interval between P and H, and the answer sits closer to H: on the most heavily weighted material it produces sound, applied resolutions on pleading, Erie, venue, appealability, the affirmative-defense summary judgment, class certification and the policy question, with real errors on some cores rather than repeated conclusory or inverted cores.

Add the unresolved 1367 analysis and an IPJ discussion resting only on effects reasoning with no long-arm, purposeful-availment or fairness work, and the answer does not match the DS or upper-H comparators' sustained canvassing of alternatives on the 25- and 11-point questions.

The Erie sequence is complete and reaches the operative forum-procedural-law sentence; the 12(b)(6) run cuts conclusory paragraphs by number and matches each tort element to record paragraphs; Celotex is applied with correct burden allocation and specific deposition citations; appealability closes every route; Semtek and the happy court rule are argued both ways on which state's preclusion law follows the transfer; Rule 23 is run with the numerosity soft middle. The P comparator, by contrast, disposes of subject-matter jurisdiction and appellate jurisdiction in bare clauses and contradicts itself on personal jurisdiction.

fixtures.label: 2021 answer — DS
fixtures.answer:
## Question 1

 We could mount the following constitutional objections.

 Notice likely wasn’t reasonable. Need reasonable notice to Montoya (Mullane).

Valerie’s PO box scheme was unreasonable; she knew from weblog that Montoya was in
Dallas and from Buttercup’s contract that P.O box was unused (they used Fedex).
However, she sent certified mail to FL.

 Chat notice may be unreasonable; courts haven’t settled whether digital notification
is sufficient. We’d say there’s potential fraud, spam, and no authentication. But Courts
might believe Montoya is looking for clients and would be actively reading chat.

 Reasonable notice includes continuing duty when earlier attempts fail (Flowers).
Valerie saw website outage and unclaimed mail receipt; she had duty to send someone to
Dallas or alternatively call RV Park because she already knew where he lived. Valerie

would respond that reasonable doesn’t imply actual notice (Dusenberry) and those
alternate methods aren’t reasonable. Our arguments seem stronger.

 Opportunity to be Heard: §4.20 is potentially unconstitutional. A judge hears the
case and there’s a timely trial with post-seizure hearing and affidavits. However, §4.20
doesn’t require pre-seizure hearing or response, or bond/counterbond for seizure. Only
§4.10 requires bonds.

207089 207089

 We’d pose both in a Mathews challenge. Private interests seem high for Montoya
since the court took his earnings (like Snaidach wage garnishment). But money is in
Paypal; he only transferred when needing funds, implying existing funds. He could use
Paypal in the interim and challenge seizure at hearing in 20 days. There is countervailing
risk that Montoya could hide his bank funds, making Buttercup/Westley’s potential life

savings disappear. Montoya’s “wages” weigh heavily but not as much as in
Snaidach/Goldberg.
 Risk of erroneous outcomes drops in proposed scheme. Bonds/counterbonds
decrease risk of money “moving” and are rough signal for meritoriousness (Doehr). If
Montoya is confident, he can post counterbond as well. Hearings are especially important
for tort claims; we need to compare witness testimony minimize error or lying; signed
affidavits or documentary evidence don’t screen truth as well (like Doehr). We don’t
know if Soprano was defective without more evidence.
 Government interest favors us. Government may want to avoid litigation costs, but
hearing is inevitable. Yes, parties could settle, but seems unlikely from Montoya’s words
(he’s confident wiring is correct). Government interest favors bonds because they might

decrease non-meritorious lawsuits.

 Quasi-in-rem failure: Court can only attach property within its jurisdiction.
Unclear where the bank account is; it’s an incorporeal entity. If address for PPoB in NV
was dispositive, attachment of NV property from TX was unconstitutional.

 State must show the account was in Dallas. On one hand, Montoya cashed the
physical checks there. However, data is “in” Reno hard drives, and he opened the account

207089 207089

in Florida. Montoya also did almost all banking and received statements online, reaching
out to NV servers. Valerie could argue that debt should travel with owner; brightline rule
easy to administer and avoids artificiality of saying bank accounts are in Nevada (like
saying all stocks in Delaware, cf. Shaffer). And placing property in NV drags people to
courts they never expected to be in, raising inter-state power issues. We could argue

setting location in NV is administrable; more efficient because that’s where the records
and system administrators are.

 IPJ: We could argue like in Shaffer that quasi-in-rem requires minimum contacts
between Montoya, Texas, and subject-matter of suit under Due Process Clause (Texas
long-arm goes to Constitutional limits). Montoya’s presence in TX has no relationship
with litigation other than cashing checks (renting a plot there irrelevant to suit); he
negotiated and shipped Soprano from Oklahoma to Michigan. Counterpoint is that quasi-
in-rem is more administrable and bound by traditional territorial approach (Pennoyer).
Undecided post-Shaffer.

-------------------------------------------

207089 207089

-------------------------------------------

## Question 2

 Closer, but probably not. Buttercup’s private interests increase, especially given she
spent life savings, but she can always sue without seizure. Under Mathews, Court weighs
more heavily interests of deprived party (Montoya’s earnings). However, if most of his
assets are in Paypal, this is just two private interests and she’s stronger on this factor.

 But Montoya wins the erroneous ruling factor; bonds signal a ruling’s
meritoriousness. Court might think price is low enough for Buttercup if she believes she
can win, or that not being able to pay is signal she’ll lose. Government’s interest also
favors screening non-meritorious claims through bonds. In any case, we could mount
Mathews challenge with only pre-seizure hearing.

 Not sure what A2J “rights” are. Bonds unfairly exclude indigent litigants, but
federal courts required bonds in Doehr anyways. Scheme, government’s interests
typically outweigh the indigent.

-------------------------------------------

207089 207089

-------------------------------------------

## Question 3

 Maybe. Montoya has SMJ issues. For SMJ in declaratory judgments, we look to the
“imaginary lawsuit” where Buttercup/Westley sue Montoya on tort and contract theories.

 No AUJ: tort and contract claims are state causes of action. No embedded federal
issue.
 DJ: DJ for Buttercup only. Buttercup (OH), Westley (MI). Montoya unclear
between MI or FL. He was born there; domiciliary changes if Montoya resides
somewhere with intent to stay. That could be Florida. He lived there for a year, registered
to vote, got PO box and listed it online, license, checking account. But he secretly closed
PO box, and one year seems insufficient for intent to stay. Other states don’t evince intent
to stay. If MI, then Westley and Montoya aren’t Strawbridge diverse. Also implies

Westley can’t join Buttercup’s claims under 1367(a).

 Assuming Montoya domiciled in FL, check AIC. Westley’s AIC are insufficient;
they’re 25K for tort, 30K for contract. No punitive damages for contract, nor for tort (no
physical injury). No stacking principle because there are multiple plaintiffs.

 Buttercup’s claims meet AIC: 80K on contract and (150K + 350K punitive
damages) on tort. Even if punitive damages barred, AIC met for both.

207089 207089

 SJ: met for Westley. He’s joined properly under FRCP20: same T+O (broad
definition includes buying Soprano and explosion) and shared issue of whether Soprano
was defective/breached warranty. Either of Buttercup’s DJ claims anchor; Westley is
included under 1367(a) as a diverse AIC-deficient party with CNOF (Exxon). Not ousted

under 1367(b) (assume Westley diverse), and no 1367(c) reason to refuse jurisdiction.

 Montoya can likely sue in N.D.Ohio, E.D.Mich, and D.Vt.

 Venue: 1391(b)(1) doesn’t apply because Buttercup/Westley reside (under
1391(c)(1) domiciliary rule) in different states. 1391(b)(2) only where substantial parts of
events happened. That includes N.D.Ohio (where Buttercup negotiated contract),
E.D.Mich (delivery location), and D.Vt (injury location). Maybe not N.D.Tx (check
cashing) nor Oklahoma districts (check delivery); linkage is weak. Also not D.DE, D.NV
(we could say “account” is here, but that’s weak). No 1391(b)(3) because we can lay
venue via 1391(b)(2).

 IPJ: GIPJ over Buttercup in Ohio, Westley in Michigan. All relevant states have
long-arm statutes to constitutional limits, which federal court “piggybacks” via
4(k)(1)(A). No Daimler. Courts haven’t decided this for individuals; however,
Buttercup/Westley don’t seem to visit for majority of their time. No consent or tag
jurisdiction. For specific jurisdiction, we need minimal contacts linking
Buttercup/Wesley, subject matter of litigation, and forum (International Shoe).

207089 207089

 Ohio: GIPJ over Buttercup. For Westley, could argue Buttercup negotiated “for
him” and kept him informed, and they identified themselves as contracting from Akron
together (McGee). If so, fair and reasonable: Soprano is there, Ohio interested in
protecting contracting citizens, convenient for Buttercup/Westley who make this drive
often, and for Montoya who drives cross-country and ships nation-wide.

 Michigan: GIPJ over Westley. Buttercup agreed to ship the Soprano there.
Buttercup (using Westley’s address) purposefully availed herself of Michigan consumer
protection law by directing goods into Michigan. Maybe fair and reasonable: the shipping
records are here, Michigan interested in protecting goods sent into the state, same
convenience arguments for litigants.
 Vermont: Probably Specific IPJ. Buttercup/Westley availed selves of VT tort law
when they transported Soprano into Burlington. Potentially fair or reasonable: electrical
wiring there, Vermont interested in safe equipment.
 Texas/Oklahoma: No IPJ. Buttercup/Westley did nothing in TX; Montoya moved
there unilaterally post-contract (like Denckla). And checks seems insignificant to
declaratory judgment issue.

 Montoya should sue in N.D.Ohio.

 Punitive: We don’t want punitive damages. They’re substantive for HCOL. Federal
court uses forum’s choice-of-law rules (Klaxon). OH/DE/NV follow 2RS; TX/VT/MI
follow 1RS. In TX/VT/MI, follow the harm. Harm felt in VT so VT law applies, which
includes punitive damages. In OH/DE/NV, start with place of blood (VT) and see if §6
factors change “center of gravity.” RS2 lets us split issues; we could argue that as to

207089 207089

liability, Ohio is center. Key evidence (the Soprano) there, contract made there,

feedback.headline: Frameworks run and applied; two bottom lines reached wrongly on the heaviest questions
feedback.overview: Question 3 is your best work: the imaginary lawsuit rule to fix the subject-matter inquiry, Westley's amount in controversy computed and not stacked, the current §1391 across three districts, personal jurisdiction defendant-by-defendant in each candidate forum, then Klaxon and the First/Second Restatement split driving the N.D. Ohio recommendation, then the Ohio deposit priced as a vertical choice-of-law cost. Question 1 works all four required lines with facts attached rather than naming them. Four things cost you. Supplemental jurisdiction over Westley is resolved backwards, and §1367(b) bars that claim. The limitations arithmetic in Question 5 is wrong, and it decides the first half of that question. Question 1 never reaches fair-and-reasonable. Question 2 sets the access-to-justice half aside.

strengths.label: Notice worked as a sequence
strengths.detail: The points come from the second step. Once the certified mail returned unclaimed and the site was down, you name the follow-up actually available — personal service at the Dallas plot counsel had already tracked. Raising Dusenberry against yourself keeps the standard at reasonableness rather than receipt.
strengths.answerExcerpt: Valerie saw website outage and unclaimed mail receipt; she had duty to send someone to Dallas

strengths.label: Balancing tied to the actual statutory features
strengths.detail: You catch the bond asymmetry between §4.20 and §4.10, a genuine error-risk factor that most answers miss. Pairing the judge-not-clerk point with the Doehr observation that tort causation here needs live testimony rather than documents is balancing done as application.

strengths.detail: Treating the account as incorporeal and then arguing Dallas, Reno and Florida on administrability and party expectation is exactly what the hint invites. Keeping both readings of Shaffer open preserves the minimum-contacts argument you need immediately afterward.

feedback.exampleRevision:
Brain off on supplemental jurisdiction — walk the steps in order:
1. Anchor: the declaratory claim against Buttercup, roughly $500,000, resting on diversity under §1332.
2. §1367(a): the claim against Westley shares a common nucleus with it — one sale of one computer, one fire, and the same contested question whether the machine was defective.
3. §1367(b): the anchor is diversity, Montoya is the plaintiff, and Westley is a person joined under Rule 20. Supplemental jurisdiction over that claim would be inconsistent with §1332's amount requirement, so §1367(b) bars it.
4. Consequence: the roughly $55,000 claim against Westley cannot ride along, so Max's single joint federal action against both defendants does not work.
Note what drops out. Westley is a defendant, so the question is never whether he may join Buttercup's claims; delete that sentence and the Exxon citation with it.
feedback.closing: The framework work here is real. What cost you was two results reached at the end of otherwise well-run paths and two halves left unwritten — so check the arithmetic and the carve-out subsections before committing to a bottom line.

fixtures.bandRationale: Pairwise verdicts. Against the same-exam H reference: stronger. That reference's own serious defects include applying §1391 venue analysis inside the Texas state-court seizure question, omitting Westley's amount-in-controversy and supplemental jurisdiction analysis from Question 3 entirely (it simply assumes complete diversity and moves on), inventing an embedded-Erie Smith-Grable theory for the declaratory action, saying issue preclusion fails because "Buttercup won on product liability," and claim-precluding Westley as a possible successor-in-interest co-signatory. The student answer covers what that reference omits on the 22-point question (amount in controversy, non-stacking, 1367 analysis even if wrongly resolved, defendant-by-defendant personal jurisdiction, three-district venue under the current statute, a full three-position vertical choice-of-law run) and is more accurate on Question 5's privity analysis and Question 4's counterclaim treatment. Against the same-exam P reference: clearly stronger. That reference disposes of subject-matter jurisdiction and venue in Question 1 with "does not matter," never canvasses the situs of the account, offers a three-sentence Question 2, mishandles transfer and choice-of-law law in Question 3, precludes Westley through virtual representation, and answers Question 6 with a Rule 23(b)(1)-versus-(b)(3) description rather than the entity-versus-joinder framing. Against the DS reference (sole DS comparator, weighted as a full comparator): weaker as a total performance, though closer than the gap to H would suggest. That reference has its own real defects — a one-sentence Rule 42(b) answer, a mislabeled appellate provision, contestable assumptions about which forum's forum non conveniens rule dismisses — yet its canvassing is sustained on every sub-question, including a genuinely argued normative essay and a numerosity discussion that works the soft middle. The student answer matches that texture on Questions 1, 3 and 4 but falls short in three places that matter: the abandoned access-to-justice half of Question 2, the missing fairness prong in Question 1, and two inverted bottom lines (1367(b) and the limitations arithmetic) on the two most heavily weighted fact-pattern questions. That places it above the H reference without meeting the DS definition, which is a high H.
fixtures.whyNotHigher: Not DS because the DS comparator's canvassing is complete on every sub-question, while this answer leaves the fair-and-reasonable prong unrun in Question 1 and expressly abandons the access-to-justice half of Question 2 ("Not sure what A2J 'rights' are"). Its two inverted resolutions also fall on the most heavily weighted items: the 1367(b) gate that decides Question 3's bottom line, and the elapsed-time computation that decides the first half of Question 5. The boundary evidence pushing it to the top of H is Question 3, where it substantially outperforms the H reference (amount in controversy, non-stacking, current §1391 across three districts, forum-by-forum personal jurisdiction, full vertical choice-of-law canvass) and Question 4, where it adds the Rule 13(a)(2)(A) pending-action exception.
fixtures.whyNotLower: Not P because core analyses are not underdeveloped or unresolved. Every weighted question receives an applied framework with named facts attached, the alternatives are preserved rather than assumed away, and the two wrong bottom lines each sit at the end of a canvassed path rather than substituting for one. The P reference by contrast disposes of whole requirements with "does not matter," never canvasses the situs of the incorporeal account, and misframes Question 6's entity-versus-joinder question outright.

-------------------------------------------

Answer-to-Question-___

 Q5

 TX will likely grant MTD. SOL are procedural for HCOL, so apply TX law. TX

SOL=3 years, so dismiss because filed 3+ years after explosion. Possibly consider SOL

substantive in which case (under FR) we might apply VT (6 year SOL) because explosion

 Issue Preclusion: Not available. Only preclude parties who lost. Buttercup won on

 Claim Preclusion: Buttercup/Wesley likely claim precluded for both claims.

 Same claim: Yes, both same T/O as L1; same evidence, origin, formed a well

integrated trial unit. Product liability is literally same claim and we know breach of

contract claim is same T/O because Valerie wanted to raise in L1 and it arose out of same

2XXXXX 2XXXXX

party. Maybe in privity as successor in interest (signees of same contract). Doesn’t

substantially control Buttercup. If court determines not same party, only Buttercup

CP’ed.

 Judgment final/on merits: On the merits? Rendering court was state. If subsequent

court federal, must give at least as much preclusive effect as TX would (Hart, Migra).

Applying TX preclusion law, SOL dismissal = on the merits. If subsequent court state,

same deal, therefore on the merits and CP’ed for both S/F subsequent. Final? Unclear

because there was no trial court judgment, but I believe on the merits = final.

Marrese no CP. If not, B/W will be claim precluded on both issues as long as Westley
