2XXXXX 2XXXXX

-------------------------------------------

Answer-to-Question-___

 Q6

 For establishing complete diversity, we treat classes as a newly created entity.

The new entity adopts only the citizenship of the named plaintiff. (Supreme Tribe).

Where we normally require all plaintiffs to be diverse from all defendants, in class

actions, there can be thousands of nondiverse class members.

 However, when unnamed class members are AIC insufficient, we treat classes as

a joinder on steroids which has to comply with restrictive 1367 diversity rules. When

named plaintiff is completely diverse (from single defendant) and AIC sufficient,

supplemental jurisdiction 1367(b) can be exercised over unnamed class members who

individually do not meet AIC. (Exxon)

 But while AIC deficient claims don’t contaminate the original jurisdiction

lawsuit, under 1367(b)they do contaminate the lawsuit when they aren’t diverse. In this

respect, we force AIC insufficient claims to comply with joinder rules, whereas we don’t

apply those rules when only looking at complete diversity/aic sufficient claims.

 For specific PJ, it’s unclear whether we treat classes as a new legal entity or

joinder-case. Under Shutts, courts can exercise IPJ over unnamed members as long as

there’s procedural protections like notice, opportunity to participate, adequate

2XXXXX 2XXXXX

representation. But Bristol Myers Squibb left unanswered whether courts can exercise

specific PJ over unnamed plaintiffs when only some of the class have minimal contacts

(International Shoe).

 If considered a new legal entity, wherever class members suffered injury would

count towards minimal contacts, meaning it would be easier to establish specific PJ. In

that sense the class operates like a trust. If treated as a joinder, it would be much harder to

establish minimum contacts and specific jurisdiction because in large suits, plaintiffs are

in almost every state.

 I believe it’s better to treat classes as newly created legal entities because it

increases efficiency and makes litigation more likely. Class actions are intended as a

remedy for plaintiffs and so we worry less about applying arbitrary laws when they class

members can only gain from litigation. If we treat it as joinder, defendants (usually

companies who do bad things) can easily overcome litigation, creating an A2J problem.

Especially for damages classes under 23(b), if plaintiffs opt into litigation they’re

signaling consent to personal jurisdiction. A middle ground would be to treat opt-in

classes as legal entities but mandatory class actions as joinder-cases. Lastly, FRCP 23’s

commonality, numerosity, typicality and representativeness requirements provide legal

safeguards for defendants worried about unfairness.

feedback.headline: Real analysis on the hardest issues; two weighted questions left incomplete
feedback.overview: Your best work is analysis, not coverage. On Question 1 you ran the opportunity-to-be-heard balancing against record facts: the frozen account as Montoya's livelihood, Buttercup's lack of any pre-existing interest in it, a fact-intensive tort needing live testimony, no bond under §4.20 where §4.10 requires one, and no exigency. On Question 3 you made punitive damages the driver of forum choice, and you ran the vertical choice-of-law problem on Ohio's 10% deposit to a concrete recommendation. Those are two of the hardest moves on this exam. The gap is completeness on the two heaviest questions. Question 3 never reaches the joinder and supplemental jurisdiction step, so the question actually asked — can he sue both together — is answered without the analysis that decides it. Question 5's issue preclusion paragraph rests on an inverted premise. Its privity conclusion also runs against your own finding that Westley controlled nothing. Question 1 applies federal venue in a state court, and that paragraph spends 17-point words you needed for the contacts argument.

strengths.label: Opportunity to be heard worked against the facts
strengths.detail: The balancing uses record facts rather than recited factors, and you caught the bond asymmetry the fact pattern plants between §4.10 and §4.20. That comparison is what turns risk of erroneous deprivation into an argument.
strengths.answerExcerpt: No litigation bond here to mitigate risk of e.d.

strengths.detail: Naming the failed certified mail and the dead website as the trigger for further attempts is what makes the notice attack work. A one-shot reasonableness answer earns far less here.

strengths.label: Location of the incorporeal account argued both ways
strengths.detail: You treated the account's location as genuinely open and gave reasons for and against each candidate, including that a 2,000-branch bank would otherwise be seizable everywhere. That is the comparative policy work the hint invites.
strengths.answerExcerpt: Bank account is incorporeal, could argue it doesn't exist anywhere.

strengths.label: Personal jurisdiction run forum by forum and defendant by defendant
strengths.detail: Separating the candidate states surfaced that each has general jurisdiction over only one of the two defendants. That is the structure the two-defendant setup is built on.
strengths.answerExcerpt: General over Buttercup (OH domicile), Specific for Westley

strengths.detail: Identifying Vermont and Michigan as First Restatement states and Ohio as Second Restatement, then arguing center of gravity toward Ohio's bar on punitive damages, is what makes this a best-forum answer rather than a list of available ones.
strengths.answerExcerpt: OH follows SR. Punitive damages are substantive, so need to look at center of gravity/state interests.

strengths.label: Vertical choice of law on the 10% deposit
strengths.detail: You worked outcome determination, the source of the federal statute's validity, and Harlan's primary-conduct approach, using Ohio's stated aim of deterring weak suits. You then priced the deposit into the recommendation instead of leaving the tension open.

improvements.label: Argue contacts for Montoya, not against him
improvements.whatHappened: You conceded that Montoya "purposefully availed of business in the forum" and that Texas has an interest in "litigating bad sales." You flagged it as a close call but never made the point that no litigation-related conduct occurred in Texas.
improvements.whyItMatters: You are arguing for Montoya. Restoration and shipment happened in Oklahoma, the negotiations were online with an Ohio buyer, and the checks were mailed to Oklahoma. Cashing a check and a four-month RV stay are unrelated to the claim, and relatedness is the whole minimum-contacts inquiry.

Add that the website is visible everywhere with nothing aimed at Texas. Fund this with the §1391 paragraph identified in the next point, and spend its last words on fairness: no Texas conduct, no Texas resident, no Texas evidence, and Texas law will not govern.

You made the parallel point correctly elsewhere in the same answer when you noted that Rule 4(k)(1)(A) does not matter in state court.

improvements.whatHappened: You called the frozen account "new property" and cited Goldberg, then analogized to Sniadach in the next sentence.
improvements.whyItMatters: In this course new property means government benefits, licenses, and permissions; bank accounts and wages are old property and sit in the Sniadach line. The mislabel undercuts an otherwise strong paragraph.

Use the recovered words to argue Delaware as a candidate location for the account: place of incorporation is certain and easy for a third party or a court to ascertain before a seizure, which the transient candidates are not.

improvements.label: Run the Mathews factors and reach the access-to-justice line

improvements.whyItMatters: Four points still expects the taught structure. Weighing Buttercup's purely monetary interest against Turner and Lassiter, where liberty and parental-rights interests still drew no appointed counsel, is what shows the argument fails. One further omission drains her interest: she can still sue for products liability or breach of written contract with no seizure at all, so she loses only protection against dissipation of assets, and nothing suggests Montoya would dissipate.
improvements.howToImprove:
Cut the speculation about how many bond issuers were available in her area. In its place run the three Mathews factors on the bond requirement:
1. Buttercup's private interest in securing assets.
2. The risk of erroneous deprivation and the value of the bond as an added safeguard.
3. The countervailing interests of Montoya and of Texas.
Then add one sentence placing her interest below the interests at stake in Turner and Lassiter, and one noting she keeps her full damages action.

improvements.label: The joinder and supplemental jurisdiction step is missing
improvements.whatHappened: You wrote "AIC ($500k) > $75k" as though one figure covered both defendants. Rule 20 is never cited and §1367 never appears, so the question's first sentence is answered without the analysis that decides it.
improvements.whyItMatters: The declaration sought against Westley is worth at most about $55,000 — his $30,000 payment plus his $25,000 demand — so that claim fails §1332 on its own. Section 1367(b) then bars supplemental jurisdiction over a plaintiff's claim against a person joined under Rule 20 where the claim is inconsistent with §1332. On this record joining both defendants federally is likely impossible, which changes your bottom line.
improvements.howToImprove:
Walk these steps before you touch personal jurisdiction:
1. Rule 20 permits joining Buttercup and Westley — one transaction, the sale and the fire, and a common question, whether the computer was defective.
2. Amount in controversy separately for each defendant; Buttercup's $500,000 anchors, Westley's roughly $55,000 does not.
3. §1367(a) — the Westley claim shares a common nucleus, arising from the same sale and fire.
4. §1367(b) — the carve-out bars a plaintiff's claim against a Rule 20 co-defendant inconsistent with §1332, so the Westley claim drops out.
Pay for this by cutting the "FC piggybacks on 4(k)(1)(a)" recital from each of the three forum sections to a single statement at the top, and by cutting "SMJ: DJ; same as above" in the Michigan section.

improvements.label: A vertical choice-of-law question is not an embedded federal issue
improvements.whatHappened: You wrote "Possible SG exception; Erie issue embedded in declaratory judgment action," then relied on it: "potential SG-exception protects against possibility of no complete diversity."
improvements.whyItMatters: The Smith-Grable route asks whether a state-law claim contains an embedded federal issue. A dispute about which court system's law supplies the deposit rule is not an element of Montoya's state claims, so it cannot support jurisdiction. Because you used it as a backstop against a diversity failure, the error spreads into your forum recommendation.
improvements.howToImprove: Delete the aside and its later use. State instead that the declaratory judgment statute supplies a remedy and not a claim, so the underlying products liability and contract theories leave no arising under route and diversity must carry the case. That is a one-line saving.

improvements.label: The issue preclusion paragraph rests on an inverted premise
improvements.whatHappened: You wrote "Only preclude parties who lost. Buttercup won on product liability." Buttercup lost: the limitations dismissal was entered against her.
improvements.whyItMatters: The premise is backwards, so the conclusion is unsupported even though "not available" happens to be right. The real reason issue preclusion goes nowhere is that the only issue actually litigated and determined was compliance with Texas's three-year period, and no other forum will face that issue because each applies its own limitations law.
improvements.howToImprove: Replace the two sentences about who won with one identifying the issue actually decided and one saying no later court will confront it. Keep claim preclusion and issue preclusion in separate paragraphs, as you already did.

improvements.label: The privity conclusion contradicts your own reasoning
improvements.whatHappened: You named the right two tests, control and successor in interest, found that Westley "Doesn't substantially control Buttercup," then concluded he "would probably be CP'ed" because he co-signed the contract.
improvements.whyItMatters: Co-signature is not succession, and no control means no privity. Westley was never a party to the Texas case, so neither claim nor issue preclusion reaches him. The payoff of this question is exactly that asymmetry: the limitations win over Buttercup does nothing against Westley.
improvements.howToImprove: State the two privity tests, apply each to Westley in one sentence, conclude he is not bound, and say plainly that he can still sue. Pay for it by cutting the final recap paragraph, which repeats conclusions you already reached.

improvements.label: Two precision slips
improvements.whatHappened: You cited §1367(b) where §1367(a) is the operative provision for amount-deficient class members, and you described damages classes as opt-in when Rule 23(b)(3) classes are opt-out.
improvements.whyItMatters: The opt-out point matters because you built the consent argument on members choosing to join, which weakens the argument as written.
improvements.howToImprove: Cite §1367(a) for the common-nucleus step and reserve §1367(b) for the carve-outs. Recast the consent point: absent members who receive notice and decline to opt out have accepted the representation. Pay for it by cutting the paragraph on non-diverse members contaminating the suit.

feedback.exampleRevision: Instead of "DJ: Complete diversity met (Strawbridge) … AIC ($500k) > $75k": Rule 20 allows joining both — one sale, one fire, and a common question whether the computer was defective. But amount in controversy runs defendant by defendant. Buttercup: $500,000, over the threshold, so that claim anchors. fixtures.bandRationale:
Equal-scrutiny defect lists first. DS reference (same exam): botches the Q5 limitations arithmetic outright ('just within three years' — wrong, which knocks out the entire preclusion premise it then builds), concludes §1367(b) does not oust Westley's AIC-deficient claim (the model's contrary holding), leaves the Q3 deposit/punitive tradeoff frankly unresolved, and hedges 'Not sure what A2J rights are' in Q2. P reference (same exam): writes off SMJ and venue in Q1 as 'does not matter,' supplies no opportunity-to-be-heard balancing at all, gives Q2 four sentences with no framework, misses §1367(b) while affirmatively using Exxon to admit Westley, concludes in Q3 that even a Second Restatement Ohio court applies Vermont law (so the punitive damages payoff that makes Ohio attractive never surfaces), rests Westley's preclusion on virtual representation, and in Q6 names Rule 23(b)(2)/(b)(3) categories instead of the taught entity/joinder doctrines with no BMS. H reference (different year, sole H comparator, treated as a full comparator): fluent and broad, but contains real errors — 'York has been largely superseded,' a numerosity statement that a class 'below 40 plaintiffs' 'easily meets the numerosity threshhold,' and several conclusions asserted with thin support — while sustaining two-sided analysis and preserved alternatives on each weighted piece.

Pairwise verdicts. Versus P: stronger, clearly. On the 17-point question the student runs the full Mathews/Doehr/Fuentes seizure balancing and a policy canvass of the account's situs, both of which P lacks entirely; on the 22-point question both miss §1367(b), but the student gets the punitive-damages HCOL driver right, runs IPJ defendant-by-defendant, and lands a concrete forum recommendation with the deposit priced in; Q4 and Q6 are stronger; Q5 is comparable (both err on Westley's privity, the student adds the correct intersystem move and Marrese but garbles issue preclusion). Versus the H comparator: comparable as a total time-pressured performance — mostly sound resolutions with rich, two-sided analysis on Q1's due process, Q3's HCOL/VCOL, Q4 and Q6, offset by real errors on some cores (the Q3 AIC/§1367 omission, the Q5 preclusion pair), which is the same defect class the H reference carries. Versus DS: weaker. DS canvasses more per question (including negative findings — which states have no IPJ, why Oklahoma fails), runs SMJ per party including Westley's AIC deficiency and all four Erie approaches, and prioritizes alternatives throughout; the student's Q3 simply never reaches the joinder/supplemental step and its Q1 minimum-contacts run leans against its own client.

fixtures.answer:
## Question 1

 I. Subject-Matter Jurisdiction

 Not federal case, does not matter.

 II. Personal jurisdiction

 Personal jurisdiction applies to both federal and state courts. In order for a seizure
of property to be valid under quasi-in-rem jurisdiction, there must be a long arm statute
(there is in TX), and the property must be subject to jurisdiction under the minimum
contacts test (International Shoe, Shaffer). First, the property must be within the bounds
of the court’s geographic jurisdiction. Judge Humperdinck seized Montoya’s bank
account. Rationale is thtt 1. Bank of Florin has a Dallas, TX branch, 2. Montoya
deposited funds into his account there, and 3. Because Montoya can withdraw and deposit
money in TX, the bank account is located there.

 Montoya has a number of defenses that quasi-in-rem jurisdiction should not be
granted. First, Bank of Florin is a Delaware company with its principal place of business
in NV. All business records for the bank are located in NV. Montoya opened an account
in FL, and used his FL plot address and FL PO Box to do so.

 Moreover, it is not clear that neither Montoya nor his bank account have had
enough business in TX to say they’ve “purposefully availed” themselves in the forum
state (WW Volkswagen). Montoya deposited checks at the Dallas branch, but did so only

153225 153225

once.

 Because Montoya has few ties to the state, it does not seem like attaching quasi-in-
rem jurisdiction to his bank account follows “traditional notions of fair play and
substantial justice” (International Shoe).

 III. Venue

 Does not matter, as not federal case.

 IV. Service of Process

 Procedural due process is characterized by notice and an opportunity to be heard.
Due Process Clause guarantees this for loss of property (Doehr, Sniadach). However, it
does not require “actual” notice (Mullane), merely a concerted effort to give notice.

Courts have ruled that certified mail, even if not delivered, still may constitute sufficient
service (Dusenbery). But in Dusenbery, the FBI sent notice to multiple locations and
published in the newspaper. Jones v. Flowers also indicates that more than undelivered
mail is likely needed for sufficiency. Because Buttercup did not take additional steps, and
Montoya did not know of his opportunity to be heard, there is a strong case for dismissal.

153225 153225

-------------------------------------------

153225 153225

-------------------------------------------

## Question 2

 It would be difficult to argue that the bond requirement would/should be waived.
Bonds are considered necessary for fail dealing when addressing the potential attachment
and loss of property (Doehr). Bonds minimize the risk that comes with such practice, as
putting up the money usually is an indication that the underlying claim is reasonable.
Furthermore, the money itself prevents defendants from suffering losses if wrongfully
incurred.

-------------------------------------------

153225 153225

-------------------------------------------

## Question 3

 I. Subject-Matter Jurisdiction

 Because the two types of claims Montoya is primarily concerned about are state
contracts and tort claims, Montoya will not have arising under jurisdiction under 1331,
because federal declaratory judgment statute does not independently create a federal
COA. Montoya will then have to sue invoking diversity jurisdiction (1332).

 It is not likely Montoya has maintained his MI citizenship. While he has lived in an
RV, he made substantial moves that would shift his citizenship to FL. He registered to
vote in FL, opened a bank account there, got a FL driver’s license, opened a FL PO Box,

and leased a plot for a year. This should shift his citizenship to FL. Since living in FL, he
has not lived in a place for any longer than 4 months. While he is on his second stint in
TX, his lease is for three months, which doesn’t indicate an inclination to make TX his
home. It is likely that he is still domiciled in FL.

 Regardless of whether Montoya is domiciled in either FL or TX, he is domiciled in
a different state than both Buttercup and Westley. Buttercup is domiciled in OH (lived all
her life in Toledo), and Westley in MI (lived all his life in Ann Arbor). The AIC

153225 153225

requirement is met for Buttercup, as her medical bills alone are over $75k. For Westley,
however, the AIC requirement is not met. Westley and Buttercup only demanded
Montoya pay Westley $25k for distress, and even if we added the $30k Westley paid for
the computer, that is still not enough. Westley would have to be included under
supplemental jurisdiction, as we cannot aggregate.

 Joinder here would be proper under FRCP 20. There is the same T/O since they
were together when the injury occurred. Also common question of law or fact, regarding
breach of contract and product liability. If Buttercup’s AIC acts as the anchor, then
supplemental jurisdiction should be allowed (1367, Exxon).

 II. Personal Jurisdiction

 FRCP 4(k)(1)(A) to determine personal jurisdiction. General IPJ is not going to be
applicable in this case, as the defendants are domiciled in different states, and have not
otherwise declared themselves “at home” in other contexts. Specific IPJ requires long

arm statute (which we assume) and minimum contacts test (International Shoe). The
defendants could likely be sued in VT. The injury occurred while both defendants were
on vacation in VT, giving both defendants contact with the forum state.

 It is plausible that personal jurisdiction could be exercised in OH. Buttercup
conducted all the negotiations regarding the computer on Westley’s behalf from her
apartment in Ohio, and mentioned Ohio in every interaction. The bulk of the money paid
came from an OH bank.

153225 153225

 Montoya was in OK, but OK is not a valid place for IPJ, as because the
conversations occurred online, unless there was purposeful targeting of OK, then there is
no IPJ (Luban).

 It is arguable that the defendants could be sued in MI, as the product itself was
mailed to MI for Westley to pick it up, so that both defendants could use it. MI also
satisfies requirements of convenience in specific IPJ, as Westley and Montoya live within
an hour of each other.

 III. Venue

 Assuming personal jurisdiction could be exercised in either VT, OH, or MI, venue
would be proper in the sole district in VT, the Northern District of OH-where Toledo is
located, or the Eastern District of MI-where Ann Arbor is located.

 Because nobody lives in VT, if it is indeed the most likely place to begin the suit,
the defendants may ask that the lawsuit be transferred to either OH or MI, which is closer
to where they live. Because we have determined that OH and MI likely have PJ, the
transferor court’s (VT) law will be applied.

 IV. HCOL

153225 153225

 To determine what would happen in each state, apply HCOL(Klaxon). Breach of
contract, products liability, emotional distress, fall under substantive law, so do
restatement analysis. VT and MI are 1st restatement, while OH is 2nd restatement. 1st
restatement means we apply the law where the “blood fell.” A federal court in VT or MI

should therefor apply VT law, since the product broke in VT (Alabama Southern). 2nd
restatement takes into consideration where the injury occurred, but considers
circumstances towards a “center of gravity.” The transaction occurred online between
someone temporarily in OK and someone in OH. The product purchased was sent to an
MI address. The money from the transaction was deposited in TX. No apparent “center of
gravity,” so VT law may still be applicable. OH, therefore, would likely use VT law too.

 V. OH’s Declaratory Judgment Statute

 Erie here, because conflicts with § 2201. Erie suggests using federal law, so OH

statute should not concern Montoya.

 York Outcome Determinative: Whether or not ruling on claim affects outcome.
Failure to comply causes dismissal, so apply state law.

 Harlan Primary Conduct Test: would conflict between state and federal law cause a
change in pre-litigation conduct? Yes, would cost Montoya money that he does not have,
so state law.

153225 153225

 Scalia Valid and Applicable Test: valid under § 2201. Applicable because the
statute is sufficiently broad to control issue. Use federal law.

 Ginsburg “narrow construal” Shady Grove Test: narrow federal provisions to

accommodate state interests, also valid + applicable. Could go either way, but policy
reasons underlying OH statute aren’t here, Montoya is not a large corporation and
Westley/Buttercup can respond to suits. Apply federal law.

-------------------------------------------

153225 153225

-------------------------------------------

## Question 4

 Usually, if a federal court has SMJ, PJ, and venue, they have to take the case. But
there are rare exceptions through the Colorado River Doctrine. If there is a parallel
proceeding in state court, federal courts will consider some factors that may lead to
rejecting the case. Here, the TX case is currently proceeding. Next, consider convenience
for the parties, avoiding piecemeal litigation, judicial efficiency, any intent from
Congress, and how it may affect the state case. It would be burdensome for all parties to
hear a case in TX and a case in either VT, MI, or OH, not only physically but financially
too. The TX state case began first. Because two concurring lawsuits run the risk of
adjudicating the same issue, there is a risk of piecemeal litigation. All things considered,
the Colorado River Exception may be applicable here.

 In common law cases, the 7th amendment of the Constitution guarantees right to a
jury trial when the value in controversy >$20. Cases in law usually include cases that ask
for compensatory damages or punitive damages. This case regards thousands of dollars
for damages related to medical bills from possible productive liability and contract
breach, and physical and emotional suffering. Unfortunately for Max, he’ll likely have to
deal with a jury trial.

153225 153225

-------------------------------------------

153225 153225

-------------------------------------------

## Question 5

 Statutes of limitations are a procedural issue for HCOL. As a result, we apply TX
law. TX law statute of limitations is 3 years for product liability claims. Periods run from
day injury occurs. Injury occurred on April 17, 2017. The lawsuit was filed on June 16,
2020. Therefore, Buttercup is beyond the SOL, and the motion to dismiss should be
granted.

 The rest of this answer assumes a dismissal would be with prejudice.

 Another state:

 Requirements for claim preclusion: 1. Same party (or privity), 2. Same claim (T/O),

3. Judgment that is final and on the merits. The first requirement certainly applies for
Buttercup. This would also be the same occurrence for her as well, regardless of whether
she sued for products liability or breach of contract. A dismissal on statute of limitations
would be intended to have finality, as courts want old issues to conclude. In TX,
dismissal is on the merits. The next question is do states have to recognize other states’
dismissals for statute of limitations. While another state may say statute of limitations
dismissals are not on the merit, they must follow the judgment of the rendering court
(Full Faith and Credit, 28 U.S.C. § 1738). Therefore, another state would preclude

153225 153225

Buttercup too.

 Westley is not the same party, but check for privity, because courts want to make
sure everyone has their day in court. No successor in interest or substantial control of
litigation. However, there is virtual representation. Westley’s and Buttercup’s claims are

essentially the same, they arose from the same occurrence, and Westley had actual notice
of the lawsuit. So, satisfies first requirement. As stated, same T/O. Judgment being final
and on the merits should not differentiate from Buttercup’s analysis above, so Westley
too would be precluded.

 Federal court:

 28 U.S.C. § 1738 holds that the subsequent court uses the rendering court’s law.
Migra was case that held that subsequent federal courts are to give the same preclusive
effects that a rendering state court would. Therefore, Buttercup and Westley ought to be
precluded here too.

 Applying Erie, as federal law clashes with state law, also infers we should use the
state judgment.

 York Outcome Determinative: Whether or not ruling on claim affects outcome.
York involved statute of limitations, so following the state law.

 Harlan Primary Conduct Test: would conflict between state and federal law cause a

153225 153225

change in pre-litigation conduct? Yes, Westley and Buttercup would be shopping a
different forum, so apply state law.

 Scalia Valid and Applicable Test: issue with judgment on the merits is governed by
federal common law rather than FRCP or statute. So not valid/applicable, and ruling in

Erie dictates to apply state law.

 Ginsburg “narrow construal” Shady Grove Test: Ginsburg also takes into
consideration Scalia’s test, while construing federal provisions to accommodate state
interests. Therefore, state law should be prioritized here too.

-------------------------------------------

153225 153225

-------------------------------------------

## Question 6

 One example of an area where class actions treat a class as a new entity is in class
actions where we do not want to create “incompatible standards of conduct” that make it
difficult for the non-class party to know how to treat the class as a whole. In cases such
as a voting rights case where a locality is infringing on rights, cases where an injunction
directing the non-class party may be necessary, this is where it is better to treat all
plaintiffs as one body, because there is a common injury to address. Members are not
allowed to opt out in these cases.

 Cases where damages are appropriate (damage class actions) may be more like a
large-scale joinder. These cases often have plaintiffs that may have a variety of claims
against a defendant, but are certified as class action because one claim predominates. In

these cases, unlike the case above, members of the class can opt out. Exxon is an example
of this case, where like a joinder case, if there is diversity jurisdiction, and at least one
named plaintiff satisfies AIC, then supplemental jurisdiction holds for all other parties.

 There are also hybrid class action cases that include both damages and injunctive
relief that blend the two sides together. Wal-Mart was an example of a case that
attempted to be certified in this regard, yet missed the issue of commonality.

153225 153225

 I prefer the first type because it seems to take the concerns of both sides and find
the most equitable way to remedy the situation. Avoiding incompatible standards
eliminates error, protecting the rights of the plaintiffs and the interests of the defendants
to avoid future suits. Second, class actions like large joinders do not actually serve
purpose of addressing plaintiffs’ individual claims like a joinder claim would, so

plaintiffs are still not made fully whole.

feedback.headline: Question 5's preclusion chain works; Questions 1 and 3 each leave a required half unwritten
feedback.overview: Question 5's limitations computation and the claim preclusion chain against Buttercup are the strongest work on the paper, and the four competing approaches to Ohio's deposit statute in Question 3 are real analysis rather than labels. The gaps sit on the questions carrying the most points. Question 1 names notice and opportunity to be heard and then analyzes only notice, leaving roughly half of a 17-point question unwritten. Question 3 resolves supplemental jurisdiction on a reading of Exxon the course forecloses. It also disposes of venue in a single clause and never names a best forum. Question 4 skips the question whether the defendants must file their own suit. Question 5's conclusion on Westley is inverted. Question 6's third slot answers a certification question rather than the entity-versus-joinder question asked.

strengths.detail: Identifying the duty to try again after the certified mail returned unclaimed is what decides this half of the issue, and distinguishing Dusenbery on its multiple attempts and publication shows you were comparing efforts rather than collecting cases.
strengths.answerExcerpt: Jones v. Flowers also indicates that more than undelivered mail is likely needed for sufficiency.

strengths.label: Domicile decided on the facts
strengths.detail: Weighing the one-year Pensacola plot, the registration, the license, and the P.O. box against the later three- and four-month stays is presence plus intent applied rather than asserted, and it produces a conclusion the diversity analysis can actually use.
strengths.answerExcerpt: Since living in FL, he has not lived in a place for any longer than 4 months.

strengths.label: Amount in controversy taken defendant by defendant
strengths.detail: Valuing the declaration against Westley on its own and refusing to aggregate is the discipline that sets up the supplemental jurisdiction question correctly, even though the answer then resolves it wrongly.

strengths.label: Four approaches to the Ohio deposit, each to a conclusion

Most answers then stop at Texas treating the dismissal as on the merits; carrying it through § 1738 to a later state court, and through Migra to a later federal court, is what makes the bar binding rather than local.

improvements.label: Question 1 — the opportunity-to-be-heard balance is not here
improvements.whatHappened: You state that due process means notice and an opportunity to be heard, then analyze only notice. Mathews is never named and the § 4.20 scheme is never weighed.
improvements.whyItMatters: This is roughly half of the exam's second-largest question, and it is the half the seizure facts were built for.
improvements.howToImprove:
Run the Mathews factors on § 4.20, naming features on each side.
1. Montoya's private interest: he needs the account to live and run the business.
2. Features lowering the risk of error: a judge rather than a clerk issues the order, a sworn short statement of facts is required, and a hearing follows within 20 days.
3. Features raising it: § 4.20 requires no bond, unlike § 4.10; causation here (the computer's power cable against the 19th-century wiring at the bed and breakfast) needs live testimony rather than documents, as in Doehr; there is no exigency after three years; Buttercup has no pre-existing interest in the account.
4. Buttercup's and Texas's interests, both thin, since an ordinary in personam suit would protect her.
Fund this from the four-approach Erie canvass that closes Question 5; that passage runs several paragraphs and covers both this addition and the issue-preclusion sentence below.

improvements.label: Question 1 — situs candidates listed but not argued
improvements.whatHappened: You name Dallas, Nevada, and Florida as possible locations for the account. No policy strength or weakness is given for any of them, and Harris v. Balk does not appear.
improvements.whyItMatters: Where the incorporeal account sits decides whether Texas has anything to seize, and the hint asked for the trade-offs rather than a list.
improvements.howToImprove: Give each candidate a reason and a cost. Dallas follows the holder: ascertainable but transient. Reno is where the records are kept, a sensible proxy for what a modern bank is. Delaware incorporation is certain but formal. Pensacola is where the relationship began but is unknowable to a plaintiff seeking seizure before notice. Harris v. Balk supplies the reasoning that the account is a debt the bank owes, pointing to the bank's location. Then pick one. Pay for it by converting your three-part recitation of Buttercup's Dallas rationale (branch, deposits, ability to withdraw) into that evaluation instead of stating it as background.

improvements.label: Question 1 — only one reading of Shaffer
improvements.whatHappened: You cite Shaffer for the proposition that quasi-in-rem requires minimum contacts and proceed on that reading alone.
improvements.whyItMatters: The course teaches two readings, and on the narrow one ordinary quasi-in-rem survives, which changes whether you reach International Shoe at all.
improvements.howToImprove: Add a clause: on the narrow reading, Shaffer reacted to the sweeping Delaware sequestration statute, so ordinary quasi-in-rem stands, with Burnham supporting presence-based theories; on the broad reading you run the minimum contacts analysis you already have. The words come from your two Question 1 headings disposing of subject matter jurisdiction and venue, which do no work in a state-court seizure.

improvements.label: Question 2 — the access-to-justice half is unaddressed
improvements.whatHappened: Two sound reasons why bonds survive scrutiny are given, both from Doehr. The access-to-justice branch the prompt names is never engaged, and Buttercup's own interest is never weighed.
improvements.whyItMatters: Half of what was asked earns nothing on a four-point question.
improvements.howToImprove: Characterize Buttercup's interest as monetary security only, and note she keeps her products liability and contract claims in an ordinary in personam suit — she loses the seizure remedy, not the courthouse. Then use Lassiter and Turner: courts declined to supply counsel where parental rights and incarceration were at stake, which makes a monetary interest a weak candidate for an access-to-justice remedy. Concede in a clause that inability to pay distorts the market signal you identified. Compress your two sentences on the bond's rationale into one to pay for it.

improvements.label: Question 3 — § 1367(b) never reached, so the answer comes out the wrong way
improvements.whatHappened: Supplemental jurisdiction is resolved by treating Buttercup's amount in controversy as an anchor that carries Westley along, citing Exxon.
improvements.whyItMatters: That is the single-plaintiff, multiple-defendant reading the course forecloses, and it inverts the answer to whether Montoya can sue them together at all.
improvements.howToImprove:
Rewrite the anchor sentence rather than adding to it.
1. Name the anchoring claim and its basis: the declaration against Buttercup, over $75,000, diversity only.
2. Under § 1367(a), say what makes the Westley claim part of the same case: one sale, one fire, one defect question.
3. Run § 1367(b): Montoya is the plaintiff, Westley was joined under Rule 20, jurisdiction rests only on § 1332, and Westley's claim is amount-deficient, so supplemental jurisdiction is barred.
4. Conclude that joint suit likely fails, then treat the forum analysis as conditional, as the question invites.

improvements.label: Question 3 — venue asserted rather than analyzed
improvements.whatHappened: Venue is a single clause naming three districts, with no statutory work behind it.
improvements.whyItMatters: Venue is mechanical and cheap in words; the points here are lost only by not walking the subsections.
improvements.howToImprove:
Take § 1391(b) in order.
1. § 1391(b)(1) fails: under § 1391(c)(1) an individual resides at his domicile, and these defendants are domiciled in different states.
2. § 1391(b)(2): Vermont plainly hosts a substantial part of the events; Toledo hosts the negotiations; Ann Arbor delivery is arguable, so say which way you take it and why.
3. § 1391(b)(3) is then unnecessary.
Pay for it with the transfer paragraph, which answers a question the prompt did not ask.

improvements.label: Question 3 — the domiciliary half of each jurisdiction analysis drops out
improvements.whatHappened: Read against a single joint suit, your point that no one state has general jurisdiction over both defendants is fair. What is missing is that Ohio has general jurisdiction over Buttercup and Michigan over Westley, so the Ohio and Michigan discussions never say whose contacts are in question.
improvements.whyItMatters: Naming the domiciliary first is what isolates the hard question in each state: jurisdiction over the non-domiciliary.
improvements.howToImprove: In each candidate state, dispose of the domiciliary in a clause, then run specific jurisdiction on the other defendant only. Westley in Ohio: whether Buttercup's Toledo negotiations count as his contacts, then fairness. Buttercup in Michigan: directing shipment to Ann Arbor, against Michigan's thin interest and the absence of evidence there. Vermont can take both together. This is reorganization, not addition, so it costs you nothing.

improvements.label: Question 3 — the best-forum sub-question is never answered
improvements.whatHappened: Your center-of-gravity reading concludes that even Ohio would apply Vermont law, and then stops. No forum is identified as best for Montoya.
improvements.whyItMatters: The client's stated worry is punitive damages, and the horizontal choice of law is the only thing that moves it. An unanswered sub-question earns nothing even where the reasoning behind it is sound.
improvements.howToImprove: Fold the answer into your existing choice of law conclusion: Vermont and Michigan are First Restatement states and under Klaxon apply Vermont law, where punitive damages are available; N.D. Ohio applies the Second Restatement and gives Montoya at least a chance at Ohio's bar on punitive damages in products liability. Name your pick and tie it to that exposure even if you think it close.

improvements.label: Question 4 — the compulsory counterclaim question goes unanswered
improvements.whatHappened: Rule 13(a) does not appear, so whether Buttercup and Westley must file their own lawsuit is never addressed.
improvements.whyItMatters: They would not file separately: Rule 13(a) pulls their tort and contract theories into Montoya's federal action, and failing to assert them risks losing them. That also anchors your jury conclusion, because the damages counterclaim carries the right and Montoya cannot avoid it by suing first for a declaration.
improvements.howToImprove: Add a short Rule 13(a) paragraph before the jury discussion, and tie the jury right to the counterclaim rather than to the size of the dispute. Then give Montoya's side of the abstention argument: Westley is not before the Texas court, there is no congressional policy of unified adjudication, and no absent party's rights are at stake, so exceptional circumstances are doubtful. Pay for it with your opening sentence on the obligation of federal courts to hear cases and with the restatement of the damages facts in the jury paragraph.

improvements.label: Question 5 — Westley precluded on a theory the course does not support
improvements.whatHappened: You rule out succession and control correctly, then reinstate privity through virtual representation based on shared claims, the same occurrence, and actual notice.
improvements.whyItMatters: That inverts the result for one of the two parties. A nonparty who neither controlled the litigation nor succeeded to Buttercup's interest is not bound, and a close relationship plus a joint purchase is not privity.
improvements.howToImprove: Keep the structure and change the conclusion: no control, no succession, no privity, so Westley may sue. Add the practical consequence in a clause — his claims are individually modest and he suffered no physical injury, which matters to punitive damages.

improvements.label: Question 5 — issue preclusion never run, and the closing canvass misfires
improvements.whatHappened: Issue preclusion is never addressed separately. The closing four-approach Erie canvass then reworks a question § 1738 and Migra had already settled earlier in your answer.
improvements.whyItMatters: A complete preclusion answer covers both doctrines. The effect of a state judgment in a later federal court is intersystem preclusion, not a vertical choice of law problem, so those paragraphs earn nothing.
improvements.howToImprove: Cut the canvass. In its place, say that the only issue actually litigated was compliance with the Texas limitations period, which is not an issue in another forum applying its own period, so issue preclusion does no work. Add that Buttercup's contract theory is barred by transactional claim preclusion rather than limitations, since the contract period is ten years everywhere relevant.

improvements.label: Question 6 — the unsettled-area slot answers a different question
improvements.whatHappened: For the area of genuine doubt you offer hybrid damages-and-injunction classes and Wal-Mart's commonality holding.
improvements.whyItMatters: Commonality is a certification question. It does not show a doctrine where the entity and joinder conceptions pull in opposite directions, so the question's central ask is unanswered.
improvements.howToImprove: Use personal jurisdiction over a defendant as to unnamed out-of-state class members: on an entity conception the Bristol-Myers Squibb limit does not bite, while on a joinder conception each member's claim needs its own jurisdictional predicate. Strengthen the entity slot as well — diversity measured by the named representative alone (Supreme Tribe of Ben-Hur) is the cleanest example. Trim your explanation of no-opt-out injunctive classes to pay for both.

feedback.exampleRevision: Instead of: "If Buttercup's AIC acts as the anchor, then supplemental jurisdiction should be allowed (1367, Exxon)." Try: "Buttercup's claim anchors on diversity alone (over $75k, FL v. OH). Westley's claim shares a CNOF under § 1367(a): one sale, one fire, one defect question. But § 1367(b) bars it — Montoya is the plaintiff, Westley is joined under Rule 20, jurisdiction rests only on § 1332, and Westley's claim is worth at most ~$55k, so supplemental jurisdiction would be inconsistent with § 1332. Montoya likely cannot sue them together. Assuming he could, as the question directs, the forum analysis follows."
feedback.closing: Four directly asked sub-questions went unanswered: access to justice in Question 2, the best forum in Question 3, whether the defendants must counterclaim in Question 4, and the unsettled area in Question 6. Listing each question's sub-questions as headings before you write would have been worth more here than any single doctrinal fix.

fixtures.bandRationale: Reference defects first, so both sides carry a real list. DS reference: miscomputes the limitations period and concludes Buttercup's suit was timely (a wrong dispositive result on Q5); assumes away § 1367(b) rather than running it; muddles whether Ohio's deposit statute is procedural for horizontal choice of law before pivoting to vertical; its Q6 venue example is arguable. H reference: injects a § 1391 venue analysis into a state-court proceeding on Q1; precludes Westley on a thin successor-in-interest privity theory (wrong result); its issue-preclusion reasoning on Q5 ("[o]nly preclude parties who lost") is garbled; floats a Smith-Grable arising-under theory premised on an embedded Erie issue. P reference (sole reference for P, treated as a full comparator): disposes of subject-matter jurisdiction in one clause, rests a Rule 50 discussion on authority no longer in the course, resolves appealability conclusorily, and speculates about a foreclosed aggregation reading — but does cover most questions and has some applied preclusion and choice-of-law reasoning. Pairwise verdicts. Versus DS: clearly weaker. The DS answer canvasses both due-process prongs on Q1 with the seizure factors named and weighed, walks venue by subsection, separates general from specific jurisdiction for each defendant in each candidate state, names N.D. Ohio as best with a Second Restatement argument, and fills all three Q6 slots correctly; this answer omits the entire opportunity-to-be-heard balance, disposes of venue in a clause, and never names a best forum. Versus H: weaker as a total performance. The H answer carries the Mathews/Doehr balance on Q1 (bond absence, documents-versus-testimony, Fuentes exigency), runs SMJ/PJ/venue/HCOL district by district on Q3, gets Rule 13(a), and fills the Q6 slots; this answer matches or beats it only on the Q5 limitations computation and the clarity of the § 1738/Migra step, while losing on the two most heavily weighted questions. Versus P: stronger, but not by a band. The Q3 vertical choice-of-law canvass and the Q5 limitations-plus-preclusion chain are sustained applied analysis of a kind the P comparator's doctrinal half largely lacks; against that, this answer's Q1 (17 points) is missing half its required analysis, Q3 leaves venue and the best-forum question unresolved, and Q4 and Q6 each skip a directly asked piece. That pattern — issue recognition broadly present, several cores underdeveloped, misframed, or unresolved — is the P definition, at its upper edge.
fixtures.whyNotHigher: Not H because the two questions carrying 39 of 65 points are each missing a required core. Q1 names notice and opportunity to be heard and then analyzes only notice: no Mathews balancing, no § 4.20 factor weighing, no bond point, no Harris v. Balk situs policy. Q3 misses § 1367(b) (and uses the foreclosed Exxon reading), disposes of venue in one clause without the statute's subsections, misstates general jurisdiction, and never answers which forum is best. Q4 skips the compulsory-counterclaim sub-question entirely. The H comparator, with its own real errors, nonetheless had rich analysis behind its conclusions on those same questions; this answer's conclusions frequently arrive without the path.
fixtures.whyNotLower: Not LP because the heavily weighted questions are not a combination of wrong results with skipped or inverted core analysis. Q5's limitations holding is right and worked through with dates, and the preclusion chain against Buttercup is complete including the § 1738 step. Q3 contains genuine applied reasoning on domicile, per-party amount in controversy, Rule 20, Restatement assignments, and a four-approach vertical choice-of-law canvass. Q1's notice analysis identifies the follow-up duty correctly, and Q4's Colorado River discussion applies named facts. judgeFindings.problem: Over-penalizes a defensible compression. Read against the question asked — one joint suit against both defendants — the student's sentence that general jurisdiction "is not going to be applicable in this case, as the defendants are domiciled in different states" is correct: no single forum has general jurisdiction over both. The real defect is incompleteness, not error: the answer never says that each candidate state has general jurisdiction over its own domiciliary, so it never isolates whose contacts need analysis.

feedback.headline: Question 1's conditional structure works; Question 2 is missing entirely
feedback.overview: The branch structure on limitations is the best work here. You ask whether the transferor New Hampshire court was happy, state that limitations are procedural for HCOL so forum-state law applies, pair that with Klaxon, and carry both branches to opposite results. Claim preclusion is then run element by element to a stated conclusion. The gaps are serious, though. Question 2, the "should" question, is not answered at all, and you had words left in the limit. Venue is named but never run, even though the limitations answer rests on it. Minimum contacts stops at a label while the facts the problem loads on both sides go unused. Issue preclusion concedes the element the problem was built around.

improvements.label: Venue in the District of New Hampshire is named but never run
improvements.whatHappened: The only venue entry is a parenthetical about how many federal districts NH has. Neither the events-based ground nor §1391(b)(2) appears.
improvements.whyItMatters: Venue is half of the happy-court test, and the happy-court answer decides the limitations answer. A named requirement that is never run leaves the whole conditional resting on nothing.
improvements.howToImprove: Walk the venue grounds in order and stop at the one that fits: the sale and the explosion happened in Concord, so a substantial part of the events giving rise to the claim occurred in NH under §1391(b)(2). One clause does it. Pay for it by cutting the parenthetical about the number of districts and the second recitation of the HCOL rule in the "If NH was unhappy" bullet.

improvements.label: Minimum contacts stops at the label
improvements.whatHappened: You name the distributor structure (McIntyre) and Mr. Olivander's encouragement, but the facts the problem loads on both sides go unused: the independent-contractor contract, the private-investigator background check, the five-wand daily cap, the removable tags, and the minimum-price control. International Shoe is never named, nor the World-Wide Volkswagen and McGee line, and there is no fair-and-reasonable step.
improvements.whyItMatters: "Questionable whether minimum contacts/purposeful availment applies" is a conclusion without the step, and this is the contested point the fact pattern was engineered around.
improvements.howToImprove:
Run the taught SIPJ sequence:
1. Long-arm statute — NH's goes to the limits of the Constitution, so Rule 4(k)(1)(A) collapses this into the constitutional question.
2. Minimum contacts under International Shoe, argued both ways — for Olivanders, no purposeful availment because it sells only in Boston, contracts its sellers as independent decision-makers, and moves a trickle of unbranded wands through an intermediary (McIntyre, World-Wide Volkswagen); for Parkinson, the express encouragement to cross the border north is purposeful availment and makes suit in NH foreseeable (McGee), and the background check, the five-wand cap, and the minimum-price control cut against genuine independence.
3. Fair and reasonable, reached only if contacts are found.
Staying at "MAYBE" is fine so long as both sides are argued. The words come from the issue-preclusion prerequisites bullet, which recites uncontested items.

improvements.label: §1738 applied as if it settled the question rather than set a floor
improvements.whatHappened: You use §1738 as a rule that MA preclusion law governs. It sets a floor: the subsequent court must give at least as much preclusive effect as the rendering state would.
improvements.whyItMatters: Because MA's floor is no preclusion, the only path on which Olivanders' claim-preclusion argument could win is the open question after Hart whether the subsequent court may give more effect than MA would. You close off that live route without addressing it.
improvements.howToImprove: After concluding MA would not preclude, add a clause: under Hart it is unsettled whether the subsequent court may give greater effect, in which case NH's on-the-merits rule could support dismissal. Flag it as open rather than resolving it. Condition the passage on the NH branch in three words — claim preclusion matters only if the suit survives limitations. Cut the "exact same situation, no concerns about a market" aside to pay for it.

improvements.label: Issue preclusion concedes the element the problem turns on
improvements.whatHappened: You answered "Same issue: Did Pansy file too late?" in the affirmative, then rescued the result through actually litigated. No conclusion is stated, and the case where MA law governs is never addressed.
improvements.whyItMatters: The course treats timeliness under a two-year period and timeliness under a six-year period as different issues, because the governing provisions differ. That is the direct route, and conceding it pushed you onto a longer, weaker one.
improvements.howToImprove: Brain off here: work the elements in order and identify what the MA court actually decided, which was timeliness under the two-year MA period. Timeliness under NH's six-year period is a different issue, so no issue preclusion on the NH branch. Then state the mirror image in a clause: if MA law governs, the identical issue was litigated, decided, and necessary between the same parties, so issue preclusion would bite, and limitations would dismiss anyway. Finish with a numbered conclusion as you did for the other two grounds. Shrink the Cromwell bullet to a fallback clause to pay for it.

improvements.label: The "should" question is unanswered
improvements.whatHappened: There is no normative discussion at all. The judge asked two things and one is blank. The answer stops short of the word allowance, so the space existed.
improvements.whyItMatters: Half the assignment is unanswered. Repeating the doctrinal analysis under a "should" heading would not have counted either, because the register has to change.
improvements.howToImprove: Take a position and defend it, then answer the strongest objection. For dismissal: Parkinson picked a forum where she was time-barred, forum shopping is what Erie's concerns target, and re-filing removes any incentive to get the forum right the first time. Against: each state is free to set its own limitations and preclusion policy and other systems must respect it, and transfer rules exist so the plaintiff keeps the law of the forum she chose. Then engage the oddity these two statutes engineer — a Boston federal court applying NH's six-year period while treating the MA dismissal as non-preclusive, producing a combination no legislature enacted. Close on the rule-design tradeoff: whether a targeted fix such as judicial discretion is worth the loss in predictability. Concluding that there is no clean answer is legitimate if you show the tension. Reserve roughly a third of your words for this from the outset.

revisionPlan: Budget words before writing: reserve about a third for Question 2.
Run venue in NH: substantial part of events, §1391(b)(2), one clause.
Rebuild minimum contacts as long-arm, then contacts argued both ways using the contract, background check, five-wand cap, tags and price control, then fair and reasonable only if contacts are found.
Frame §1738 as a floor and flag the question left open after Hart.
Redo the same-issue element as different issues because the periods differ, state a conclusion, and add the mirror image if MA law governs.
Answer Question 2 as policy: position, counterargument, the hybrid the transfer creates, and the cost of fixing it.
feedback.exampleRevision: Same issue? What MA decided was timeliness under its 2-yr period. Under NH's 6-yr period the governing provision is different, so different issue → no issue preclusion on the NH branch. Mirror image: if MA law governs, same issue, actually litigated, necessary, same parties → preclusion would apply, though limitations alone dismisses. Conclusion: no issue preclusion if NH was happy. (This reaches the result through the element the problem was built on, and states an outcome under either branch.)
feedback.closing: The branch structure and the claim-preclusion run show you can hold a conditional together across an answer. Next time, run the steps you name, and budget words for the second question before you start writing.

feedback.headline: Strong transfer and preclusion work; the 25-point question and the short answers are where the points went
feedback.overview: Question 2 is your best work. You establish personal jurisdiction in Oregon and venue under 1391(b)(2) on the purchase and the accident before you reach convenience, then run the procedural-versus-substantive characterization and the full Erie sequence through York, Harlan and the twin aims. Question 1's waiver point is the pivot of that question and you have it. The rest is a distribution problem. Question 7 carries 25 of 70 points and receives four bullets. It contains no assessment of who gains and who loses under the appearance ban. It also contains no procedural due process discussion, which part (b) expressly requires. All five short answers are blank, another 12 points. Question 1's domicile holding is asserted rather than reasoned, and Questions 3 and 6 stop at a conclusion.

strengths.label: The waiver sequence on remand

strengths.label: Transferee-forum jurisdiction and venue settled before any balancing

strengths.label: Characterization plus the full vertical choice-of-law run
strengths.detail: Asking first whether enforceability is procedural or substantive, and then identifying the competing federal law as federal common law, is what puts you into the twin aims instead of a mistaken Federal Rule analysis. That step is where the points are on this question.

strengths.label: Two tracks of issue preclusion, elements applied on each

improvements.label: Question 1: domicile is the question and it is a bare conclusion
improvements.whatHappened: "probably both NJ (probably not OR)" states an outcome with no reasoning. The Oregon condo and the Oregon residency filing for tuition never appear.
improvements.whyItMatters: Diversity turns entirely on where Hermione is domiciled, and the facts genuinely pull both ways, so this is where the points sit.
improvements.howToImprove: Mas is the cite; what the bullet needs is the facts on each side of the intent question. The condo and the residency filing point to Oregon. A fixed three-year law school term and a stated hope of moving to northern California show no intent to remain indefinitely. Delete the Rule 20 and 1367 bullets to pay for it.

improvements.label: Question 1: the joinder and supplemental jurisdiction run needs a step to justify itself
improvements.whatHappened: The declaratory judgment Malfoy sought covered only Hermione. Reading Farley into the imagined coercive suit is defensible given the joint demand letter, but you never supply the step that puts his claim in the case. The bullets then close on jurisdiction over a claim the New Jersey court was not asked to decide.
improvements.whyItMatters: The doctrine inside the run is mostly sound, so the loss is the unstated premise plus a bottom line that answers a question the exam did not pose.
improvements.howToImprove: Before any joinder machinery, name the parties and claims in the imagined coercive suit and say in a clause why Farley is or is not in it. If he is out, those words go to domicile and to Question 7.

improvements.label: Question 2: carry the domicile finding through, and support the venue bullet
improvements.whatHappened: The opening bullet gestures at an unhappy transferor court but never follows it through. If Hermione is an Oregon domiciliary, diversity fails and the case goes back to state court rather than to the District of Oregon. Separately, "Venue proper because removed" is a conclusion with no reason.
improvements.whyItMatters: The examiner is testing whether the domicile determination is carried forward. Naming the consequence on the losing branch costs one clause.
improvements.howToImprove: Add a clause saying that Oregon domicile means remand, not transfer, and a clause giving the reason venue in the removal court is not an obstacle. Apply the private and public factors once rather than restating the labels on both branches, which frees the words.

improvements.label: Question 3: no bottom line, and no weighing of Oregon against Mexico City
improvements.whatHappened: You state the fork and stop. You never resolve which branch obtains, even though Question 2 concluded she is likely a New Jersey domiciliary. You never say whether the motion should be granted. "FNC analysis would be as above" points back to a New Jersey-versus-Oregon weighing, which is a different comparison.
improvements.whyItMatters: The question asks whether to dismiss in favor of a foreign forum. Forum non conveniens, not the transfer statutes, is the route there, and the factors that decide it are Mexico-specific.
improvements.howToImprove: Resolve the branch, then weigh what actually differs: Oregon's regulatory interest as the site of the sale, the warranty and the accident against the Mexico City situs of design and manufacture. State the result. Cross-referencing your Question 2 Erie work instead of restating it is fine and pays for this.

improvements.label: Question 4: the appealability list is not walked
improvements.whatHappened: The conclusion is right and the collateral order route is named, but the reasoning is one clause. The final-order requirement is never the starting point. The other enumerated routes are never ruled out.
improvements.whyItMatters: This is a brain off topic. The points come from walking the list in order, and each entry is a few words.
improvements.howToImprove:
Run the taught steps, one compact line each:
1. 28 U.S.C. 1291 — final order? No, the case continues.
2. FRCP 54(b) — a claim fully resolved? No.
3. 28 U.S.C. 1292(a)(1) — an injunction? No.
4. 28 U.S.C. 1292(b) — a certified controlling question? No district judge statement.
5. FRCP 23(f) — a class certification ruling? No.
6. Collateral order under Cohen — fails the effectively-unreviewable element; Lauro Lines is on point for forum clause rulings.
7. Mandamus — no extraordinary circumstances.
The Question 1 joinder bullets are the words.

improvements.label: Question 5: the judge's question goes unanswered
improvements.whatHappened: You set the two bodies of preclusion law side by side and never choose between them. Neither side of the open question is argued. You never tell the judge whether Farley's argument has merit.
improvements.whyItMatters: The open point is which state's preclusion law follows a transferred diversity judgment, and the judge expressly asked for a view on it. A fork left unresolved leaves the analytical work undone.
improvements.howToImprove: Argue both sides in a sentence each: transfer is only a change of courtroom, so New Jersey preclusion law travels with the judgment, against the simplicity of reading preclusive effect off the face of the judgment where it was entered. Then pick, and say whether the argument has merit. Add that the Oregon state court may allow preclusion as a matter of discretion even if not compelled, citing Hart. Drop the stray Rule 50 bullet, which belongs to no part of this question.

improvements.label: Question 6: right element, no reason attached
improvements.whatHappened: "Not same party / in privity no claim preclusion" is a conclusion with no supporting step. In outline form that is as conclusory as a one-sentence disposal.
improvements.whyItMatters: Privity is the contestable element on these facts, and the grader is looking for why it fails.
improvements.howToImprove: Give the reason and answer the obvious counterargument: Farley did not control Hermione's litigation, did not step into her shoes, and suffered his own injuries, so co-purchase of the car and the family relationship do not create privity. Add a clause conceding what is met — same transaction, valid final judgment on the merits. Two clauses; the stray Rule 50 bullet in Question 5 pays for them.

improvements.label: Question 7(a): no analysis of who gains and who loses
improvements.whatHappened: Lassiter and Turner are used accurately for the point that there is no civil right to counsel even where weighty interests are at stake. Past that, part (a) does not evaluate the scheme. Nothing on the repeat-player advantage for collection and insurance entities. Nothing on the fact that the ban reaches only courtroom appearances, so lawyers still draft the complaint, the dispositive motions and the discovery and coach the client. No access to justice assessment, though the question names it.
improvements.whyItMatters: This is 25 of 70 points, more than a third of the exam, and it is where distribution cost you most.
improvements.howToImprove: Work part (a) as winners and losers. Say who benefits from a steady diet of litigation in this court. Say who benefits from education and social capital when required to speak for themselves, with Lassiter as the object lesson. Name devices that are impracticable without counsel, such as class actions. Then frame the proposal as leveling down rather than up, drawing on Barton and Bibas on cost. The Question 1 joinder detour pays for this.

improvements.label: Question 7(b): proposals without reasons, and no procedural due process discussion
improvements.whatHappened: Part (b) is two fragments. "FRCP wouldn't apply, need simpler rules" and "Simplify rules of preclusion?" carry no reasons. The procedural due process defense that part (b) expressly requires is absent.
improvements.whyItMatters: A modification without a reason earns nothing, and an express requirement left out is a guaranteed loss on the heaviest question.
improvements.howToImprove: Make each proposal concrete with a reason attached: court-supplied claim forms, expanded mandatory disclosures with interrogatories and requests for admission eliminated, joinder and class actions scrapped on complexity grounds, inquisitorial judging on the small claims model. feedback.headline: Questions 1 and 5 are largely finished; Questions 4, 6, and 7 leave their central arguments unmade
feedback.overview: Question 1 carries the answer. The 12(b)(6) run strikes paragraph 16 as conclusory and then matches each element of fraud in the inducement to numbered complaint paragraphs, and the vertical choice-of-law run walks the whole taught sequence in the expected Rules Enabling Act and Sibbach form. Personal jurisdiction and venue are run rather than asserted, and Question 5 is complete at the right size. The rest is where the points went. Question 6 never identifies the renewed Rule 50 motion and states no standard for either post-verdict motion. Question 7, worth twenty-five points, answers part of the constitutional prompt and neither of the other two. Question 4 concedes numerosity, which was the ground that defeats certification. Within Question 1, the amount in controversy is one clause and transfer, expressly asked, is three fragments. Question 3 reaches the right destination without stating the reason that gets there.

strengths.label: Plausibility pleading worked paragraph by paragraph
strengths.detail: Setting paragraph 16 aside first and then tying each element to numbered paragraphs is the taught order, and it lets you show that materiality survives independently through Spinnet's own recited statements about wanting only safe investments. That independent route is the step most answers skip. (The course's term for the standard is plausibility pleading, not the portmanteau.)
strengths.answerExcerpt: Plausibility pleading, cross out conclusory elements: most of paragraph 16

strengths.label: The Erie sequence is complete and correctly ordered
strengths.detail: You state the operative horizontal choice-of-law sentence, then York, Harlan on primary conduct, Hanna validity in the Sibbach "really regulates procedure" form, Scalia on applicability, and Ginsburg's floor-and-ceiling narrowing — and you say what dismissal looks like under each branch. Naming the consequence both ways is what makes the branches worth writing.
strengths.answerExcerpt: Valid: FRCP under REA valid if doesn't A/E/M, really regulates procedure (Sibbach)

strengths.label: Personal jurisdiction and venue each run to the end
strengths.detail: You reject Daimler at-home on a single branch, dispose of consent and tag, then run long-arm plus 4(k)(1)(A), purposeful availment and minimum contacts anchored to the Houston negotiation, and fairness on named facts. Venue is then resolved at district level with reasons under (b)(1) and (b)(2) and the fallback correctly foreclosed — the district-level move is what makes venue the strongest ground here.
strengths.answerExcerpt: Not Daimler at home- only one branch there, unless 50%+ of business flowed through

strengths.label: Commonality argued from the facts
strengths.detail: Using the Greyback email as the concrete common policy, and the identical contracts as supplying a common answer on the statutory materiality element, is the right way to distinguish Wal-Mart, where the alleged policy was decentralized discretion. Keeping the counterpoint that each oral misstatement may need individual proof earns credit rather than costing it.

strengths.detail: You apply the final-order rule to the actual posture — a verdict with no judgment entered — and then dispose of each taught exception with a reason rather than a list. Citing Cohen instead of writing out its elements is correct technique on a three-point question.
