improvements.label: Question 1: the amount in controversy rides on the punitive damages claim
improvements.whatHappened: You wrote "AIC over 75k (770k)" and moved on. The $70,000 compensatory figure is below the threshold on its own, so the whole question is whether the $700,000 punitive claim is viable.
improvements.whyItMatters: Texas allows punitive damages for fraud in the inducement and Louisiana bans them by statute, so the amount in controversy depends on your horizontal choice-of-law result. You ran that analysis and never connected it back, leaving the diversity conclusion unsupported on the heaviest question. You do make the link in Question 2, which shows you had it available.
improvements.howToImprove: Add one clause after your Second Restatement conclusion: if Texas law governs, the punitive claim counts and the threshold is met; if Louisiana law governs, punitives are unavailable and only $70,000 remains, defeating diversity. That is a clause, and you are well under the word limit.

improvements.label: Question 1: transfer is half the prompt and gets three fragments
improvements.whatHappened: Transfer appears as "GIPJ in TX and NDNY / SDTX is proper in TX, ED LA." There is no could-have-been-brought test, no district-by-district check, no convenience weighing, and no recommendation. "GIPJ in TX" also contradicts your own Daimler point — general jurisdiction lies in Delaware and New York.
improvements.whyItMatters: The question asks for grounds to dismiss or transfer, and once venue is improper transfer is the live remedy. A list of districts with no test attached earns little.
improvements.howToImprove:
Walk it as steps, citing Hoffman for the controlling limit:
1. Name the candidates: S.D. Tex., E.D. La., N.D.N.Y., D. Del.
2. For each, say whether personal jurisdiction exists and on what basis.
3. For each, say whether venue is proper and under which subsection of section 1391.
4. Weigh convenience and the interest of justice on the named facts — witnesses, documents, the Houston signing.
5. Recommend one district.

improvements.label: Question 1: the domicile facts are available and unused
improvements.whatHappened: You preserve both sides of Spinnet's domicile but marshal no evidence. The discarded cold-weather clothes, the condo shopping, the promised post-graduation job, and the demand that the boyfriend relocate never appear.
improvements.whyItMatters: Domicile is presence plus intent to remain, and intent is proved only by facts. "Maybe reason to believe she's never leaving TX" states the conclusion those facts would have earned.
improvements.howToImprove: Replace that clause with the two or three strongest facts on each side, note that she has not yet bought the condo or started the job, and say which way it tips — adding that a Delaware domicile destroys complete diversity.

improvements.label: Question 2: the on-the-merits element is asserted, not run
improvements.whatHappened: You list the claim preclusion elements and reach Texas preclusion law through Semtek, but "[j]udgement that was final and on the merits under TX preclusion law" is where the analysis stops.
improvements.whyItMatters: That element is the question. The exam tells you a FRCP 11 dismissal is not on the merits, while Weasley holds that a TXRCP 11 dismissal is. Which rule the one-sentence dismissal rested on therefore decides preclusion.
improvements.howToImprove: Say which rule the dismissal rested on given your Question 1 Erie result, use Weasley for the Texas treatment, and state the consequence for the new case. Fund it by cutting the E.D. La. personal jurisdiction and venue re-run, which the prompt asked you not to repeat.

improvements.label: Question 2: the First Restatement does not point to the defendant's citizenship
improvements.whatHappened: You wrote that Louisiana "will probably apply NY or DE law (PPoB/incorporation of the bank)."
improvements.whyItMatters: The First Restatement looks to the place of the wrong — the last event completing the tort, which the exam tells you is the plaintiff suffering damages, possibly before she discovers them. Routing to incorporation or principal place of business changes the substantive law and so changes the punitive damages answer.
improvements.howToImprove: Name the last-event rule, locate the loss on these facts (the bonds becoming worthless), and say plainly what makes the location hard — where the bonds were, and whether the rig accident happened in Louisiana at all. Your Question 3 attempt at the location shows you can do this; move it here.

improvements.label: Question 3: the reason the transferee's choice-of-law rules apply is never stated
improvements.whatHappened: "LA procedural law, probably LA substantive 1R" is a conclusion with no supporting step. A bullet can be conclusory, and this one is.
improvements.whyItMatters: The step you skipped is the four points. Because venue in the N.D. Tex. was improper, that court was not a happy court, so its choice-of-law analysis does not follow the transfer.
improvements.howToImprove:
Walk it in order:
1. Venue was improper in the N.D. Tex., so it is an unhappy court.
2. Under the happy court rule, the transferor's choice-of-law analysis does not follow (Van Dusen, Ferens).
3. The E.D. La. therefore uses Louisiana choice-of-law rules (Klaxon), and so the First Restatement.
4. Locate the last event completing the tort and say what is indeterminate.
5. Connect the result to punitive damages and the amount in controversy.
The prompt also asks what you want from the investigator: add where the Voldemort bonds were held and where Spinnet was when the account hit zero, with a reason for each.

improvements.label: Question 3: the summary judgment burdens are inverted
improvements.whatHappened: You wrote "We bear burden of persuasion on the elements at trial." You are the bank.
improvements.whyItMatters: Spinnet carries the burden on the elements of fraud in the inducement. That changes what your motion must show: the absence of a genuine issue on one element she must prove, not proof of every element by you.
improvements.howToImprove: Say who bears the burden at trial, then name the element your motion attacks and the record material that makes it undisputed.

improvements.label: Question 4: numerosity is the winning ground and it is conceded
improvements.whatHappened: "Numerosity: satisfied by over 40 accounts" concedes the element from the raw account count.
improvements.whyItMatters: This was the question's pivot. The E.D. La. cannot entertain the claims of account holders in Jackson, Oklahoma City, Atlanta, or Houston, because those transactions have no Louisiana contacts. Filter the table and three or four Louisiana accounts remain, which is not numerous.
improvements.howToImprove: Apply the personal jurisdiction filter to the account distribution table before counting, then measure the survivors against the rule: roughly forty or more satisfies numerosity, roughly twenty or fewer does not, and in between it turns on dispersion and claim size. Note too that small per-member amounts push toward certification, so drop "Don't know how big the claims are" from superiority and spend those words here.

improvements.label: Question 4: the jurisdictional predicate is a heading
improvements.whatHappened: "SMJ, IPJ, Venue" appears with nothing under it.
improvements.whyItMatters: A heading earns nothing, and the point is one line: in a class action you look to the named plaintiff for complete diversity (Ben-Hur), so absent members' citizenship and their small individual amounts do not independently defeat jurisdiction.
improvements.howToImprove: Replace the heading with that line — Spinnet anchors diversity and carries the amount in controversy — and go straight to Rule 23.

improvements.label: Question 6: the renewed Rule 50 motion is missing
improvements.whatHappened: You name only Rule 59, with "verdict against the great weight of the evidence, lying witness." No standard is stated for either motion, and neither is applied to the trial record.
improvements.whyItMatters: Six points sit on two motions. Spinnet moved for judgment as a matter of law at the close of all the evidence and the judge deferred ruling, which preserves the renewal — the facts were built to hand you that motion. The two motions also produce different results: judgment for Spinnet, versus a new trial.
improvements.howToImprove:
Cover both, in order:
1. Renewed judgment as a matter of law under Rule 50: view the trial evidence favorably to the verdict winner without weighing credibility, and ask whether a reasonable jury could have found as it did.
2. Apply that to this record — the emails Lestrange concedes came from her account, her forgery-and-hacking story with no account of who, how, or why the hacker knew about the poker winnings, her testimony conceding materiality and reliance, and the deposit receipt on damages.
3. Rule 59 new trial: the trial judge may weigh credibility, so the great-weight ground fits comfortably.
4. State the different consequence of each.
The words are there — this question got one line.

improvements.label: Question 7: two of the three prompts are unanswered
improvements.whatHappened: The balancing analysis is framed correctly and each factor gets some named facts. But there is no worked access-to-justice discussion and no normative position. "makes sense for A2J reasons // to NP for lawyers" is too compressed to carry an argument.
improvements.whyItMatters: This is twenty-five points, and the constitutional prompt is only one third of it. The advantages and disadvantages and the recommendation are where most of the credit lives.
improvements.howToImprove: List the tradeoffs with a reason attached to each: low cost, speed, and accessibility to unrepresented parties on one side; no appellate correction, non-lawyer decisionmakers with unconstrained evidentiary discretion, the bar on counterclaims and joinder forcing claim splitting, and the $5,000 cap excluding meritorious claims on the other. Then take a position and propose one or two fixes — a minimal record, a limited right of review — naming what each costs. Also reach the jury issue: the court issues money judgments only, which is classically legal relief, so the total absence of a jury has to be confronted. This is your shortest answer relative to its weight, so it is added coverage rather than a trade.

improvements.label: Questions 1, 4, and 7: no bottom line for the client
improvements.whatHappened: Question 1 ends without recommending dismissal or transfer and to where. Question 4 never says whether certification can be defeated. Question 7 never says whether the scheme is a good idea.
improvements.whyItMatters: Each is written as a request from a supervisor. Canvassing grounds without recommending one leaves the reader to do the work you were asked to do, and the closing line is cheap in words.
improvements.howToImprove: End each of those three answers with one line naming the result you recommend and the single strongest reason for it.

feedback.exampleRevision: Numerosity, reworked: 118 is the wrong denominator. Start with the account table and ask which claims this court can hear. The Jackson, Oklahoma City, Atlanta, and Houston accounts were opened and serviced outside Louisiana, so those transactions supply no contacts linking Gringotts, Louisiana, and those claims — the E.D. La. cannot entertain them. What remains is the three New Orleans accounts plus Spinnet's, whose deposit was made in New Orleans. Three or four members sits below the roughly twenty-member line where numerosity generally fails, and joinder of four plaintiffs is plainly practicable. So lead with numerosity: even granting commonality on the Greyback email, the class this court can certify is too small. Note what this does not require you to say — the small size of individual claims cuts toward certification, so it is not a defense point here.
feedback.closing: Question 1 shows you can run a long taught sequence to the end. Do that on Questions 6 and 7, where the points are and the sequences are shorter.

judgeFindings.problem: This reverses the exam's own law. The exam states that Texas permits punitive damages for fraud in the inducement and that Louisiana has banned them by statute, and the instructor model answer says the same ("TX allows the punitive damages for fraud, LA does not"). The draft appears to have imported the reversed facts from a different year's assignment. Left uncorrected it would teach the student a wrong result on the heaviest question and would also contradict the student's own correct Question 2 line about Louisiana banning punitive damages.

Discovery is the 2018 assignment's Louisiana rule, not this exam's. The instructor model answer locates the last event at the loss of the money when the Voldemort bonds became worthless and treats the location of that event as genuinely hard.

The submission is also well under the 2300-word limit.

submissions.answer:
Here are some analytical decisions that underpin my answers throughout the exam
Spinnet is domiciled in Texas, not Delaware. Normally, going out of state for college does not change your domicile. However, Spinnet’s actions show an affirmative intent to stay in Texas with no definite leave date; she loves it there for clear reasons including the lack of income tax (a prospect that’ll only become more enticing as she ages and makes more money), she has thrown away her cold weather clothes (supporting argument she never intends to return to a cold climate like Delaware), she is shopping for a condo, and she is close to securing a job with no set end date (she will be a “permanent” TA), and she told her boyfriend to “come live here with me.” Given all these factors, it is very unlikely a court will find she is domiciled in Delaware. Mas.

However, there is likely personal jurisdiction as there are minimum contacts liking Gringott’s, the subject matter of the litigation, and the forum state (Contract’s were a party to the contract at issue, and that contract was signed in their TX branch). Assuming the defendant does not consent to venue, improper venue is grounds for dismissal or transfer.
Motion to Transfer
This is an unhappy court because venue is improper, so we must transfer. Several other courts we could transfer to that would be happy, including in DE, NY, and LA.
Next: Motion to Dismiss for Failure to State a complaint?
We should not dismiss this case for failure to state a complaint; it satisfies the Twiqbal standard.
Federal law uses Twombly/Iqbal plausibility pleading. It does not seem like Texas has a different pleading standard that would implicate Erie questonis.
Under Iqbal/Twombly, we eliminate paragraph 16 as legally conclusory.
Paragraph 8 and 9 describes the contracting party’s intentional statement.
Paragraph 11-13 describes why that stastement was false or misleading
Paragraph 9 and 11 describes why that statement was material
Paragraph 9 describes the plaintiff’s reasonable reliance
Paragraph 9 and 15 describes the damages
The complaint is not just possible but plausible and contains sufficient specificity.
Next: Motion to dismiss bc violates TXFCP 11 (ERIE ALERT!)
TXRCP require an attorney’s signature on each page of the complaint, otherwise the complaint will be dismissed immediately and without notice to the affected party. FRCP 11(a) requires a signature, but does not specify that it be on every page, and allows the party to promptly correct an error.
First, under York, whether we apply state vs federal law determines whether the complaint will be dismissed, so it is outcome-determinative and we should go with the state law.
Second, under the Hanna/Scalia version, the FCRP is valid, because it “abridge, enlarge, or modify” any obvious substantive right and per Sibbach really does regulate procedure. Reading it broadly and straightforwardly, FRCP is applicable here, as it also deals with signature requirements and opportunities to correct it. This supports going with federal law.
Third, under the Hanna/Ginsburg version, the FCRP is valid, because it “abridge, enlarge, or modify” any obvious substantive right and per Sibbach really does regulate procedure. We might be able to interpret the signature requirement narrowly, arguing that FRCP sets a floor (sign in one place) and the state law adds requirements (sign in multiple places). It’s harder to interpret the notice requirement narrow to avoid conflict; FRCP prevents dismissal if the omission is promptly corrected after being called to the attorney's or party's attention, but TXRCP requires immediate dismissal. This supports using federal law.
Fourth, under the Harlan Hanna test, we need to assess whether applying federal law would cause an alteration in the primary conduct of the parties. Under Harlan, it’s substantive because TX enacted this rule to force attorneys to do more accurate review, suggesting applying federal law would change their conduct.
Should i argue it’s proecural bc it alterswhat lawyers do?
This supports applying state law.
Overall, while the tests offer support for both, given the clear legislative intent as articulated by the TX SC, we should probably use state law and dismiss the complaint.

feedback.headline: Question 1's threshold analyses are sound; 31 of 85 points went unanswered
feedback.overview: The strongest work here is Question 1's threshold sequence. Domicile is argued from five specific facts in the email rather than taken from the complaint's allegation. Personal jurisdiction moves through general jurisdiction, consent and tag, the long-arm and 4(k)(1)(A), minimum contacts, and fairness in order. Venue is rejected subsection by subsection with a reason on each, and the pleading analysis strikes paragraph 16 and then maps each fraud element to surviving paragraph numbers. Question 2's claim preclusion run and Question 5 are also complete. The cost is elsewhere. Question 7 is worth 25 points and is not answered at all — the text under that heading is Question 6 material on appellate standards of review. Question 6 is worth 6 points and is not answered either. Inside Question 1, arising-under jurisdiction never appears even though the complaint pleads 1331, and the transfer half of the memo is one sentence.

strengths.label: Domicile argued, not asserted
strengths.detail: Naming the presumption that college attendance does not shift domicile and then arguing against it from the discarded winter clothes, the condo search, the permanent TA offer, the tax remark, and the boyfriend ultimatum is how a contested threshold requirement should be run. It also secures the diversity conclusion the rest of the memo depends on.
strengths.answerExcerpt: Normally, going out of state for college does not change your domicile. However, Spinnet's actions show an affirmative intent to stay in Texas

strengths.label: Venue rejected subsection by subsection
strengths.detail: Each basis gets its own reason — events in the Southern District, no residence in the Northern District, and the fallback unavailable because the Southern District exists. That is what turns "venue improper" from a conclusion into a holding, and it feeds the happy-court consequence you carry forward.
strengths.answerExcerpt: § 1391(b)(3) does not apply because tehre are districts the action could have otherwise been brought it.

strengths.label: Pleading tested at the paragraph and element level
strengths.detail: Setting aside paragraph 16 as conclusory and then naming which paragraphs plead which element of fraud in the inducement is the taught sequence performed rather than described. That is what makes the plausibility conclusion credible.
strengths.answerExcerpt: Under Iqbal/Twombly, we eliminate paragraph 16 as legally conclusory.

strengths.label: Four vertical choice-of-law approaches carried to a commitment
strengths.detail: York, the two Hanna variants with the Rules Enabling Act and Sibbach's "really regulates procedure," and Harlan's primary-conduct question are each run, and then you pick a side instead of leaving the approaches side by side. Flagging your own doubt about the Harlan reading is the right instinct on a close point.
strengths.answerExcerpt: Overall, while the tests offer support for both, given the clear legislative intent as articulated by the TX SC, we should probably use state law and dismiss the complaint.

strengths.label: Preclusion elements plus the new amount-in-controversy problem
strengths.detail: Semtek gets you Texas preclusion law because the rendering court sat in diversity, and then finality, on the merits, same parties, same claim, and same transaction each get a reason. You also find the separate Louisiana problem on your own, run lex loci delicti, canvass the candidate places for the last event, and admit the answer is close. Living with genuine indeterminacy is an analytical move, not a hedge.
strengths.answerExcerpt: Factors could go either way but prob lean toward LA

strengths.label: You spotted the jurisdictional limit on out-of-state class claims
strengths.detail: Canvassing both branches — Shutts for absent members and Bristol-Myers Squibb treating a class as mass joinder — is the hardest move in this question, and it is the door to the winning defense.

strengths.label: Complete and proportionate on three points

improvements.label: Arising-under jurisdiction is never raised
improvements.whatHappened: The complaint pleads jurisdiction under 1331 as well as 1332, and the federal disclosure statute is embedded in the state fraud claim through the rule that a required disclosure makes a statement conclusively material. Your answer analyzes diversity only.
improvements.whyItMatters: This is a whole component of a 35-point question, and the 1331 allegation in the complaint is the signal to run it.
improvements.howToImprove:
Run it in three short steps.
1. No federal cause of action appears on the face of the well-pleaded complaint, so there is no arising-under jurisdiction (Mottley).
2. Ask whether the Smith-Grable exception applies, because the state claim contains an embedded federal issue.
3. Ask whether that federal issue is actually disputed and substantial, and whether recognizing it would sweep ordinary state fraud claims into federal court. Step one is mechanical; step three is the judgment call, so argue both sides.
The words come from the Question 4 bullets on venue and pleading, which that question did not put in play.

improvements.label: Transfer is disposed of in one sentence
improvements.whatHappened: After correctly finding the Northern District of Texas an unhappy court, you list Delaware, New York, and Louisiana with no analysis. The Southern District of Texas — the district your own venue analysis identified as where the events happened — is not mentioned.
improvements.whyItMatters: The boss asked about transfer as the alternative to dismissal, so a bare list answers half the assignment conclusorily. A transferee is only available if the case could have been brought there.
improvements.howToImprove:
For each candidate district, run the check in order.
1. Could the case have been brought there — personal jurisdiction plus proper venue (Hoffman)?
2. Weigh the public and private interest factors (Gulf Oil): location of witnesses and documents, the parties' convenience, and the forum's interest.
Start with the Southern District of Texas and the Eastern District of Louisiana, where the events, witnesses, and documents are. The words come from the Question 3 bullets that repeat Question 1's venue and personal jurisdiction analysis.

improvements.label: Two stated errors in the amount-in-controversy analysis
improvements.whatHappened: You write that the amount in controversy is met under both Texas and Louisiana law. Louisiana bans punitive damages for this tort, so under Louisiana law the amount fails — which is the whole reason the horizontal choice-of-law fight decides jurisdiction. Separately, you label the Texas discussion "Lex loi delicti," which is the First Restatement's rule, and the sentence beginning "Looking at section 3" stops before the Second Restatement factors are named.
improvements.whyItMatters: The first error undercuts the analysis you then do correctly. Mislabeling the Restatements reads as confusion about which framework Texas uses.
improvements.howToImprove: State the stakes in one line: Texas allows the punitive damages and the amount is met, Louisiana bars them and it is not, so the choice of law decides subject matter jurisdiction. Then name the Second Restatement factors you are weighing and reserve lex loci delicti for the Louisiana analysis in Question 2. Incidentally, the course term is plausibility pleading rather than the portmanteau.

improvements.label: The contested element rests on an unstated assumption
improvements.whatHappened: The dismissal order cites only "applicable signature requirements," so which signature rule the dismissing court applied is deliberately ambiguous. You carry the Texas rule over from Question 1 without saying so.
improvements.whyItMatters: On the merits is the only contested claim preclusion element here, and it turns entirely on that choice. Naming the assumption is what makes the conclusion argued.
improvements.howToImprove: Add one line stating the assumption and its consequence: the Question 1 vertical choice-of-law analysis pointed to the Texas rule, Texas treats such dismissals as on the merits, so preclusion follows; had the federal rule applied, the dismissal is not on the merits and this ground disappears. Pay for it by deleting the "Issue Preclusion" heading and its two general lines, which state a rule without applying it.

improvements.label: The question asked for facts and you named none
improvements.whatHappened: The question expressly invites you to say what additional facts the investigator should find and why they matter. None are named, even though the Question 2 lex loci discussion had just identified which facts are unknown.
improvements.whyItMatters: On a four-point question, answering the express invitation is most of the available credit.
improvements.howToImprove: Name the facts and tie each to a consequence: where the Voldemort bonds were held, and where Spinnet was and what her domicile was when the account went to zero, because those locate the last event under Louisiana's First Restatement and therefore decide whether the punitive damages claim, and with it the amount in controversy, survives. Add one clause on why Louisiana's rules apply at all — venue in the transferor court was improper, so its choice-of-law analysis does not follow the transfer. The words come from this question's venue and personal jurisdiction bullets, which repeat Question 1.

improvements.label: The jurisdictional limit never reaches numerosity
improvements.whatHappened: You see that the Louisiana court cannot hear the claims of account holders whose transactions have no Louisiana connection, then state that numerosity is satisfied because the total exceeds forty. Later you concede a state-by-state class works in Georgia and Oklahoma but not Louisiana. The two positions are never reconciled, so the boss's question gets no answer.
improvements.whyItMatters: Numerosity is where the defense wins. Once the out-of-state claims drop out, only the three New Orleans accounts plus Spinnet remain, which is not numerous.
improvements.howToImprove:
Run Rule 23(a) in order and let the jurisdictional ruling feed the first element.
1. Numerosity — count only the members whose claims the forum can hear.
2. Commonality — already argued from the supervisor's email and the identical form contracts.
3. Typicality.
4. Adequacy.
Then reach predominance and superiority for a damages class; the common scheme and the geographic spread of the accounts support superiority. Close with a yes-or-no for the boss. Note also that the five-million-dollar aggregate threshold comes from the class-action fairness statute, not Shady Grove. Pay for this with the venue and pleading bullets in this question.

improvements.label: Not answered
improvements.whatHappened: The Question 6 heading is followed immediately by Question 7. The only Rule 50 and Rule 59 material in the submission sits under the Question 7 heading and consists of general notes on appellate standards of review.
improvements.whyItMatters: Those notes describe what a court of appeals does, not whether the trial judge should grant the renewed motion. Six points are forgone on a record that is unusually easy to argue from.
improvements.howToImprove:
Answer it in this order.
1. Preservation — she moved at the close of all the evidence and the judge deferred, so the renewed motion under Rule 50(b) is available.
2. The standard — view the evidence in the light most favorable to the verdict winner and ask whether a reasonable jury could have found as it did, credibility normally being the jury's.
3. Apply it to the testimony — the emails Lestrange concedes came from her account, her concession on materiality, Greyback's authentication, Spinnet's testimony about her own signature, and the absence of any account of who forged, who hacked, or how a hacker knew about the poker winnings.
4. The alternative Rule 59 motion that the verdict is against the great weight of the evidence, where the judge has more latitude on credibility, and how the two remedies differ.
Time for this comes from reserving it up front — see the allocation note below.

improvements.label: Not answered
improvements.whatHappened: Nothing under this heading addresses the small claims scheme; the text there is displaced Question 6 material.
improvements.whyItMatters: This is 25 points, the second heaviest item on the exam, and it needs real space.
improvements.howToImprove:
The question has three parts, so answer all three.
1. Constitutionality — run procedural due process against the scheme's features: the interest at stake in a claim capped at five thousand dollars, the risk of error from non-lawyer judges with no evidence rules, no record, no motions and no appeal, and the government's interest in cheap fast adjudication; six weeks' notice with the complaint and a trial date goes to notice. Then address whether the absence of a jury raises a problem in a state court system.
2. Access to justice both ways — low cost, speed, and usability without counsel on one side; error rates with no appellate correction, no record, the counsel-at-your-own-expense asymmetry against a repeat-player institution, the cap excluding larger meritorious claims, and the bar on counterclaims and joinder on the other.
3. A bottom line defended against the strongest objection, with a concrete fix and its cost.
Budget words here in proportion to 25 of the 85 points.

Pick one of the two ways listed above. Add to it one other way, not listed, of expanding either issue or claim preclusion, a way that you think of yourself. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of these ideas. Include in your discussion a consideration of the access to justice concerns involved.
Question 6: The second suggestion would eliminate the distinction between permissive and compulsory joinder (including counterclaims) currently in FRCP13 & 20. Particularly given the declaratory judgment statute, so doing would provide sophisticated parties with additional power to compel litigation on all disputes in that party’s chosen forum. How much this will matter is hard to guess. For sophisticated and reasonably financed opponents, it will probably matter little. Such parties can take advantage of modern transportation and information transmission mechanisms to render location less important. Geographic location can sometimes matter to HCOL (Klaxon), but given the similarity in HCOL rules across the country (see how NY’s experience with HCOL resulted in the R2 = R1 except in unusual cases), this will infrequently. The big divide currently, and likely in the future, is whether litigation occurs in court at all (as opposed to some kind of arbitration), and if so, whether it occurs in a United States court using United States law (“US law, who needs it?”). The FRsCP already encourage resolution of as many disputes as possible in a single lawsuit, and this change seems consistent with that policy, with Rule 42 providing the needed complexity-reducing discretion to the trial judge. Whatever efficiency gains are result from the litigation, but most likely settlement, of multiple matters would be welcome. An additional suggestion to expand the preclusion doctrine would be to expand the rules of privity, such that (say) the Gonzalez district court’s decision would have been affirmed. As applied to claim preclusion, this would create a rule of near-compulsory intervention for anyone who wanted to have a say in litigation of their interests, when those interests were effectively represented by a party to that litigation, knowing that if they do not intervene, they will be precluded anyway. As applied to issue preclusion, this would effectively expand the rules of precedent (which does not require any form of mutuality) to include factual determinations. This proposal could result in some efficiency gains from reduced relitigation of claims and issues, particularly on large matters of public interest, such as the behavior of large corporations, or the legality of government policies. The proposal would, however, involve acute information costs. Depending on how much privity is expanded, it could result in parties being bound by litigation about which they had no notice and no prior knowledge, which would implicate PDP doctrines (Mullane). Parties unsure of whether changes in PDP doctrines were ripe for relaxation might need to begin to monitor courts closely; information systems regarding the nature of ongoing litigation are not currently in place for such monitoring. Moreover, large public-interest litigation might become absurdly unwieldy (think Smuck) unless class action certification rules were relaxed (we’d need to reverse the trend in Walmart). Both proposals could involve difficult access to justice costs. The declaratory judgment statute, plus the inability of low-income parties to use modern methods of transportation and information transmission, will make it difficult for smaller parties or low-income individuals to combat a sophisticated party’s choice of forum for tort cases (contract matters probably have FSCs anyway). And only sophisticated parties would have a chance to monitor cases that might affect their interests, as would be required in by the second proposed change. As is often true, the usefulness of these doctrines depends on which world we consider, that of sophisticated and reasonably resourced parties or the other 99%.

feedback.headline: Broad coverage across Questions 1 through 5, with several outcome-controlling steps announced rather than reasoned
feedback.overview: The four-branch vertical choice-of-law run on the summons rule reaches all four tests and states a bottom line that depends on which one the court adopts. The plausibility work maps elements onto numbered complaint paragraphs. Supplemental jurisdiction lands where the course now puts it: Rule 20 as the only route in, 1367(b) as the bar, no stacking of the $50,000 claim across defendants. But the steps that decide each question carry the least reasoning. Riddle's domicile, which controls whether any of the complaint survives, is disposed of as debatable with none of the record facts weighed. Venue is one clause. On Question 2 the discovery record behind HG's liability motion is never marshaled. On Question 4, "Actually Litigated -no" drives the entire issue-preclusion outcome with no reason attached.

improvements.label: Question 1 — Riddle's domicile and the other parties' citizenships
improvements.whatHappened: Riddle's domicile is disposed of in one clause as debatable under Mas, with none of the competing facts weighed. The Rhode Island birth, the continuous voter registration, and the weekends with his parents never appear. Neither do the Boston apartment, the business office there, and fifteen years of Massachusetts income taxes. HG's citizenship and Droobles' citizenship are never stated for diversity purposes.
improvements.whyItMatters: This fact decides whether any of the complaint survives. If Riddle is a Massachusetts citizen, complete diversity fails under Strawbridge and Count II against your client falls with the rest, independent of the amount-in-controversy defect you correctly spotted.
improvements.howToImprove: Establish the parties first: HG by incorporation and principal place of business under nerve-center reasoning, Droobles as New Hampshire. Then set the Rhode Island facts against the Massachusetts facts in one line each, note that student years alone do not shift domicile under Mas, pick a side, and state the consequence under Strawbridge. Pay for it by cutting the Erie section's recital of the Rules Enabling Act quotation and the Sibbach test down to the conclusion that FRCP 4 really regulates procedure.

improvements.label: Question 1 — venue asserted rather than run
improvements.whatHappened: Venue is one clause: 1391(b)(2) applies because events were substantially in Massachusetts. No Massachusetts event is named, and 1391(b)(3) is never mentioned.
improvements.whyItMatters: Venue is a brain-off topic. Walk the enumerated bases in statutory order and the points are there. It also matters downstream, because your happy court reasoning in Question 2 rests on venue having been proper in Massachusetts.
improvements.howToImprove:
Turn your brain off and take the subsections in order.
1. 1391(b)(1) — unavailable, because the two defendants reside in different states.
2. 1391(b)(2) — name the Massachusetts events: the endorsement, Harry's side of the email exchange, HG's Massachusetts operations, and the situs of the loss in value.
3. 1391(b)(3) — unavailable, because a proper district exists.
The words come from the personal jurisdiction section, where the Second Restatement section 6 digression belongs in Question 2 instead.

improvements.label: Question 1 — the plausibility analysis stops before the step that decides it
improvements.whatHappened: After striking P20 and mapping paragraphs to elements, the analysis ends. You never ask whether what survives nudges Droobles' own participation from possible to plausible, and you never say whether the motion should be granted.
improvements.whyItMatters: Steps one and two are bookkeeping. Step three is the holding, and the contested element here is element (i), participation in production — not falsity, reputational harm, or loss of value.
improvements.howToImprove: Add one line applying step three to element (i), using paragraph 16 and the exam's discovery facts: the recording was made on Droobles' own phone at his explicit request, and Harry never met either defendant. Then state whether the motion is granted. Take the words from the repeated validity analysis in the Erie section, which states the same point twice. The course calls this plausibility pleading rather than the portmanteau you used.

improvements.label: Question 1 — make the direct-sale contrast on availment
improvements.whatHappened: The specific jurisdiction analysis runs the long-arm, 4(k)(1)(A), the 25% Massachusetts shipments, the McIntyre concurrence on volume, and the McGee fairness factors. The contrast between Droobles' direct sales and a distributor-intermediary posture is gestured at rather than made.
improvements.whyItMatters: Direct shipment to the customer's own address with no distributor in between is the strongest purposeful availment point available to you, and it takes this out of stream-of-commerce territory entirely.
improvements.howToImprove: Add a clause where you write "minimal contacts": Droobles ships to the address the customer supplies, with no intermediary, so the volume question is not a stream-of-commerce question. One clause, taken from the sentence that repeats that the business is unincorporated.

improvements.label: Question 2 — HG's liability motion resolved without the record
improvements.whatHappened: On HG's motion you cross-referenced the pleading analysis from Question 1 and then referred to "very clear evidence of the vid/email." The FluNetwork report, the matching 5:22 running time and identical scripted language, and Lily Evans' uncontradicted testimony that Droobles summoned her and directed the recording on his own phone never appear.
improvements.whyItMatters: A pleading tests allegations; Rule 56 tests the discovery record. Pointing back to the complaint answers a different question, so the inference chain a jury would have to draw is not on the page. Denying summary judgment is a defensible conclusion, but it needs the record it is denying judgment on.
improvements.howToImprove: Replace the cross-reference with the record items, each tied to what it proves: the two email exchanges to motive, the report plus the 5:22 match and identical script to how the fake was made, Evans to Droobles' participation. Then say why the cold-medicine and flu memory testimony does or does not controvert documents. The words come from the Public Access paragraph, where "HP's online connections" can be swapped for the deposition testimony to paragraphs 6-8 at no extra length.

improvements.label: Question 2 — only one path to Massachusetts law
improvements.whatHappened: The Public Access defense reaches the case only through the happy court route, and the horizontal choice-of-law reasoning behind it sits back in the personal jurisdiction section compressed to a sentence.
improvements.whyItMatters: Your conclusion rests entirely on Massachusetts having had proper venue and personal jurisdiction, which you yourself treated as uncertain in Question 1. A second route exists that does not depend on that.
improvements.howToImprove: Add the alternative: if New Hampshire's own First Restatement analysis governs, lex loci delicti still points to Massachusetts, because the last event completing the tort is HG's loss of value there. Pay for it by cutting the Celotex burden recital, which states the standard twice before applying it.

improvements.label: Question 3 — Rule 54(b) missing from the checklist
improvements.whatHappened: You cleared 1291, the collateral order doctrine, mandamus, injunctions, and the double-discretion route, but never mentioned Rule 54(b).
improvements.whyItMatters: Rule 54(b) is the one remaining category, and it is the natural argument for a ruling that resolves liability but reserves damages.
improvements.howToImprove: Add a clause: no Rule 54(b) direction of entry of final judgment as to fewer than all claims or parties was made, so that route is closed. Everything else here was correctly proportioned to three points.

improvements.label: Question 4 — "Actually Litigated -no" carries no reason
improvements.whatHappened: That bullet decides the whole issue-preclusion outcome and has no supporting step. The tort elements were resolved on a granted summary judgment motion, which you never engage. The related question — whether a summary judgment ruling never reduced to judgment is firm enough to support preclusion — is never raised.
improvements.whyItMatters: A bullet that states a result with no reason is as conclusory as a sentence doing the same, and this one produces your bottom line. The firmness question is genuinely two-sided, and either resolution earns credit when reasoned.
improvements.howToImprove: Say what happened: the elements were litigated on a granted summary judgment motion, then the case ended by stipulated dismissal. Then argue firmness both ways in one line each — such rulings are revisable in principle but rarely revised, weighed against the interest in not relitigating — and land on an answer.

improvements.label: Question 4 — Harry and Ginny treated as one party
improvements.whatHappened: Privity rests on a combined figure: "Own 70% of the stock and are VP," producing a single claim-precluded result for both plaintiffs.
improvements.whyItMatters: The question turns on the difference between them. Harry's 65% stake and his control of the HG litigation supply privity; Ginny's 5% with no control evidence does not. Aggregating them also closes off Ginny's nonmutual offensive issue preclusion, the only live use of preclusion on the plaintiffs' side.
improvements.howToImprove: Run privity separately for each. Ground Harry's in substantial control with his percentage and his role in the first suit. Say Ginny is not in privity on a 5% stake with no control shown, and note that discovery could develop control facts. Then take her nonmutual offensive issue preclusion on its own.

improvements.label: Question 4 — which state's preclusion law the transferred judgment carries
improvements.whatHappened: You named intersystem preclusion correctly and cited Semtek for the rule that the rendering federal diversity court's state supplies the preclusion law. You then wrote "the State Law where the federal court sits" without asking whether that is Massachusetts or New Hampshire after the transfer. The passage ends up saying both that New Hampshire mutuality will not block preclusion and that there is no preclusion.
improvements.whyItMatters: Massachusetts has abolished mutuality and New Hampshire requires it strictly, so the transferor-versus-transferee question is the fulcrum here. You already had the tool in hand from Question 2.
improvements.howToImprove: Carry the happy court reasoning forward: if Massachusetts had proper venue and personal jurisdiction, its preclusion law follows the transfer and mutuality is no obstacle; if not, New Hampshire's requirement defeats Ginny. State which you think it is.

improvements.label: Question 5 — typicality and adequacy recited without facts
improvements.whatHappened: Both prongs appear as rule text with no facts attached.
improvements.whyItMatters: On a three-point question the rule text buys nothing; the application does. The named plaintiffs' outsized stakes relative to the absent members are exactly what adequacy asks about.
improvements.howToImprove: Replace the quoted rule language with one line: Harry's and Ginny's claims arise from the same scheme on the same legal theory as the absent members', and their much larger stakes raise the only adequacy question worth naming.

improvements.label: Outcome-controlling steps stated as results
improvements.whatHappened: Four bullets decide their questions with no supporting step: Riddle's domicile, venue under 1391(b)(2), "Actually Litigated -no," and the combined stock figure for privity.
improvements.whyItMatters: The pattern is not the note format. It is that the steps carrying the most weight have the least reasoning behind them, while fully reasoned work sits on steps that were never in doubt.
improvements.howToImprove: Before leaving any step, ask whether the answer changes if that step flips. If it does, give it a reason, and where the facts are close, a sentence for each side. Take those words from the steps that are not close.

improvements.label: Question 1 — no arising-under step, and diversity is never assembled
improvements.whatHappened: You went straight to diversity. The well-pleaded complaint rule and the Smith-Grable exception never appear, so the other basis for subject matter jurisdiction is never ruled out. You also never state HG's own citizenship, so complete diversity is never actually put together.
improvements.whyItMatters: On a 25-point dismissal survey the grader checks whether each threshold was tested. Diversity without the plaintiff's citizenship is incomplete even when the conclusion is right.
improvements.howToImprove:
Walk the taught steps in order.
1. Arising under: no federal cause of action (Mottley), then run the two-step Smith-Grable exception and say why a state business-disparagement claim embeds no substantial federal issue.
2. HG's citizenship: MA incorporation plus principal place of business under Hertz; shareholder residences are irrelevant.
3. Droobles: NH by birth, no move.
4. Riddle: argue both sides under Mas — RI birth, parents' home, and RI voter registration against the Boston apartment, the business office, and 15 years of MA taxes.
5. State the consequence: if Riddle is a MA citizen, complete diversity fails under Strawbridge and the whole complaint goes, not just Count II.
Pay for this by stating the Rules Enabling Act formulation once in your Erie run instead of twice.

improvements.label: Question 1 — the personal jurisdiction analysis never reaches an answer
improvements.whatHappened: Your fairness bullets stop at "Forum's interest-" and no conclusion on specific jurisdiction over Droobles appears. Relatedness is never named as the problem: the MA contacts are gum sales, while the suit is about the video.
improvements.whyItMatters: Relatedness is the weak link on these facts, and a memo that lists contacts without deciding whether jurisdiction exists gives the partner nothing to act on.
improvements.howToImprove: Take the bases in order and finish each: no general jurisdiction under Daimler (25% is not at home), no consent or in-state service, then specific jurisdiction. State purposeful availment — direct internet sales with no intermediary, unlike McIntyre — then argue relatedness both ways: the gum sales do not give rise to this claim, but the endorsement, HG's MA-anchored reputation, and knowledge that the loss would land in MA connect the video to MA. Complete the fair and reasonable factors and state a conclusion. Analyze contacts through purposeful availment and relatedness only; do not reach for an aimed-at-the-forum shortcut. The words come from the repeated "Longarm + 4k1a" line and the place-of-harm bullets sitting in this block, which belong in Question 2.

improvements.label: Question 1 — venue subsections blur, and the summons rule is never characterized
improvements.whatHappened: "B2 likely satisfied if MA found to have SIPJ over Droobles" imports the (b)(3) test into (b)(2). Separately, you enter the Erie analysis without first characterizing MARCP 4(a)(1)(H) as procedural for horizontal choice of law under Klaxon.
improvements.whyItMatters: Section 1391(b)(2) turns on where substantial events occurred, not on personal jurisdiction, and (b)(3) opens only when no district qualifies under (b)(1) or (b)(2). And the Erie question does not arise until the state rule is the one a MA court would supply.
improvements.howToImprove: Say (b)(1) fails because the two defendants reside in different states. Say (b)(2) is satisfied by the MA events — the endorsement, Harry's side of the emails, HG's operations, the loss of value — with the NH filming as the counterweight. Say (b)(3) is therefore unavailable. Then add one clause before the Erie run: anything arguably procedural is procedural for horizontal choice of law, so MA's summons rule supplies the requirement under Klaxon. Put that clause where the fragment "Big question: where is the place" now sits.

improvements.label: Question 2 — three elements decided by label alone
improvements.whatHappened: On HG's motion you disposed of utterance, falsity, and reputational harm with a bare "GIMF" and no reason. Falsity in particular is hard to call disputed when Harry's testimony that the video is fake is uncontradicted.
improvements.whyItMatters: A bullet that states a conclusion with no supporting step is conclusory, and these are the elements the motion turns on. Your reasoning on the remaining element shows you can do this work.
improvements.howToImprove: For each element, name the record item and say what a jury could find: the FluNetwork report plus the matching 5:22 length and identical language on falsity; Evans' uncontradicted testimony that Droobles summoned her and had her record on his own phone on production. Then say which element genuinely stays disputed. Fund it by cutting your list of candidate locations for the lost business value down to the two that matter.

improvements.label: Question 2 — the Second Restatement work is cross-referenced, not run
improvements.whatHappened: You point back to Question 1 for the choice-of-law analysis rather than working it for the Public Access defense itself.
improvements.whyItMatters: The defense exists only in MA, so this step decides half the question. A presumption plus a contacts canvass is what earns the point.
improvements.howToImprove: State the place-of-injury presumption, canvass the competing contacts — the NH meeting and recording against the endorsement, the emails, and the loss of value in MA — and say why a court is unlikely to depart from the presumption for a defense keyed to a MA party's public access. The exam tells you the last event completing the tort is the loss of value, so lean on it. Name Ferens for the point that the transfer does not change which choice-of-law rules apply. The place-of-harm bullets you wrote in the Question 1 jurisdiction block do this work — run them here instead.

improvements.label: Question 3 — name the statute and the missing Rule 54(b) element
improvements.whatHappened: You never name §1291 as the provision the order fails. Your Rule 54(b) reason — "not multiple claims" — understates the posture, since there are two defendants and two counts.
improvements.whyItMatters: Naming the element that failed is what shows the route was actually run. Here the operative point is the absence of the required determination and direction entering judgment on fewer than all claims or parties.
improvements.howToImprove: Two swaps, no added length: "no final decision under §1291 because damages are reserved," and "54(b) unavailable — no express determination and no direction for entry of judgment."

improvements.label: Question 4 — the happy-court branch is inverted and attached to the wrong court
improvements.whatHappened: You wrote that if the rule applies and NH was happy, strict mutuality governs. The rule keys on the transferor court, which is MA, and it runs the other way.
improvements.whyItMatters: This is the pivot of the whole issue-preclusion half. Whether Ginny can use nonmutual offensive issue preclusion depends entirely on which state's preclusion law follows the transfer, so an inverted mapping loses the answer even though you preserved both outcomes.
improvements.howToImprove:
Run it in order, in place of the two inverted branch lines.
1. Semtek: a federal diversity court's judgment takes the preclusion law of the state where that court sat.
2. The transfer makes the question which state that is.
3. If the MA court was happy — personal jurisdiction and venue proper there — MA law follows the transfer, MA has abolished mutuality, and Ginny may use NMOCE.
4. If the MA court was unhappy, NH law governs and its strict mutuality bars her because she was not a party in the first suit.

improvements.label: Question 4 — "actually litigated" undervalues the granted summary judgment
improvements.whatHappened: You concluded nothing was actually litigated because the claim was dismissed after settlement. The court had already granted summary judgment on the tort elements before that dismissal.
improvements.whyItMatters: That grant is the event the actually-litigated and necessary-to-the-judgment inquiries are about. Skipping it means you never reach the genuine question.
improvements.howToImprove: Say the elements were litigated and decided on the motion, then argue firmness both ways: a summary judgment grant is revisable before final judgment and was followed by a stipulated dismissal, which cuts against firmness, but the issues were fully presented and decided on a developed record, which cuts for it. Attach your stealth-factor bullets to that ruling rather than to the settlement.

improvements.label: Question 5 — superiority has no reason and certification has no answer
improvements.whatHappened: Superiority is "maybe not, maybe yes" with no reason on either side, and no overall conclusion on certification appears.
improvements.whyItMatters: An answer that opens every requirement without closing any leaves nothing to credit at the end, and superiority is the requirement your own predominance work has already set up.
improvements.howToImprove: Replace "maybe not, maybe yes" with a reason: near-identical issues across 22 shareholders make one adjudication better than 22 suits, subject to the horizontal choice-of-law wrinkle you already flagged. Then state a conclusion on certification. This costs no net words.

improvements.label: Question 6 — the required original proposal is missing
improvements.whatHappened: The slot for your own proposal contains the exam's second listed option, restated: expanding claim preclusion to reach claims that could have been brought, including permissive counterclaims.
improvements.whyItMatters: The prompt expressly requires an addition of your own on a 15-point question, so this is a straight loss of the points reserved for it.
improvements.howToImprove: Cut that restatement and use the space for one concrete expansion of your own, with its mechanism in a sentence — for example, extending preclusion to non-parties who were effectively represented, or relaxing the necessary-to-the-judgment requirement. Then work the consequences: the notice and procedural due process limits on binding non-parties under Mullane, the monitoring costs pushed onto absent parties, the pressure toward near-compulsory intervention, and the strain on class certification and manageability.

improvements.label: Question 6 — the chosen proposal gets no mechanism and no authority
improvements.whatHappened: Your reason for tolerating preclusion of unraised issues — that issues are narrower than claims — is a start. The second listed option gets one line, "Encourages judicial economy," with no mechanism and no downside. No case or rule is cited anywhere in this question.
improvements.whyItMatters: This is the second-heaviest question on the exam and it received fewer words than the 3-point appealability question. A policy answer earns points by naming the mechanism by which each consequence follows and by using specific course material.
improvements.howToImprove: Say that extending claim preclusion to permissive claims would collapse the permissive/compulsory line in Rules 13 and 20, and that it would let a sophisticated party use a declaratory judgment to force all disputes into a forum of its choosing. Then ask how much forum choice actually costs the other side, given Klaxon and the convergence of the Restatements. Keep your access to justice point about the unrepresented defendant and develop it — that is the strongest thing in this question. Pay for the space by stating the MA and NH mutuality regimes once in Question 4 instead of twice.

improvements.label: Across Questions 1, 5, and 6 — sequences opened but not closed, and effort not matched to points
improvements.whatHappened: The specific jurisdiction analysis, superiority, and certification each stop before a stated bottom line. The 15-point policy question received less development than the 3-point appealability question.
improvements.whyItMatters: An unfinished sequence forfeits the credit its completed steps had already earned. Points follow the exam's stated weights, not the questions that are quickest to run.
improvements.howToImprove: Before moving on, write one line beginning "so" for each sequence you open. Budget words against the point values first: Questions 1 and 6 are 40 of 65 points and should take most of the answer.

feedback.exampleRevision: Instead of "Don't know if happy court rule applies for preclusion, if it does and NH was happy / Strict mutuality": L1 was a federal diversity judgment, so under Semtek the NH state court applies the preclusion law of the state where the rendering federal court sat — and the transfer makes that the question. If the MA court was happy (personal jurisdiction over Droobles and venue proper under §1391(b)(2)), MA law follows the case to NH. MA requires no mutuality, so Ginny — not in privity with HG and therefore not bound — can assert NMOCE against Droobles on the elements decided on summary judgment, subject to firmness. If the MA court was unhappy, NH's own preclusion law governs, and its strict mutuality bars her because she was not a party in L1.
feedback.closing: The habit worth building is the one-line "so" at the end of every sequence you open — you already reach the hard steps in Questions 1 and 5 and lose the credit only at the last line.

feedback.headline: Question 1 is handled at a high level; several later questions leave part of the prompt unanswered
feedback.overview: Your strongest work is Question 1. You ran the taught sequences instead of announcing results: long-arm plus 4(k)(1)(A), then minimum contacts, then F&R, separately for XH and Faith. Venue is run subsection by subsection. The Erie ladder is complete, including the Rules Enabling Act validity step. The plausibility work is done at the paragraph level. And you correctly treated the availability of the per se theory as an HCOL question that then drives the 12(b)(6) result. What holds the answer back is completeness elsewhere. Question 2 never converts the new facts into a pleading theory and never mentions venue. Question 5 does not answer the jury-trial half of the prompt and never uses Parklane. Question 6 names two doctrines without the explanation or the assessment the question required. Question 7 supplies one drawback where three or four were asked. Those four questions carry 26 of the 65 points.

strengths.detail: Splitting XH from Faith is what let you reach different results with reasons: Faith's Pennsylvania advertising as purposeful availment, and for XH the point that the truck reached Pennsylvania through Faith's own act and through a distributor. That separation is what the question was built to test.
