improvements.label: Question 1 — the section 6 relationship factor covers only one of two relationships
improvements.whatHappened: You wrote that the "relationship between parties [is] centered in PA." That is right for Buffy and Faith. The XH–Faith relationship, formed and performed at The Spike, is not accounted for.
improvements.whyItMatters: The relationship factor is one of the reasons a Second Restatement court departs from the place of injury, and the whole 12(b)(6) outcome turns on whether Pennsylvania or Virginia law supplies the per se theory. Your Pennsylvania conclusion is defensible, but it needs to survive the Virginia-side facts rather than omit them.
improvements.howToImprove: Split the factor into two lines: Buffy–Faith centered in Pennsylvania, XH–Faith and the failure to test in Virginia. Then say why the presumption still holds despite the second line, or why it gives way. Shrink "B3- irrelevant because we have B2" to a clause to pay for it.

improvements.label: Question 1 — characterize the state pleading requirement before the Erie ladder
improvements.whatHappened: The outline moves from Klaxon straight into York, Harlan, and Hanna without saying that the Pennsylvania pleading requirement is procedural for HCOL purposes.
improvements.whyItMatters: That characterization is what makes the state rule a candidate to apply at all, and it is the hinge connecting the HCOL run to the Erie run.
improvements.howToImprove: Add one clause: anything arguably procedural is procedural for HCOL, so the Pennsylvania specificity requirement is procedural and Pennsylvania would apply it, which sets up the conflict with FRCP 8. Cut "Can we use NPS? Probably not (see HCOL below)" to pay for it, since the HCOL section resolves that point.

improvements.label: Question 2 — the amended complaint is never pleaded
improvements.whatHappened: Part (i) is one bullet advising more specificity and reference to the state pleading rule. None of the Zoom-call facts appear.
improvements.whyItMatters: The question supplies those facts so you can build the ordinary-negligence theory that survives even if the per se theory is unavailable. Without it, the amendment advice earns almost nothing.
improvements.howToImprove: Convert the facts into allegations tied to elements: Maclay saw three trucks hit light poles and did nothing; Chase saw two trucks hit vehicles and waived the required test; respondeat superior links both employees' conduct to XH and Faith; the photographed front-left damage supports the inference that the truck that hit Buffy was one of that set. Say which element each fact goes to. The MD bullets in part (ii), which restate Question 1's GIPJ and SIPJ formula, pay for the words.

improvements.label: Question 2 — venue is missing, and the MD/DE bullets skip relatedness
improvements.whatHappened: You canvass MD, DE, and VA on jurisdiction but never mention 1391 for any of them. The MD and DE bullets assert SIPJ over Faith from advertising and selling in those states.
improvements.whyItMatters: The question asks where filing makes dismissal or transfer less likely, so venue is half the answer. And SIPJ requires that this suit arise out of the forum contacts; Faith's MD and DE sales have nothing to do with Buffy's accident, so those bullets do not survive relatedness.
improvements.howToImprove: Run 1391(b)(1) then (b)(2) for your chosen district, and say plainly that the failure to test and the waived test at The Spike put a substantial part of the events in the Eastern District of Virginia. Collapse the DE bullets to a single line — no relatedness for Faith, so DE fails — to pay for it.

improvements.label: Question 3 — class jurisdiction disposed of by cross-reference
improvements.whatHappened: IPJ and venue for the class are each answered with "Discussed above."
improvements.whyItMatters: The class raises a jurisdictional problem Question 1 does not: class members injured outside the forum may lack the contacts connecting their claims to the defendant.
improvements.howToImprove: Add two lines. Whether Bristol-Myers Squibb reaches class actions is unresolved, so pick a view: class as joinder on a large scale, in which case out-of-state members' claims fail, or class as a new entity, in which case they do not. The "Rules: FRCP 20 can join Faith & XH same T&O" bullet and the two "Discussed above" lines pay for it.

improvements.label: Question 4 — say what Rule 52 findings are for
improvements.whatHappened: You identified the defect but not its consequence, which is what the hint about Rule 52's purposes was pointing at.
improvements.whyItMatters: The appellants' argument is that findings this vague are no findings at all: the appellate court cannot review a basis it cannot identify, and a later court cannot tell what was decided.
improvements.howToImprove: Extend the existing "Didn't say why negligent" bullet with both purposes, and point forward to Question 5, where the vagueness is what defeats necessary to the judgment. The duplicated line under your Question 1 IPJ heading — "HCOL: PA is 2R, LLD was PA, very likely to apply PA law" — repeats your HCOL section and pays for it.

improvements.label: Question 5 — the jury-trial sub-question is not answered
improvements.whatHappened: The prompt asks whether a jury-trial right in the second court changes the result. Nothing in the outline addresses it.
improvements.whyItMatters: A squarely asked sub-question on a ten-point item earns nothing when skipped, however strong the rest of the question is.
improvements.howToImprove: One line at the end: an issue tried to a judge can still bind a party who demands a jury in the second case (Parklane). Beacon Theatres is available if you want a clause on the tension. Your claim preclusion bullets, reduced to a clause once you have said the parties differ, pay for this line and for the mutuality line below.

improvements.label: Question 5 — the NMOCE standard is stated backwards
improvements.whatHappened: You wrote that federal common law "doesn't usually let you use ONMCE because of bad incentives, unless couldn't have litigated in L1."
improvements.whyItMatters: That inverts the framework. Non-mutual offensive preclusion is permitted at the court's discretion under Parklane, and whether the second plaintiff could easily have joined the first suit is one factor within that discretion rather than an exception to a bar. Framing it as a bar also hides the other factors you had facts for.
improvements.howToImprove: Replace that line with the discretionary standard and run your could-have-joined point inside it (Parklane). Then finish the step you assert: Dawn is a South Carolina domiciliary, so she is not diverse from Faith, and 1367(b) would bar supplemental jurisdiction over her AIC-deficient claim against a defendant joined under Rule 20. This is a replacement, so it costs no words.

improvements.label: Question 5 — Virginia's mutuality rule is never mentioned
improvements.whatHappened: The facts tell you Virginia requires strict mutuality, and the second court is a Virginia state court. Your analysis runs entirely on the rendering court's law.
improvements.whyItMatters: Either route can earn credit, but the answer has to show it saw the choice. Silence on a fact the exam supplied reads as missing it rather than resolving it.
improvements.howToImprove: One line naming the tension and picking a side: the rendering forum's law governs the judgment's preclusive effect, so Virginia's mutuality rule does not control — or the opposite, with a reason.

improvements.label: Question 6 — doctrines named, question unanswered
improvements.whatHappened: You name JAMOL under Rule 50 and a Rule 59 new trial. Neither bullet says how the doctrine reflects belief that trial judges get things right, and no assessment of that belief appears.
improvements.whyItMatters: The question asked for two things per doctrine: the mechanism and your judgment on whether the confidence is warranted. Naming the doctrine is the setup, not the answer, so this five-point question currently scores near nothing.
improvements.howToImprove: For each doctrine write one sentence on the mechanism and one on whether the trust is deserved. Your Rule 59 bullet is a clause away: it lets a judge override a verdict a reasonable jury could have reached, which assumes the judge's read of the evidence beats the jury's — then say whether you believe that. The two "No consent/tag" bullets in Question 1 pay for the words; consent and tag jurisdiction were never in play.

improvements.label: Question 7 — one drawback where three or four were asked
improvements.whatHappened: The scalability point is a real, mechanism-based drawback, and it is the only one. The outline also spends a bullet on advantages the question did not request.
improvements.whyItMatters: All of this question's value sits in the drawbacks, so each undeveloped one is points forgone.
improvements.howToImprove: Cut the "Pro: cheap, easy" bullet and spend those words on two more drawbacks with a mechanism each — the difficulty of putting doctrine into language a non-lawyer can act on, and the device and connectivity barrier for the litigants who most need the tool. Close by saying whether it would actually have helped someone like Buffy or Dawn.

revisionPlan: Question 1: give each F&R factor a reason from the facts, funded by the duplicated long-arm lines under GIPJ.
Question 1: add the XH–Faith relationship to the section 6 factor, then resolve the presumption.
Question 1: add a clause characterizing the Pennsylvania pleading requirement as procedural before the Erie ladder.
Question 2: plead the ordinary-negligence theory from the Maclay and Chase facts, with respondeat superior and the front-left-damage inference.
Question 2: run 1391(b)(1) and (b)(2) for the Eastern District of Virginia, and reduce MD and DE to a relatedness failure.
Question 3: address class-member relatedness under Bristol-Myers Squibb and pick a view.
Question 4: extend the Rule 52 bullet with the two purposes findings serve.
Question 5: answer the jury-trial sub-question, restate the standard as Parklane discretion with the 1367(b) step completed, and name Virginia's mutuality rule as a choice you resolve.
Question 6: add a mechanism sentence and an assessment sentence for each doctrine.
Question 7: drop the advantages bullet and develop two more drawbacks.
feedback.exampleRevision: Instead of "FCL doesn't usually let you use ONMCE because of bad incentives, unless couldn't have litigated in L1", the analysis should read closer to: NMOCE is permitted at the court's discretion (Parklane). Could Dawn easily have joined L1? No — she is SC domiciled and so not diverse from Faith, and 1367(b) would have barred supplemental jurisdiction over her AIC-deficient claim against a defendant joined under Rule 20, so no wait-and-see problem. Did XH and Faith have incentive to litigate? Yes — bench trial with testimony, injunction on the line. But necessary to the judgment still fails: the findings do not say whether the judge decided per se or ordinary negligence. Jury-trial right in VA: no obstacle, because an issue tried to a judge can still bind a party seeking a jury later (Parklane).
feedback.closing: The habit to carry forward is the one Question 1 already shows: every conclusion gets a reason attached. Where it lapsed — the F&R factors, the class jurisdiction cross-reference, the two doctrines in Question 6 — the analysis stops at the label.

judgeFindings.problem: Blonder-Tongue appears nowhere in the exam, the instructor model answer, or the retrieved course sources, so a claim about what it does and does not stand for rests on outside law.
judgeFindings.correction: Removed the assertion about Blonder-Tongue's holding. The card now criticizes only the substance the sources support: the standard is discretionary permission under Parklane, not a general bar with an exception, and the model answer runs the could-have-joined point as a Parklane factor.

judgeFindings.problem: Overstates the defect. The Buffy–Faith relationship is in fact centered in Pennsylvania; what is missing is the second relationship (XH–Faith, formed and performed at The Spike). The evaluation records this as weakening, not invalidating, a defensible conclusion.
judgeFindings.correction: Recast the card as an incompleteness point: the factor covers one of two relevant relationships and needs the second before the LLD presumption is resolved.

judgeFindings.problem: Implies the whole 26 points were forfeited, when the answer earns real credit inside Question 5 and partial credit in Questions 2 and 7.
judgeFindings.correction: Rewritten as "Those four questions carry 26 of the 65 points," which states the weight without inflating the loss.

judgeFindings.problem: The exam is strictly word-limited, so an instruction to add content without naming what it displaces is not actionable.
judgeFindings.correction: Each of those cards now names the specific bullet whose words fund the addition, and the Parklane fix is reframed as a replacement that costs nothing.

judgeFindings.problem: Asks for a full rule statement plus a citation, which this course does not require.
judgeFindings.correction: Both instructions now model the single line the answer needed, with the case name deployed inside it.

judgeFindings.problem: Multiple distinct points per sentence; the drafting rules require one idea per sentence.
judgeFindings.correction: Split into separate sentences and shortened.

submissions.label: FC bullets
submissions.bandNote: Outlines are not banded here: the graded reference answers are all written-out drafts, so a band would measure the format rather than the analysis.
submissions.answer:
2021 Practice Exam
You are an associate at Rungen & Max. Max, a partner, asks you for a miracle. He has interviewed Montoya and has otherwise used his wizard-like powers to find out the facts detailed above. Max asks what doctrines and arguments discussed in your civil procedure class he could assert on Montoya’s behalf to argue against the court’s seizure order and/or its assertion of jurisdiction. Explain your answer
Jurisdiction in in a Texas state court
Mas test: say that Montoya never left MI with an intention to stay in one place, so no at home GPJ. Frame the RV more as a car than as a house. so no GPJ. Marketed his products all over the world, no evidence of Daimler applying (plus may not apply to people at all.) No GPJ.
SIPJ: Long arm. Minimal contacts between Montoya and Texas (currently based there, worked from there). Minimal contacts with the subject matter of the litigation? Mailed the computer from Oklahoma, received the checks in OK, but did cash the checks in Dallas. Unclear if this is sufficient, but likely because it is minimal.
F&R factors: high extent of contacts, convenient (he is there), P decided there so it should be fine, Texas may be interested in resolving disputes for an online seller currently operating in its borders, evidence probably in the RV currently leased to stay in Texas. HCOL: Texas is 1R, LLD. Apply law of state where blood spilled/last element for the tort of products liability–Vermont, a point against Texas. Given strength of other factors, probably PJ in TX.
Seizure
Tex. L. Ann. § 4.20 requirements are met.
Tex. L. Ann. § 4.50: directly meets 20 day hearing req,
use means reasonably likely of success to provide the respondent/defendant with notice
Try to argue notice was not reasonably provided bc Montoya didn’t get it. However, like Mullane, this word reasonable doesn’t require actual notice. They mailed it to the PO box on Montoya’s website, seems reasonable to mail it to the place where mail would go. Did not get sent back (contra Flowers). While there was an error message on the chat function, analogous to Jones, there didn’t seem to be another reasonable way to contact. Notice probably fine.
a state court can constitutionally seize property only if that property is located within that state’s geographic limits.
Could try to say per Balk bank accounts are debts, and debts follow the debtor, so debt would have been in Bank of Florin’s PPoB of NV or INC of DE–more likely NV because all the business records were outside Reno. Balk viewed more broadly would say property follows the defendant, would not work for Montoya because Montoya was in Texas. Texas interest in allowing its people to sue sellers in that state, where Montoya might reasonably expect to be called into court, where key evidence is located, and most ascertainable and definite all point in that direction. Probably will not succeed on this.
Shaffer
Interp 1: Don’t take shaffer seriously
Property in forum enough for QIRJ–because it probably is, probably QIRJ
Interp 2: Shaffer requires IntlShoe
Needs minimal contacts between Montoya’s interest in the property, Texas forum, and the tort claim. Montoya should argue Texas has nothing to do with this claim, he did not stay there until after he had mailed his computer. In that view, no QIRJ.
Mathews v Eldridge
Balance of private interests here (like Doehr). Falls in favor of Montoya because a bank account is needed to live life
risk of an erroneous deprivation: a judge did decide, but there was no opportunity for Montoya to be heard until after the seizure (and he did not have actual notice at all even for his hearing), the pre-seizure evidentiary requirement was low, and expert testimony would likely be needed to assess the fitness of the product and its possibility of causing the injuries, it’s being seized just for security not as evidence that would be tampered with, and there was no bond requirement. [BOND REQ WOULD HAVE BEEN A SAFER SCHEME.]
Government scheme not directly implicated here, but while an instant seizure may have efficiency benefits, government must focus on accuracy as well to inspires trust in the judicial system. This little process with no bond requirement erodes that.
Question 2 (4 points): Max asks you whether you think Valerie’s argument on the litigation bond will succeed. What do you think? Explain your answer.
I think it will not succeed. The civil legal system does not provide automatic protections or changes in process for low income litigants. The state law requires a bond for a reason and must be followed. A lack of a bond req has the problems I outline above.
Question 3 (22 points): Can Montoya sue Buttercup and Westley, together in one lawsuit, in any federal court for a declaratory judgment of the type that Max describes? Assuming he could do so, in what federal court (geographically) can he sue? And which location would be best for Montoya? Explain your answers.
SMJ for Declaratory judgment. First Federal Savings, Imaginary Lawsuit Rule Applies.
Contesting the products liability claim. This is state law, so no AUJ. No substantial federal issue, no SmithGrable.
DJ and SuppJ
DJ base claim: AIC would come from the amount paid for product (plus PDs for injured person if available in the state.) Even without PDs, at 80k Buttercup meets the AIC. Montoya has no claim to Ohio citizenship, completely diverse
Westley would be brought in under rule 20. Same T/O, CNOF. But AIC deficient, also breaking complete diversity if Montoya is MI resident.
Is the plaintiff making a claim against a person made a party through Rule 20? Depends on whether you see people suing for DecJudg as plaintiffs, or if you view them as defendants through the coercive action. I view them as plaintiffs, so because the joinder of these parties would be inconsistent with the jx requirements of 1332 (i.e., destroy complete diversity or be AIC deficient), there is no supplemental jurisdiction (Exxon) and this cannot be brought together.
If DecJudg was allowed: Where (PJ and Venue)
Texas 3 year SOL, will apply if suit is filed in Texas bc its procedural. The SPL claim should have run out. [WANT TO SUE HERE IF YOU CAN.]
PJ
Long arm/4k1a. Minimal contacts? Could argue, as above that this SPL claim had nothing to do with Texas. Buttercup already availed herself to litigation in Texas through the state claim, but Westley hasn’t. No major extent of contacts from W, convenient for Montoya but not him, evidence will be in Texas for the RV where it is made but may also be in Vermont where it blew up, Texas is 1R, LLD. Apply law of state where blood spilled/last element for the tort of products liability–Vermont, a point against Texas. ALSO: VT HAS SUBSTANTIVE PD LAW, DONT WANT IT.
Venue
1391(b)(3) at a minimum would apply if at least one D had PJ (and they both must)
Ohio
PJ
GPJ for Buttercup. SPJ for Westley? Minimum contacts because he was knowingly supporting a negotiation based in Ohio for the product. F&R: fairly easy to travel an hour to Ohio, but not much evidence there. Ohio may have an interest in litigating because funds from an Ohio bank were used, but not much evidence there. HCOL: 2R. LLD (VT) presumption, but section 6 factors: evidence probably in Vermont, the relationship between the parties is centered more in Ohio from the conversations, one of the parties is an OH resident while none are VT, OH has an interest in applying OH law to transactions in the state. Might use OH law. [THIS IS BEST FOR MONTOYA BC THERES A CHANCE OF NO PDs]
But problem: has no money! plaintiff shall deposit with the court 10% of the amount in controversy in the lawsuit, to be held by the court until final judgment in the lawsuit to pay the defendant’s litigation costs and attorneys’ fees if the court ultimately decides not to issue the declaratory judgment. Any lawsuit in which the plaintiff does not comply with this requirement shall be immediately dismissed. 2201 does not have this req.
Venue fine resident here
Erie issue?
York: outcome determinative, use state law.
Scalia
Statute is a valid law Art III Sec 1 (power to create lower fed courts), this law was Necessary and Proper to regulate them.
Applicable: Apply plain meaning of statute to see if it fits (usually does, so use fed law)
Ginsburg
Valid: see Scalia
Applicable: this is just an additional step above the 2201. Apply narrower meaning of statute to avoid infringing on state law (more likely to use state law). Laboratories of democracy.
Harlan
Does the law impact the parties’ primary conduct? No, just a thing when you sue. Hard to link it to investment or something else. Procedural, use state.
This is only a good option if the Ohio law on DecJudg doesn’t apply.
Michigan
PJ: Westley at home GPJ. Buttercup SPJ: Minimal contacts from knowingly buying a product partially with Michigan money and getting it shipped there. F&R: convenient and visits all the time, forum wants to litigate products shipped there. R1 analysis like Texas.
Venue fine resident here
Vermont
PJ- no GPJ at home. SPJ: minimal contacts from the defendants being there when it all went down. But F&R: far away, low contact, inconvenient for all. Good on evidence and choice of law.
Venue fine, b2 substantial
Question 4 (6 points): Max is thinking some more about the idea of a federal court declaratory judgment lawsuit. He has two additional questions. First, are there any arguments (from our civil procedure class) not covered in your answer to Question 3 that Valerie might assert on Buttercup’s behalf to prevent the federal court lawsuit from going forward, and if so, would any such arguments work? Second, Max would rather not bother with a jury in these circumstances. If Montoya sues for a declaratory judgment, will Buttercup and Westley have to respond with their own federal court lawsuit; and regardless of whether they have to respond, if they demand a jury trial, will they be entitled to one? Explain your answers.
Prevent a suit from going forward? Colorado river maybe. Yes Parallel concurrent state/federal proceedings, Amongst substantially the same issues. Not the same parties, though, because Westley is not in the state action (but are they substantially similar?). There is a preponderance of state law, might argue state court more specialized in these claims. State case has probably moved further. If in TX court, equally convenient. Ohio more convenient for Buttercup and Westley. Will probably not grant because of the differences in the parties.
Will Buttercup and Westley have to respond with their own federal court lawsuit? If they want to make an assertion in the federal court beyond just requesting the end of the decjudg, it will be for the same T/O and will have a compulsory counterclaim per Rule 13. Should do this in case the fed case goes to judgment before the state case, and thus may have a preclusive effect.
Right to a jury: 7th amendment did not create right to a jury, only “preserves” the right: meaning that there is a right to a jury trial if there would have been one in 1791. Products liability did not exist in 1791. Chauffeurs test: legal remedy, damages. Entitled to a jury probably. Markman functional test: Jury good at reflecting community standards and assessing credibility of testimony in the case. Probably right to a jury.
Question 5 (8 points): Max asks whether you think the Texas court, as a matter of horizontal choice of law, is likely to grant the motion to dismiss Buttercup’s products liability lawsuit on limitations grounds? Next, Max asks you, suppose the Texas court does dismiss on limitations grounds. Max is worried about another lawsuit by Buttercup, maybe joined this time by Westley, for either products liability or breach of contract, in a court of a different state, or in federal court. If Buttercup or Westley or both together sue Montoya in another state or federal court, could Montoya use the doctrine of preclusion against either or both? Explain your answers.
1: yes HCOL is procedural, will apply law of the forum
Claim
Same claim (BROAD) Same transaction + occurrence (Heyward-Robinson)
Same party or in privity or a successor in interest? I would say Westley is in privity because it is based on the same product.
Judgement (doesn’t matter who wins) that is both final and on the merits
Final, went to judgment
On the merits?
Assume it was dismissed with prejudice. No Marrese issue. Texas would say yes.
If sued in a state court where they would not be on the merits: Art IV s1 (Full Faith and Credit Clause); §1738; *At least as much preclusive effect as state A. Claim precluded.
If sued in federal court: §1738; (Invoke power to regulate federal courts because Congress created them); *At least as much preclusive effect as state A. Claim precluded.
Issue
Nothing was actually litigated, would not be relevant.
Question 6 (8 points): In our last few sessions of the semester, we discussed how the law sometimes treats a certified class as a new legal entity (separate from the individual class members’ claims), and sometimes treats a certified class as “joinder on steroids,” that is, a large-scale case of joinder. Identify one legal doctrine we discussed in which a class is treated as a separate legal entity [BEN HUR ONLY NAMED PLAINTIFF NEEDED FOR SMJ], and one legal doctrine in which a class is treated as a large-scale joinder [COMMONALITY WALMART]. Next, identify one doctrinal area in which it is still not clear whether the court system will treat classes as new legal entities or large-scale joinders [PJ]. Explain your response briefly. Then write a few sentences explaining which of the two treatments you prefer, and why.
Prefer one entity, easier to sue

feedback.headline: Question 3 is your strongest work; Question 1's notice analysis rests on an inverted fact
feedback.overview: The best analysis here is Question 3. You framed declaratory subject matter jurisdiction with the imaginary lawsuit rule, computed the amount in controversy defendant by defendant, and then asked whether a declaratory-judgment plaintiff counts as "the plaintiff" for 1367(b) before using the answer to bar the Westley claim. You also chose N.D. Ohio for a stated reason and named the Ohio 10% deposit as the vertical choice of law cost of that choice. The other heavily weighted questions do not hold up as well. Question 1 reasons away its most available argument on a misreading of the record: the certified mail came back unclaimed, and you wrote that it did not. Question 5 decides Westley's preclusion on a same-product theory of privity rather than the control or successor-in-interest test. Questions 2 and 6 are twelve points delivered as bare conclusions.

strengths.label: Both readings of Shaffer, run separately
strengths.detail: Splitting the narrow reading from the reading that requires an International Shoe analysis let you reach two different results and say what contacts each one needs. That is the structure this question rewards, because the course treats the split as genuinely unresolved.
strengths.answerExcerpt: Interp 1: Don't take shaffer seriously … Interp 2: Shaffer requires IntlShoe

strengths.label: The bank account treated as an incorporeal object
strengths.detail: Canvassing candidate locations rather than asserting one is what the situs question calls for, and you named the trade-off that Nevada is where the bank's records actually sit.
strengths.answerExcerpt: Balk viewed more broadly would say property follows the defendant

strengths.label: The 1367(b) step, resolved rather than asserted
strengths.detail: Most answers reach for supplemental jurisdiction to rescue the Westley claim and never run the carve-out. You took a position on whether a declaratory plaintiff is the plaintiff for that purpose and drew the consequence that the single lawsuit fails.
strengths.answerExcerpt: because the joinder of these parties would be inconsistent with the jx requirements of 1332 … there is no supplemental jurisdiction (Exxon) and this cannot be brought together

strengths.label: Forum choice tied to the punitive damages consequence
strengths.detail: You tested personal jurisdiction over both defendants in each candidate state instead of over "the defendants" collectively, then picked the forum for a reason that changes Montoya's exposure rather than for general convenience.
strengths.answerExcerpt: [THIS IS BEST FOR MONTOYA BC THERES A CHANCE OF NO PDs]

strengths.label: Colorado River argued both ways, and the Rule 13 consequence stated
strengths.detail: You named factors on each side and resolved on the party difference. On the counterclaim you did not stop at "compulsory" — you said why filing matters, which is the preclusive effect if the federal judgment lands first.
strengths.answerExcerpt: Should do this in case the fed case goes to judgment before the state case, and thus may have a preclusive effect.

strengths.label: Intersystem preclusion named and run twice
strengths.detail: You separated the subsequent state court from the subsequent federal court and applied the at-least-as-much-preclusive-effect rule to each. Using the course's own name for that step keeps it clear of the choice of law analysis, which is where students usually blur it.
strengths.answerExcerpt: *At least as much preclusive effect as state A.

improvements.label: Question 1 — the notice conclusion rests on an inverted fact
improvements.whatHappened: You wrote that the mail was not returned, so Flowers did not apply. In fact the certified mail came back unclaimed and the chat function was down. You also concluded there was no other reasonable way to reach him, when Valerie had noted the exact Dallas RV plot, where personal service was easy.
improvements.whyItMatters: The continuing duty to try again is the strongest argument available against the seizure on these facts, and it is what decides notice here. Getting the record backwards turns your best point into a concession.
improvements.howToImprove: Split notice into two moments. First ask whether the plan was reasonable when made — the P.O. box was listed on his own site, so probably yes. Then ask what the plaintiff learned afterward: mail returned unclaimed and the site down means both methods visibly failed, which triggers the duty to try something else. Name the available follow-up, personal service at the noted Dallas plot, and conclude that the failure to try it likely invalidates the seizure. Pay for this with the opening Mas and Daimler general jurisdiction discussion of Montoya, which is not what a quasi-in-rem attack needs.

improvements.label: Question 1 — the situs canvass resolves toward Texas on reasons the record contradicts
improvements.whatHappened: After listing good candidates you concluded Montoya "probably will not succeed" because Texas has an interest in letting "its people" sue and because key evidence is there. Buttercup is not a Texan, the computer is in Ohio, and the outlet wiring is in Vermont. The contacts line, "likely because it is minimal," is a conclusion with no supporting step.
improvements.whyItMatters: The canvass earns its points only if the choice among candidates rests on facts that survive the record. Here the reasons given push toward the answer the facts do not support.
improvements.howToImprove: Finish the canvass with the ascertainability point you already had: Nevada as the proxy for the bank's records is certain and knowable to third parties, while follow-the-holder is transient and unknowable before seizure. Then, on minimum contacts, list what did not happen in Texas — the computer work, the negotiations, the shipment, and the receipt of the checks were all elsewhere — and say that check-cashing plus temporary RV stays is thin. Recover the words from the general jurisdiction opening.

improvements.label: Question 2 — the right result with no balancing
improvements.whatHappened: You concluded the argument fails and supported it with the statement that the law "requires a bond for a reason and must be followed." That is circular, and the Mathews framework is never named on this question.
improvements.whyItMatters: Four points still buy the balancing, and the balancing is what shows you know whose interest sits on which side. As written the conclusion could be right by luck.
improvements.howToImprove:
Run the balance in three steps.
1. Buttercup's interest is purely monetary — assurance that assets exist if she wins — and she keeps her ordinary lawsuit with no seizure at all.
2. Rank that below the interests at stake in Lassiter (parental rights) and Turner (incarceration), which is where the course's access to justice cases set the bar.
3. The bond protects the party whose property is seized, the same interest that made the Question 1 scheme look thin, so striking it down cuts against Montoya.
The words come from deleting the "requires a bond for a reason" sentence.

improvements.label: Question 3 — domicile is asserted, not tested
improvements.whatHappened: "Montoya has no claim to Ohio citizenship, completely diverse" skips the analysis, and the later parenthetical "if Montoya is MI resident" flags the Michigan branch without working it.
improvements.whyItMatters: Domicile decides complete diversity as to Westley on the heaviest question. If Michigan survives as his domicile, the joint suit fails for a second, independent reason.
improvements.howToImprove: Apply the Mas test — presence plus intent to remain indefinitely — to the facts given: the Pensacola year, the voter registration, the driver's license, and the P.O. box on one side; Michigan birth and upbringing plus the itinerant RV life on the other. Pick one and trace it. If Florida, diversity is complete and the amount in controversy does the work against Westley. If Michigan, complete diversity fails as to Westley regardless. Two clauses of the Texas personal jurisdiction run duplicate the Question 1 contacts analysis and can pay for this.

improvements.label: Question 3 — venue takes the fallback first
improvements.whatHappened: "1391(b)(3) at a minimum would apply if at least one D had PJ" reverses the statute; (b)(3) is available only when no district qualifies under (b)(1) or (b)(2). The Ohio, Michigan, and Vermont districts each get one clause: "Venue fine resident here."
improvements.whyItMatters: Venue is brain off. Walking the subsections in order costs almost nothing and reaches the right districts; starting at the fallback produces a wrong method even where the destination is defensible.
improvements.howToImprove:
Take them in order and stop reasoning.
1. 1391(b)(1): unavailable, because the two defendants reside in different states under 1391(c)(1).
2. 1391(b)(2): N.D. Ohio on the negotiations, D. Vt. on the fire, and E.D. Mich. arguably on the pickup.
3. 1391(b)(3): never reached, because (b)(2) supplies districts.
This is shorter than what you wrote across the four state headings, so it pays for itself.

improvements.label: Question 3 — Harlan's primary-conduct question missed the fact that answers it
improvements.whatHappened: You answered "No, just a thing when you sue" and moved on. The Ohio legislature stated a purpose of deterring risky pre-litigation conduct, which is what makes the primary-conduct question arguable.
improvements.whyItMatters: Your conclusion (apply state law) survives either way, so naming the deterrence finding and the bond analogy under Cohen costs nothing and buys the harder half of the analysis.
improvements.howToImprove: Add one clause noting the stated deterrence purpose and the Cohen bond analogy, then keep your conclusion. The Ginsburg and Scalia passages already say more than they need to; trim one to pay for it.

improvements.label: Question 4 — the jury path skips the cleanest legal claim
improvements.whatHappened: You leaned on "products liability did not exist in 1791" and then reached the right answer through the legal-remedy prong. The breach of written contract counterclaim is the cleanest legal claim, and Beacon Theatres is the course's authority for trying legal counterclaims to a jury despite the equitable declaratory posture.
improvements.whyItMatters: That route reaches the same result in fewer words and forecloses the argument that Montoya's equitable framing controls.
improvements.howToImprove: Say that the damages counterclaim on the written contract is legal, cite Beacon Theatres, and conclude that Max cannot avoid a jury. Drop the 1791 products liability aside, which is doing no work here.

improvements.label: Question 5 — privity decided on the wrong test
improvements.whatHappened: "I would say Westley is in privity because it is based on the same product." Privity here turns on control over the first action or successor-in-interest status, not on a shared interest in the same object.
improvements.whyItMatters: This inverts the answer to one of the two things Question 5 asks. Westley was not a party to the Texas action, did not control it, and is not Buttercup's successor, so no preclusion runs against him.
improvements.howToImprove: Keep the claim preclusion elements you listed and run them twice — once for Buttercup, once for Westley. For Westley, ask only two things: did he control the Texas action, and is he a successor in interest to Buttercup. Both are no, so the same-party element fails and he sues freely. The sentence about the same product is the sentence to replace.

improvements.label: Question 5 — the dispositive dates and the issue preclusion route
improvements.whatHappened: "yes HCOL is procedural, will apply law of the forum" never puts the arithmetic on the page: injury April 17, 2017, filing June 16, 2020, roughly 38 months against Texas's three-year period. Separately, "Nothing was actually litigated" misdescribes the record, because compliance with the Texas limitations rule was litigated and decided.
improvements.whyItMatters: On the limitations half the numbers are the answer, and without them the conclusion is unsupported. On issue preclusion you reach the right bottom line by a route that cannot be credited.
improvements.howToImprove: Put the two dates and the month count into the line where you say limitations are procedural, and add that the motion should be granted; that is a clause inside a sentence you already wrote, so nothing needs cutting. Then swap "Nothing was actually litigated" for the accurate version: the only issue decided was compliance with the Texas limitations period, which is not an issue in any other state's court, so nothing travels.

improvements.label: Question 6 — the joinder example is a certification requirement
improvements.whatHappened: You offered Wal-Mart commonality as the doctrine treating a class as large-scale joinder. Commonality is a Rule 23(a) certification requirement, not a treatment of the class as joinder. Ben-Hur for the entity side is right but unexplained. The unsettled area is a single bracketed word. The preference is five words with no reason and no counterargument.
improvements.whyItMatters: Eight points, four required parts, and only one part is currently correct — the same weight as Question 5.
improvements.howToImprove:
Give each part a sentence, which is all the question asks for.
1. Entity: diversity is measured by the named representative's citizenship alone under Ben-Hur, so the class is one litigant for jurisdictional purposes.
2. Joinder: Exxon's supplemental jurisdiction reasoning, which analyzed the joinder case and the class case together on one rationale.
3. Unsettled: personal jurisdiction as to unnamed out-of-state members' claims — the entity view means Bristol-Myers Squibb poses no bar, the joinder view means it defeats jurisdiction.
4. Preference: state one, give a reason, and name the strongest point against it.
This question currently uses almost none of its word budget.

improvements.label: Bullets that state a result with no supporting step
improvements.whatHappened: "likely because it is minimal" on Texas contacts, "must be followed" on the bond, and "Prefer one entity, easier to sue" on the class preference each announce an outcome without the step that produces it.
improvements.whyItMatters: Outline form is fine, but a bullet with no reason earns what a sentence with no reason earns. Where you did supply reasons — the Doehr balance, the 1367(b) step — the analysis is visibly stronger.
improvements.howToImprove: Before leaving any conclusion bullet, add one "because" clause tied to a named fact or rule. Three such clauses cost fewer words than the general jurisdiction opening in Question 1.

feedback.exampleRevision: Notice, in two moments. When made, the plan was probably reasonable: certified mail to the Pensacola P.O. box Montoya himself listed, plus the chat function he habitually used, is what someone who actually wanted to reach him would try (Mullane). But the plaintiff then learned that both methods had failed — the certified mail came back unclaimed and the site returned an error. Under Jones v. Flowers that knowledge revives the duty, and the question becomes what else was reasonably available. Valerie had noted the exact Dallas RV plot, so personal service there was cheap and highly reliable. Actual notice is not the standard; the failure to try the obvious next step is. Notice was therefore likely constitutionally insufficient, which is enough to attack the seizure order without reaching the situs question at all.
feedback.closing: Question 3 shows you can hold a long sequence together and make a hard call inside it with a stated reason. Bring that same habit — name the element, then the fact that decides it — to Question 1's notice analysis, Question 5's privity test, and the four parts of Question 6.

feedback.headline: Situs and preclusion carry their own reasons; the Ohio recommendation is made without pricing its cost
feedback.overview: Question 1's situs work and Question 5's preclusion chain are the two places where a conclusion rests on stated reasons. The situs run treats the account as an incorporeal object, uses Harris v. Balk for the debt characterization, argues Nevada or Delaware on ascertainability against an unpredictable branch-based rule, and concludes the account is not in Texas. Question 5 reaches every correct bottom line on stated rules, including §1738 and the refusal to bind Westley. Elsewhere the pattern is that an issue is named and then left. Question 3 is worth 22 points and omits the vertical choice-of-law problem that would decide whether the recommended forum is available at all, and asserts domicile with no facts. Question 2 states no conclusion. Question 4 never reaches Rule 13(a). Question 6 states a preference with no reason.

strengths.label: Situs of the account, argued with policy reasons
strengths.detail: Locating an incorporeal object by ascertainability rather than by where a deposit happened to occur is what makes the quasi-in-rem attack work, and it defeats jurisdiction without needing the contacts argument at all.
strengths.answerExcerpt: Makes sense to be located at banks PPoB / place of incorporation (NV or DE) more certainty/ease of adjudication than ATM where someone made a deposit/withdrawl could be super unpredictable

strengths.label: Both branches of Shaffer preserved
strengths.detail: Splitting the analysis into quasi-in-rem surviving and quasi-in-rem dead keeps the alternative holding alive, so the argument does not collapse if a court reads Shaffer narrowly.
strengths.answerExcerpt: QIR is dead: minimum contacts

strengths.label: Two-sided balance on the seizure scheme
strengths.detail: The balance is worked against actual features of the Texas provisions — judge rather than clerk, sworn statement, 20-day hearing, no bond or counterbond, no pre-existing interest in the property, subsistence interest in the account. That is application, not recitation.
strengths.answerExcerpt: Judge decisionmaker (Snidach), party seizing doesn’t have property interest, 20 days for hearing, no Fuentes

strengths.label: Imaginary lawsuit rule as the frame, and the §1367 result
strengths.detail: Opening with the imaginary lawsuit rule is the right frame for jurisdiction over a declaratory action. The amount-in-controversy split is right, and the conclusion that Westley's claim is ousted despite sharing a case or controversy reaches the correct result. Arising-under jurisdiction is rejected with the embedded-federal-issue check under Smith and Grable.
strengths.answerExcerpt: SMJ: Imaginary lawsuit rule

strengths.label: Preclusion rules correctly chained
strengths.detail: Limitations as procedural for horizontal choice of law, then §1738 sending the second court to Texas preclusion law, then Texas treating a limitations dismissal as on the merits — each step supplies the next, and the no-privity result for Westley is right.
strengths.answerExcerpt: Rendering court is state court: either way 1738 tells us to use preclusion law of state where rendering court is sitting

improvements.label: Question 1 — the notice argument stops before the point that wins it
improvements.whatHappened: The bullets reach Jones v. Flowers and the continuing duty, then move on. They never name what could reasonably have been tried after the mail came back unclaimed, and never state the consequence.
improvements.whyItMatters: Under Jones v. Flowers the duty is to try something reasonable that was available. Without naming the available step there is no violation, only a rule. Without the consequence, the argument Max asked for never lands.
improvements.howToImprove: Name personal service at the Dallas RV plot, whose exact location Valerie had from the website, and conclude that notice was inadequate so the seizure order falls. Pay for it by converting the Dusenbury and Mullane bullets into the application they are missing: the initial plan was reasonable because Montoya communicated through the site and listed that P.O. Box there.

improvements.label: Question 1 — the contacts and fairness runs are under-supported
improvements.whatHappened: The contacts bullets find a likely relationship among defendant, subject matter and forum on four months' presence and check deposits. The fairness bullets note convenience and that evidence may be in Oklahoma, and stop there.
improvements.whyItMatters: A finding of contacts on presence plus banking is defensible, but a defensible conclusion still has to face the other side: none of the refurbishing, the negotiations, the shipment or the receipt of the checks happened in Texas. Fairness also asks about Texas's interest and whether Texas law will apply, and both point away from Texas.
improvements.howToImprove: Add those counter-facts to the contacts bullet, and add two fairness clauses: Texas has no interest with no Texas conduct and no Texas party, and Texas substantive law will not apply. Separately, move the point that fact-heavy tort allegations need live testimony to Doehr; Mathews is the documents case, so the current attribution is inverted.

improvements.label: Question 2 — no answer and no balance
improvements.whatHappened: The bullets gather useful material — the bond's deterrent purpose, the market-signal point, filing fees as an accepted price of access — but never say whether the argument succeeds, and never run Mathews.
improvements.whyItMatters: The question asks whether the argument wins. A four-point question rewards a bottom line with reasons, and the balance is what produces one.
improvements.howToImprove: Run Mathews in three lines, factor by factor: the private interest (Buttercup's is purely monetary, and she can still sue for breach of written contract or products liability with no seizure at all); the risk of erroneous deprivation and what the bond adds (it protects Montoya's own interest in compensation if the seizure was wrongful); and the state's slight interest. Then state that the argument fails. The market-signal bullet can shrink to a clause to pay for it.

improvements.label: Question 3 — the vertical choice-of-law problem is missing
improvements.whatHappened: Ohio is recommended as the best forum, but Ohio's 10% deposit requirement against 28 U.S.C. §2201 never appears.
improvements.whyItMatters: Montoya's account is frozen. If the deposit requirement applies in federal court, the recommended forum dismisses his suit, so a recommendation that never prices this risk is not usable advice. This is the largest gap on the most heavily weighted question.
improvements.howToImprove:
Add a short run in this order:
1. Name the conflict: Ohio requires a 10% deposit, §2201 requires none.
2. Under York it is outcome-determinative here, because Montoya cannot pay and the case ends.
3. Cohen supports applying the state rule, given the legislature's stated aim of deterring strike suits.
4. A Scalia-style approach treats §2201 as valid and as controlling what federal courts do on declaratory judgments, so no deposit.
5. A Ginsburg-style approach agrees on validity but may read §2201 as silent on deposits, leaving the state policy room to operate.
Pay for it with the Oklahoma personal jurisdiction entry, which is not a viable forum for a suit that includes Westley, plus the duplicated venue lines.

improvements.label: Question 3 — domicile is asserted, not analyzed
improvements.whatHappened: "Montoya: MI, maybe FL domiciled" carries the whole complete-diversity branch, with no facts marshalled either way.
improvements.whyItMatters: Whether diversity is complete as to Westley turns on this one choice, and everything downstream inherits it. A bare assertion here is as conclusory in an outline as in prose.
improvements.howToImprove: Under Mas, put the facts on both sides in one or two lines: the one-year Pensacola plot lease, the voter registration, the driver's license and the P.O. box against Michigan origin and continued itinerancy. Pick one, say why, and run the rest consistently with it. The words come from the venue block, where three entries currently repeat conclusions.

improvements.label: Question 3 — venue worked defendant by defendant
improvements.whatHappened: The venue block lists subsections separately for Buttercup and for Westley, each getting a §1391(b)(1) district.
improvements.whyItMatters: Venue is one inquiry for the single suit, and this is a brain-off topic: walk the subsections in order. Because the two defendants reside in different states under §1391(c)(1), §1391(b)(1) is unavailable at all, which is exactly the point the split-by-defendant format hides.
improvements.howToImprove: Run the subsections once for the case: §1391(b)(1) fails because the defendants reside in different states; §1391(b)(2) supports D. Vt. (the fire and the wiring evidence), N.D. Ohio (Buttercup's negotiations), and arguably E.D. Mich. (the pickup); §1391(b)(3) is therefore irrelevant. That is shorter than what is there now.

improvements.label: Question 3 — the comparison that makes Ohio best is only half stated
improvements.whatHappened: Ohio is chosen for the punitive damages reason, with the Second Restatement plus lex loci delicti and the §6 factors named, but the answer never says what the other forums would do. The Ohio conclusion is then hedged to "But unlikely" with nothing following.
improvements.whyItMatters: "Best" is a comparison. Without the First Restatement half — that the Vermont and Michigan federal courts apply Vermont law, where punitive damages are available — there is no baseline against which Ohio is better. A hedge with no consequence also leaves the recommendation unresolved.
improvements.howToImprove: Add one line that the D. Vt. and E.D. Mich. apply First Restatement rules and so land on Vermont law with punitive damages available. Then say what follows if the Ohio court applies Vermont law anyway. Recover the words from the Vermont personal jurisdiction entry, which can stay as short as it is.

improvements.label: Question 4 — Rule 13(a) is the answer and it is not here
improvements.whatHappened: "DJ: don't have to respond with own lawsuit" states the right half of the conclusion. The reason is absent.
improvements.whyItMatters: They need not file their own suit because Rule 13(a) makes their tort and contract theories compulsory counterclaims in this one, arising from the same transaction or occurrence. The flip side is the trap: if they do not plead them here, they forfeit them once judgment enters.
improvements.howToImprove: Replace that bullet with the Rule 13(a) point and the forfeiture consequence. Add Beacon Theatres to the jury bullet as well: your historical-analogue-plus-damages reasoning reaches the right result, but the point that carries it here is that a plaintiff cannot defeat a jury right by racing to declaratory relief first.

improvements.label: Question 4 — Colorado River is named with no content
improvements.whatHappened: One bullet names a Colorado River stay and parallel state litigation. No standard, no factors, no answer whether the motion would work.
improvements.whyItMatters: The question asks whether the additional argument succeeds. Naming the doctrine earns little; the exceptional-circumstances standard applied to these facts is the point.
improvements.howToImprove: Add the standard and two facts each way in note form. For the stay: the Texas case is further along, and a Texas court has already seized the asset most likely to satisfy a judgment. Against it: the federal case adds Westley, no comparable congressional policy is at stake, no absent parties' rights are being adjudicated, and northern Ohio is convenient for the defendants. Then say the motion likely fails.

improvements.label: Question 5 — elements listed but not applied, and issue preclusion skipped
improvements.whatHappened: Same claim, same party or privity, and final judgment on the merits are listed but never run against facts. Westley's escape rests on "wasn't a party." Issue preclusion does not appear at all.
improvements.whyItMatters: A listed element is not a satisfied element. The arithmetic matters: injury April 17, 2017, filing June 16, 2020, roughly 38 months against a three-year period. Same-transaction scope is what bars Buttercup's contract theory as well as her products liability theory. Privity has a test — control or successor in interest — which is what shows her relationship with Westley is not enough. And issue preclusion is the doctrine that limits how far the Texas dismissal travels, because the only issue litigated was compliance with Texas's limitations period.
improvements.howToImprove: Convert each listed element into a one-clause application: the dates and the arithmetic, the single sale and fire as one transaction covering both theories, and the control or successor-in-interest test failing as to Westley. Then add two lines of issue preclusion identifying the issue actually litigated and saying it decides nothing about another state's period. The words come from the restated element list.

improvements.label: Question 6 — the preference has no reason and the open question is not separated
improvements.whatHappened: "Prefer joinder on steroids" is the entire preference. The uncertainty item is folded into the Exxon bullet as "SIPJ over the defendant," so a reader cannot tell what the open question is.
improvements.whyItMatters: The question asks you to explain the preference, so a one-line preference is conclusory even in an outline. The open question is a distinct third item: whether a court can exercise specific personal jurisdiction over a defendant as to unnamed out-of-state class members' claims, which turns on the entity-versus-joinder characterization after Bristol-Myers Squibb.
improvements.howToImprove: Give the uncertainty its own line, name Bristol-Myers Squibb, and say why the characterization decides it. Then give the preference two reasons — for example that absent members do not in practice control their own claims, or that entity treatment reduces jurisdictional gamesmanship. Your two identifications are already explained, so this costs almost nothing.

improvements.label: Cross-cutting — naming a doctrine without disposing of it
improvements.whatHappened: The same shape recurs on Questions 2, 3, 4 and 6: the doctrine is identified, then the answer moves on before the step that disposes of it.
improvements.whyItMatters: Issue recognition here is broad, which is the harder skill. What the answer loses is the step between naming a doctrine and resolving it, and that step is where most of the credit sits.
improvements.howToImprove: Give every doctrine you name one line of reason and one line of result before moving on. If a doctrine cannot earn those two lines, cut it and spend the words on one that can.

feedback.exampleRevision: Instead of ending Question 3 at "OH- no PDs," price the cost of that forum: "Ohio best on HCOL — 2R, so §6 factors (negotiations centered in OH, computer and records in OH, OH interest) can displace LLD in VT and bar punitive damages, where D. Vt. and E.D. Mich. apply 1R and land on VT law with punitive damages available. But N.D. Ohio carries a VCOL risk: OH's 10% deposit vs. §2201, which requires none. Under York this is outcome-determinative — M's account is frozen, so the suit ends — and Cohen supports the state rule given the anti-strike-suit findings. Scalia-style: §2201 is valid and controls what federal courts do on declaratory judgments, so no deposit. Ginsburg-style: valid but arguably silent on deposits, leaving room for the state policy. So M trades a real shot at no punitive damages for a real risk of dismissal on the deposit." What this adds is the comparison forum's rule, so "best" means something, and the cost of the recommendation, so the advice is usable.
feedback.closing: The situs canvass and the Question 5 preclusion chain show you can carry a conclusion on stated reasons. Do that for the doctrines you currently only name.

Erie Tests

Apply MARCP

Apply FRCP
Hanna Scalia

Applicable: Directly answers the question we are asking
Outcome: FRCP
Hanna Ginsburg
Valid: under REA if it doesn’t abridge, enlarge, modify a substantive right. Sibbach really regulates procedure.
Applicable: FRCP doesn’t specifically apply because no Congressional statute speaks to SOL for pet death/injury
Outcome: MARCP
Stevens Shady Grove
Laws governing pet ownership, relationship to a right: by including in rights governing pet ownership, could argue that it is entwined with state substantive right and FRCP would interfere
In shady grove, the fact that the class action killer was in procedural code/used procedural language indicated that it wasn’t tied up with a state substantive right
But- what does SOL for pet injury really have to do with the right to pet ownership?
How should the court rule?
Follow Hanna Ginsburg- 1) under federalism rule, federal government has limited power and the rest is left to the states, federal government should avoid preempting if it can, even if the FRCP is valid. If there is an interpretation where the FRCP wouldn’t run into state law, should choose that one. 2) under equal protection, out of state plaintiff could trap defendant in federal court and bring a claim that would be barred in state court, violating due process concerns. 3) Prudential justification: not ideal to have two substantive regimes going at once, if we know that we will always try our best to apply state law when there isn’t a direct conflict with federal- easier for planning purposes.
Question 2
Class Actions- Access to Justice, SCOTUS reluctance to appoint counsel in civil cases. Situation where CA is useful/less useful to A2J
A2J Promotion
CA is useful to promote A2J: no lawyer in civil cases, even where significant rights are at stake
Benefit from named plaintiff / their counsel, only cost is giving up right to sue later
In cases where plaintiff isn’t incentivized to sue themselves, e.g. lacks resources, potential recovery is too low basically provides them with a free option to benefit from bringing a claim they wouldn’t have brought themselves and compensating them for a harm done
A2J Failures
Lack of control over the litigation strategy, situations where named plaintiff might pursue a strategy that isn’t in the interest of class members, e.g. Amchem- named plaintiff incentivized to pursue a litigation strategy that didn’t benefit all class members
Requirements for class action try to resolve this with Typicality requirement, but class members could still disagree with strategy and lack recourse
Also, incentivized to get a big settlement quickly- plaintiff’s counsel likely works on commission- doesn’t consider the ways in which this strategy might contradict interests
What if an injunction is more important to class members than damages?
Those lawyers also take a huge cut of the money for victims who need/deserve it
High transaction costs
Emphasis on requirements to a fault- Amchem failed on typicality after long negotiations would finally give money to a lot of sick people
Question 3
