feedback.headline: Taught sequences run properly; the heaviest questions stop one step short, and venue drops out entirely
feedback.overview: Your best work here is real analysis rather than recitation. On Question 7 you correctly identified Sylvania as the movant carrying the trial burden of persuasion on its own affirmative defense, stated the heightened production standard, and treated Groucho's lack of memory as an absence of evidence rather than a genuine dispute. On Question 8 you broke the negligence ruling into three candidate issues and tested each against actually litigated and necessary to the decision, landing on the multiple-independent-grounds problem under Russell. Question 3's supplemental jurisdiction chain runs in order and reaches the right partial-remand result. The recurring cost is that several analyses stop where the question actually begins. Question 4 never raises venue or 1391. Question 5 names the Gulf Oil factors and applies none. Question 7 settles its dispositive choice-of-law step on a forum preference rather than the last-event rule you had just invoked. Question 8 reaches the Oklahoma point the facts were built to trigger only in a truncated closing clause. That is roughly ten points of venue and transfer analysis missing, plus the payoffs of both twelve-point questions left unresolved.

strengths.label: All four Erie tests separated with an outcome for each
strengths.detail: Attaching a grant-or-deny result to each test is what makes the run scoreable, and stating the stakes first (two years dismisses, three years survives) is what gives each outcome meaning.
strengths.answerExcerpt: York: SOL period is OD, if 2 years, dismissed and if 3 years not dismissed

strengths.label: Stevens analyzed on the fact the question was built around
strengths.detail: You located the Massachusetts period inside the statute creating the pet cause of action and contrasted Shady Grove, where the class-action bar sat in the procedural code. That is the as-applied validity inquiry Stevens actually runs, not a description of him as a middle position.
strengths.answerExcerpt: by including in rights governing pet ownership, could argue that it is entwined with state substantive right

strengths.label: Supplemental jurisdiction walked as steps to the right remedy
strengths.detail: You anchored on the Zeppo claim, found a common nucleus under Gibbs, then let 1367(b) oust a plaintiff's claim against a Rule 20 defendant. Remanding only the Sylvania claim rather than the whole case is the consequence most answers get wrong.
strengths.answerExcerpt: Under 1367b- claim by a plaintiff against a person made a party by FRCP 20 that violates the requirements of 1332

strengths.label: Every appellate route canvassed with a record-specific reason
strengths.detail: Nothing is skipped: 1291, 1292(a)(1), Rule 54(b), the absent 1292(b) certification, Cohen, and mandamus. The Cohen effective-reviewability element is genuinely reasoned rather than asserted, and you answered the standard-of-review half conditionally instead of dropping it after finding no jurisdiction.
strengths.answerExcerpt: The issue is reviewable later, can appeal judgement and if not a harmless error, trial can occur in the right place.

strengths.label: Happy-court framework drives the choice-of-law step
strengths.detail: Deciding whose choice-of-law rules follow the transfer before doing any choice-of-law work is the sequencing this question needs. Your incorporeal-object reasoning also does real work: the three-server option rejected because all three parts are needed, and the Balk analogy used to place the artwork with Sylvania.
strengths.answerExcerpt: Transfer from TX unhappy court for Sylvania, so DE will apply its own choice of law

strengths.label: Claim and issue preclusion kept separate, each run through its elements
strengths.detail: Claim preclusion is resolved on a reason rather than a label: we want a market in these artworks, so each is a separate transaction, contra the land reasoning in Gonzalez. You then stated the governing preclusion law with its reasoning, which is a complete form under the word limit, and tested three candidate issues one at a time.
strengths.answerExcerpt: the NFTs are something we’d want a market for like bonds (contra how the court phrased its reasoning about land in Gonzalez)

improvements.label: The Ginsburg applicability reason runs backwards
improvements.whatHappened: You concluded Rule 87 is inapplicable because no congressional statute speaks to a limitations period for pet death. On the Rule's own text, that is the condition under which Rule 87 does govern.
improvements.whyItMatters: Ginsburg's move is a creative narrow construction of the federal rule, so the reason has to be a reading the text can bear. A backwards reading leaves the state-law outcome unearned even though the outcome is right.
improvements.howToImprove: Use the construction the course teaches for this shape of rule: Rule 87 sets a three-year outer limit and is silent on whether a shorter state period may also bar the suit, so the two operate together and Massachusetts law applies. Swap that clause in for your current applicability clause; it costs no extra words.

improvements.label: No stated bottom line
improvements.whatHappened: "FRCP would interfere" implies Rule 87 is invalid as applied and the suit is dismissed, but you never say so.
improvements.whyItMatters: This subpart asks how Stevens comes out. An implied outcome is not scored as an outcome.
improvements.howToImprove: Add one clause naming the result: invalid as applied, so state law governs and the case is dismissed. Pay for it by cutting the rhetorical question about what a pet-injury limitations period has to do with pet ownership down to a short counter-clause.

improvements.label: One justification is mislabeled, and the other side is never weighed
improvements.whatHappened: Your second justification is described as equal protection and due process. The substance is recognizable, but the taught label is avoiding inequitable administration of the laws, the discrimination concern that ran through Swift. Separately, you argue only for the Ginsburg result and never take on the case against it.
improvements.whyItMatters: This subpart carries as much weight as the four-test run and asks for a defended position. A position that never meets the counterargument is asserted rather than defended.
improvements.howToImprove: Rename the second justification as inequitable administration of the laws. Then give the strongest reply to your own position in two clauses: Rule 87 came from Congress through the Rules Enabling Act rather than from judges finding general law, and uniform limitations across federal districts is itself a value. Pay for it by trimming your third justification, which repeats the planning point already made in the first.

improvements.label: Amchem's failure is attributed to the wrong requirement
improvements.whatHappened: You wrote that Amchem failed on typicality. The conflict between members who were already sick and those who were not is an adequacy-of-representation problem under Rule 23(a)(4).
improvements.whyItMatters: Amchem carries your unfavorable scenario. Naming the wrong requirement makes the mechanism wrong, and the mechanism is what this question rewards.
improvements.howToImprove: Say that the sick and not-yet-sick members wanted different things, so one representative could not adequately represent both, and subclasses would have been needed. Pay for it by cutting the sentence about lawyers taking a large cut, which repeats your fast-settlement point.

improvements.label: The Texas server never appears in Sylvania's contacts analysis
improvements.whatHappened: You concluded there is no specific jurisdiction over Sylvania on a unilateral-plaintiff rationale contra McGee. Sylvania maintained a server in Texas holding part of the stolen data, and that fact appears nowhere in the contacts discussion, though you discuss the three servers elsewhere.
improvements.whyItMatters: That server is the best Texas contact against Sylvania, and it reflects the defendant's own choice rather than anything Groucho did. A conclusion that never meets the strongest counter-contact reads as if the fact was missed.
improvements.howToImprove: Put the server into the purposeful-availment step and argue both sides: Sylvania chose to store this data in Texas, which is a contact related to the claim, against the response that Groucho opened the account in South Dakota and returned home on his own. Then state your resolution. Pay for it by moving the horizontal choice-of-law discussion out of Question 3 into Question 7.

improvements.label: Venue is never raised
improvements.whatHappened: You correctly identified that each claim now independently satisfies 1332, so supplemental jurisdiction and remand drop out, and you preserved the personal jurisdiction conclusion. Venue is not mentioned, and 1391 appears nowhere in the answer.
improvements.whyItMatters: Venue is the reason the exam switches from removal to original filing. In Question 3 venue was proper because the case was removed; on an original filing in the Western District of Texas it must be tested from scratch, and it fails. You also lose the predicate for Question 5, since transfer needs a venue problem to explain it.
improvements.howToImprove:
Walk 1391(b) in the order the statute lists.
1. 1391(b)(1): all defendants must reside in the district. Zeppo is a Delaware domiciliary, so this fails.
2. 1391(b)(2): a substantial part of the events. The gathering at Chico's house was in Dallas, the account was opened in Pierre, and the access came from San Diego. Groucho's own viewings in the Western District are not the substantial events.
3. State the consequence: venue is improper, so the case is dismissed or transferred.
Pay for it with the words spent re-stating the Question 3 personal jurisdiction conclusion; one clause saying it is unchanged is enough.

improvements.label: The Gulf Oil factors are named and never applied, and no district is tested for venue
improvements.whatHappened: Your last line is "Where is mostly likely to transfer: Gulf Oil factors," with no factor applied and no district chosen. Separately, your per-defendant jurisdiction lists are never intersected into a district that works against both defendants, and venue is not tested in any candidate district.
improvements.whyItMatters: The question asks which district is the most likely destination, and a transferee court must be one where the action could have been brought against both defendants. A framework recited without application earns nothing.
improvements.howToImprove: Run venue in one clause per district: Delaware works under 1391(b)(1) because both defendants reside there, and the Northern District of Texas works under 1391(b)(2) because the meeting at Chico's house happened there. Say which districts survive against both defendants, and say expressly whether naming the Northern District of Texas revisits your earlier conclusion that Texas lacks jurisdiction over Sylvania. Then apply three facts you already have: Chico's testimony and computer sit in the Northern District of Texas; Texas burdens Zeppo while Delaware burdens Groucho about equally; a Texas court using the Second Restatement might apply Texas law, while Delaware's advantage is that jurisdiction and venue there are beyond argument. Name your pick. Pay for it by compressing the per-district bullets that repeat the Question 3 contacts reasoning.

improvements.label: Mandamus and clear-error review are named without content
improvements.whatHappened: Mandamus appears as a heading disposed of in a fragment. The standard-of-review breakdown gives de novo for interpretation and abuse of discretion for application, but omits clear error for underlying findings of fact.
improvements.whyItMatters: Mandamus is the realistic vehicle in this posture, so the exceptional-circumstances requirement is what a reader looks for. Zeppo's domicile is a factual finding, and separating fact from law shows you are matching the standard to the character of the question.
improvements.howToImprove: Add one clause saying mandamus requires an exceptional circumstance and nothing here supplies one. Add one clause applying clear error to Zeppo's domicile. Pay for both out of the Rule 54(b) bullet, which needs only the absence of an entered judgment.

improvements.label: The choice-of-law step ends on a forum preference, not the last-event rule
improvements.whatHappened: You correctly said Delaware is a First Restatement state and that the last event controls, then concluded that "DE probably more likely to apply its own law" and hedged with "really could go either way." That is a court's preference for its own law, which is not what the First Restatement asks.
improvements.whyItMatters: Whether recovery is barred or merely reduced is the payoff of this twelve-point question, and it turns entirely on where the artwork was when it was taken. Leaving the location unresolved leaves the answer without a bottom line, even though you had already done the hard locating work earlier.
improvements.howToImprove: Move your Balk reasoning here and finish it. Choose a location and say why: Oklahoma City is where Sylvania keeps the account and made the security decisions, which is ascertainable and matches party expectations, against the objections to Pierre as accidental and to the three physical server sites as too scattered to pick one. Then state the consequence, since Oklahoma bars recovery while Delaware, Texas, Massachusetts and South Carolina only reduce it. Pay for it by deleting the location discussion from Question 3, where it earns nothing.

improvements.label: The password ground and the 2FA ground are not analyzed separately
improvements.whatHappened: You treated the affidavit and Chico's transcript as establishing contributory negligence in one move, without asking whether the password facts alone would compel the finding and whether the absence of two-factor authentication alone would.
improvements.whyItMatters: They are independent grounds, and that independence is exactly why the unexplained ruling creates your Question 8 preclusion problem. Combining them here makes the Question 8 point look incidental rather than earned.
improvements.howToImprove: Run the compelled-finding standard once on the password facts and once on two-factor authentication, saying whether each alone would carry Sylvania's burden. Pay for it by cutting your written-out statement of the movant's production standard to its operative words, since you state it at length and then apply it twice.

improvements.label: Oklahoma's rejection of Russell is left as a truncated clause
improvements.whatHappened: Your answer ends mid-sentence with the observation that in some states failure to enable two-factor authentication could have been found actually decided. The exam supplies the fact that Oklahoma does not follow Russell, and the second court's freedom to give more preclusive effect than the rendering court would is never stated.
improvements.whyItMatters: This is the point the facts were engineered to produce. Your Russell analysis is correct, and the answer stops just before the payoff, so the Oklahoma court's likely ruling is never given.
improvements.howToImprove:
Finish the chain in two steps.
1. Oklahoma treats multiple independent grounds as all decided, so the necessary-to-the-decision problem does not defeat preclusion there.
2. A second court may apply more preclusion than the rendering court would, so the Oklahoma court can issue-preclude Groucho on the two-factor authentication finding.
Pay for it by collapsing your three-issue table: the username and written-paper issues fail for the same reason, so handle them in one line and spend the recovered words here.

improvements.label: The Rule 54(b) conclusion rests on box-checking
improvements.whatHappened: You confirmed there are multiple claims, that judgment was entered on one, and that the judge said there was no just reason for delay, then concluded the certification was correct. The overlap between the two claims is never weighed.
improvements.whyItMatters: Rule 54(b) asks whether there is a just reason for delay, which is a judgment about efficiency rather than a form check. Groucho's theory is that Zeppo succeeded only because Sylvania was negligent, so the claims share facts and piecemeal appellate review is wasteful.
improvements.howToImprove: Add the weighing in two clauses: the claims overlap factually and the Zeppo claim continues, so there is a just reason for delay and the certification was probably improper. Note in passing that the judge gave no reasons. Pay for it out of the definitional bullet explaining what counts as multiple claims.

improvements.label: Analysis placed under the wrong question
improvements.whatHappened: Question 3 carries an extended horizontal choice-of-law discussion that belongs to Question 7, where the affirmative-defense question turns on it.
improvements.whyItMatters: Under a strict word limit, misplaced analysis is paid for twice: once in words, and once in the venue and transfer analysis that Questions 4 and 5 never received.
improvements.howToImprove: When a question does not ask for an analysis, leave a one-line cross-reference and save the analysis for the question that does. Here that would have freed the words Question 4's venue run and Question 5's factor application needed.

revisionPlan: Question 1(a): replace the Ginsburg applicability reason with the narrow reading — Rule 87 sets an outer three-year limit and is silent on shorter state periods.
Question 1(b): state the outcome — invalid as applied, state law governs, case dismissed.
Question 1(c): rename the second justification as inequitable administration of the laws, and add the counterargument that Rule 87 came out of the Rules Enabling Act process.
Question 2: attribute the Amchem conflict to adequacy of representation under Rule 23(a)(4).
Question 3: put the Texas server into Sylvania's purposeful-availment analysis and argue both sides; move the choice-of-law material to Question 7.
Question 4: run 1391(b)(1) then (b)(2), and state that venue in the Western District is improper so the case is dismissed or transferred.
Question 5: test venue in each candidate district, name the districts available against both defendants, then apply the Gulf Oil factors to a stated pick.
Question 6: add the exceptional-circumstances requirement for mandamus and clear error for Zeppo's domicile.

submissions.label: Mock full draft — 2022 (DS answer)
submissions.answer:
## Question 1
 a) Under the outcome-determinative test (York), the case will be dismissed if SoL is
2 years and will survive otherwise, so the case is dismissed under state law. Under the

Harlan concurrence in Hanna, we find that SoL doesn’t alter primary (non-lawyer)
conduct since SoL only comes into play after you’ve decided to file a lawsuit, so the case
survives under federal rule. Both Scalia and Ginsburg would find that the federal rule is
valid because it “really does regulate procedure” (Sibbach) and thus does not conflict
with the REA. It concerns what period of time a plaintiff must initiate a lawsuit in.
Regarding applicability, MA sets a shorter SoL than the federal rule, so Scalia would
likely find there to be a conflict, so the case survives under the federal rule. Ginsburg
might interpret the MA SoL as specifically pertaining to the death or injury of pets, for
which there is no federal equivalent, so there is no conflict and the state rule applies (and
case dismissed).

 b) Stevens in Shady Grave would actually apply the validity test beyond a nominal
citation to Sibbach by finding that FRCP 87 enlarges the scope of a substantive right

defined by state law. In this case, SoL is substantive because it determines how difficult it
will be for a plaintiff to seek remedy by setting a time limit (and Stevens cites Guaranty
Trust as an example of a state procedural rule creating a substantive right). Stevens would
then apply the same applicability test as Ginsburg to dismiss the case under state law.

 c) I think the court should apply state law and dismiss. Doing so upholds
constitutional values albeit at the expense of uniform federal procedure. However, I
believe preserving federalism and state-specific policy-making is more important than

124383 124383

creating a national market for lawyers. Furthermore, even the RDA, which Scalia relies
heavily upon in formulating his Erie test, presumes that state law applies unless Congress
“require[s]” otherwise. In this case, since MA specifically passed a law concerning cases

involving pets, it’s not clear whether the general federal rule actually requires us to
abandon the state standard. Perhaps Congress just didn’t think about pets as a special
case, and we need a stronger statutory justification before abandoning state law. Finally,
practically speaking, applying state law prevents forum shopping between state and
federal court (as Erie intended) by preserving vertical uniformity. We have other
protections (IPJ and venue) to prevent horizontal forum shopping, so it arguably isn’t as
important to also make Erie preserve horizontal uniformity.

-------------------------------------------

124383 124383

-------------------------------------------

## Question 2
 On balance, I think class actions are not useful to promoting access to justice. On
one hand, because Turner/Lassiter together basically rule out the right to counsel in civil
cases, a would-be plaintiff might still be able to seek remedy as an unnamed member of a
class if she doesn’t want to appear pro se in litigation. Supreme Tribe of Ben-Hur and
Exxon both set class actions up to allow this, by eliminating the diversity of citizenship
and AIC requirements for unnamed plaintiffs.

 However, class actions are ultimately still an efficiency-motivated litigation
mechanism, allowing (and sometimes requiring) claims to be consolidated. An unnamed
plaintiff has very little control over the litigation process and, in 23(b)(1)/(2) lawsuits,
cannot opt out if they want to. Furthermore, even in 23(b)(3) lawsuits, a plaintiff may not
have adequate notice of an ongoing class action to make any meaningful decision

pertaining to the lawsuit. And though the plaintiff also has a choice to opt out of (b)(3)
lawsuits and pursue the litigation on her own without being precluded, someone who
needs class actions as an access to justice mechanism probably doesn’t have other viable
options. Therefore, by failing to provide plaintiffs with a meaningful choice in how they
pursue litigation before precluding them from making future claims, class actions can’t
reasonably be construed as an alternative avenue to justice.

-------------------------------------------

124383 124383

124383 124383

-------------------------------------------

## Question 3

 Both defendants agreed to remove and likely within time limit. As explained below,
the basis for SMJ is likely DJ, and neither Sylvania (incorp. DE, PPoB OK) nor Zeppo
(DE) is from TX, so no “home court” advantage prevents removal.

 SMJ: No AUJ because negligence and conversion are both state claims. No federal
issue embedded, so no Smith-Grable exception. Groucho (TX domiciliary) is completely
diverse from the parties. His claim against Zeppo ($250K) meets the AIC threshold
($75K), but his claim against Sylvania ($50K) does not. Joinder is proper under FRCP 20
(same T&O of “Duck in Soup” theft). By the same logic, the claim against Sylvania is
part of the same case or controversy as Zeppo (1367(a)). No reason for the federal court
to decline to exercise jurisdiction under 1367(c). However, 1367(b) prevents SuppJ in

diversity cases over a party joined under FRCP 20 where it would violate requirements of
1332 (Sylvania is AIC-deficient), so likely no SuppJ (Exxon dictum).

 Groucho could remand to TX state court for lack of SMJ at any time.

 Assuming the remand is denied, the defendants could also dismiss for lack of SMJ.

 IPJ: We have a TX long-arm going to constitutional limits. Under FRCP

124383 124383

4(k)(1)(A), TX federal court can “piggy-back” off state long-arm. No GIPJ in TX over
either defendant (they’re from DE/OK). Sylvania also doesn’t meet the Daimler threshold
(only one known sale in TX, only 1/3 of servers in TX). For SIPJ minimal contacts (Int’l

Shoe), Sylvania has purposely availed itself to TX by maintaining servers there without
an intermediary (contra Nicastro), even though it hasn’t advertised or maintained an
office there (WWVW). Fair and reasonable analysis points to TX: servers in TX (extent of
defendant contacts and convenience), Groucho lives there (plaintiff’s interests and
convenience), TX has interest in protecting its residents, some evidence/witnesses might
be in TX (Groucho’s computer, Chico) but not all (Sylvania tech support), TX law likely
applies (see Q7 for full HCOL analysis).

 SIPJ over Zeppo is unlikely, since he was in CA when the theft happened and his
only known contact with TX was his visit. As a Hail Mary for minimal contacts, we
could argue that Zeppo projected harm “generally targeted” (Griffis) at Groucho’s
experience of “Duck in Soup” in TX (Calder). However, since virtual reality can be
experienced from anywhere in the world and not necessarily in TX, the harm to Groucho

probably doesn’t rise to the threshold of harm to a Hollywood actress’s reputation in CA.
Alternatively, Zeppo’s visit to Chico might be “reach[ing] into the state” (where he first
encounters Groucho and the simulation) (McGee). Fair and reasonable analysis is mostly
the same: weaker extent of contacts, though still convenient because Zeppo visited the
state, with other factors unchanged.

 Venue: No 1391(b)(1)/(c), since not all defendants (Zeppo) “reside” in TX. Likely
also improper under 1391(b)(2), since Groucho’s purchase of “Duck in Soup” (D.SD),

124383 124383

creation of his Sylvania account (D.SD), Zeppo’s visit (N.D.TX), Zeppo transferring the
code (S.D.CA) were all outside of W.D.TX, even though Groucho discovered the theft in
San Antonio. That doesn’t seem like a substantial portion of events “giving rise” to the

claims. Can maybe argue that trying to “locate” all events makes no sense for Internet-
related crimes. Can also try to use 1391(b)(3), depending on if there is IPJ over either
defendant (likely Sylvania).

 Defendants could motion to transfer for lack of IPJ over Zeppo.

-------------------------------------------

124383 124383

-------------------------------------------

## Question 4
 Changing the AICs would cure the SMJ problem above, since both Zeppo ($200K)
and Sylvania ($100K) would now meet the threshold. The FRCP 20 joinder would be
okay now under 1367 since SuppJ over Sylvania would not violate 1332 requirements.
Groucho could not remand and defendants could not dismiss for lack of SMJ.

-------------------------------------------

124383 124383

-------------------------------------------

## Question 5
 Only DE and TX could be argued as having contacts with both defendants. We look
at IPJ for both states and venue for their available districts (N.W.TX and DE).

 IPJ
 TX: See above. Unclear if IPJ exists for Zeppo.
 DE: Has GIPJ over both defendants as DE residents.

 Venue
 N.D.TX: See above. Analysis is almost exactly the same, except Zeppo’s visit
occurred in the district. Could arguably now lay venue under 1391(b)(2), since Zeppo’s
visit precipitated his stealing the code.
 D.DE: Proper under 1391(b)(1)/(c).

 Assuming Judge Teasdale may transfer to either N.D.TX or D.DE: Applying Gulf
Oil factors: on one hand, some of the evidence/witnesses are in TX, the cost of litigation
would be lower in TX due to convenience for parties involved, TX has an interest in
having theft involving its residents decided in-state, DE has no real connection to the
incident other than the residence of defendants, a DE jury would have no relationship to
the litigation, and TX law would likely apply. On the other, since both defendants reside
in DE, it may be easier to enforce a judgment and would be unfair to force defendants to

124383 124383

litigate in another state when they have much stronger contacts elsewhere. Overall, this
analysis favors transferring to N.D.TX, assuming we don’t have an IPJ problem.

-------------------------------------------

124383 124383

-------------------------------------------

## Question 6

 The transfer motion is not immediately appealable. The court has not rendered a
final judgment under 1291. No injunction, so no 1292(a)(1). No further explanation
provided, so no double discretion (1292(b)) or FRCP 54(b). No irreparable harm or
repeated trial judge mistake, so no writ of mandamus. No Cohen exception: though the
order is final and collateral to the merits, it is not effectively unreviewable later, as the
right to be sued in a particular forum is not “essentiall destroyed” by allowing the trial
finish first (Lauro Lines wrt. forum selection clauses).

-------------------------------------------

124383 124383

-------------------------------------------

## Question 7
 If, as a matter of HCOL, contributory negligence is available as a defense, Judge
Marcal should grant Sylvania’s motion. Otherwise, she will probably deny it.

 As a substantive rule, contributory negligence is likely not available. Under Van
Dusen/Ferens, DE court will apply the transferor court’s (TX) COL rules (as W.D.TX
would have, Klaxon) if venue was laid properly and the court properly exercised IPJ.
Assuming TX was “happy”, TX uses 2R, so we begin with a strong presumption of LLD
and look for countervailing interests that shift the “center of gravity” (Babcock). The
challenge here is locating the digital asset at the time of theft. The candidates are SC,
MA, and TX (where Sylvania’s servers are). Luckily, all three states only have the
“comparative fault” defense available. Per our analysis above, TX does have an
especially strong interest in this litigation, which may center the parties’ relationship

there. Alternatively, even if TX was “unhappy”, we apply DE’s COL rules under 1R to
find the HCOL result unchanged under LLD (though it’s unclear what we would do if
SC/MA/TX laws diverged).

 Under the “comparative fault” theory, the motion would fail, since only
contributory negligence totally bars the plaintiff from recovery.

 If contributory negligence were available, the motion would succeed. Movant

124383 124383

Sylvania has the burden of proving the affirmative defense at trial (Celotex). Sylvania
must show that, drawing all reasonable inferences in Groucho’s favor, there is no genuine
issue of material fact and Sylvania is entitled to judgment as a matter of law. Sylvania can

meet its production burden by pointing to the affidavit from its engineer (bad
username/password and lack of 2FA) and the transcript of Chico’s deposition (showing
his username/password to everyone) to show that Groucho’s own negligence was a causal
factor of the theft/loss of “Duck in Soup”. Groucho has not produced any evidence to
counteract Sylvania’s production, and it’s hard to see how Groucho would otherwise be
able to rebut this evidence of his negligence in managing his account.

-------------------------------------------

124383 124383

-------------------------------------------

## Question 8
 Rule 54(b) was applied correctly. We have multiple claims: different legal theories
(negligence and conversion) against different parties (Sylvania and Zeppo) (Liberty
Mutual). The negligence claim is severable from conversion. Besides, Marcal’s judgment
will be reviewed with “substantial deference” (Curtiss-Wright). Finally, Marcal expressly
directed entry of final judgment and found there was “no just reason for delay”.

 Sylvania cannot invoke claim preclusion against Groucho. We have the same
parties (Groucho and Sylvania) and a judgment that is final and “on the merits”
(Sylvania’s liability in Groucho’s negligence claim). However, the theft of “Duck in
Soup” is not the same T/O as the theft of another artist’s work (“To War!”). Contra
Gonzalez, allowing preclusion here would inhibit the market for digital art.

 Sylvania might try using ONMCE on Groucho’s negligence/inability to recover.
First, we have mutuality, since these are the same parties in the same procedural posture.
Second, the issue was actually litigated in the MSJ proceedings. It’s unclear if SJ grant is
sufficiently firm, since they can be revised at any time (but hardly ever are). Finally, in
diversity cases, we apply the preclusion law of the state where the rendering federal court
sat (Semtek). However, since this case was transferred from TX to DE, it’s unclear which
state that is. Since TX was likely “unhappy”, and the plaintiff shouldn’t get their COL
when IPJ/venue are improper, DE preclusion rules should arguably apply.

124383 124383

 Since Sylvania alleged multiple independent grounds for SJ in L1, if DE preclusion
law applies, issue preclusion will not run against Groucho in L2 (Russell v. Place). If TX

preclusion law applies, however, the fact that Groucho did not enable 2FA will prevent
him recovering in L2, because this was one of the independent bases supporting the MSJ
in Sylvania’s favor in L1.

feedback.headline: Committed, well-structured answers on all eight questions; the gaps are in canvassing alternatives and in the standard of review Question 6 never gives
feedback.overview: The best work here is analysis rather than recitation. Question 3 runs supplemental jurisdiction as steps instead of asserting a result. Question 7 makes the summary judgment ruling expressly conditional on the choice-of-law answer, then notices that under comparative fault a motion asking for a complete bar fails even if Groucho was negligent. Every question ends in a committed disposition. The gaps are completeness and canvassing. Question 6 never states the standard of review the question asks for. Question 7 stops the location of the incorporeal artwork at the three server states, and because all three use comparative fault, the complete bar is never tested. Question 8 never uses the planted fact that Oklahoma rejects Russell v. Place. Question 3 never says which claim goes back to state court.

strengths.label: All four Erie tests carried to an outcome
strengths.detail: Naming the tests is not the credit; resolving each one on these facts is. Validity and applicability stay separate, and Ginsburg's move is correctly described as narrowing the federal rule rather than invalidating it.
strengths.answerExcerpt: Ginsburg might interpret the MA SoL as specifically pertaining to the death or injury of pets, for which there is no federal equivalent, so there is no conflict

strengths.label: An independent forum-shopping argument
strengths.detail: Separating vertical from horizontal uniformity, and observing that personal jurisdiction and venue already police horizontal shopping, is an argument of your own rather than a second helping of the federalism point.
strengths.answerExcerpt: We have other protections (IPJ and venue) to prevent horizontal forum shopping

strengths.label: Supplemental jurisdiction run as steps
strengths.detail: You anchor on the Zeppo claim, establish the common nucleus under 1367(a), consider declination under 1367(c), then reach the 1367(b) carve-out — with Exxon used to deny jurisdiction, which is the correct direction.
strengths.answerExcerpt: 1367(b) prevents SuppJ in diversity cases over a party joined under FRCP 20 where it would violate requirements of 1332

strengths.label: Every appealability route walked in order
strengths.detail: You take the routes in sequence rather than jumping to the one that decides it, and you give the right reason the collateral order route fails — the forum right is not destroyed by waiting.
strengths.answerExcerpt: No injunction, so no 1292(a)(1). No further explanation provided, so no double discretion (1292(b)) or FRCP 54(b).

strengths.label: The summary judgment ruling made conditional
strengths.detail: Tying the grant or denial to the choice-of-law result up front is stronger than a flat answer, and it lets you see that comparative fault defeats the relief Sylvania actually sought.
strengths.answerExcerpt: If, as a matter of HCOL, contributory negligence is available as a defense, Judge Marcal should grant Sylvania's motion.

strengths.label: Issue preclusion worked element by element
strengths.detail: Actually litigated, an honest doubt about the firmness of a revisable summary judgment, Semtek for which system's law governs, and Russell v. Place applied to the two independent grounds — sequenced rather than scattered.
strengths.answerExcerpt: Since Sylvania alleged multiple independent grounds for SJ in L1, if DE preclusion law applies, issue preclusion will not run against Groucho in L2 (Russell v. Place).

improvements.label: Question 1(a) — the Harlan pass needs the other side
improvements.whatHappened: Harlan gets one sentence: limitations periods bite only after a plaintiff decides to sue, so federal law applies.
improvements.whyItMatters: The course materials use the limitations-period hypothetical to make the opposite point — repeat players such as insurers do adjust pre-litigation behavior to litigation risk. A one-sided pass on a close test reads as an unexamined conclusion.
improvements.howToImprove: Add a clause acknowledging that sophisticated parties may set rates or investment strategy against the limitations period, then say which way you come out. Pay for it by cutting the sentence "It concerns what period of time a plaintiff must initiate a lawsuit in," which restates the conclusion you already reached.

improvements.label: Question 1(a) — the validity test is not a conflict test
improvements.whatHappened: You write that the rule "really does regulate procedure" and "thus does not conflict with the REA."
improvements.whyItMatters: Validity under 2072(b) asks whether the rule abridges, enlarges or modifies a substantive right. The phrasing blurs a test you are otherwise applying correctly.
improvements.howToImprove: Swap "does not conflict with the REA" for "does not abridge, enlarge or modify a substantive right." Same word count.

improvements.label: Question 1(b) — Stevens fights on validity, not applicability
improvements.whatHappened: You identify Stevens's as-applied Rules Enabling Act inquiry correctly, then say he "would then apply the same applicability test as Ginsburg."
improvements.whyItMatters: That is the one place Stevens and Ginsburg part company. Stevens accepts the rule's plain language on applicability and locates the whole fight in whether applying it would enlarge a state substantive right.
improvements.howToImprove: Close the subpart by saying Stevens agrees the rule applies by its terms and would dismiss on validity instead. Bring up the placement fact you use later in 1(c): the two-year period sits inside the pet statute that creates the cause of action. Pay for both by cutting the clause explaining that a limitations period "determines how difficult it will be for a plaintiff to seek remedy."

improvements.label: Question 1(c) — the RDA attribution is off
improvements.whatHappened: You attribute Scalia's Erie test to the Rules of Decision Act.
improvements.whyItMatters: The Hanna majority route rests on the Rules Enabling Act and the Supremacy Clause; the Rules of Decision Act drives the unguided track and the twin aims. The slip sits at the center of your strongest normative argument.
improvements.howToImprove: Recast the same argument under the Rules Enabling Act: a general federal limitations rule promulgated under 2072 may not have been meant to displace a state rule embedded in the statute creating the claim. One word changes and the argument survives.

improvements.label: Question 2 — the central access-to-justice mechanism is missing
improvements.whatHappened: You deliver the Turner and Lassiter component with its relevance stated. You never reach the mechanism that makes class actions an access-to-justice device: pooling claims too small for anyone to litigate alone.
improvements.whyItMatters: The question asks for a situation where a class action promotes access to justice, and low-value claims are that situation. Without it your position rests only on the counterarguments.
improvements.howToImprove: Add one sentence on claims no individual would rationally bring alone, and tie the unfavorable example to commonality under Wal-Mart or to a defensive posture where there is no class to join. Pay for both by cutting the Ben-Hur and Exxon sentence down to a clause.

improvements.label: Question 3 — say which claim is remanded
improvements.whatHappened: After correctly finding no supplemental jurisdiction over the $50,000 Sylvania claim, you write that "Groucho could remand to TX state court for lack of SMJ at any time." That reads as remand of the whole case.
improvements.whyItMatters: The 1367(b) analysis earns its points only when you state the consequence. The Zeppo claim independently satisfies 1332 and stays in federal court; only the amount-deficient Sylvania claim goes back.
improvements.howToImprove: Replace that sentence with the split disposition: the Sylvania claim is remanded, the Zeppo claim remains. Pay for it by cutting the Calder and Griffis passage, which spends four lines on a weak theory when the strong point is one clause — Zeppo's Dallas visit is where he encountered the artwork.

improvements.label: Question 3 — the fallback venue provision is closed here
improvements.whatHappened: You float 1391(b)(3) as usable "depending on if there is IPJ over either defendant."
improvements.whyItMatters: The fallback applies only when no district qualifies under (b)(1) or (b)(2). Delaware qualifies under (b)(1), as your own Question 5 shows.
improvements.howToImprove: Brain off on this one: walk the three bases in order and close (b)(3) with the reason the statute gives — another district is available. No extra words.

improvements.label: Question 4 — name the defect that survives the fix
improvements.whatHappened: You correctly say the higher amounts cure the subject matter jurisdiction problem, and stop. Your venue analysis showing the Western District of Texas is improper sits back in Question 3 and is never flagged here.
improvements.whyItMatters: The question asks what changes. What changes is that the jurisdictional defect disappears and venue becomes the live one, so the case must still be dismissed or transferred. A reader of Question 4 alone thinks the suit can proceed.
improvements.howToImprove: Add one sentence: venue in the Western District remains improper under 1391(b)(1) because Zeppo does not reside in Texas, and under 1391(b)(2) because the substantial events occurred in the Northern District, so dismissal or transfer still follows. Question 4 runs four lines, so the room is there; cross-reference rather than repeat.

improvements.label: Question 5 — resolve the jurisdictional doubt your recommendation depends on
improvements.whatHappened: You recommend the Northern District of Texas "assuming we don't have an IPJ problem," leaving the doubt about Zeppo unresolved.
improvements.whyItMatters: A transferee district must be one where the action could have been brought, which requires personal jurisdiction over every defendant there. If Zeppo is not amenable in Texas, the district you pick is not available at all, so the assumption is doing the whole job.
improvements.howToImprove: Commit: Zeppo's Dallas visit is where he encountered the artwork, so specific jurisdiction over him is likely there. Name Hoffman for the point that the transferor court's improper venue does not enlarge the set of permissible transferee districts. Pay for both by cutting the clause that a Delaware jury would have no relationship to the litigation, which repeats the clause just before it.

improvements.label: Question 6 — the standard of review is never given
improvements.whatHappened: The appealability canvass is complete and correct. The second half of the question — what standard the court of appeals would use if an appeal did lie — gets nothing, not even a conditional sentence.
improvements.whyItMatters: The question asks for it expressly, so that half is unclaimed. Concluding that no appeal lies does not excuse the conditional ask.
improvements.howToImprove:
Match the standard to the type of question rather than giving one global standard:
1. Interpretation of the venue statute: de novo.
2. Findings of fact such as Zeppo's domicile: clear error.
3. A discretionary transfer decision, if venue were proper: abuse of discretion.
Pay for it by compressing the mandamus and 1292(b) sentences to one clause each; both are already conclusions.

improvements.label: Question 7 — the incorporeal artwork's location needs a real canvass
improvements.whatHappened: You identify the hard problem, then limit the candidates to the three states holding Sylvania's servers and note that all three use comparative fault.
improvements.whyItMatters: This is the signature move of a twelve-point question, and the truncation decides the outcome. Because every server state uses comparative fault, the complete bar is never tested. The candidates you skipped are the strong ones. Pierre is where the account was opened and control given up. San Antonio is the owner's home. Oklahoma is where the security decisions were made, and Oklahoma and South Dakota are the contributory negligence states.
improvements.howToImprove: List the candidates and give each a reason for and against — definiteness, whose expectations it matches, whether it scatters entrusted data wherever owners happen to live — then pick one and carry it to the contributory or comparative result. Pay for it by cutting the restated standard, "Sylvania must show that, drawing all reasonable inferences in Groucho's favor, there is no genuine issue of material fact and Sylvania is entitled to judgment as a matter of law," which you then apply anyway.

improvements.label: Question 7 — your own venue finding controls the happy court question
improvements.whatHappened: The primary path assumes Texas was "happy" and applies the transferor's choice-of-law rules. Your Question 3 analysis concluded venue in the Western District of Texas was improper. The alternative gets one clause.
improvements.whyItMatters: Under the Greiner Happy Court Rule, an unhappy transferor court means the transferee applies its own choice-of-law rules — here Delaware's First Restatement approach, which points to the place of the last event and forces exactly the location problem the question is built on.
improvements.howToImprove: Lead with the unhappy-court path, since your own findings compel it, and reduce the happy-court branch to one clause. No net words added.

improvements.label: Question 8 — use the fact that Oklahoma rejects Russell v. Place
improvements.whatHappened: You reach the multiple-independent-grounds problem and route the alternative through Texas preclusion law. The exam supplies the fact that Oklahoma does not follow Russell v. Place, and that fact never appears.
improvements.whyItMatters: The second suit is in Oklahoma. Under Hart, the second court may give a judgment more preclusive effect than the rendering court would, so Oklahoma's rule is the direct route to preclusion running against Groucho on the 2FA ground.
improvements.howToImprove: After the Semtek step, add the Hart point and apply Oklahoma's rule. Say explicitly that the changed password removes the password ground from the second suit, leaving 2FA as the only shared issue. Pay for it by cutting the Curtiss-Wright deference sentence. One substantive labeling point: you call this offensive non-mutual collateral estoppel and then say mutuality is present, which cannot both hold — with the same parties it is ordinary issue preclusion.

improvements.label: Question 8 — meet the argument against the Rule 54(b) certification
improvements.whatHappened: You approve the certification on multiple claims and the judge's recitation of no just reason for delay. The strongest argument the other way never appears, even to be rejected.
improvements.whyItMatters: Groucho's theory is that Zeppo could take the artwork only because Sylvania was negligent, so the two claims are factually intertwined and the Zeppo claim is still live. That is a just reason for delay, and appellate efficiency favors treating the case as one unit.
improvements.howToImprove: State the intertwinement argument in one sentence, then say why you still come out where you do. Pay for it by cutting "The negligence claim is severable from conversion," which restates the multiple-claims point you already made.

submissions.answer:
## Question 1

 (a)

 York:
 Applying state SoL leads to dismissal, FRCP87 wouldn’t. Outcome-determinative,
apply state law.

 Harlan:
 Harlan would analogize to Ragan, which involved whether tolling of SoL
commenced upon service or filing. Harlan believed Ragan was wrongly decided, because
SoL tolling didn’t affect litigant’s “primary conduct.” Harlan would view a three-year
versus two-year SoL as solely affecting the behavior of lawyers to know when filing is
proper, and not “primary conduct” of clients. Thus, apply federal rule.

 One could argue SoLs affect “primary conduct” because longer SoLs could raise
insurance premiums (keeping claims on insurance books longer) and, in turn, deter risky
driving.

 Scalia:
 Scalia asks whether FRCP87 is valid and applicable. REA says rule mustn’t

802386 802386

“abridge, enlarge, or modify substantive right” and Scalia applies Sibbach test of whether
rule “really regulates procedure.” Because FRCP87 affects how litigants file complaints,
it regulates procedure. Reading plain text of FRCP87, Scalia would find it applicable,

because it states “any” lawsuit in federal district court “shall” have 3-year SoL, which
applies here. Apply federal rule.

 Ginsburg:
 Ginsburg uses Scalia validity test, finds FRCP87 valid.

 While Ginsburg is willing to narrowly construe FRCP to advance state policy
objectives, she probably wouldn’t do so here. FRCP87 is unambigous that it “shall” apply
to “any lawsuit” in federal court, unless Congress has otherwise specified. No federal
statute speaks to SoL for death/injury to pets. Apply federal rule.

 If Ginsburg narrowly construed FRCP87, she might say the parenthetical is a non-

comprehensive list of exceptions, because it states “for example.” In doing so, she could
advance Massachusetts’ interest in dictating when pet injury/death claims are too stale.

 (b)
 Stevens might argue FRCP87 isn’t valid under REA by avoiding the atextual
Sibbach interpretation of §2072.

802386 802386

 SoLs are tied up in the enforcement of rights (in fact, MA SoL is part of pet statutes
and NOT MRCP), and thus are arguably substantive. By imposing a longer SoL, FRCP87

enlarges substantive rights of pet-owners, which violates REA.

 If Stevens reached applicability, he’d side with Scalia since he’s willing to read
FRCP in light of state aims but less so than Ginsburg, who already struggles to construe
FRCP87 narrowly.

 (c)
 We should adopt Ginsburg’s test. Her test promotes robust federalism principles
that were at the heart of Erie initially. Reading federal rules/statutes in light of state
policies promotes “laboratories of democracy.”

 While Ginsburg’s use of Sibbach involves an atextual reading of §2072, it’s easier
to operationalize than Harlan’s or Stevens’ approach. It’s hard to determine whether
something affects “primary conduct” (see SoL discussion above). For Stevens’ approach,
it’d be tremendously challenging to determine FRCP validity by interpreting state law,
because state laws often don’t have requisite clarity/legislative history and federal judges
won’t have expertise. Babcock and Neumeier demonstrate the perils of interpreting
another sovereign’s law.

802386 802386

 I disfavor Scalia’s unabiding commitment to formalism. Substantive rights are
intertwined with procedural rights and Scalia unduly limits state efforts to apply
normative judgments in structuring their procedures to affect substantive outcomes.

-------------------------------------------

802386 802386

-------------------------------------------

## Question 2

 Class actions promote access to justice by allowing persons with small claims to
have a cost-justified avenue for bringing suit by pooling their claims with others. There’s
potential for substantial damages in class actions (and substantial attorney’s fees) as the
defendents are often multinational corporations. Economies of scale allow classes to more
easily find/afford a lawyer on a contingency-based fee, which mitigates the need for state-
provided counsel. The Turner court worried about lawyers making proceedings more
complex and undercutting judicial efficiency, but class actions, by their nature, promote
efficiency in adjudicating many claims simultaneously.

 Class actions are not uniformly positive on access to justice. A class member can
get stuck with a settlement they view as inadequate which they’ll be forced to accept if

the court adjudges it “fair” under Rule 23(e). Individual suits could produce more
fulsome relief to some litigants, and yet some class action categories don’t allow class
members to opt out (FRCP23(b)(1)(B)).

-------------------------------------------

802386 802386

-------------------------------------------

## Question 3

 Remand:

 Joinder is proper under FRCP 20, because claims against Zeppo/Sylvania arise
from same T+O (Groucho losing “Duck in Soup”) and common issue of fact is present in
whether Zeppo stole based on weak Sylvania cybersecurity protocols.

 W.D.TX lacks SMJ over claim against Sylvania. No federal question is present
because conversion and negligence are state law causes of action, and no federal issue is
embedded (Smith-Grable). Therefore, FQJ isn’t present for either defendant. Groucho
(TX domicile) is completely diverse from Zeppo (DE domicile) and Sylvania (DE inc.
/OK PPOB) (Strawbridge). However, claim against Sylvania is AIC-deficient.

 Claim against Zeppo meets AIC, so could pursue supplemental SMJ, but Groucho’s
claim is by plaintiff against person/corporation (Sylvania) made party under Rule 20, and
thus must independently comply with §1332, according to §1367(b), which we’ve shown
above it doesn’t.

 Motion to remand against both defendants should be granted (§1441(c)(2)
inapplicable because claim against Zeppo is DJ not AUJ).

802386 802386

 MTD/transfer:

 SMJ -
 See above.

 IPJ -
 No general IPJ since neither “at home” or Daimler “essentially at home” in Texas
(Sylvania’s sales mostly abroad, <50% in Texas).

 Texas has long-arm statute, federal court can “piggy-back” (FRCP 4(k)(1)(A)).

 Zeppo has “minimum contact” in Texas by visiting Chico’s Dallas home and noting
Groucho’s username/password there (International Shoe). Prudential factors support
exercising SIPJ since Texas is convenient to Groucho, interested in preventing theft

within its borders, TX substantive law likely applies (see below), and witnesses (Chico)
reside in Texas. While slightly inconvenient for Zeppo (DE domicillary), he’s traveled to
TX before.

 No slam-dunk “minimum contact” for Sylvania. Sylvania doesn’t advertise in
Texas (McIntyre) and Groucho purchased their product online in South Dakota. WWVW
tells us unilateral action of a plaintiff to move property into another state doesn’t create
minimal contacts. Groucho’s strongest argument for SIPJ is Sylvania’s servers in Dallas,

802386 802386

but unclear if that’s enough.

 HCOL -

 Texas federal court sitting in diversity apply HCOL rules of state in which it sits
(Klaxon). Texas applies 2nd Restatement, starting with lex loci presumption. Digital
artwork is incorporeal, but one would theorize it’s “located” where its owner is, similar to
debt moving with debtor (Balk). Here, that means artwork resides where Groucho is when
it’s stolen, and thus “blood spills” in TX. The §6 factors point towards using TX law as
the “center of gravity” of the action since Groucho/Zeppo’s interaction was in Texas, and
Texas has interest in protecting Groucho.

 One could argue artwork was located where Sylvania’s servers are in TX, MA, and
SC. This scrambles lex loci presumption, but “center of gravity” still likely in Texas.

 Venue -
 Defendants both residents of same state, so venue proper in D.DE under

§1391(b)(1), but not in W.D.TX. Substantial part of events happened at Chico’s Dallas
home (N.D.TX), but not in San Antonio (W.D.TX), where all that happened was Groucho
trying to access art (probably not substantial enough). Venue not properly laid in W.D.TX
(§1391(b)(2)).

 Transfer -
 W.D.TX would likely grant transfer motion given improper venue (§1406(a)) or
lack of IPJ over Sylvania (§1404/§1631).

802386 802386

-------------------------------------------

802386 802386

-------------------------------------------

## Question 4

 Higher AIC in claim against Sylvania negates SMJ issue (§1332). Joinder still
proper. Issues with improper venue in W.D.TX and IPJ over Sylvania in Texas remain.
Transfer/dismissal remains likely.

-------------------------------------------

802386 802386

-------------------------------------------

## Question 5

 Judge Teasdale can transfer to any district where IPJ/venue proper:

 D.DE - Both defendants citizens of Delaware (general IPJ, §1391(b)(1)).

 Possibly N.D.TX - Zeppo has minimal contacts in TX (see above), and substantial
portion of events in Chico’s Dallas home (§1391(b)(2)). Murkier for Sylvania. They have
server in Dallas housing one-third of artwork in question. Possibly enough for “minimum
contact.” Venue proper under §1391(b)(2) as theft drew from server in Dallas.

 Any district where all parties consent to transfer (§1404(b)).

 Judge Teasdale will transfer “in the interest of justice” (§1404(a)), looking to FNC
doctrine. FNC factors point towards most likely transfer is to N.D.TX (assuming IPJ over
Sylvania). Evidence exists in N.D.TX including Sylvania’s Dallas server, Chico’s
testimony, and any evidence on Chico’s VR headset. Texas shouldn’t be too inconvenient
for defendants since Zeppo traveled there before and Sylvania has a server in Texas.
Public interest factors favor N.D.TX because Texas law applies (see above).

802386 802386

 Factors weighing towards transfer to D.DE include greater convenience to
defendants and possibility that evidence of theft exists at Zeppo’s Delaware home.

-------------------------------------------

802386 802386

-------------------------------------------

## Question 6

 Groucho is unlikely to succeed in immediately appealing.

 Transfers aren’t final orders under §1291 (no judgment entered), so Groucho needs
to find an applicable interlocutory appeal.

 Cohen exception is most appealing. Cohen requires decision be collateral to the
merits (met here), final in that it won’t be revisited by court (technically D.DE could
revisit transfer, but unlikely), and issue must be effectively unreviewable later (here,
Groucho’s argument fails). Lauro Lines tells us SCOTUS viewed denial of a transfer
motion pursuant to a forum-selection clause as effectively reviewable later, so Cohen
didn’t apply. It logically follows that granting a transfer is reviewable later. Collateral

order doctrine isn’t concerned with saving costs of unnecessary litigation.

 Groucho’s case doesn’t fit other interlocutory appeals. There’s no written statement
seeking additional guidance (§1292(b)), no final judgment on any claim (FRCP 54(b)),
no injunctive relief (§1291(a)(1)), and no exigent circumstances (writ of mandamus).

 If an appeal immediately lies, Fifth Circuit would apply de novo review, as transfer
is question of law.

802386 802386

-------------------------------------------

802386 802386

-------------------------------------------

## Question 7

 Is contributory/comparative negligence procedural or substantive for HCOL
purposes? It seems substantive because establishing party’s right to recovery. However,
FRCP 8(c) lists contributory negligence as an affirmative defense, suggesting procedural.
Either way, comparative negligence controls.

 D.DE applies HCOL rules of state in which it sits (Klaxon). If affirmative defense
available is procedural, will use law of the forum state, Delaware, which uses
comparative negligence. If substantive, applying DE’s 1st Restatement principles
(Klaxon), we use law of state where “blood lies,” Texas, which uses comparative
negligence.

 Comparative negligence is an affirmative defense, so burden of persuasion lies with
Sylvania at trial. Judge Marcal will apply “burden shifting” analysis to MFSJ (Celotex, J.
Brennan dissenting). Sylvania meets its burden of production by producing evidence
from its engineer and Chico that Groucho had a simple password, showed it to Zeppo,
and didn’t use 2FA. Any rational factfinder would see this as failing to exercise due care
and contributing to potential theft. No genuine issue of material fact emerges, entitling
Sylvania to JAMOL. Burden of production then shifts to Groucho. Groucho’s assertions

802386 802386

that he’s forgotten his password, whether he wrote password down, and whether he used
2FA doesn’t create a genuine issue of material fact, because he doesn’t dispute Sylvania’s
assertions. Groucho fails to meet his burden of production. MFSJ granted to establish

Groucho as causal factor in theft.

 However, because DE/TX use comparative negligence, Groucho shouldn’t be
barred from recovering from Sylvania. Rather, his $100,000 claim against Sylvania will
be reduced by his comparative fault, a question of fact decided at trial. If Groucho
establishes Sylvania was also negligent, he can partially recover.

-------------------------------------------

802386 802386

-------------------------------------------

## Question 8

 Judge Marcal’s use of FRCP 54(b) was correct.

 Marcal complies with 54(b)’s requirements to expressly determine there’s “no just
reason for delay” and expressly direct judgment be entered. The only potential issue with
Marcal’s 54(b) determination is whether the Sylvania claim is intertwined with the Zeppo
claim. Because the MFSJ dealt only with Groucho’s comparative fault, and Zeppo cannot
assert that defense to a conversion action, the issues are arguably distinct. There are
factual similarities between the claims, but they’re likely not inseparable as to reverse a
Rule 54(b) determination (Sears).

 In evaluating issue preclusive consequences of Sylvania’s MFSJ, we note that the
rendering court was a federal court sitting in diversity. There are arguably two “rendering
courts,” the transferror court in W.D.TX and transferee court in D.DE.

 Semtek says that a subsequent state court must apply at least as much preclusive
effect as state in which the federal rendering court sat. Hart tells us Oklahoma state court
could apply more preclusive effect.

802386 802386

 If W.D.TX had proper venue/IPJ, Ferens suggests transfer is just changing
courthouse, and we could therefore apply Texas’ preclusion law. Texas considers all
independent bases possible to support a judgment as decided against the losing party.

There were two bases for Sylvania’s MFSJ in D.DE (Groucho’s weak password
protection and Groucho’s not using 2FA). The same issue is present in whether
Groucho’s failure to use 2FA makes him a causal factor in theft, the issue was actually
litigated and previously decided, and Texas’ application of general verdicts says it was
“necessary to the decision.” Texas would have IP run, thus Oklahoma must preclude.

 Alternatively, one could argue that Ferens’ holding on HCOL shouldn’t extend to
preclusion law because Delaware has greater interest in seeing their judgment respected
than Texas. Also, if W.D.TX didn’t have proper venue/IPJ, Ferens says apply HCOL
rules of transferee court (Delaware), and it follows we should apply transferee’s
preclusion law. In either case, apply Delaware preclusion law.

 Delaware uses FCL (Russell) and there were two possible grounds for Sylvania’s

MFSJ. Groucho changed his password and never wrote it down, which eliminates one
basis for the prior judgment. Since it’s unclear which basis Judge Marcal relied on
because she didn’t state her reasons in compliance with FRCP 56(a), Russell says IP
wouldn’t run in Delaware.

 Hart suggests Oklahoma could apply greater preclusive effect to the Delaware
judgment, and since Oklahoma doesn’t follow Russell, it might do so.

802386 802386

feedback.headline: Strong jurisdictional and preclusion work; the two 12-point questions lost their heaviest halves
feedback.overview: Question 8's preclusion run is the best work in the answer: you separated the two candidate rendering courts, worked both transfer branches, and used the judge's silence about which of the two independent grounds she relied on to defeat the necessary-to-the-judgment element. Question 3's subject matter jurisdiction is fully worked — citizenship party by party, amount in controversy claim by claim, Rule 20 T/O, then 1367(b) — though it ends with the wrong disposition. Question 7's summary judgment half correctly puts the persuasion burden on the movant asserting its own defense and refuses to treat a failure of memory as contradictory evidence. The losses are concentrated where the points are. Question 7's choice-of-law half never runs the transferee-court rule and never locates the artwork, so you never confront that a different location bars recovery outright rather than reducing it. Question 1(c) supplies one Erie justification where three were required, and Question 2's two required situations never become concrete.

strengths.label: Four separate rulings, argued both ways
strengths.detail: Each Erie test produced a ruling on these facts rather than a description of the test. The Harlan run is the best of them, because you gave the lawyer-conduct reading and then the insurance-premium counter — the two-sided treatment a close test invites.
strengths.answerExcerpt: Harlan would view a three-year versus two-year SoL as solely affecting the behavior of lawyers to know when filing is proper, and not "primary conduct" of clients.

strengths.label: Stevens's move identified, and paid for with the planted fact
strengths.detail: You saw that Stevens takes Rules Enabling Act validity seriously rather than nominally, and you supported that with the statute's placement. That is the fact the question was built on, and the answer stayed proportionate to two points.
strengths.answerExcerpt: MA SoL is part of pet statutes and NOT MRCP

strengths.label: Jurisdiction run defendant by defendant
strengths.detail: The 1367(b) step lands for the right reason: Groucho's claim against a party joined under Rule 20 must independently satisfy 1332. You also refused to treat the two defendants as a package on personal jurisdiction, and naming Sylvania as a close case rather than forcing it is the honest move.
strengths.answerExcerpt: must independently comply with §1332, according to §1367(b)

strengths.label: Each appealability route worked in turn
strengths.detail: Cohen is run element by element — collateral to the merits, final in the sense that the court will not revisit it, and effectively unreviewable later — with the first two conceded and the third identified as the failure point. The extension from Lauro Lines is carried by an argument rather than by assertion.
strengths.answerExcerpt: Collateral order doctrine isn't concerned with saving costs of unnecessary litigation.

strengths.label: Burden structure on a movant's own affirmative defense
strengths.detail: You placed the persuasion burden where it belongs and drew the consequence that decides the motion: an absence of recollection controverts nothing, so no genuine dispute forms and the burden never shifts back. Each independent ground is tied to its own evidentiary source.
strengths.answerExcerpt: he doesn't dispute Sylvania's assertions

strengths.label: Both transfer branches worked in the preclusion analysis
strengths.detail: You saw that the transfer creates two candidate rendering courts and resolved both paths instead of picking one. You also caught the changed password, which is what removes that ground from the shared-issue set, and closed with the Oklahoma point about a forum giving more preclusive effect than the rendering court would.
strengths.answerExcerpt: Groucho changed his password and never wrote it down, which eliminates one basis for the prior judgment.

improvements.label: Question 1(c) — three justifications were required; one appears
improvements.whatHappened: Federalism is developed. The remainder compares the four tests for administrability, which argues about the tests rather than about why Erie exists. The answer also picks a test instead of ruling on these facts.
improvements.whyItMatters: The prompt sets the count. On five points, two missing justifications cost more than any refinement of the one you gave.
improvements.howToImprove: Add the twin aims — discouraging forum shopping and avoiding inequitable administration of the laws — and separation of powers, meaning Congress's authority over the lower federal courts exercised through the Rules Enabling Act. Then say how the court should rule on Rule 87 against the two-year period. Pay for it by cutting the Babcock and Neumeier sentence and reducing the critique of Scalia's formalism to one line.

improvements.label: Question 2 — neither required situation is concrete
improvements.whatHappened: The pooling mechanism is right and the Turner point is used well. But no claim type is named where a class action opens the courthouse, and the downside you give concerns settlement control rather than a setting where a class action fails as an access-to-justice device.
improvements.whyItMatters: Six points ride on naming a situation on each side. A general account of the mechanism supplies neither.
improvements.howToImprove: Name a low-value or negative-value claim that no one would rationally bring alone, and say that the small per-member recovery is what makes the class necessary. Then name a setting where the device fails: parties in a defensive posture, or fact-specific claims that cannot clear commonality. Lassiter, which the prompt names alongside Turner, can carry the right-to-counsel point in a clause. The answer is short for six points, so this is space you can afford.

improvements.label: Question 3 — the disposition does not follow your own analysis
improvements.whatHappened: You show that the Zeppo claim satisfies 1332 on its own and that only the Sylvania claim is deficient, then remand both.
improvements.whyItMatters: The reasoning is the hard part and you did it. Losing the disposition discards the points that reasoning earned.
improvements.howToImprove: Split it: the Sylvania claim goes back to state court for want of the amount in controversy; the Zeppo claim stays because 1332 supports it independently. This is a brain-off area — run diversity and supplemental jurisdiction through the steps and let the disposition fall out mechanically. The words come from your 1441(c)(2) parenthetical, which can shrink to a clause.

improvements.label: Question 3 — Sylvania's personal jurisdiction is left unresolved
improvements.whatHappened: You canvass Sylvania's contacts well, stop at "unclear if that's enough," and never run the fair and reasonable prong for Sylvania.
improvements.whyItMatters: The exam asks for a prediction. Naming a close case and declining to resolve it leaves nothing to credit on the second half of the inquiry.
improvements.howToImprove: Take a position on whether the Dallas server holding part of the artwork is a suit-related contact, then run F&R for Sylvania — Texas's interest, the burden on a company already keeping a server there, and where the witnesses are. McGee supports treating acceptance of an out-of-state customer as a contact. Pay for it by reducing the repeated statement of the long-arm and the 4(k)(1)(A) piggyback to a single clause.

improvements.label: Question 4 — venue is carried by cross-reference
improvements.whatHappened: The three changes are correctly identified, but the venue conclusion rests on a pointer back to Question 3. You also never confront that your Question 3 theory locating the artwork with its owner would make venue in the Western District arguable under the property strand of 1391(b)(2).
improvements.whyItMatters: Venue is the live defect once the amount in controversy is cured, and a conclusion carried by cross-reference is not an application.
improvements.howToImprove:
State the two failures by number:
1. 1391(b)(1) fails because Zeppo is domiciled in Delaware, so not all defendants reside in the district.
2. 1391(b)(2) fails because the Chico gathering and the server are in the Northern District.
Then answer the tension your own location theory creates, and add a clause noting that nothing was removed, so there is nothing to remand. The answer is four sentences, so there is room.

improvements.label: Question 5 — the permissible set is never closed
improvements.whatHappened: You work D. Del. and N.D. Tex. properly but never rule out the other candidate districts.
improvements.whyItMatters: The question asks which districts the case could go to. Naming two without eliminating the rest answers half of it.
improvements.howToImprove: Add one sentence eliminating the others by defendant: no contacts connecting Sylvania to S.D. Cal. or D.S.D., and none connecting Zeppo to D. Mass., W.D. Okla., or D.S.C. Name the could-have-been-brought limit (Hoffman) that supplies the constraint you are already applying. Cut the 1404(b) consent sentence to pay for it.

improvements.label: Question 6 — the standard of review half is one clause
improvements.whatHappened: The appealability run is complete. The conditional second half is answered with a single global de novo.
improvements.whyItMatters: It is half of a five-point question, and once you have said no appeal lies it is free ground.
improvements.howToImprove:
Separate the standard by type of question:
1. De novo for interpretation of the venue statute.
2. Clear error for factual findings such as Zeppo's domicile.
3. Abuse of discretion for the transfer decision itself, if venue in the Western District were proper, because that is application of law to fact.
Pay for it by trimming the mandamus and 1292(a)(1) sweep to a single sentence.

improvements.label: Question 7 — the transferee-court choice-of-law step is skipped
improvements.whatHappened: You apply Klaxon to say the Delaware court uses Delaware's rules but never say why Delaware's rather than Texas's. The transfer rule is missing, and so is the connection to the improper venue in the Western District that you established in Question 3.
improvements.whyItMatters: This step decides which state's rules govern, and everything downstream depends on it. You run precisely this analysis correctly in Question 8, so the omission is one of sequence, not knowledge.
improvements.howToImprove: Say it in the course's terms: the Western District of Texas was an unhappy court because venue there was improper, so the transferee's choice-of-law rules apply and Delaware's govern (Ferens). One sentence. Pay for it by cutting the FRCP 8(c) procedural-or-substantive detour, which ends in "either way, comparative negligence controls" and so buys nothing. While you are there, the conclusion that Sylvania is entitled to JAMOL should read as entitlement to judgment under Rule 56 — Rule 50 is a different posture.

improvements.label: Question 7 — the artwork is never located
improvements.whatHappened: Delaware follows the First Restatement, so the question is where the last event occurred, which the prompt fixes as where the artwork was when stolen. You assert Texas by importing the Balk theory from Question 3 without argument and canvass no alternatives. Oklahoma and South Dakota never appear.
improvements.whyItMatters: Those two are the contributory-negligence states. They are the only reason the question asks whether Groucho is barred from recovering anything, and the locating exercise is where most of the twelve points sit.
improvements.howToImprove: Canvass the candidates with a reason on each: Pierre, where the account was opened and control relinquished; San Antonio, the owner's domicile, definite but scattering Sylvania's holdings across every customer's home state; Delaware or Oklahoma, definite and tied to the company and its security decisions; and the three server sites, each holding part of the data, which undercuts all three. Then pick one and say what it does — a comparative-negligence state reduces recovery, Oklahoma or South Dakota bars it. Fund it by cutting the FRCP 8(c) detour and the sentence restating the burden-shifting conclusion after you have already reached it.

improvements.label: Question 8 — claim preclusion is never addressed
improvements.whatHappened: The issue preclusion analysis is thorough. Claim preclusion does not appear, and the actually-litigated and mutuality elements are assumed rather than stated.
improvements.whyItMatters: The question asks whether Sylvania can use the judgment in some way, which opens both branches. An answer that runs only one reads as not separating them.
improvements.howToImprove: Run claim preclusion briefly: same plaintiff, a final judgment on the merits, and the pending appeal does not defeat finality — but the second suit is a different claim, because the second theft involved a different artwork, months later, viewed elsewhere, taken by a different person. No bar. Then name the two assumed elements in a clause each before the two-independent-grounds problem. Pay for it from the Rule 54(b) half, where the intertwinement argument can lose a sentence.

revisionPlan: Question 1(c): add the twin aims and separation of powers, and rule on these facts; cut the Babcock and Neumeier sentence.
Question 2: name one low-value-claim situation where a class action helps and one setting where it fails.
Question 3: remand only the Sylvania claim, and resolve Sylvania's personal jurisdiction with the F&R prong.
Question 4: state the 1391(b)(1) and 1391(b)(2) failures by number and answer the property-location tension your own theory creates.
